The advantages and disadvantages of\\nboth approaches are discussed. It is also necessary to implement learning outcomes regarding\\npersonal  or  social  competences,  such  as  employees’  attitudes  towards  rapid  technological\\nchanges, motivation to learn and competences regarding interdisciplinary cooperation.\\nSocial implications: Implementing changes in study programs will allow for more effective\\neducation  of  health  care  specialists  in  the  area  of  new  technologies,  which  is  necessary  to\\nimprove the quality of treatment.\\nOriginality/value: The conducted study showed gaps in study programs, which will allow for\\ntheir  improvement  and,  as  a  result,  increase  the  quality  of  teaching  in  the  field  of  new\\ntechnologies.\\nKeywords: education, health care, medicine 4.0, revolution 4.0, new technologies.\\nCategory of the paper: Research paper.\\n\\nhttp://dx.doi.org/10.29119/1641-3466.2025.215.1  http://managementpapers.polsl.pl/\\n\\n## [PDF page 10]\\n\\n10  K. BarBóg, I. Mendryk\\n\\n1.  Medicine 4.0\\n\\nThe  fourth  industrial  revolution  (revolution  4.0),  resulting  from  the  development  of\\ntechnology, leads to many organizational transformations in subsequent sectors of the economy,\\nimproving  communication  processes,  data  analytics,  and  various  simulations  (Bujak,  2017;\\nFurmanek, 2018; Kiraga, 2016). The 4.0 revolution also increasingly covers the health care\\nsector. Modern technologies enable personalization of therapy, which can reduce costs and at\\nthe same time increase its quality (Gaciong, 2016; Jose et al., 2022; Mathur, Sutton, 2017).\\nNew technologies in medicine significantly improve the effectiveness of treatment, enabling\\nmore precise disease diagnosis and analysis of specific disease indicators. Through increasing\\naccess  to  clinical  databases,  the  use  of  artificial  intelligence  (AI)  and  big  data  analysis\\nalgorithms, specialists are able to treat increasingly complex medical cases (Seyhan, Carini,\\n2019; Sgro, Blancafort, 2020).\\nDespite the numerous benefits associated with the implementation of new technologies,\\nmedicine remains one of the slowest adapting sectors (Chanchaichujit, Tan, Meng, Eaimkhong,\\n2019; Jose et al., 2022). One of the key challenges of modern medicine in the area of technology\\nis  the  integration  of  telemedicine,  server  applications  and  machine  learning  algorithms.\\nTheir synchronization can increase the level of health care (Rakhimov, Mukhamediev, 2022).\\nAt the same time, the development of technology requires improving the competences of health\\ncare specialists. Although technologies are widely used in various fields of medicine, the level\\nof their use and their necessity vary depending on the specialization (Konttila et al., 2019).\\nThe result is a diversified demand for competences in the field of health technologies among\\nthe staff of individual specialties (Foadi, Varghese, 2022; Kirchberg, Fritzmann, Weitz, 2020;\\nTorrent-Sellens, Soler-Ramos, 2018). However, most physicians are not adequately trained in\\nnew  technologies,  which  limits  their  ability  to  fully  utilize  these  tools.  Low  technological\\ncompetences may lead to medical errors and also cause psychological barriers in the use of\\nmodern  solutions  (Foadi,  Varghese,  2022).  Therefore,  there  is  a  need  to  improve  European\\neducational standards in this area. The European Union should develop uniform standards for\\ncompetencies related to Medicine 4.0 and adapt them to the needs and capabilities of member\\nstates, taking into account differences in the level of digitization of healthcare systems across\\nthese countries. It is also necessary to standardize terminology and establish precise guidelines\\nregarding  the  scope  of  training  for  physicians  in  the  field  of  Medicine  4.0.  Postgraduate\\neducation  programs  should  be  based  on  clearly  defined  competencies  that  physicians  will\\nacquire  upon  completing  their  studies.  The  current  lack  of  coherence  in  this  field  leads  to\\nsignificant discrepancies in the programs offered. At the same time, it is essential to outline\\na  strategy  in  which  technology  is  viewed  as  an  integral  tool  in  medical  practice,  with  its\\nimportance appropriately reflected in physician training programs. In addition to investing in\\nthe digitalization of healthcare facilities, the European Union should simultaneously focus on\\n\\n## [PDF page 11]\\n\\nEducation of health care personnel…  11\\n\\ndeveloping digital competences among healthcare workers, as it is crucial to maintain a balance\\nbetween  the  use  of  technology  and  fostering  empathetic  relationships  between  doctors  and\\npatients (Jidkov et al., 2019).\\n\\n2.  Educational needs in health care from the perspective of the development\\nof new technologies\\n\\nThe implementation of new technologies generates the need to improve the education of\\nspecialists  in  health  care  4.0  (Jose  et  al.,  2022).  It  is  important  for  the  development  of\\ntechnology in medicine  to create appropriate conditions by health care  managers, who play\\na decisive role in shaping an environment open to innovation and in change management (Jose\\net  al.,  2022).  Key  technological  competencies  that  should  be  developed  in  doctors  include:\\ninformation  management  and  security,  digital  communication,  empowering  the  patient  in\\ntherapy and the ability to use new technologies (Jidkov et al., 2019; Foadi, Varghese, 2022).\\nIn addition to hard competences in the field of technology, critical thinking, independent\\nacquisition of knowledge and the ability to use technology are important, which is becoming\\nan increasing challenge because some tasks are taken over by machines and some still remain\\nhuman (Kao et al., 2023). The development of technology in medical education solves many\\nproblems related to traditional education, e.g. medical simulators solve the problem of access\\nto actors playing various disease states, and machines enable safe training and improvement of\\nskills in controlled conditions. However, it is important to understand the relationship between\\nthe  costs  of  implementing  new  technologies  and  the  benefits  for  the  development  of\\ncompetences (Scalese, Obeso, Issenberg, 2008), including social ones, because technologies\\ncan improve communication between health care specialists and patients (Blahun et al., 2022).\\nDespite  the  increasing  precision  of  technological  innovations  and  their  popularity  in\\nmedicine,  there  are  doubts  about  the  reliability  of  tools,  the  accuracy  of  diagnoses  and  the\\nsusceptibility of algorithms to errors (Seyhan, Carini, 2019). It is worth emphasizing, however,\\nthat technology alone is not enough for the full development of medicine. Social aspects and\\nfocusing on the needs of individual patients are also important (Ioppolo, Vazquez, Hennerici,\\nAndres, 2020). When working with a patient, although precise diagnosis, data collection and\\nanalysis  using  technology  are  crucial,  they  are  not  enough  to  achieve  therapeutic  success.\\nAn important element of therapy, especially in the case of chronic treatment, is the patient’s\\nmotivation. As health improves, patients may lose determination, which negatively affects the\\neffects  of  treatment  (Chen,  Tang,  Guo,  2022;  Tavakoly,  Behzhad,  Ferns,  Peyman,  2020).\\nFor  this  reason,  apart  from  technology,  the  patient’s  psychophysical  and  emotional  aspects,\\nas well as the reactions of his loved ones, are also important.\\n\\n## [PDF page 12]\\n\\n12  K. Mendryk\\n\\nCurrently,  the  literature  on  the  subject  lists  several  key  competencies  regarding  the\\nimplementation  of  changes  related  to  the  Industrial  Revolution  4.0,  these  are  technical,\\nmethodological,  social  and  personal  competencies  (Hecklau  et  al.,  2016;  Jose  et  al.,  2022).\\nTechnical  competencies  refer  to  the  use  of  technology  information  and  communication,\\nincluding processing large amounts of data, while methodological competences are the area of\\nbeing innovative, engaging in strategic tasks and solving emerging problems, and continuous\\nlearning. The area of social competences in the implementation of Industry 4.0 is the ability to\\ncooperate with people from various backgrounds, use knowledge and skills and share them with\\nothers. In turn, a key personal competence is flexibility, which manifests itself, among other\\nthings, in adapting to changes resulting from the development of technology, supporting new\\ninitiatives and coping with emerging  challenges. Own research methodology\\n\\n3.1.  Subject and purpose of research\\n\\nThe research purpose of the work was to identify the necessary competences of health care\\nspecialists in the context of the development of Industry 4.0 based on the learning outcomes of\\npostgraduate studies dedicated to the implementation of technologies in health care. It is also\\nimportant to compare the assumed effects in study programs to the model of key competencies\\nof Industry 4.0: technological, methodological, personal competencies and social. The practical\\npurpose of the work was to formulate recommendations for people building programs and study\\nplans in the field of health care, as well as to present the possibilities of developing current staff\\nthrough postgraduate studies or certification courses. The main research question posed in the\\n\\n## [PDF page 13]\\n\\nEducation of health care personnel…  13\\n\\nstudy was: what key competencies for the effective implementation of Industry 4.0 are included\\nin postgraduate study programs addressed to health care specialists?\\n\\n3.2. BarBóg, I. Mendryk\\n\\n4.  Presentation of results\\n\\nCommon to the studies surveyed is a focus on artificial intelligence (AI), 3D printing issues\\nand big data analytics. These are key issues for the implementation of Industry 4.0. In addition\\nto universal knowledge, there are also issues specific to medical technologies.\\nAs  part  of  the  postgraduate  studies  \\"Technologies  of  the  future  in  clinical  application\\",\\nlearning outcomes are assumed that relate, among others, to:\\n\uf0b7  standards and management of medical data (e.g. source data analysis, cleaning, pseudo-\\nanonymization, data quality assessment),\\n\uf0b7  the process of designing and improving three-dimensional representations of biological\\nobjects and structures used in medicine, preparing pre-operative processes,\\n\uf0b7  3D printing process and three-dimensional visualizations using immersive technologies,\\n\uf0b7  design and implementation of applications using immersive technologies for medical\\neducation and improvement of medical practices,\\n\uf0b7  design, synthesis and development of drugs using three-dimensional models,\\n\uf0b7  programming neural networks and analyzing medical data, creating predictive models,\\nautomating processes and creating medical applications.\\nThe  presented  learning  outcomes  therefore  focus  on  technical  and  methodological\\ncompetences (problem solving, decision making, analytical skills, research skills). Conclusions\\n\\nThe analyzes carried out lead to the conclusion that the study programs largely refer to the\\narea of technological and partly methodological competences. The creators of the studies focus\\non hard competencies, on current knowledge, technical skills, and understanding of processes,\\nincluding new technologies, applications and devices.\\nFew effects refer to other areas of key competencies for Industry 4.0, such as: ability to\\nwork under pressure, team, interprofessional and intercultural cooperation, leadership skills,\\nand flexibility in adapting to new challenges. Postgraduate study programs pay little attention\\nto social and personal competences, which are as important as technological competences for\\nthe challenges of Industry 4.0 (Hecklau et al., 2016; Jose et al., 2022). Unfortunately, the above-\\nmentioned areas are covered only to a small extent in study programs.\\nSome universities try to show the importance of technology in various areas of health care:\\ndrug production, surgery, medical diagnosis (data analysis), or the use of 3D printing. In turn,\\nsome universities focus their content on key areas of medicine where Industry 4.0 technology\\nis particularly useful, such as: biophysics, anatomy, surgery, cardiology, neurorehabilitation.\\nThe  question  remains  open  about  the  effectiveness  of  both  approaches  to  acquiring\\ntechnological competences by health care specialists and the coherence between first-cycle,\\nsecond-cycle or uniform studies (enabling participation in postgraduate studies) and the content\\ntaught during postgraduate studies. The basic learning outcomes of medical studies include\\noutcomes relating to new technologies and their use in medicine (Regulation of the Minister of\\nScience and Higher Education, 2019, 2023, 2024), universities also independently expand the\\nbasic effects listed in the regulations with content related to industry 4.0 technologies (BarBóg,\\nMendryk, 2024), however, in practice, there are large differences in this area of competence\\namong specialists in various fields of medicine (Foadi, Varghese, 2022; Kirchberg, Fritzmann,\\nWeitz, 2020; Torrent-Sellens, Soler-Ramos, 2018). This is not a Polish problem only; in other\\nEuropean countries, including the UK, postgraduate programs related to medicine 4.0 also focus\\non selected areas of medicine, completely omitting some of them, e.g. psychiatry (Jidkov et al.,\\n2019).\\nIt seems that some of the content planned for postgraduate studies should also be included\\nin  long-cycle  studies,  so  that  each  graduate  has  the  basic  competences  necessary  for  the\\nimplementation of industry 4.0 technologies in health care facilities. It is important to take into\\naccount not only technological and methodological, but also social and personal competences\\n(Hecklau et al., 2016; Jose et al., 2022). Additional, expanded research should address specific\\n\\n## [PDF page 19]\\n\\nEducation of health care personnel…  19\\n\\nareas  of  medicine  and  competency  needs  for  future  developments.  However,  the  presented\\ntheses require empirical verification through research on health care staff, both managers and\\nspecialists - practitioners.\\nThe presented study has limitations regarding the size of the research sample and to a large\\nextent it can be understood as a pilot, but particularly important due to the growing trend of\\ntechnological  directions  addressed  to  health  care  specialists.  The  analyzed  fields  of  study\\nappeared to a large extent in the university’s offer in recent months, which is an important need,\\nconsidering  the  strategic  importance  of  health  care  for  the  functioning  of  society  and  the\\nfinancing of these postgraduate study programs from external funds. It is also worth noting that\\npostgraduate studies are not the only ones recently offered by universities that combine the\\nissues of industry 4.0 and medicine. This article is limited to postgraduate studies, taking into\\naccount their specificity, including (Article 160 of the Act of 20 July 2018 - Law on Higher\\nEducation and Science): length of study (studies last no less than 2 semesters) or obtaining\\nqualifications (postgraduate studies enable only partial qualifications at level 6, 7 or 8 of the\\nPolish Qualifications Framework). The adoption of partial effects results in concentration on\\na relatively narrow thematic scope and omission of teaching/developing other, more general\\nskills. It would be interesting to see how the graduates of these studies use the acquired skills\\nand whether they feel they are sufficient.\\nThe considerations presented in the article are based on analyses of the learning outcomes\\nof postgraduate studies conducted at selected Polish universities. It is important to emphasise\\nthat  the  problems  associated  with  the  education  of  health  professionals  in  the  context  of\\ncontemporary challenges are global in nature. The development of technology and techniques\\nbrings new possibilities for diagnosis and treatment of patients. It is becoming necessary to\\ndevelop new competencies. Universities around the world are facing this challenge. The issues\\nraised  in  the  article  and  the  research  method  used  can  be  used  both  for  research  based  on\\ninternational  comparisons  and  for  analyses  aimed  at  changing  the  educational  programmes\\nimplemented at universities in every region of the world.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Introduction\\n\\nResearch  and  development  (R&D)  projects  are  inherently  associated  with  risks,\\nuncertainties,  and  barriers,  which  often  manifest  as  threats  (Parys,  2012),  preventing  the\\nachievement of the value sought by project stakeholders. Today, it is widely accepted that the\\nsuccess of any project is tied to achieving the value sought by its stakeholders (Kerzner, 2017).\\nRisks and uncertainties in projects (defined in various ways), including R&D projects, are\\nfrequently analyzed (e.g. Klaus-Rosińska, 2019). However, the concept of barriers, which is\\nindeed  related  to  risks  and  uncertainties  but  is  not  synonymous  with  them,  can  offer  new\\ninsights into the management of R&D projects and is less frequently a subject of scientific\\nresearch. In R&D projects, barriers are closely linked to the project lifecycle, and the risk of\\ntheir occurrence is typically associated with a specific timeframe during which the project is\\nimplemented (Szyjewski, 2004). Due to the complexity and characteristics of R&D projects,\\nthese barriers can be highly diverse and often arise unexpectedly during different phases of the\\nproject (Morris et al., 1991). To minimize the impact of these unforeseen failures, it is essential\\nto plan corrective actions and select appropriate tools to support the process of overcoming\\nencountered barriers (Duncan et al., 1983). The existence of barriers should not be viewed as\\nobstacles that prevent project implementation but rather as a foundation for developing actions\\nto address them effectively. Moreover, they can serve as potential sources for increasing the\\nvalue generated by R&D projects.\\nThe primary aim of this article is to identify barriers in managing R&D projects conducted\\nat universities, based on literature and case studies. The secondary objectives are as follows:\\n\uf0b7  To define the specificity of the concept of barriers in managing R&D projects conducted\\nat universities in the context of the concepts of risks and uncertainties.\\n\uf0b7  To propose the fundamentals for barrier management in R&D projects conducted at\\nuniversities.\\nThe achievement of these objectives is intended to serve the general purpose of maximizing\\nthe value delivered by R&D projects conducted at universities.\\nThe structure of the article is as follows: In Section 2, we present the concept of barriers in\\nproject management. In Section 3, we discuss the issue of values sought to be attained in R&D\\nprojects  implemented  at  universities,  noting  that  without  achieving  the  desired  values,\\nthe projects will not be considered successful. In Section 4, we identify barriers to R&D projects\\nconducted at universities, and in Section 5, we propose a concept for the management of R&D\\nproject barriers. The paper concludes with some final remarks.\\n\\n## [PDF page 25]\\n\\nBarriers in achieving project value…  25\\n\\n2.  The Concept of Barriers in Project Management\\n\\nLet  us  begin  by  comparing  the  concepts  of  risk  and  barrier  in  the  context  of  project\\nmanagement.\\nAccording  to  the  Polish  Language  Dictionary  (https://sjp.pwn.pl/),  risk  is  defined  as\\n\\"the possibility that something will fail; also: an undertaking with uncertain outcomes\\" and\\n\\"taking on a specific danger\\". Risk in a project is defined as the possibility of undesirable results\\nor failure to achieve set goals, which may disrupt the course of the project (Smith, Merritt,\\n2002).\\nA  barrier,  on  the  other  hand,  is  defined  by  the  Polish  Language  Dictionary\\n(https://sjp.pwn.pl/) as \\"a natural obstacle that hinders or prevents movement\\" and \\"a thing that\\nhinders the occurrence of a phenomenon or situation\\". In the context of project management,\\nbarriers are defined in the literature as obstacles that prevent the occurrence or execution of\\na specific group of tasks within a given undertaking (Liebert, Trzeciak, 2016).\\nBased on a synthesis of the literature (Smith, Merritt, 2002, Kerzner, 2017), a definition of\\nbarriers tailored to the general understanding of project management and the needs of R&D\\nprojects can be proposed:\\nA barrier in a project is a condition or characteristic, existing at the time of project analysis\\nand  considered  permanent,  that  pertains  to  the  project  or  its  environment,  or  a  set  of  such\\nconditions or characteristics. These factors may hinder or prevent the achievement of project\\nobjectives by causing delays, increasing costs, limiting resources, or negatively affecting the\\nquality  of  outcomes.  Barriers  can  be  internal  (e.g.,  lack  of  team  competencies,  insufficient\\nplanning) or external (e.g., changes in legal regulations, unforeseen events). In other words,\\na barrier may trigger a risk of not meeting project objectives. In this sense, a barrier is a source\\nor cause of risk, though not every source or cause of risk qualifies as a barrier, as a barrier is\\ncharacterized by its permanence and is an inherent feature of the project or its environment.\\nA barrier ceases to be a source of risk once it is removed. Similarly, mitigating a barrier will\\npositively influence the attributes of the risk it generates.\\nBond and Houston (2013) identify three main types of barriers to innovation projects, which\\nare also significant in the context of R&D projects:\\n1.  Strategic-structural barriers, related to regulations and bureaucracy.\\n2.  Technological-market  barriers,  stemming  from  technical  limitations  and  market\\ndemands.\\n3.  Socio-cultural barriers, associated with resistance to change and cultural differences.\\n\\n## [PDF page 26]\\n\\n26  O. Bezgin, D. Kuchta\\n\\nSome researches (Grusza, Trocki, 2013) add that barriers can be categorized as internal or\\nexternal. Internal barriers include organizational and project-specific issues, such as a lack of\\nresources  or  inadequate  management  procedures.  External  barriers,  whether  closer  to  the\\nproject  (e.g.,  stakeholder  relations)  or  more  distant  (e.g.,  legal  or  economic  environments),\\nalso significantly impact project progress.\\nVarious  barriers  exist  in  new  product  development  projects,  arising  from  both  internal\\ncompany resources and external relationships (Liebert, Trzeciak, 2016). Research in different\\ncountries, such as Brazil (Feldens et al., 2012), Australia (Kotey, Sorensen, 2014), and Spain\\n(Madrid-Guijarro  et  al.,  2009),  highlights  severe  financial  constraints  and  insufficient\\nintellectual capital as key obstacles in new product development. Additional challenges, such\\nas corruption, lack of transparency (Feldens et al., 2012; Lekovic, 2013), improper resource\\nallocation, or infrequent product updates (Engberg et al., 2015), further hinder R&D activities.\\nRelationships with the company’s environment, including suppliers and partners in strategic\\nalliances, often lead to conflicts that can result in project abandonment (Athaide et al., 2011;\\nChin, Lam, 2004).\\nCommunication barriers play  a  significant role in the idea selection process and project\\nexecution. These issues include difficulties in employee communication (Felekoglu et al., 2013;\\nLechler, Thomas, 2015; Sojkin, 2003), lack of specialized project teams (Gerwin, Barrowman,\\n2002; Sandmeier, 2008), and insufficient project manager competencies (Badir et al., 2012;\\nBonner et al., 2002; Nauman et al., 2010). Additionally, a lack of trust and differing perceptions\\nof requirements for new products also pose significant challenges (Lynch et al., 2014).\\n\\n3. Barriers in research and development projects conducted at universities\\n\\n4.1.  Barriers identified in the literature\\n\\nResearch and development projects carried out at universities encounter numerous barriers\\nthat can limit the maximization of their value. It is important for these barriers to be viewed\\nmultidimensionally, and their minimization should be a priority for both the project manager\\nand  other  stakeholders.  The  active  involvement  of  all  interested  parties  during  the  project\\nplanning  stage  allows  for  better  preparation  to  address  barriers  in  the  later  phases  of  the\\nendeavor.\\n\\n## [PDF page 28]\\n\\n28  O. Kuchta\\n\\nAccording to Eckes-Kondak (2021), considering the specifics of research and development\\nprojects at universities, the following barriers to maximizing their value can identified:\\nA.  improperly defined project goals,\\nB.  lack of a realistic project plan, including scope, timelines, and budget,\\nC.  insufficient resource base,\\nD.  inadequate competence and experience of the project manager,\\nE.  insufficient skills and misalignment of the project execution team,\\nF.  improper or limited communication,\\nG.  lack of or inappropriate use of project management methodologies,\\nH.  complex administrative structure and prolonged procedures,\\nI.  ineffective collaboration with stakeholders and failure to consider their expectations in\\nthe project.\\nThe phenomena or circumstances listed above will be considered barriers only if they are\\nof  a  permanent  nature.  For  instance,  ineffective  collaboration  with  stakeholders  must  have\\npersisted over a significant period despite efforts made to improve it. Each of the listed barriers\\nsignificantly impacts the maximization of the value generated by research and  development\\nprojects. Managing these barriers requires a comprehensive approach that includes planning,\\nmonitoring,  and  collaboration  with  stakeholders.  Early  identification  of  these  barriers  and\\nappropriate responses to them can significantly increase the chances of project success and the\\nmaximization of its value.\\n\\n4.2. Barriers identified in the case study\\n\\nCase study description\\n\\nThe case study pertains to an R&D project conducted at one of the largest Polish universities\\nbetween 2009 and 2011. The objective of the project was to develop a concept for a costing\\nsystem tailored to the university’s needs. The problem intended to be partially addressed through\\nthe  project  was  that  the  costs  associated  with  all  university  activities4teaching,  research,\\nand administration4and all cost objects, such as students, employees, courses, and projects,\\nwere calculated in a manner that did not accurately reflect the actual utilisation of financial and\\nmaterial resources.\\nThe proposed concept was based on the Activity-Based Costing (ABC) approach, which\\nmeasures the resource usage for each activity individually, ensuring that the resulting costs of\\nactivities  and  cost  objects  are  more  closely  aligned  with  reality.  This  approach  necessitates\\na significant amount of detailed information regarding how individual activities are performed,\\nthe resources consumed, and the time spent on them. The design of such a system could not\\nsucceed  without  the  active  involvement  of  all  university  employees  across  all  departments.\\nIt is worth emphasising that interviews and thorough documentation reviews were conducted,\\n\\n## [PDF page 29]\\n\\nBarriers in achieving project value…  29\\n\\nrequiring  complete  transparency  and  the  potential  exposure  of  hidden  inefficiencies  in  the\\ncurrent cost calculation system.\\nRegrettably, the project was only partially successful. Conclusions\\n\\nIn this paper, we propose addressing barriers that hinder the creation of desired values in\\nR&D projects implemented at universities. Barriers are defined as permanent obstacles or issues\\nwhose removal requires time and must be strategically planned for the future. The approach\\ninvolves  using  lessons  learned  from  each  R&D  project  at  universities  to  contribute  to  the\\nstepwise elimination of these barriers. In the long term, this will reduce the risks associated\\nwith R&D projects and enhance the benefits they deliver to both the university and society.\\nA  proposal  for  a  barrier  management  system  has  been  outlined.  Naturally,  further  case\\nstudies are required to verify and refine the system to ensure its practical effectiveness.\\nWithout such a system, problems related to R&D projects will not be mitigated but will\\nrecur repeatedly. This leads to a waste of money, effort, and enthusiasm, while also diminishing\\nthe societal benefits derived from R&D projects. For this reason, we hope that our research will\\ncontribute to enhancing the effectiveness of R&D activities at universities.\\n\\nAcknowledgements\\n\\nWroclaw  University  of  Science  and  Technology,  Minigrant  for  doctoral  students,  Grant\\ntitle: Identification of Metrics for Hard-to-Measure Human Factors Negatively Affecting the\\nImplementation of Research Projects, 2024\\n\\n## [PDF page 33]\\n\\nBarriers in achieving project value…  33\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Introduction\\n\\nGastronomy is considered to be one of the oldest and most widespread service activities\\nworldwide ([wiątkowska et al., 2017; Zanetta et al., 2024). Every year, an increasing number\\nof people use catering services, not only because of the lack of time to prepare meals, but also\\nbecause  of  the  lack  of  skills  to  prepare  them,  the  greater  involvement  of  women  in  the\\nworkforce, and the increase in income (Czernyszewicz et al., 2023; Rutkowska, Czarniecka-\\nSkubina, 2015). It is important to note that the growth rate in eating out varies, with the fastest\\nbeing recorded in the Asia-Pacific region (Edwards, 2019; Chowdhury, 2021). According to\\nthe  National  Restaurant  Association  (State  of  the  Restaurant  Industry  Report,  2023),\\nfor 84% of consumers, going to a restaurant with family and friends is better use of time than\\ncooking or cleaning. In their opinion, the amount of money spent eating out is similar to that\\nspent at home. In Poland, about 67% of consumers enjoy dining out, spending on average about\\n4.2% of their total expenditure, up from only 1.4% as of 2000 (PMR Report, 2023). It should\\nbe noted that customers now have an increasing choice of dining establishments, from fast food\\nto fine-dining restaurants (Dziadkowie, 2018; Zanetta et al., 2024). Street food is important in\\nmany  countries  (Shi  and  Nuangjamnong  2023;  Kaewmahaphinyo  et  al.m  2020).  Choosing\\nan establishment depends on situational factors, that is, the dining occasion (celebrating special\\noccasions, social gatherings, business meetings, quick meals, or leisure activities) (Kopacki,\\nBogacka, 2020; Gheribi, 2016).\\nTherefore, this study was undertaken to determine the influence of selected attributes on\\ncustomers’  purchasing  decisions  in  the  food  service  market,  considering  the  moderating\\ninfluence  of  customer  gender.  This  research  is  an  important  contribution  to  understanding\\nopinions  about  food  service  establishments  and  consumer  purchasing  behavior,  particularly\\nabout perceptions of hygiene compliance and the quality of food served, as well as the type of\\nfood service establishments chosen, frequency and purpose of consumption.\\n\\n## [PDF page 37]\\n\\nFactors influencing customers’ purchasing decisions…  37\\n\\n2.  Literature review\\n\\nIn  addition  to  situational  factors,  many  other  factors  related  to  menus,  services,  service\\nconditions, and prices influence the choice of dining establishments. As  indicated by many\\nauthors  (Barrera-Barrera,  2023;  Española,  Janaban,  2024;  Mathayomchan,  Taecharungroj,\\n2020; [więtkowska et al., 2017; Zanetta et al., 2024), factors such as the quality of food (meals),\\nquality of the service (e.g. empathy, professionalism, and responsiveness), service environment\\n(e.g. décor, ambience), and value of money also influence the choice of a dining establishment.\\nThese factors are referred to as the ’big four attributes of a restaurant’. Other authors further\\npoint  to  menu  variety,  restaurant  reputation,  location,  and  promotion  (Chua  et  al.,  2020;\\nChiciudean  et  al.,  2019;  Medeiros,  Salay,  2013).  The  relationship  between  these  aspects  is\\ncomplex,  as  consumers  make  decisions  based  on  trade-offs  that  balance  costs  and  benefits,\\nwith attributes related to the quality of meals served and the quality of service being the most\\nimportant  in  most  studies  (Mathayomchan,  Taecharungroj,  2020;  Majid  et  al.,  2021).\\nCustomers perceive food quality to be at a high level when meals are made with fresh and good-\\nquality  ingredients,  are  tasty,  and  when  there  are  a  variety  of  menu  items  to  choose  from,\\nand portions are large enough and aesthetically served. In turn, when assessing the quality of\\nservice,  the  key  elements  are  the  neat  and  clean  appearance  of  the  service  staff,  courtesy,\\nattentiveness, product knowledge, accuracy, and speed of service. These attributes play a key\\nrole in shaping customer choices while influencing customer behaviour in different ways (Sari,\\nSunarti,  2023).  Research  has  also  pointed  to  other  important  factors  affecting  consumers’\\nrestaurant choices and experiences. For example, one can observe the role of ’healthy menus’\\n(Jeong, Jang, 2015), plant-based menu options (Choi et al., 2022), environmentally conscious\\nattitudes (Shin et al., 2018), the use of local products (Kim et al., 2020),  and technological\\naspects (Teng, Chen, 2021). Factors influencing customers’ restaurant choices vary depending\\non the occasion of eating out, as well as the type of dining establishments (Yrjölä et al., 2019).\\nWhen planning special occasions (e.g. birthdays and anniversaries), restaurants are most often\\nchosen, while other catering establishments are chosen to satisfy hunger. Consumer preferences\\nwhen choosing a catering establishment should guide entrepreneurs in adapting to customer\\nexpectations.  The  customer  evaluation  of  service  quality  is  crucial  for  the  survival  and\\ndevelopment  of  service  businesses.  With  this  in mind,  the  following  research  question  was\\nposed:\\nRQ1. What attributes influence customer purchasing decisions in the food service market?\\nAlthough many studies have been conducted on food service quality, few have addressed\\nthe  moderating  effect  of  gender  on  the  relationship  between  service  quality  and  customer\\nsatisfaction (Omar et al., 2016; Gasiorowska et al., 2023; Wolf, Zhang, 2016). Women have\\nhigher levels of service satisfaction than men (Omar et al., 2016). Gender is also an important\\n\\n## [PDF page 38]\\n\\n38  E. Czernyszewicz, J. Król\\n\\ndeterminant  of  food  preference  (Gasiorowska  et  al.,  2023).  Hence,  the  following  research\\nquestions were posed.\\nRQ2. Does gender moderate the choice of food outlet?\\nRQ3. Does sex influence opinions about the characteristics of a quality meal?\\nRQ4.  Does  gender  influence  judgements  about  the  hygiene  compliance  of  catering\\nestablishments and does cleanliness of the establishment influence judgements about the quality\\nof meals on offer?\\nThe  answers  to  the  above  research  questions  are  important  in  terms  of  customers’\\nperceptions  of  the  key  factors  in  choosing  an  establishment  and  in  developing  marketing\\nstrategies to help attract and attract existing and potential customers to catering establishments.\\n\\n3.  Methods\\n\\nThe study was conducted in 2023 in the period May-August on a group of 262 economically\\nactive Generation Y people using catering establishments in one of the large cities in eastern\\nPoland. The choice of the research group was based on the fact that Generation Y dominates\\nthe contemporary labour market. Above all, they prioritise personal development and devote\\ntime to their passions. They value their free time and are more willing to use entertainment and\\nservices,  including  catering,  than  other  groups  (Muszyńska,  2021).  The  majority  of  the\\nrespondents were women (53.4 %), while men were 46.6%.\\nThe research tool was a survey questionnaire and the research method used was a diagnostic\\nsurvey.  The  survey  questionnaire  consisted  of  10  questions  concerning  the  choice  and\\nfrequency  of  visiting  catering  establishments  and  the  reasons  respondents  chose  a  catering\\nestablishment. In addition, respondents were asked whether they paid attention to the quality of\\nthe  meals  they  received,  the  characteristics  of  high-quality  meals,  the  fulfilment  of  their\\nexpectations from the dishes they order, how compliance with the principles of hygiene in the\\npremises manifests itself, whether the maintenance of cleanliness in the premises influences the\\nquality of the meals offered, and whether the maintenance of hygiene principles by the staff\\ninfluences their feelings of safety in the premises. The form mainly contained closed single-\\nchoice questions and three multiple-choice questions.\\nThis study complied with the ethical standards set for all studies involving human subjects.\\nPrior to entering the study, the participants were informed about the entity conducting the study,\\nthe purpose of the study, and how the data obtained in the study would be used. The participants\\nautomatically consented to participate in the study and voluntarily completed the questionnaire.\\nEach survey participant was allowed to refuse to answer a specific question and withdraw from\\nthe survey at any time without providing a reason. Participants were assured of the anonymity\\nand confidentiality of their responses.\\n\\n## [PDF page 39]\\n\\nFactors influencing customers’ purchasing decisions…  39\\n\\nThe  results  of  the  study  were  analysed  using  the  statistical  programme  IBM  SPSS\\nStatistics  29.  Descriptive  statistics  (%  of  indications)  were  used  for  data  analysis,\\nand correlations between variables were analysed using Pearson’s r correlation coefficients.\\n\\n4. Conclusions\\n\\nThis study aims to determine the influence of selected attributes on customers’ purchasing\\ndecisions in the catering market, considering the moderating influence of customers’ gender.\\nThe results of the study confirmed the moderating influence of  gender  on the frequency of\\nattendance at different types of catering establishments, identification of organoleptic attributes\\nthat  characterise  a  quality  meal,  assessment  of  the  fulfilment  of  expectations  regarding  the\\ndishes  ordered,  perception  of  the  manifestation  of  hygiene  principles  in  the  establishment,\\nand opinion that the maintenance of cleanliness in the establishment influences the quality of\\nthe meals offered.\\nThis study was conducted among customers of catering establishments in only one large\\ncity in Poland. The characteristics of the respondents included economically active people of\\nGeneration Y and their gender. Therefore, it would be advisable to conduct similar research\\namong people representing other generations, such as Generation Z or Millennials. In addition,\\nthe  scope  of  the  research  could  be  broadened  to  include  issues  related  to  the  specific\\ncircumstances  of  eating  out  in  catering  establishments,  detailed  expectations  regarding  the\\norganoleptic qualities of meals, and hygiene issues in the establishment.\\nInvestigating the key factors influencing customers’ choice of eating out establishments can\\nnot only help entrepreneurs understand customers’ perceptions of the key factors in choosing\\nan establishment but also create appropriate marketing strategies to attract existing and potential\\ncustomers and to outperform the competition. Particular attention was paid to\\nidentifying subject areas.\\nDesign/methodology/approach:  The  design,  compilation,  analysis,  visualization,\\nand interpretation phases of a bibliometric analysis were all used. The Scopus database provided\\n340 publications overall after a thorough search. In the examined research, science mapping\\nand performance indicators pertaining to publications and citations were employed.\\nFindings: Since 1997, when the first article on HBE was released, 340 publications indexed in\\nthe Scopus database have been published. These publications have achieved 5671 citations with\\nan h-index of 40. The country with the most affiliations was the United States, followed by\\nIndia  and  China.  Using  the  minimum  number  of  documents  at  level  3,  36  countries  were\\nidentified  in  8  clusters.  The  SuBE-related  studies  provided  1,371  keywords  in  10  clusters\\nrelated  to  brand  creation,  brand  management,  and  competitiveness  in  the  context  of\\nsustainability;  green  and  circular  economies;  consumer  behavior  and  social  media;\\ncommunication and consumer decisions; and modern research methods in marketing.\\nResearch  limitations/implications:  SuBE  was  analysed  in  general,  indicating  sustainable\\nmanagement  and  marketing.  First,  there  is  the  diversity  of  regional  and  cultural  contexts.\\nThe influence of culture, local economic conditions, and the level of environmental awareness\\ncan  vary  from  region  to  region  and  was  not  analysed.  Second,  time  frames  were  also  not\\nanalysed.\\nPractical  implications:  Theoretical  and  practical  implications  for  SuBE  were  formulated.\\nThe  theoretical  implications  include  the  need  to  integrate  theories  from  marketing,\\nmanagement, sustainability, and communications to understand how brands can meet consumer\\nexpectations  and  achieve  environmental  goals.  As  practical  implications,  companies  must\\ninclude  sustainability  as  a  central  element  of  their  branding  strategy  to  build  lasting\\nrelationships with environmentally conscious consumers.\\nOriginality/value: There were no studies demonstrating the present level of development of\\nthis  field  of  study;  hence  our  bibliometric  analysis  study  on  SuBE  closes  a  research  gap.\\nThe originality of this study is in the identification of clusters that represent current research\\nareas in the field of SuBE.\\nKeywords:  sustainable  brand  equity,  sustainable  brand,  sustainable  branding,  sustainable\\nmanagement, bibliometric analysis.\\nCategory of the paper: literature review.\\n\\nhttp://dx.doi.org/10.29119/1641-3466.2025.215.4  http://managementpapers.polsl.pl/\\n\\n## [PDF page 52]\\n\\n52  H. Górska-Warsewicz\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nSustainable branding is an important research area in marketing and management (Kaur,\\nGupta, 2024; Kaur, Monisha, 2023; Mebtrovi\\u0007, 2023; Muchenje et al., 2023; Ryals, Macdonald,\\n2015; Swaroop, Gade, 2023). Both marketing and sustainable branding are related to advancing\\nsustainability  through  various  complementary  approaches.  While  sustainable  marketing\\nconveys  these  ideals  to  customers,  sustainable  branding  supplies  the  identity  and  values\\n(Kumar,  Christodoulopoulou,  2014;  Popescu  et al.,  2023).  In  this  aspect,  brand  loyalty  and\\nresponsible  consumer  behavior  are  subsequently  fostered  by  sustainable  marketing,  which\\nimproves  brand  image  (Jia  et  al.,  2023;  Kumar,  Christodoulopoulou,  2014).  Sustainable\\nbranding  initiatives  can  boost  customer  happiness  and  engagement  through  sustainable\\nmarketing. This is especially true  in industries like sustainable food production, where it is\\nessential  to  raise  awareness  and  improve  the  perception  of  sustainability  brands  (Franco,\\nCicatiello,  2018).  Through  the  incorporation  of  sustainability  principles  into  business\\noperations,  creative  management  techniques,  strategic  marketing,  and  effective\\ncommunication,  sustainable  branding  and  sustainable  management  are  closely  related.\\nBusinesses may create powerful, long-lasting brands that support a more sustainable future and\\nprovide them a competitive edge in the market by coordinating these factors (Foroudi, Palazzo,\\n2020).\\nThe issue of brand equity is widely analyzed in the literature. This includes general aspects\\n(Almestarihi et al., 2021; Rojas-Lamorena et al., 2022; Dropuli\\u0007 et al., 2022) as well as various\\nproduct and service sectors (Juga et al., 2018; Hazée et al., 2017; Çifci et al., 2016; Dwivedi,\\nMerrilees,  2013;  Andéhn  et  al.,  2014;  Florek,  Kavaratzis,  2014;  Górska-Warsewicz,  2020;\\nDe Heer, 2020; Gupta et al., 2019; Vijay MallikRaj et al., 2017). Literature review\\n\\nThe issue of sustainable brands has been studied extensively in the literature. Sustainable\\nbrands integrate economic, social, and environmental concerns into their brand management\\nand commercial operations. This all-encompassing strategy guarantees that the brand prioritizes\\nnot just financial gain but also the well-being of the environment and society (Fallström et al.,\\n2018; Foroudi, Palazzo, 2020). In this concept, the identity of organizations and their brands\\nreflects  a  commitment  to  sustainability,  linking  management  methods  to  the  Sustainable\\nDevelopment  Goals  (SDGs)  (Caldana  et  al.,  2022).  This  is  because  sustainable  branding\\nextends above standard brand management by taking into account wider viewpoints, including\\ncorporate social responsibility, the circular economy, and environmental ecosystems (Foroudi,\\nPalazzo,  2020).  Effective  implementation  of  sustainable  branding  is  demonstrated  by  best\\npractices from a variety of industries (Fallström et al., 2018; Foroudi, Palazzo, 2020).\\nSustainable  branding  involves  integrating  brand  identity  and  operations  with\\nenvironmentally  friendly  values  to  create  interest  in  eco-aware  customers  and  support\\na sustainable future (Surmanidze et al., 2024).  In this concept,  to gain consumers’ trust and\\nloyalty,  sustainable  brands  frequently  highlight  ethical  behavior,  transparency,\\nand environmental responsibility in their marketing campaigns (Eyada, 2024; Gutiérrez et al.,\\n2024). At the same time, connecting with customers and setting the business apart in a crowded\\nmarket require effective communication of sustainability initiatives (Caballero-Castaneda et al.,\\n2021; Surmanidze et al., 2024). Brands that effectively promote their sustainability initiatives\\ncan observe a rise in consumer satisfaction, loyalty, and willingness to pay (Franco, Cicatiello,\\n2018).  Additionally,  long-term  business  success,  competitive  advantage,  and  improved\\ncompany image can all be attributed to sustainable branding (Fallström et al., 2018; Saraiva,\\n2022).\\nSustainable  branding  is  closely  related  to  sustainable  marketing,  which  requires\\na comprehensive strategy that takes into account the entire life cycle of a product and its broader\\nenvironmental  and  social  impact  (Kaur,  Gupta,  2024;  Kaur,  Monisha,  2023).  In  this  area,\\ndesigning, advertising, selling, and distributing goods in a way that has the least negative impact\\non  the  environment  is  known  as  sustainable  marketing.  Using  eco-friendly  raw  materials,\\n\\n## [PDF page 54]\\n\\n54  H. Górska-Warsewicz\\n\\npackaging,  and  procedures  are  also  part  of  these  activities  (Kaur,  Gupta,  2024;  Ryals,\\nMacdonald, 2015). It emphasizes the entire production process, from sourcing raw materials to\\ndisposal,  ensuring  that  each  step  is  environmentally  sustainable  (Kaur,  Gupta,  2024;  Kaur,\\nMonisha,  2023;  Swaroop,  Gade,  2023).  Sustainable  branding  encompasses  ethical  issues,\\nensuring  that  marketing  activities  positively  impact  society  and  respect  the  needs  of  future\\ngenerations (Mebtrovi\\u0007, 2023; Ryals, Macdonald, 2015; Swaroop, Gade, 2023). At the same\\ntime, sustainable marketing tactics must be profitable and competitive to guarantee long-term\\ncorporate success while preserving sustainability standards (Muchenje et al., 2023).\\nSustainable brand equity combines traditional brand equity  (Aaker, 1991; Keller, 1993)\\nwith sustainability initiatives to demonstrate a brand’s dedication to social and environmental\\nresponsibility (Kara et al., 2024). This idea emphasizes how crucial environmental and non-\\nfinancial activities are in influencing consumer attitudes and brand value. Environmental and\\nnon-financial activities have an impact on a company’s sustainable brand equity. Businesses\\nuse  social  responsibility  and  green  efforts  to  show  customers  how  committed  they  are  to\\nsustainability. Compared to other brands, this strategy aids in creating a competitive position in\\nsustainability  (Kara  et  al.,  2024).  Sustainable  brand  equity  is  perceived  as  the  consumer\\nperceptions  of  a  brand’s  sustainability  efforts.  In  this  concept,  customer  trust,  satisfaction,\\nand loyalty are influenced by brand identification, brand awareness, physical quality, lifestyle\\ncongruence, staff behavior, and ideal self-congruence (Dananjoyo, Udin, 2023). Additionally,\\nby increasing market share, creating barriers to entry for competitors, expanding production\\nand  market,  offering  premium  pricing,  attracting  top  talent,  guaranteeing  customer  loyalty,\\nand fostering innovation, sustainable brand equity improves the overall success of the company\\n(Veselinova, Samonikov, 2018).\\n\\n3. Discussion of results and implications\\n\\nThe purpose of this study was to identify the state of research in the field of SuBE using\\nbibliometric  analysis  with  special  attention  given  to  thematic  areas.  The  current  level  of\\nknowledge on the subject of SuBE, the identification of known authors, countries, and sources,\\nas well as the identification of thematic areas that are significant for SuBE, were all included in\\nthe three research questions.\\nThe  first  question  was  assessing  the  level  of  development  of  the  SuBE  field  of  study.\\nBy the end of 2024, 340 publications on SuBE had been published, with an average value of\\n12.1 publications per year. The largest number of publications was published in the 2021-2024\\nperiod; there were 170. In comparison, 150 studies were published in the 2011-2020 period.\\nThe difference can be seen in the average number of publications; in the 2011-2020 period,\\nan average of 15 studies per year were published, while in the 2021-2024 period, this average\\nvalue was 42.5 studies per year. The importance of this area is also evidenced by the number\\nof  citations.  In  total,  publications  indexed  in  the  Scopus  database  were  cited  5,671  times.\\nThis means an average number of citations of 202.5 per year. The highest number of citations\\nwas recorded in the 2021-2024 period; there were 3,848 citations. In comparison, in the 2011-\\n2020 period, the number of citations of publications related to SuBE was 1,749. The comparison\\nof the average annual number of citations shows an increase in the importance of the subject.\\nIn the 2011-2020 period, the number of citations was 174.9 per year, while in the 2021-2024\\nperiod, this number increased to 962 citations per year.\\nThe second research question focused on identifying authors and countries relevant to the\\nSuBE  research  area.  The  authors  of  the  largest  number  of  publications  were  Gil-Saura  I.,\\nRuiz-Molina  M.E.,  and  Marín-García  A.,  who  published  12,  9,  and  7  studies,  respectively.\\nThe  United  States  turned  out  to  be  the  most  affiliated  country,  followed  by  India,  China,\\nthe  United  Kingdom,  and  South  Korea.  These  five  countries  accounted  for  50%  of  all\\npublications on SuBE indexed in the Scopus database. The bibliographic coupling identified\\n68 countries. However, considering the minimum number of documents at level 3, 8 clusters\\n\\n## [PDF page 65]\\n\\nSustainable brand equity…  65\\n\\nwere identified. South Korea and India belonged to the first cluster, the United Kingdom and\\nthe United States to cluster No. 3, while China was in the sixth cluster.\\nAnswering  the  third  question,  analysis  of  the  keyword  co-occurrence  using  mapping\\nanalysis allowed the selection of 10 clusters. According to the cluster research, globalization\\nand regional socioeconomic changes present both opportunities and problems for modern brand\\nmanagement,  marketing,  and  communication  strategies.  An  interdisciplinary  and  dynamic\\nresearch and practice environment was created by combining issues like consumer behavior,\\ncircular  economics,  sustainable  development,  branding  and  competitiveness  building,  brand\\nmanagement in the context of tourism services, and contemporary marketing research methods\\n(Buckley et al., 2022; Hassan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2015).\\nOne crucial area of marketing and management is brand development and competitiveness\\nin relation to sustainable development (Javed et al., 2024; Tung, Vigneron, 2023). Brands must\\nset  themselves  apart  in  the  face  of  intense  global  competition  and  shifting  consumer\\nexpectations by being able to connect emotionally with their target audiences in addition to\\noffering  high-quality  goods  and  services.  In  the  tourism  services  industry,  where  customer\\nexperience, authenticity, and a region’s or city’s image are crucial in fostering enduring loyalty,\\nbrand management is especially crucial (Bordian et al., 2024; Chan, 2019).\\nThe circular economy and sustainability are significant components of modern marketing\\nplans. Brands must incorporate social and environmental responsibility into their operations\\ndue  to  the  increasing  environmental  consciousness  of  societies  and  global  environmental\\nresponsibilities. The circular economy, which is founded on the ideas of reducing waste and\\noptimizing resource value, is evolving into both a goal and a chance to develop creative business\\nsolutions.  Customers  expect  firms  to  be  open,  accountable,  and  dedicated  to  eco-friendly\\npractices as they become more conscious of their influence on the environment (Kumar et al.,\\n2022; Matteucci, 2020). A crucial part of this process is communication, which affects customer\\nchoices.  Since  today’s  consumer  is  both  highly  demanding  and  knowledgeable,  effective\\ncommunication needs to be real-time, authentic, and individualized. Social media has grown to\\nbe  a  significant  platform  for  brand-consumer  communication,  providing  fresh  chances  to\\nengage  audiences,  examine  behavior,  and  form  connections.  Online  reviews,  suggestions,\\nand opinions frequently influence consumer choices, making reputation management and user-\\ngenerated content marketing even more crucial (Duh, Uzezi Wara, 2024; Qi et al., 2024).\\nAdditionally,  marketing  innovations  are  embracing  customer  loyalty,  particularly  in  the\\nhotel  sector,  where  a  significant  difference  is  the  combination  of  outstanding  service  and\\nsustainable  practices.  Consumers  are  more  inclined  to  select  companies  that  provide\\ncontemporary,  tailored  solutions  while  exhibiting  respect  for  the  environment  and  local\\ncommunities. A deeper comprehension of consumer behavior and the efficacy of marketing\\ninitiatives is made possible by modern marketing research methodologies. Using social media\\ndata, artificial intelligence, and advanced analytics enables the development of tailored tactics\\nin addition to trend forecasting (Golob et al., 2020; Kumar, Bagchi, 2020; Wang et al., 2014).\\n\\n## [PDF page 66]\\n\\n66  H. Górska-Warsewicz\\n\\nIn summary, the previously mentioned concerns  highlight the increasing  significance of\\na  multidisciplinary  approach  in  marketing  that  incorporates  consumer  behavior  analysis,\\ncutting-edge technologies, communication methods, and sustainability. To succeed in a world\\nthat is changing quickly, today’s brands and organizations must exhibit not only innovation but\\nalso social and environmental responsibility.\\nBased on the bibliometric analysis, theoretical and practical implications for sustainable\\nbrand  equity  can  be  formulated.  The  theoretical  implications  include  the  need  to  integrate\\ntheories from marketing, management, sustainability and communications to understand how\\nbrands  can  simultaneously  meet  consumer  expectations  and  achieve  environmental  goals.\\nThis will make it possible to present fresh theoretical frameworks that consider how circular\\neconomics  affects  brand  equity,  brand  value,  and  brand  loyalty.  The  approach  to  consumer\\nbehavior needs to change, and studies on consumer choices need to consider how social media\\nis becoming a more significant influence on sustainable preferences. When creating analytical\\nmodels, it is important to consider how sustainability, loyalty, and consumers’ perceptions of\\nbrand value interact. From the perspective of the development of tools and methodologies using\\nartificial intelligence, big data, and real-time analytics for the analysis of changing consumer\\nsustainable behavior, it is also vital to highlight contemporary research methods in marketing.\\nPractical implications should be pointed out that companies must include sustainability as\\na central element of their branding strategy to build lasting relationships with environmentally\\nconscious consumers. To attract clients who are searching for unique and ethical experiences,\\ntravel  agencies  might  highlight  authenticity  and  locality  in  their  activities.  Additionally,\\norganizations should use social media to assess customer behavior and instantly determine their\\nneeds in addition to using it for communication.\\nTo  promote  sustainability,  companies  can  introduce  loyalty  programs  that  promote\\nconsumers’ green choices, such as discounts for repeated use of goods and services with a low\\ncarbon footprint. Implementing circular economy practices in business processes can not only\\nreduce operating costs but also increase consumer involvement in green activities. Additionally,\\ncompanies  should  employ  sophisticated  data  analytics  in  conjunction  with  contemporary\\nresearch  methods  to  forecast  market  trends  and  make  real-time  strategy  adjustments.\\nIn this sense, the creation of digital platforms and mobile applications can aid in the study of\\ncustomer behavior and make it easier to use creative marketing strategies.\\n\\n6.  Conclusions, limitations, and future research\\n\\nSuBE is an important issue in the context of management, marketing, and sustainability.\\nIt  is  related  to  the  importance  of  sustainability  in  marketing  strategies.  In  this  context,\\nsustainability  is  becoming  a  key  factor  in  determining  the  competitiveness  of  brands.\\n\\n## [PDF page 67]\\n\\nSustainable brand equity…  67\\n\\nAt the same time, the role of social media and technology is growing dynamically. Social media\\nhas significantly influenced the way consumers interact with brands. In turn, new technologies\\nenable  precise  analysis  of  their  behavior  and  preferences.  Shaping  SuBE  considered  in  the\\ncontext of brand management requires the integration of knowledge from various fields, such\\nas marketing, economics, technology, and social sciences.\\nThis study also has limitations. First, there is the diversity of regional and cultural contexts.\\nThe influence of culture, local economic conditions, and the level of environmental awareness\\ncan vary from region to region. This issue was not analysed. Second, time frames were not\\nanalysed. The dynamics of technological change, evolving consumer behavior, or approaches\\nto sustainability can affect the issues analysed in the context of SuBE.\\nSeveral issues should be identified as directions  for future research. First, the long-term\\nimpact of sustainability strategies should be studied. Research should focus on analysing how\\nbrands’ pro-environmental and pro-social activities affect their long-term consumer loyalty and\\nmarket value. Second, loyalty in the context of the circular economy would be an interesting\\nresearch area. Currently, there is a lack of extensive research indicating how circular strategies\\naffect consumers’ brand perceptions and purchase decisions. Third, research analysing the post-\\npandemic reality should continue. Introduction\\n\\nProject  management  is  one  of  the  key  tools  of  modern  organisations  to  achieve  their\\nstrategic  objectives  in  a  dynamically  changing  economic  environment.  It  is  the  process  of\\nplanning,  organising,  controlling  and  closing  project  work  in  order  to  achieve  specific\\nobjectives within a set time and budget constraint. The importance of projects in the modern\\nworld  is  steadily  increasing  and  this  is  an  ongoing  trend.  This  is  due  to  a  number  of\\ncircumstances, notably the increasing complexity and variety of problems and projects required\\nto solve them (Trocki, 2012).\\nThe  choice  of  topic  for  this  study  was  prompted  by  the  growing  demand  for  project\\nmanagement  professionals,  including  junior  project  managers  (Junior  Project  Managers).\\nAs more organisations adopt project-based approaches, recruiters are looking for talent that\\ncombines theoretical knowledge with practical skills, as well as the ability to work in multi-\\ndisciplinary teams (Crawford, 2005).\\nThe  purpose  of  this  study  is  to  identify  and  analyse  the  key  requirements  placed  on\\ncandidates  for  the  position  of  Junior  Project  Manager  in  job  offers  on  recruitment  portals.\\nThe  study  focuses  on  two  main  aspects:  the  identification  of  the  most  common  mandatory\\nrequirements, such as work experience or knowledge of project management tools, and the\\nanalysis of non-standard requirements that may set candidates apart from the competition.\\nThe study used a literature review and quantitative research using a survey questionnaire.\\nThe analysis was based on job vacancies available on recruitment portals. The study provides\\npractical guidance for young candidates as well as for organisations responsible for recruitment\\nprocesses and universities training in project management.\\n\\n2.  Literature analysis\\n\\nBoth  academic  literature  and  practical  project  management  standards  point  to  the  vital\\nimportance  of  project  managers’  competencies  in  achieving  an  organisation’s  objectives.\\nThe Project Management Institute, in its PMBOK guide, defines the role of the project manager\\nas the person responsible for managing the project team to achieve project objectives and meet\\nstakeholder  expectations  (Project  Management  Institute,  2017).  The  IPMA  ICB  standard,\\non  the  other  hand,  emphasises  the  development  of  individual  competence  in  project\\nmanagement (International Project Management Association, 2015).\\nAs the demand for project managers grows, so does the interest in their competencies and\\nin  standards  for  competence  development  and  assessment  (Crawford,  2005).  A  project\\nmanager, in order to carry out his or her tasks effectively and efficiently, must possess the right\\n\\n## [PDF page 77]\\n\\nResearch on key requirements…  77\\n\\ncompetencies,  which  can  be  defined  as  dispositions  in  knowledge,  attitudes  and  skills  that\\nenable professional tasks to be carried out at an appropriate level (Filipowicz, 2019). A number\\nof studies have been conducted on the competencies of project managers. They show that the\\nmost  important  competencies  of  a  project  manager  are  behavioural  (human)  competencies.\\nThese  include  interpersonal  communication,  teamwork,  entrepreneurship  and  creativity,\\nself-reflection and self-management, professionalism and ethics, result orientation, leadership,\\nnegotiation, conflict management, among others (Marek-Kołodziej, 2024). Another study also\\nindicates that interpersonal skills as the most important area of a leader’s competency, such as:\\ncommunication  skills,  inspiration,  motivation,  building  trust,  and  cooperation  (Balcerzyk,\\nŽukovskis, 2024). For Junior Project Managers, on the other hand, it is particularly important\\nto  combine  technical  and  interpersonal  skills  to  enable  effective  collaboration  in\\nmultidisciplinary and multicultural teams (Borg et al., 2023). The findings show that through\\ninitiatives  aimed  at  increasing  self-efficacy,  organisations  can  support  the  development  of\\njunior project managers, improving their work readiness and potential for further development\\n(Borg  et  al.,  2023).  At  the  same  time,  the  findings  of  junior  project  managers  can  provide\\na basis for integrating project management issues into university curricula (Nijhuis et al., 2024).\\nUnderstanding  the  requirements  for  Junior  Project  Managers  is  an  essential  part  of\\nan effective recruitment process. These expectations include knowledge of project management\\ntools such as MS Project or Jira, time management skills, as well as interpersonal competencies\\nsuch as communication and teamwork. In addition, organisations often expect candidates to be\\nadaptable and to work under time pressure.\\nIn the light of the theoretical issues presented, the following section of the study will present\\nthe results of an analysis of job offers for the position of Junior Project Manager posted on\\nrecruitment portals, showing the detailed requirements for candidates at this career stage.\\n\\n3.  Research process\\n\\nThe  research  presented  in  this  article  was  conducted  by  a  team  of  five  people  who  are\\nmembers  of  the  Project  Management  Group  Scientific  Association  at  the  Faculty  of\\nManagement, Wrocław University of Science and Technology. The aim of the research was to\\nidentify and analyse the requirements for candidates for the position of Junior Project Manager\\non  the  labour  market,  including  what  competencies,  work  experience  and  personality  traits\\nconsidered key.\\n\\n## [PDF page 78]\\n\\n78  J. Iwko, B. Kubek, J. PiwiDski\\n\\nThe survey consisted of four stages:\\n1.  Stage I - creation of a tool to collect data.\\n2.  Stage II - data collection.\\n3.  Stage III - data selection.\\n4.  Stage IV - analysis of results.\\nA detailed description of the different stages of the study is presented later in the paper.\\n\\n3.1.  Creation of a tool to collect data\\n\\nIn  Stage  I,  an  analytical  questionnaire  developed  using  GoogleForms,  which  allowed\\ninformation to be collected from job vacancies for the position of Junior Project Manager posted\\non recruitment portals. The form was designed to allow the research group to enter all details\\nof the mandatory requirements, type of contract, full-time hours and required competencies.\\nSections of the form included:\\n\uf02d  Job publication site (e.g. recruitment portals, company websites).\\n\uf02d  Mandatory requirements (language, technical, soft, project management).\\n\uf02d  Type of contract and full-time hours.\\n\uf02d  Experience required.\\n\\n3.2.  Data collection\\n\\nThe data presented in this article was sourced from the most popular Polish recruitment\\nplatforms, which play a key role in the recruitment and candidate selection process, as well as\\nthe ’Careers’ section from the websites of companies based in Wrocław. The offers came from\\nvarious industries, including IT, finance, marketing and business services. PiwiDski\\n\\nFrom the analysis of the results regarding the work experience requirement, the following\\nconclusion can be drawn: there is a prevailing trend on the labour market where employers\\nprefer  to  hire  people  with  project  management  experience  in  the  range  of  2  to  5  years.\\nThese types of candidates already have the basic skills and knowledge, but are still able to adapt\\nquickly to the specifics of an organisation that can offer further career development in project\\nmanagement. By contrast, offers are rare for those with no work experience or very extensive\\nexperience. Such figures suggest that the Junior Project Manager position is seen as a role that\\nrequires some experience, but candidates are not expected to have a high level of autonomy and\\nresponsibility.\\nAnother important aspect that was considered in the analysis of job offers for the position\\nof Junior Project Manager is the scope of work and the full-time hours that appear in the\\nadvertisements (Figure 7). Required hourly working hours for the Junior Project Manager position (%).\\nSource: own elaboration based on survey.\\nFull-time hourly work in this context can be considered the industry standard, especially in\\nlarge  organisations  where  designing,  coordinating  and  monitoring  the  progress  of  projects\\nrequires systematicity and the full commitment of the employee. Full-time employment also\\nprovides  the  opportunity  to  be  fully  integrated  into  the  team,  to  participate  in  daily  project\\nmeetings and to collaborate with other departments of the organisation on an ongoing basis,\\nwhich is particularly important in the case of the Junior Project Manager position. Employers,\\nwhen deciding on this working time, usually expect candidates to be fully  available, which\\nfosters effective project management and enables young professionals to develop quickly by\\nengaging in a variety of tasks on a daily basis.\\n\\n## [PDF page 85]\\n\\nResearch on key requirements…  85\\n\\nDespite the predominance of full-time employment, positions with indefinite working hours\\nappeared  in  around  8%  of  the  offers  analysed.  This  may  mean  that  employers  are  offering\\ngreater flexibility in working hours, which is particularly attractive in the context of a dynamic\\nlabour  market,  the  growing  importance  of  work-life  balance  and  well-being  (Procházka,\\nBočková, 2024). In such offers, employers may suggest the possibility of part-time work or\\noffer flexible working hours, allowing the employee to adjust their schedule to accommodate\\nother  commitments  or  personal  preferences.  These  types  of  options  may  be  particularly\\nattractive to those who are studying, working on different projects at the same time or seeking\\na better work-life balance.\\nFlexible working hours may also result from the organisational policies of companies that\\nplace trust in their employees and allow them to manage their own working time. On the other\\nhand,  the  offer  of  a  job  with  non-standard  working  hours  may  also  refer  to  employment\\ncontracts that do not require a full commitment to a standard working mode, but allow tasks to\\nbe completed on a flexible basis. In this case, employers may expect Junior Project Managers\\nto work on a project in a more structured way, based on flexibility of working hours, which\\nmay involve less stress and more autonomy in organising their own working time.\\nThis type of offer, although a minority, can be attractive in the context of new trends in the\\nlabour market, such as remote working, hybrid  working and offering non-standard working\\nhours. Flexibility in terms of working hours can attract people who value the ability to tailor\\nworking  hours  to  their  individual  needs,  while  also  enabling  companies  to  attract  younger\\nworkers who are more willing to be flexible.\\n\\n5.  Conclusions\\n\\nThe study presented in this paper aimed to identify and analyse the key requirements for\\ncandidates for the position of Junior Project Manager. The analysis was based on 70 offers from\\nvarious recruitment platforms, providing a picture of recruiters’ expectations of young project\\nmanagement  professionals.  The  study  focused  on  the  identification  of  the  most  common\\nrequirements in terms of work experience, technical and soft skills, as well as an analysis of the\\nscope of work, including full-time equivalents.\\nIn  terms  of  technical  competence,  offers  most  often  required  knowledge  of  project\\nmanagement  tools  and  technical  knowledge  related  to  IT  systems  architecture  and\\nIT infrastructure markets, which may reflect the growing influence of technology on project\\nmanagement  processes.  In  addition,  emerging  requirements  for  knowledge  of  agile\\nmethodologies (including SCRUM) reflect the current trend in the IT industry, where flexibility\\nin project management methodologies is key. Another interesting finding of the survey is the\\n\\n## [PDF page 86]\\n\\n86  J. Iwko, B. Kubek, J. PiwiDski\\n\\nlack of explicit requirements for certification in the area of project management, which may\\nsuggest that practical experience is valued more than formal proof of skills.\\nIn terms of working hours, the survey found that the predominant form of employment is\\nfull-time, accounting for 92% of the offers analysed. This type of offer ensures employees are\\nfully  integrated  into  the  project  team  and  have  a  permanent  presence  in  the  organisation,\\nwhich is important in the context of delivering projects that require ongoing coordination and\\ncommitment. Only 8% of offers provide for flexible working hours or non-standard full-time\\nhours, which may indicate the growing role of flexibility in the workplace, especially in the\\ncontext of the changing expectations of today’s employees, who are looking for more autonomy\\nin organising their working time.\\nIn the context of the work experience analysis, the survey results reveal a dominance of the\\n2-5 years of experience category, indicating that recruiters prefer candidates who have some\\nproject management experience, but at the same time do not require excessive experience that\\ncould limit the flexibility of hired employees. The least sought after were those with no work\\nexperience and those with more than 5 years’ experience, which may indicate a preference for\\npeople who can quickly get into complex project processes but do not yet expect a high level\\nof responsibility.\\nThe conclusions of the survey indicate the increasing importance of soft competencies such\\nas  communication  and  self-management,  which  are  key  in  the  work  of  a  project  manager,\\nespecially in the position of Junior Project Manager. Iwko, D. Kuchta, O. Bezgin\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nR&D  projects  at  universities  consume  significant  amounts  of  money  and  effort.\\nUnfortunately, they are not always successful. For instance, according to one research study,\\nExploratory  Research  Projects  had  a  success  rate  of  24.2%,  Postdoctoral  Research  Projects\\naveraged 43.4%, and Research Projects for stimulating young independent teams had a success\\nrate of 18.5% (Rusu, Mocanu, Bibiri, 2022).\\nTwo aspects are increasingly recognised as important in project management, including in\\nthe  context  of  R&D  projects:  value-based  management  (The  Knowledge  Academy,  2024),\\nand metrics-based management (Kerzner, 2013). A project cannot be considered successful if\\nthe values desired by its stakeholders are not achieved. Additionally, it is possible, at least to\\nsome extent, to measure the likelihood of attaining these values during project implementation,\\nthrough carefully selected metrics. However, these concepts have been scarcely developed for\\nR&D projects implemented at universities.\\nFor this reason, the purpose of this paper is to investigate the potential for using metrics to\\nmeasure the likelihood of achieving the values desired by project stakeholders of R&D projects\\nin the university context and to propose a selection of metrics for practical application.\\nA literature review was conducted to identify the metrics proposed for R&D projects in the\\nexisting literature and the values expected from such projects by stakeholders, particularly in\\nthe university context. Furthermore, interviews with R&D project managers from universities\\nwere carried out to determine the current use of metrics in R&D projects at universities and\\ntheir preferences regarding different groups of metrics.\\nFinally,  as  the  findings  indicate  a  very  low  maturity  in  value-based  and  metrics-based\\nproject management at universities, an initial attempt was made to identify metrics that could\\nbe prioritised to demonstrate to project managers the feasibility and usefulness of using metrics\\nto measure the likelihood of achieving the values desired by stakeholders in university-based\\nR&D projects.\\nThe structure of the paper is as follows: In Section 2, we present the state of the art from the\\nliterature on values and stakeholders in R&D projects at universities. In Section 3, we review\\nthe metrics proposed in the literature for R&D projects in the university context. In Section 4,\\nwe  present  the  results  of  an  interview-based  study  on  the  use  of  metrics  in  R&D  projects\\nimplemented at universities. In Section 5, we propose an initial selection of metrics to be used\\non an obligatory basis in the management of R&D projects at universities.
