Value and stakeholders in R&D projects at the university\\n\\nThe  task  of  project  management  is  to  achieve  the  project’s  goal,  which,  in  the  case  of\\nresearch  and  development  (R&D)  projects,  takes  on  an  innovative  context.  Under  such\\nconditions, the final value of the project is not fully known, as are the research results that will\\nbe  achieved.  Therefore,  determining  the  fundamental  objectives  of  an  R&D  project  is\\ncomplicated,  and  their  final  form  is  sometimes  unexpected  (Elmquist,  Le  Masson,  2009).\\nThe ultimate goal of an R&D project, considering its specifics, is to achieve value, which may\\nmanifest as profit, collaboration, or the dissemination of new technology to society.\\nTraditional approaches to project management, despite their efficiency, may limit learning\\nprocesses,  innovation  development,  and  creativity,  thereby  negatively  impacting  the  value\\ngenerated by the project (Kerzner, 2015). For this reason, viewing a project through the lens of\\nvalue becomes crucial, enabling not only the achievement of objectives but also the creation of\\nnew benefits for stakeholders.\\nCreating value in R&D projects at universities presents a significant challenge associated\\nwith identifying and measuring the value generated at various stages of their implementation.\\nA  key  issue  is  that  the  outcomes  of  R&D  projects  do  not  always  translate  directly  or\\nimmediately into process improvements or innovation creation. R&D projects are inherently\\naimed at advancing science and specific disciplines, yet their positive impact on practice often\\nbecomes observable only after some time.\\nManaging the value of R&D projects at universities involves assessing the effectiveness\\nand efficiency of project activities and estimating the significance of the achieved outcomes.\\nThe  fundamental  problem  in  building  value  in  R&D  projects  at  universities  is  not  the  low\\nquality of research but rather the lack of knowledge and skills among researchers in steering\\nthe  development  of  their  research  work  (Aukasiewicz,  2007;  Klaus-Rosińska,  2019)  and\\ninsufficient  knowledge  about  managing  the  value  of  a  given  project.  Without  systematic\\nmeasurement and identification of value indicators, it is difficult to develop an effective method\\nfor analyzing and evaluating the value of a project (Zaskorski, 2012). According to Ellis et al.\\n(2005),  in  the  early  stages  of  project  implementation,  where  problems  are  often  complex,\\ndynamic, and poorly defined, value management is particularly crucial. Project managers and\\nresearch team members are typically unable to precisely estimate the value generated by the\\nproject  at  the  outset,  as  it  is  dynamically  shaped  during  implementation.  This  creates  both\\nchallenges and opportunities for generating new value.\\nWhen seeking criteria for measuring and evaluating value in R&D projects at universities,\\nit  is  essential  to  distinguish  between  value  evaluation  criteria  and  value-generating  factors\\n(Collins,  Baccarini,  2004).  Criteria  are  used  to  measure  the  value  achieved,  while  factors\\nfacilitate  its  creation  and  are  an  integral  part  of  project  management.  A  key  aspect  is\\n\\n## [PDF page 92]\\n\\n92  J. Iwko, D. Kuchta, O. Bezgin\\n\\nunderstanding who evaluates the project’s value and for whom it is created, highlighting that\\nthe primary criterion is meeting the needs of all stakeholders (Collins, Baccarini, 2004).\\nIn managing R&D projects, it is important to understand that value is created when it is\\nperceived as valuable by the project’s recipients (Lepak et al., 2007). Therefore, conducting an\\nin-depth analysis of stakeholder expectations is crucial, as it allows for precise targeting of\\nactions and enables participants to capture the expected benefits from the project. The goal of the analysis is to identify and classify key stakeholders\\nbased on established criteria that should be tailored to the project’s specifics. Metrics in the context of value-based project management\\n\\nKerzner (2013) identifies three approaches to measuring value in projects:\\n1.  An approach based solely on return on investment (ROI),\\n2.  An approach focused exclusively on intangible values,\\n3.  An approach that disregards intangible values entirely (Kerzner, 2013, p. 181).\\nAccording  to  the  author,  an  optimal  solution  may  involve  a  compromise  that  combines\\nquantitative methods with qualitative assessments of value.\\nThe timing of value measurement in a project plays a critical role, and the choice between\\nqualitative and quantitative metrics may require flexibility throughout the project’s lifecycle.\\nKey issues related to measuring value include the feasibility of defining specific metrics, their\\nusefulness in predicting actual value, and the appropriateness of using particular metrics in the\\nproject.\\nThe perception of value metrics in projects can vary depending on the perspective from\\nwhich they are evaluated. Each stakeholder group may prioritize different aspects of the project,\\ninfluencing how they interpret values such as time, cost, quality, or risk. Project expectations\\nmay shift based on the priorities of a given group, meaning that the same metrics can hold\\ndifferent significance and weight depending on the goals being pursued. Understanding these\\ndiverse interpretations is critical for effective project management and communication among\\nstakeholders to ensure harmonious achievement of objectives and overall project success.\\nViewing  metrics  through  the  lens  of  stakeholder  value  highlights  the  diversity  of\\nperspectives and expectations associated with project implementation. Each stakeholder group\\nmay interpret the same metrics differently, emphasizing the importance of adopting a flexible\\napproach to project management. Although project metrics may appear identical, they are often\\nunderstood differently by various stakeholder groups. Recognizing these differences enables\\nbetter project management by tailoring the approach and communication to meet the specific\\nexpectations of each group.\\n\\n## [PDF page 94]\\n\\n94  J. They  now  include  elements  such  as  maximizing  the\\nefficiency of the project team. Intangible values encompass aspects such as corporate culture,\\nintellectual  capital  and  its  accompanying  knowledge  management  systems,  executive  and\\nproject  leadership,  employee  talents,  job  satisfaction,  trust  and  credibility,  and  employees’\\nability to innovate. While these values may seem more challenging to measure, Kerzner (2022)\\nproposes  metrics  that  enable  effective  evaluation  of  intangible  values,  providing  essential\\ninsights into the potential benefits of project implementation.\\n\\n3.2.  Metrics in R&D projects\\n\\nMetrics in research and development (R&D) projects play a crucial role in monitoring and\\nassessing progress. However, they differ significantly from traditional metrics used in other\\ntypes of projects. In projects such as construction or IT, metrics are typically based on time,\\ncost, and quality of execution. In contrast, R&D projects, where results are often uncertain and\\ndifficult to predict, require a different approach. This is primarily due to the nature of these\\nprojects, which prioritize creativity, innovation, and the discovery of new solutions, and where\\nfinal outcomes may not be known until the project is completed (Kerzner, 2015).\\nR&D projects are often characterized by a high degree of uncertainty regarding both results\\nand  progress.  Designing  effective  metrics  to  measure  progress,  especially  in  the  context  of\\ninnovation,  is  therefore  a  significant  challenge.  For  example,  the  introduction  of  new\\ntechnologies or the development of intellectual property may occur only in the later stages of\\na project, making it impossible to establish clear indicators of success early on. As noted by\\nKerzner  (2015),  creativity  and  innovation  often  emerge  only  after  a  project’s  completion,\\ncomplicating the evaluation of progress during implementation (Kerzner, 2015; Kuchta et al.,\\n2017; Klaus-Rosińska, 2019).\\nFurthermore,  the  success  or  failure  of  R&D  projects  is  often  difficult  to  define\\nunequivocally.  Even  if  a  project  does  not  deliver  the  expected  results,  it  may  generate\\nintellectual value that leads to future innovations or opens new research paths. In this context,\\nit becomes essential to identify the point at which further funding will no longer yield benefits\\nand  to  recognize  termination  as  a  success  in  avoiding  unnecessary  losses.  Therefore,\\nR&D projects require flexible metrics that account for these less obvious aspects.\\nThe  literature  lacks  precise  metrics  dedicated  exclusively  to  R&D  projects.\\nMany organizations still use traditional metrics that fail to capture the unique characteristics of\\nthese types of projects. For this reason, Yakivets proposes introducing metrics that measure the\\nlikelihood of R&D project success based on a subjective definition of success (Yakivets, 2022).\\nThis concept involves presenting metrics for identifying the causes of failure in R&D projects,\\nallowing  for  the  prediction  of  certain  problems  that  could  contribute  to  a  project’s  failure.\\nSuch  an  approach  enables  better  adaptation  of  metrics  to  the  variable  and  unpredictable\\nconditions of research projects, which can lead to more effective management.\\n\\n## [PDF page 95]\\n\\nMetrics for measuring the achievement…  95\\n\\nWith the increasing number of R&D projects conducted in collaboration between industry\\nand academia (Perkmann et al., 2011), the need for monitoring and evaluating the outcomes of\\nsuch initiatives has also grown (Grimaldi, Von Tunzelmann, 2002).\\nThe  literature  indicates  that  R&D  projects  carried  out  within  partnerships  between\\nuniversities and industry are critical for economic growth, knowledge and technology transfer,\\ninnovation  acceleration,  and  skill  development  (Cunningham,  Link,  2015;  Guimon,  2013).\\nMany  research  centers  are  established  at  universities  because  they  are  vital  sources  of  new\\nscientific  knowledge  and  technological  advances.  Academic  research  plays  a  key  role  in\\nsupporting innovation (Mowery, Sampat, 2009; Garcia et al., 2019).\\nStudies show that defining evaluation metrics to measure effectiveness is one of the most\\nimportant  factors  influencing  the  success  of  R&D  collaborations  between  academia  and\\nindustry  (Skute  et  al.,  2019;  Kulatunga  et  al.,  2011;  Perkmann  et  al.,  2011;  Philbin,  2008).\\nPerformance metrics are effective tools for evaluating and demonstrating the value of research\\nactivities and collaborative projects involving researchers and practitioners (Daoud et al., 2017).\\nPrevious research has shown that assessing the outcomes of such collaborations and setting\\nclear goals are key challenges in managing academia-industry partnerships (Perkmann et al.,\\n2011). However, further research is needed to better understand the effectiveness of academia-\\nindustry  alliances,  as  no  structured  and  widely  accepted  system  of  performance  metrics  for\\nR&D projects currently exists (Piva, Rossi-Lamastra, 2013; Bekkers, Freitas, 2011).\\nA  review  of  previous  studies  on  defining  performance  metrics  for  R&D  projects  in\\nacademia-industry collaborations provides insights into how this issue has been addressed:\\n\uf0b7  Success  factors  in  R&D  project  management  for  both  sides  of  academia-industry\\npartnerships were identified (Barnes et al., 2002), and tools were developed to raise\\nawareness of key issues affecting the success of such partnerships.\\n\uf0b7  Theoretical  frameworks  based  on  clustering  concepts  were  introduced  to  assess\\napproaches  to  measuring  performance  in  research  departments  (Samsonowa  et  al.,\\n2009).\\n\uf0b7  Challenges related to assessing the outcomes of university-industry collaborations and\\nsetting clear goals for R&D projects were addressed (Perkmann et al., 2011).\\n\uf0b7  It  was  emphasized  that  no  structured  and  widely  accepted  system  of  performance\\nindicators for R&D projects exists (Bekkers, Freitas, 2011).\\n\uf0b7  A performance measurement system for R&D activities conducted by public research\\ncenters was developed (Agostino et al., 2012).\\n\uf0b7  The lack of a widely  accepted R&D performance indicator system and the need  for\\nfurther research on the effectiveness of performance indicators in such collaborations\\nwere highlighted (Piva, Rossi-Lamastra, 2013).\\n\uf0b7  A methodology based on logic models was proposed to analyze the impact and improve\\nthe  future  performance  of  R&D  partnerships  involving  universities,  industry,\\nand governments (Daoud et al., 2017).\\n\\n## [PDF page 96]\\n\\n96  J. Respondents indicated that these issues are often handled by specialists outside\\nthe project teams.\\n\uf0b7  A metric that did not apply to the projects of any of the people interviewed was the\\ncontrol  of  overtime.  This  applied  to  people  from  both  business  and  academic\\ninstitutions. Individuals from project teams are not billed on an hourly basis, and even\\nthose  on  a  full-time  basis  do  not  have  a  practice  of  accounting  for  overtime  in  the\\nworkplace.\\n\uf0b7  Metrics related to the monitoring of financial aspects are used by specialised individuals\\nor departments, not by project managers.\\n\\n## [PDF page 101]\\n\\nMetrics for measuring the achievement…  101\\n\\n\uf0b7  Most of the metrics reported by respondents were monitored reactively, in response to\\ncurrent  events  and  problems  in  project  implementation.  The  responsibility  for\\nmonitoring these metrics was often due to unforeseen situations or guidelines from the\\ninstitutions/project funders.\\n\uf0b7  Failure  to  use  certain  metrics  did  not  mean  that  respondents  considered  the\\ncorresponding issues irrelevant. It was indicated that it was important to monitor these\\nareas and that metrics could serve as a tool to support memory.\\nIn summary, respondents appreciated the potential of metrics to increase the effectiveness\\nof research project management and to create good practice but noted that some metrics (also\\nused  in  the  quantitative  survey  (Iwko  et  al.,  2023)  are  not  well  understood  and  need  to  be\\nclarified to become a useful element in research project management.\\n\\n5. Conclusions\\n\\nIn this paper, our starting point is two statements that are generally accepted today in the\\nfield of Project Management:\\n\uf0b7  A  project  is  successful  only  if  it  delivers  the  values  expected  from  it  by  the  key\\nstakeholders.\\n\uf0b7  It is possible, at least to some extent, to measure during project implementation the\\nlikelihood of achieving these values.\\nWe  applied  these  statements  to  R&D  research  projects  implemented  at  universities.\\nWe conducted a literature review, which revealed that research on metrics for measuring the\\nlikelihood of achieving values in R&D projects is largely limited to industry-academia projects,\\ndoes not encompass other types of projects, and often does not refer directly to values but rather\\nto concepts such as performance.\\nAdditionally,  we  carried  out  qualitative,  interview-based  research  with  R&D  project\\nmanagers from three universities. We asked them about their use of specific metrics identified\\nin the literature. The results indicate that the metrics currently used do not effectively measure\\nthe likelihood of achieving the most important values expected by stakeholders in R&D projects\\nimplemented at universities.\\nConsidering  the  low  maturity  of  universities  in  project  management,  we  propose\\nimplementing several metrics (Groups 2,3, and 4 in Table 2, new metrics should be proposed\\ntoo)  in  the  R&D  project  management  process  at  universities  on  an  obligatory  basis.\\nThese metrics should be clearly linked to the values that R&D project managers aim to achieve,\\nsuch  as  gaining  new  experiences,  enriching  skills  and  personal  development,  enhancing\\nemployee skills, establishing new business relationships, enabling the research team to fulfil\\ntheir  professional  aspirations,  and  obtaining  an  academic  title  (a  full  list  is  provided  in  the\\n\\n## [PDF page 103]\\n\\nMetrics for measuring the achievement…  103\\n\\npaper).  The  results  should  be  monitored,  and  feedback  from  project  managers  should  be\\ncollected to improve the system and increase its acceptance rate. Such measures will contribute\\nto a higher success rate for R&D projects implemented at universities and greater satisfaction\\namong project managers and team members.\\n\\nAcknowledgement\\n\\nThe research was funded by the Faculty of Management, WrocBaw University of Science\\nand  Technology  (Poland),  as  part  of  the  \\"Mini-Grant  WuZetka\\"  competition  for  the\\nimplementation of a single scientific activity entitled \\"Metrics in research projects - definition\\nand selection\\".\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Literature review and research hypotheses development\\n\\nP. Asquith and D.W. Mullins Jr. (Asquith, Mullins, 1983) indicate that, when investing in\\ndividend companies, it is important for investors, that the issuer pays dividends with a positive\\ngrowth rate on a continuous basis. On the other hand, A. Cwynar and W. Cwynar (Cwynar,\\nCwynar, 2007) and M. Kowerski (Kowerski, 2011) point out, that the investor’s income, in the\\nform of expected dividends, is more important than the expected gain from the sale of stock,\\nbecause the dividend is certain, while the possible gains from an increase in the stock price are\\nuncertain. Therefore, one of the basic criteria for investing in stock of public companies should\\nbe  the  systematic  distribution  of  financial  results  to  stockholders.  Studies  conducted  by\\nH. Rubin and C. Spaht II (Rubin, Spaht, 2011, pp. 11-19), A. Williams and M. Miller (Williams,\\nMiller, 2013, pp. 58-69), as well as K.P. Fuller and M.A. Goldstein (Fuller, Goldstein, 2011,\\npp. 457-473) confirm the legitimacy of such investments. The mere fact of paying dividends\\nhas consequences for both the company itself and stockholders. Therefore, the dividends paid\\nby issuers, in light of the theory and the research conducted, on the one hand, remain in relation\\nto the value of the company (dividends determine the value of the company) and, on the other\\nhand,  depending  on  the  dividend  payment  strategy  adopted,  affect  the  behavior  of  capital\\nmarket  investors  (the  dividend  policy  adopted  determines  the  behavior  of  investors).\\nThree theories of the determination of a company’s value by the level of dividends paid are\\ncharacterized in the literature. The conservative (pro-dividend) group assumes, that the value\\nof  the  company  will  be  maximized  by  a  high  rate  of  dividend  payments  (M.  Gordon  and\\nJ. Lintner). Discussion and conclusions\\n\\nThe obtained results of the research on the comparison of Polish and American dividend\\ncompanies  confirm  the  existing  practices  of  the  latter  in  terms  of  the  stability  of  dividend\\npayments  and  the  number  of  companies  systematically  transferring  profits  to  stockholders.\\nThe  largest  companies,  that  are  components  of  the  WIG  index,  do  not  show  as  much\\nconcentration of dividend payment systematics as the companies in the S&P500 index, which\\nwere  characterized  by  a  lower  diversity  of  dividend  breaks  between  2017  and  2023.\\nThe considerations presented and the research performed also made it possible to conclude, that\\nPolish dividend companies, if they actually paid dividends characterized by higher dynamics\\nof change, were, at the same time, burdened with higher variability of payments.\\nOn the other hand, studies of stock valuation using the classical form of the Gordon-Shapiro\\nmodel in the Polish and U.S. markets have shown shortcomings regarding the model’s overly\\ndemanding  assumptions,  which  are  difficult  for  dividend  companies  to  meet  in  practice.\\nAccordingly, for no company in the Polish market was it possible to value stock according to\\nthe constant dividend growth rate model. Companies from the U.S. stock market performed\\nmuch  better,  although  it  was  possible  to  make  a  practical  valuation  for  only  9  of  the\\n24 companies, with only 2 companies having a fixed dividend growth rate, and 7 estimated as\\nan average growth rate from 2017-2023. Unfortunately, the discrepancies that occurred between\\nthe model valuation of stocks and their stock market prices were significant, suggesting the\\nimpossibility of correctly valuing stocks in practice using the classical form of the Gordon-\\nShapiro model in the U.S. market as well.\\nBased on the conducted research, the adopted research hypotheses were verified, and on\\nthis basis, it was concluded that:\\nH1: The average rate of change in dividends paid by dividend companies included in the WIG\\nindex is actually higher than the average rate of change in dividends paid by issuers that\\nare components of the S&P500 index.\\nH2: The standard deviation of the rate of change of dividends is significantly lower for U.S.\\ndividend companies than for dividend companies in the WIG index.\\nH3: The use of the classical form of the Gordon-Shapiro model for stock valuation actually in\\npractice does not allow for a reliable assessment and proper selection of listed companies\\nfor an investment portfolio in both the Polish and U.S. markets.\\nHowever, it should be noted, that there is a certain insufficiency in the research conducted\\nregarding the set of dividend companies analyzed (especially for companies in the WIG index)\\nand the time range of the analyses. The authors intend to conduct extended analyses of the\\nissues raised in the article in the future with a more extensive dataset. Analyses were performed using Statgraphics plus 4.1. Due to the\\nlack of normal distribution and unequal groups, the significance of differences was tested using\\nnon-parametric  Mann-Whitney  U  statistical  tests  for  two  grouping  variables  and  Kruskal-\\nWallis  ANOVA  test  for  questions  where  there  were  more  than  three  grouping  variables.\\nA significance level of α = 0.05 was used in the analyses.\\nFindings: In the last years, Poles began to appreciate fruits health-promoting properties more.\\nIn addition, as a result of changes in consumer preferences and tastes, looking for more and\\nmore new flavors and preferring healthy lifestyles, it is difficult to expect a significant decline\\nin  the  consumption  of  fruits  in  general,  even  with  an  increase  in  their  prices,  which,\\nin the context of the current organization of the market, is a positive development.\\nOriginality/value:  The  article  shows  current  trends  in  fruit  consumption  in  Poland.\\nIt also presents guidelines for further organization of the fruit market, as well as policies for\\nshaping correct attitudes about fruit consumption.\\nKeywords: fruit, consumer preferences, consumption.\\nCategory of the paper: research paper.\\n\\nhttp://dx.doi.org/10.29119/1641-3466.2025.215.8  http://managementpapers.polsl.pl/\\n\\n## [PDF page 130]\\n\\n130  K. Juszczak-Szel\\u0006gowska, W. CzerwiDska, D. Olewnicki, K. Zmarlicki, B. Nosecka\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nFruit production plays an important role in Polish agriculture. With its volume at 5.4 million\\ntons in 2022, our country is among the largest producers of this assortment in the European\\nUnion. Also noteworthy is the fact that with apple production at 3-4 million tons, Poland is the\\nlargest producer of apples in the European Union, and the third largest producer in the world,\\njust behind China and the US (FAO, 2024). Similar results are achieved in the production of\\nraspberries, cherries, currants and blueberries, although their volume is much lower than apples,\\nestablishing our country as a significant producer on world markets. It should be added that the\\nproduction of this assortment has a major impact on the food market, and thus on the formation\\nof prices and demand for fruit.\\nDespite such a large scale in the production of many fruits, however, household surveys\\npublished  by  the  Central  Statistical  Office  show  that  the  consumption  of  fruits  in  Poland,\\nespecially fresh ones, has been at a low level for many years, and is further declining, especially\\ndomestic  ones.  Taking  into  account  the  still  lower  level  of  consumption  of  fruits,  but  also\\nvegetables  in  Poland  in  relation  to  the  recommendations  of  the  World  Health  Organization\\n(WHO), it therefore becomes important to study the reasons for this decline, in order to create\\nthe basis for proper organization of the market, but also for the promotion of their consumption\\nwhich  aims  to  increase  consumer  interest  in  these  products.  Therefore,  based  on\\nmacroeconomic analysis and survey research, the purpose of the study was to assess the demand\\nfor  fruits  among  consumers.  Identification  of  factors  influencing  consumers’  purchase\\npreferences was carried out, such as frequency of purchase and consumption, choice of place\\nof purchase, factors influencing purchase decisions, level of spending on fruits and vegetables\\nand changes in consumption with respect to the previous year, among others. Changes in fruit\\nconsumption in Poland based on data from the Central Statistical Office (CSO) were shown as\\na background to the study.The literature shows that consumption and consumer behavior are\\ndetermined by a number of factors, both consumer-dependent and environment-related. Internal\\nfactors include disposable income, owned assets and savings, labor force participation, as well\\nas the previous level and structure of consumption. External factors, on the other hand, include\\nthe  country’s  socio-economic  situation  and  the  influence  of  the  international  environment\\n(Sobczyk, 2018). Hence, it should be added that the events that were observed in part during\\nthe years under analysis, such as the Sars-Cov 2 virus pandemic and the outbreak of armed\\nconflict in Ukraine, had a huge economic impact. In addition, the increase in prices of goods\\nand services, entailed an increase in inflation from 3.2% in 2021 to 17.5% in 2022 (|urek,\\n2023).  Problems  with  product  availability  also  became  apparent,  all  of  which  could  affect\\nconsumers’ purchasing decisions.\\n\\n## [PDF page 131]\\n\\nPreferences of Polish consumers…  131\\n\\n2.  Factors shaping demand and the role of fruits and vegetables\\nin the human diet\\n\\nFood  supply  and  demand  are  the  main  factors  that  affect  the  operation  of  the  market\\nmechanism,  with  prices  playing  an  important  role  in  the  formation  of  these  two  factors.\\nPrice  is  a  fundamental  element  of  any  offer  and  is  a  key  factor  that  influences  consumers’\\npurchasing decisions. Its importance and the ability to effectively manage this marketing tool\\nbecomes  increasingly  important,  especially  in  crisis  situations  (Waniowski,  2021).\\nThis was evident in 2021, when, as a result of the pandemic and warfare in Ukraine, the rise in\\nfood  prices  contributed  to  a  sharp  increase  in  inflation,  although  according  to  a  survey\\nconducted by SekściDska (2022) on a group of consumers aged 18-81, it appears that inflation\\ncontributed very little to the reduction in food spending in Poland. Nearly half of those surveyed\\nhave  not  changed  their  eating  habits.  In  contrast,  only  1%  of  respondents  have  definitely\\nreduced their food spending.\\nFruits as well as vegetables are the foundation of the Food Pyramid, which emphasizes their\\nkey  role  in  the  human  diet.  Health  organizations  recommend  diets  based  on  their  regular\\nconsumption (Bieniek-Majka, 2022). Many scientific studies point to the effects of a shortage\\nof fruits and vegetables in the diet and the increasing incidence of chronic non-communicable\\ndiseases.  According  to  the  WHO,  malignant  tumors  are  the  most  common  cause  of  death\\nworldwide, causing more than 8 million deaths annually. Dietary factors are estimated to be\\nresponsible for about 30% of cancer cases in industrialized countries. An adequate diet is the\\nsecond most important factor, after avoiding smoking, in reducing cancer risk. Regular physical\\nactivity, combined with a balanced diet based mainly on fruits and vegetables, is crucial for the\\noptimal  development  and  health  of  children  and  adolescents.  Fruits  and  vegetables  provide\\na variety of nutrients, such as vitamin C, pro-vitamin A, zinc, selenium and potassium, which\\nplay  an  important  role  in  neutralizing  free  radicals  in  the  body.  In  addition,  the  method  of\\npreparation  and  heat  treatment  affect  the  mineral  and  nutrient  content  of  these  products\\n(Oleśków, 2017; Doniec et al., 2020). One of the key factors influencing the consumption of\\nfruits and vegetables is their quality. The quality of food products is most often defined by their\\ncharacteristics. According to one of the most well-known and frequently quoted definitions,\\nfood  quality  includes  the  degree  of  health  safety,  sensory  appeal  and  availability  from  the\\nperspective of the consumer and society, taking into account the constraints of raw materials,\\ntechnology and price provided for these products (Kijowski, Sikora, 2003). According to the\\nrecommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO), daily consumption of an adequate\\namount of fruits and vegetables is an essential part of a healthy diet. According to the latest\\nWHO position for adults, it is recommended to consume about 400 g of fruits and vegetables\\nin five servings per day (Devirgiliis et al., 2024). According to Eurostat (2019), it appears that\\none in three EU citizens do not consume any fruits and vegetables during the day. Research by\\n\\n## [PDF page 132]\\n\\n132  K. Juszczak-Szel\\u0006gowska, W. CzerwiDska, D. Olewnicki, K. Zmarlicki, B. Nosecka\\n\\nFreshfel  Europe  (2021),  as  well  as  GoryDska-Goldmann  (2024),  shows  that  in  2021,\\nthe  daily  consumption  of  fruits  and  vegetables  in  EU  countries  was  365  grams  per  person.\\nWhich  indicated  that  the  level  of  fruit  and  vegetable  consumption  in  all  EU-27  countries,\\nhowever, corresponded to WHO dietary recommendations. Moreover, according to the data,\\nPoles were the few who met the WHO recommendations. It should be added that the above\\nstudy was carried out on the basis of FAO balance sheet data, which differ significantly from\\nthe data from the CSO’s survey of household budgets. Thus, in Poland, the average annual\\nconsumption of fruits and vegetables in 2019-2021 per capita according to the balance sheet\\ndata was 180.9 kg (GoryDska-Goldmann, 2024), while the survey of household budgets shows\\nthat the Polish consumer on average annually consumes a total of 102.3 kg of fruits and in\\nvegetables  (own  calculations  based  on  CSO,  2023).  The  amount  of  fruit  and  vegetable\\nconsumption depends on gender. Women were more likely than men to declare that they eat\\nfruit at least once a day. Women consume more fruits and vegetables than men, which may be\\nrelated  to  greater  knowledge  about  healthy  eating.  Men  are  less  aware  of  dietary\\nrecommendations and the risks associated with unhealthy habits, while women are more likely\\nto link a healthy diet with a higher intake of fruits and vegetables (Bieniek-Majka, 2022).\\nAccording to GoryDska-Goldman (2024), Polish society, in terms of the amount of fruit and\\nvegetable  consumption  on  a  macroeconomic  scale,  was  most  similar  to  many  societies  in\\nCentral Europe (i.e., Latvia, the Czech Republic, Lithuania, Hungary, Slovakia and Bulgaria),\\nas well as to that of Cyprus. Poland ranked 38th as a fruit producer in the world in 2022, while\\nin terms of vegetables it ranked 27th (Hałasiewicz et al., 2023). According to the Institute of\\nAgricultural  and  Food  Economics,  there  was  a  negative  trade  balance  for  both  fruits  and\\nvegetables in 2022. This meant that more of these products were imported to Poland than were\\nexported to other countries (Nosecka, 2023). This also demonstrates the changes taking place\\nin the structure of fruit and vegetable consumption, which is the result of changing consumer\\npreferences, seeking more and more new products and flavors.\\n\\n3.  Material and methods\\n\\nIn  the  study,  as  a  background  for  the  study  of  consumer  preferences,  the  results  of\\nmacroeconomic analyses were presented on changes in the consumption of fresh as well as\\nprocessed fruits, broken down by their individual categories, in Poland over the years 2015-\\n2022. The primary source of information for macroeconomic analyses was data from the survey\\nof household budgets, conducted by the Central Statistical Office. The year 2015 was taken as\\n100%, from which the basic statistical parameters giving a summary description of the analyzed\\nphenomenon were calculated, including fixed-base indices, with the help of which changes in\\nthe size of absolute data in the last analyzed year in relation to the base year were analyzed.\\n\\n## [PDF page 133]\\n\\nPreferences of Polish consumers…  133\\n\\nBy calculating chain indices (with a variable base), the average annual rate of the changes under\\nstudy was determined, the measure of which in the period under study (t0, t1) was the difference\\nbetween the average chain index of the period and unity (GórczyDski, 2004). The coefficients\\nof variation, which are the quotient of the standard deviation and the arithmetic mean of the\\nvalues studied, were also calculated.\\nThe main part of the paper consists of analyses of primary data from surveys conducted\\nusing the CAWI method, on a group of 255 respondents, throughout Poland, in 2023. Women\\naccounted for the largest share of the surveyed population, i.e. 60.0% of the total, taking part in\\nthe research. Men, on the other hand, accounted for 40.0%. The survey also established four\\nage  groups  of  respondents,  i.e.  18-30  years  old,  31-45  years  old,  46-60  years  old  and\\nover  60  years  old.  The  largest  group,  116  people  (45.5%),  were  respondents  aged  18-30.\\nThe  percentage  of  respondents  aged  31-45  was  30.2%,  while  those  aged  46-60  and\\nover  60  were  15.7%  and  8.6%,  respectively.  Another  factor  characterizing  the  survey\\npopulation was the place of residence. The largest group of study participants were residents of\\ncities  with  a  population  of  less  than  50,000  (30.2%).  The  second  smaller  group  among  the\\nsurvey participants were residents of cities with more than 250,000 residents accounting for\\n27.5%. The share of rural residents was 26.7%, while the smallest group, only 5.9% of people,\\nlived in a city of 52 to 99.9 thousand residents.\\nTaking into account the monthly disposable income per person in the household, the largest\\nnumber,  44.7%,  of  respondents  had  incomes  above  PLN  3000.  The  second  largest  group,\\nin terms of numbers, were respondents with income between 2001 and 3000 PLN. The least\\nnumerous group of respondents (6.3%) were those with per capita incomes of up to PLN 1000.\\nThis division made it possible to assess the diversity of respondents’ opinions depending on\\nselected  factors.  In this  case, it was investigated whether there were statistically significant\\ndifferences between selected factors, including the size of consumption or feelings about the\\nincrease  in  the  price  of  fruit,  and  factors  characterizing  the  respondents.  Analyses  were\\nperformed  using  Statgraphics  plus  4.1.  Due  to  the  lack  of  normal  distribution  and  unequal\\ngroups,  the  significance  of  differences  was  tested  using  non-parametric  Mann-Whitney  U\\nstatistical tests for two grouping variables and Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA test for questions where\\nthere were more than three grouping variables. A significance level of α = 0.05 was used in the\\nanalyses.\\n\\n## [PDF page 134]\\n\\n134  K. Juszczak-Szel\\u0006gowska, W. CzerwiDska, D. Olewnicki, K. Zmarlicki, B. Nosecka\\n\\n4.  Analysis of fruit consumption based on CSO data\\n\\nThe analysis carried out showed that the per capita consumption of fruit and preserves in\\ntotal in Poland, in households, throughout the whole of the analyzed multi-year period increased\\non average annually by only 0.4% kg/person and was at the level of 44.4 kg/person in 2022,\\nwhich means that it was only 3.1% higher than in 2015 (Table 1). It is noteworthy that in the\\ncase of fresh and chilled fruits, consumption in 2022 was at the same level as in the first year\\nof the analyzed period. Over the entire multi-year period under study, the highest decrease in\\nconsumption (by 3.3% on average from year to year) was recorded for apples, and this was\\na  total  decrease  of  20.9%  from  13.2  kg/person  in  2015  to  10.4  kg/person  in  2022.\\nAlso, a negative rate of change was recorded in the consumption of stone fruits and berries,\\nwhich averaged 2.5% and 1.3% annually. As a result, stone fruit consumption was 16.2% lower\\nin 2022 than in 2015, while berry fruit consumption was 8.5% lower. Of the group of fresh and\\nrefrigerated fruits, the highest average annual rates of change of 4.4% and 4.3% were recorded\\nfor  the  consumption  of  bananas  and  the  group  of  other  fruits,  respectively.  Thus,  in  2022.\\nPoles consumed 35.3% more bananas on average than in 2015. Noteworthy is the increase in\\nthe consumption of other southern fruits, including a 9.2% increase in citrus fruits in the last\\nyear of analysis compared to the base year. The highest, 13.3% and 10.4% average annual rates\\nof change over the entire analysis period were recorded in the consumption of processed fruit\\nand  frozen  fruit,  respectively.  Thus,  the  increase  in  consumption  of  fruit  preparations,\\nwhich include jams, mousses, purees, among others, was at 140% in 2022 compared to 2015.\\nIn turn, the consumption of frozen fruits doubled in the same period. It should be added that\\nthese were the groups of fruits with the highest coefficient of variation, which for frozen fruits\\nwas at 37.6%, while for fruit preparations it reached 31.8%. In contrast, all other fruit groups\\nanalyzed recorded low variability, as evidenced by coefficient of variation values below 25%.\\n\\n## [PDF page 135]\\n\\nTable 1.\\nFruit consumption in Summary and conclusions\\n\\nThe analysis shows that fruit consumption showed an upward trend from 2015 to 2022,\\nbut it was a small increase, averaging 0.4% per year. The highest growth rate was recorded for\\nfrozen fruit, processed fruit and citrus fruit bananas and the group of other fruits. In contrast,\\nthe largest decrease in consumption was in apples, berries and stone fruits.\\nThe results presented in the survey allow us to conclude that almost half of the surveyed\\nconsumers consume fruit on a daily basis. The most frequently consumed fruits are apples and\\nbananas,  whose  consumption  was  indicated  by  80.8%  and  76.5%  of  surveyed  consumers,\\nrespectively. In addition, the survey showed that most respondents purchase fruit very often.\\nPurchases are mainly made at hypermarkets and discount grocery stores. Slightly less important\\nare markets and local vegetable stores. In addition, the most important factor in respondents’\\nchoice of where to buy fruits and vegetables is the location close to where they live, which was\\nindicated by more than 70% of respondents. A significant proportion of respondents choose\\nplaces that offer a wide assortment and high quality produce. When shopping, respondents pay\\nattention primarily to the freshness and quality of fruits.\\n\\n## [PDF page 145]\\n\\nPreferences of Polish consumers…  145\\n\\nBased on the analysis, it can be indicated that 46.7% of all respondents felt very strongly\\nabout the increase in the price of fruits, compared to the previous year, i.e. 2022. And although\\nas many as 73.3% of all respondents spent more money on fruit purchases, compared to the\\nprevious  year,  this  was  not  reflected  in  an  increase  in  the  consumption  of  these  products.\\nThus, the survey showed that more than half, 58.4%, of respondents in 2023 consumed the same\\namount of fruit compared to the previous year, indicating that the amount of fruit consumed is\\ndue to certain eating habits. The price increase did not significantly decrease fruit consumption.\\nInstead,  consumers  may  have  opted  for  lower-quality  or  substitute  products.  In  addition,\\nit is noteworthy that despite the increase in inflation during the period under review, as well as\\nthe  increase  in  prices,  as  many  as  22.4%  of  the  total  respondents  increased  their  fruit\\nconsumption  compared  to  the  previous  year.  It  is  worth  adding,  as  the  literature  shows,\\nthat during the pandemic period there was a very strong increase in fruit consumption, but also\\nin vegetable consumption. This is due to the fact that in the face of massive COVID cases,\\ntaking care of their health, Poles began to appreciate their health-promoting properties more.\\nIn addition, as a result of changes in consumer preferences and tastes, looking for more and\\nmore new flavors and preferring healthy lifestyles, it is difficult to expect a significant decline\\nin the consumption of fruits and vegetables in general, even with an increase in their prices,\\nwhich, in the context of the current organization of the market, is a positive development.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Introduction\\n\\nIn  an  era  of  rapid  technological  development,  globalisation  of  markets  and  increasing\\ncompetition, the importance of work-life balance is growing and becoming an integral part of\\nhuman resource management strategies in companies around the world. Today’s labour market\\nis characterised by dynamic change, with challenges for employees to adapt, time pressures and\\na constant need for upskilling. In the face of these challenges, work-life balance is no longer\\na luxury or an add-on to employee benefits, but is becoming a key tool to influence employee\\nmotivation, productivity and loyalty (Tomaszewska-Lipiec, 2014).\\nProfessional  work,  despite  its  potential  for  development  and  the  opportunity  to  realise\\nprofessional ambitions, often leads to excessive strain, stress and a lack of work-life balance.\\nThe  negative  consequences  of  this,  such  as  job  burnout  and  a  decline  in  productivity,\\nare increasingly recognised by employers, who realise that satisfied and motivated employees\\nare the key to an organisation’s success (Currie, Eveline, 2011).\\nToday, work-life balance, often referred to as work-life harmony, has become a key area of\\nresearch  and  human  resource  management  practices.  Despite  the  apparent  simplicity  of  the\\nconcept, its complexity and multidimensionality make it challenging to fully understand and\\neffectively implement in an organisational context (Sadowska-Snarska, 2013).\\nThe modern approach to work-life balance is based on the belief that employees should be\\ntreated not only as a source of labour, but also as individuals with a life of their own outside the\\nworkplace. Therefore, the concept promotes the harmonious integration of work and personal\\nresponsibilities,  aiming  to  provide  individuals  with  satisfaction  and  fulfilment  in  both  the\\nprofessional and private spheres (Wierda et al., 2008).\\nThe term 8work-life balance9 (WLB) gained popularity in the 1970s in the United States,\\nmainly as a response to the challenges of the traditional family model and the increasing labour\\nforce participation of women. In the following decade, the concept expanded to include any\\ninitiative to support employees in balancing their work and personal commitments, regardless\\nof the family context. In practice, this means that work-life harmony is achieved when neither\\nsphere dominates at the expense of the other (Wiradendi et al., 2021).\\nResearch  shows  a  variety  of  approaches  to  analysing  the  concept  of  work-life  balance\\n(WLB), focusing on work-life relationships. According to the literature, there are three main\\napproaches to describing this relationship. The first approach suggests the independence of the\\ntwo spheres, according to segmentation theory. The second approach describes unidirectional\\ninfluences,  where  mainly  work  interacts  with  private  life,  as  presented  by  spillover  theory.\\nThe third approach refers to reciprocal influences, according to theories such as facilitation,\\nenrichment,  domino  effect  and  compensation  theory,  which  implies  a  certain  compatibility\\nbetween work and personal life (Menderak, 2019).\\n\\n## [PDF page 151]\\n\\nThe role of work-life-balance…  151\\n\\nThe relationship between the spheres of work and life is often described in different ways.\\nFirstly, they can generate conflicting expectations. Secondly, they can be mutually beneficial,\\nwhere resources and experiences from one sphere benefit the other. And finally, they can be\\ncomplementary, where deficiencies in one sphere are compensated by the other (Wiradendi\\net al., 2021).\\nResearch on WLB in Poland often mirrors research directions observed in other parts of the\\nworld and faces similar challenges. According to the findings of StaDczak and other researchers\\n(2017), there are six key thematic areas specific to Polish WLB research:\\n1.  Identification of the obstacles to achieving work-life balance and the associated need\\nfor support in developing a WLB strategy.\\n2.  Analysis of companies’ approaches to WLB and their proposed solutions.\\n3.  Exploring  the  experiences  of  women  who  harmonise  work  life  with  family\\nresponsibilities.\\n4.  Defining and varying interpretations of the concept of WLB.\\n5.  Analysing awareness of the benefits of work-life balance.\\n6.  Evaluating the implementation of WLB strategies in practice.\\n\\n2.  Motivation theories in the context of WLB\\n\\nBoundary theory emphasises the existence of two separate but related spheres: work and\\npersonal life. Depending on their values, attitudes and thinking patterns, people manage these\\nareas variously, aiming for a harmonious combination. Balance is about minimising conflict\\nand functioning smoothly in both areas. These boundaries can take many forms: psychological\\n(emotions,  thoughts),  physical  (e.g.  space)  or  temporal  (e.g.  working  hours)  (Karassvidou,\\nGlaveli, 2015).\\nContemporary research suggests that the strength of a boundary depends on its flexibility,\\npermeability and ability to bridge different aspects of life. Boundary crossers play an important\\nrole in shaping the work-life dynamic. Not only are they participants, but they also shape the\\ndirection  and  rules  of  both,  based  on  their  influence  and  identity.  In  the  Polish  scientific\\nliterature,  the  analysis  of  work-life  dynamics  from  the  perspective  of  boundary  theory  is\\nrelatively  rare.  Only  a  few  publications  on  work-life  boundaries  in  the  context  of  remote\\nworking have been noted so far. There is also research on the impact of mobile technologies on\\nwork-life interactions and on work-family dynamics (Kubacka, Mroczkowska, 2020).\\nThe  research  model  described  allows  the  analysis  of  different  aspects  of  work-life\\nboundaries:  physical,  temporal  and  psychological.  It  focuses  on  key  variables  such  as\\ninterpersonal  relationships  or  subjective  interpretations  and  valuations  in  the  context  of\\norganisational factors such as working time policies. In addition, it emphasises the importance\\n\\n## [PDF page 152]\\n\\n152  A. Kasperczuk, M. Ćwi\\u0006kaBa, E. Górka, P. R czajski, P. MrzygBód et al.\\n\\nof  the  psychological  shaping  and  feeling  of  these  boundaries  to  understand  the  subjective\\nexperience of balance (Kubacka, Mroczkowska, 2020).\\n\\n3.  Impact of work-life balance on commitment and job satisfaction\\n\\nMaintaining a work-life balance has become an important issue in the context of quality of\\nworking  life.  This  balance  implies  a  smooth  harmonisation  of  professional  and  personal\\nresponsibilities,  which  theoretically  translates  into  improved  well-being,  satisfaction  and\\nefficiency at work. Being professionally active implies a deep commitment to the tasks at hand,\\na strong emotional bond with the organisation and a willingness to put in extra effort to achieve\\ncommon  goals.  Research  shows  that  employees  who  are  able  to  achieve  a  better  work-life\\nbalance tend to show greater commitment to their responsibilities. This balance also promotes\\nbetter time allocation between work and private life, which reduces the risk of burnout and\\nincreases the willingness to engage with the company (Paszkiewicz, Wasiluk, 2022).\\nJob satisfaction is about positively evaluating one’s own experiences and expectations of\\nwork. People who are able to manage their time effectively and find a work-life balance often\\nexperience  higher  job  satisfaction.  Maintaining  a  work-life  balance  can  contribute  to\\nan improved sense of well-being, reduced stress levels and an increased sense of control over\\none’s life, resulting in overall job satisfaction (Skrok et al., 2023).\\nFor  companies  that  care  about  the  wellbeing  of  their  employees,  promoting  work-life\\nbalance is becoming an important priority. Employees who value this balance are more loyal to\\ntheir  employer,  less  likely  to  change  jobs  and  more  likely  to  recommend  it  to  others  as\\nan attractive place of employment. Moreover, high levels of engagement and job satisfaction\\ntranslate into higher productivity, innovation and a favourable company image (Skrok et al.,\\n2023).\\n\\n4.  Research material and method\\n\\nThe  aim  of  this  study  was  to  analyse  the  role  of  work-life  balance  as  an  instrument\\ninfluencing  employee  motivation  in  the  context  of  the  contemporary  labour  market.\\nBy  exploring  the  mechanisms  influencing  work-life  balance  and  identifying  the  benefits  of\\nmaintaining it, an attempt was made to understand what strategies and actions can contribute to\\nincreasing employee satisfaction and commitment in the current work environment.\\n\\n## [PDF page 153]\\n\\nThe role of work-life-balance…  153\\n\\nResearch  hypothesis:  Organisations  that  actively  support  the  work-life  balance  of  their\\nemployees  through  various  initiatives  and  programmes  have  more  motivated  employees\\ncompared to organisations that do not offer such support.\\nThe following research questions were posed to complement the research hypothesis:\\n1.  Are employees satisfied with their own level of work-life balance?\\n2.  Which work-life balance instruments can be considered the most effective in the opinion\\nof respondents?\\nThe survey took place between May and July 2023, where the Internet was the main tool\\nfor data collection. The survey questionnaire was prepared using the Google Forms platform\\nand  made  available  through  thematic  forums  and  other  online  platforms.  Participants  were\\nassured  of  the  anonymity  of  their  responses  and  the  purpose  of  the  survey  was  presented.\\nIn addition, participants were given the option to stop completing the questionnaire at any time.\\nThe collected data were statistically analysed and presented in the form of tables and graphs.\\nFrequency analysis and basic descriptive statistics for quantitative data, such as mean, median\\nand standard deviation, were used to analyse the data. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) with\\nrepeated  measures  was  performed  to  compare  motivator  ratings.  Comparisons  between  two\\nindependent  samples  were  made  using  the  Student’s  t-test  or  the  Mann-Whitney  test  when\\nassumptions  about  the  normality  of  the  data  distribution  were  not  met.  On  the  other  hand,\\nfor  comparison  of  values  between  more  than  two  independent  groups,  analysis  of  variance\\n(ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test was used. When significant differences were detected,\\nPOST-HOC tests were used for more detailed analysis. The normality of the data distribution\\nwas  checked  using  the  Shapiro-Wilk  test.  Analysis  of  the  relationship  between  quantitative\\nvariables was performed using Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation analysis. The significance\\nlevel was taken at α = 0.05. All analyses were performed using Statistica 13.3 software from\\nStatSoft.\\nThe survey involved 102 economically active people, of whom 61.76% were women and\\n38.24% were men. The age range of 18 to 25 years was 9.80% of the respondents, 26 to 35\\nyears was 48.04% and 36 to 45 years was 29.41%. The remaining 12.75% were employees\\naged 46 and over. Summary\\n\\nIn today’s fast-changing world, where the boundaries between work and personal life are\\nbecoming increasingly fluid, the concept of WLB is becoming extremely important for both\\nemployees and employers. Maintaining a healthy balance between these two spheres of life is\\ncrucial  for  an  individual’s  wellbeing,  job  satisfaction  and  professional  effectiveness.\\nConsequently, a growing body of research is focusing on identifying the factors that influence\\nWLB and the tools that can help improve it (Tomaszewska-Lipiec, 2014).\\nA study by Zheng and colleagues (2015) identified that work-life balance strategies and\\ninitiatives implemented in companies play a key role in supporting employees to achieve this\\nbalance. In addition to the programmes and initiatives offered, individual factors such as type\\nof  job,  age,  marital  status  and  level  of  earnings  influence  the  ability  to  balance  work  and\\npersonal  life.  It  is  therefore  important  to  regularly  monitor  and  adapt  organisational  WLB\\nstrategies and policies to better meet the individual needs of employees.\\nThe results of the study showed that there is a slight but statistically significant difference\\nin  the  assessment  of  WLB  levels  between  men  and  women.  There  are  several  potential\\nexplanations for this phenomenon. Women may be more likely to express the need for work-\\nlife balance, which may be due to their traditional role in managing the home and caring for the\\nfamily. On the other hand, men may experience more social pressure to devote more time and\\nenergy to work, which may affect their perception of their own balance (Krzykus, 2019).\\nThe above results highlight the importance of understanding and supporting the needs of\\ndifferent age groups in the context of WLB. Organisations and HR decision-makers should take\\nthese differences into account when approaching policies and programmes that aim to support\\nwork-life balance.\\nThe  results  of  the  survey,  which  identified  flexible  working  hours  as  the  highest-rated\\ninstrument  in  the  WLB  concept,  reflect  the  growing  need  to  adapt  work  schedules  to  the\\nindividual needs and wishes of employees. Flexible working hours enable employees to better\\nadapt their working time to their private commitments and preferences, which can contribute to\\ntheir satisfaction and commitment in the workplace. In addition, highly rated instruments such\\nas private medical care or a company car also used for personal use emphasise the importance\\nof employer support for aspects of life that go beyond the professional sphere (Krzykus, 2019).\\nThe  results  indicate  that  companies  are  increasingly  recognising  and  responding  to\\nemployees’ individual needs, offering solutions that support a harmonious work-life balance.\\nThis  holistic  and  flexible  model  of  approaching  WLB  can  benefit  both  employees  and\\norganisations,  contributing  to  increased  productivity,  employee  retention  and  building\\na positive employer image.\\n\\n## [PDF page 157]\\n\\nThe role of work-life-balance…  157\\n\\nBecause of its ideological background, work-life balance (WLB) is seen as a value worthy\\nof  achievement.  It  is  also  a  perceptual  tool  that  shapes  the  way  individuals  interpret  the\\nsurrounding  reality,  emphasising  selected  elements  of  it.  The  concept  of  WLB  inspires\\nindividuals to maintain the belief that harmony can be achieved in life, and its ideological nature\\nmanifests itself in a dualistic conception of everyday life, understood as two separate domains\\n(Ross i Vasantha, 2014).\\nThe central idea of the WLB concept presented is to understand the ideological as well as\\nthe institutional, i.e. political, influence on the perception of work-life balance. It is these two\\nspheres  -  work  life  and  private  life  -  that  are  the  key  areas  that  shape  the  daily  choices  of\\nindividuals and the relationships between them. With the concept of WLB, a clear division is\\nmade into two distinct spheres: work and private life. This classification not only makes it easier\\nto  analyse  and  understand  individuals’  daily  activities,  but  also  enables  an  in-depth\\nunderstanding of how the two spheres interact. This division helps individuals identify areas in\\nwhich they can strive to achieve harmony and balance (Skrok et al., 2023).\\nThe introduction of the WLB concept is an important step in understanding the dynamics\\nof work-life relationships. It provides a better understanding of how actions taken in one sphere\\nof life can affect the other and what strategies can be adopted to make these relationships more\\nharmonious. This concept provides a foundation for further research into work-life balance and\\nfor the development of organisational strategies and policies to support individuals in achieving\\nthis balance (Mroczkowska, Kubacka, 2020).\\nIn  conclusion,  although  most  employees  rate  their  work-life  balance  as  average  or\\nsatisfactory,  there  is  a  need  to  better  understand  the  individual  needs  and  expectations  of\\nemployees in order to fully address the challenges of work-life harmony. Introduction\\n\\nModern organizations increasingly decide to outsource as a tool enabling cost optimization,\\naccess to specialist knowledge and increased operational flexibility. Along with the dynamic\\ndevelopment  of  this  cooperation  model,  the  importance  of  issues  related  to  data  security  is\\ngrowing, which is becoming one of the key challenges in the process of outsourcing functions\\nto external entities (Uhl-Bien, Arena, 2017). The problem of data protection in outsourcing is\\nbecoming particularly important in the face of the growing number of cyber threats, tightening\\nlegal  regulations  and  the  growth  of  expectations  of  customers  and  business  partners.\\nData is a strategic resource of an organization, and its loss, theft or unauthorized access can\\nlead to serious financial, legal and image consequences (Yin et al., 2020).\\nTaking up the topic of data security determinants in outsourcing processes results from the\\nneed to deepen knowledge in an area that is crucial for maintaining the integrity and stability\\nof  modern  enterprises.  The  importance  of  this  issue  is  particularly  visible  in  the  context  of\\nglobalization  and  digitalization  of  the  economy,  where  data  is  often  processed  and  stored\\noutside national borders, which additionally complicates their protection. This article attempts\\nto analyze the factors influencing the effectiveness of data security activities in outsourcing,\\nfocusing on technological, organizational and educational aspects.\\nThe article consists of several parts, which in a  way lead to a full understanding of the\\ndiscussed  problem.  The  introduction  presents  the  justification  of  the  undertaken  topic  and\\ndiscusses its importance in the context of contemporary business challenges. Then, a literature\\nreview and the most important theoretical concepts related to data security in outsourcing are\\npresented. The next part describes the research methodology, including the use of multivariate\\ncorrespondence analysis (MCA) and the characteristics of the studied sample. The results of\\nthe study are presented in the form of a detailed analysis, which identifies the most important\\ndeterminants  of  data  security.  The  final  part  discusses  the  conclusions  from  the  conducted\\nresearch, presents practical recommendations for companies and indicates future directions of\\nresearch in this area.\\nThe  aim  of  the  article  is  to  identify  and  analyze  factors  that  increase  data  security  in\\noutsourcing processes and to indicate practical solutions that can be used by organizations to\\nminimize risk. The added value of the work is to combine a theoretical perspective with the\\nresults  of  empirical  research,  which  allows  not  only  to  understand  the  complexity  of  the\\ndiscussed problem, but also to develop practical tips for enterprises. The article contributes to\\nthe  development  of  knowledge  on  data  security  management  in  the  context  of  outsourcing,\\nwhile  emphasizing  the  importance  of  a  multi-faceted  approach  to  information  protection  in\\na dynamic and global business environment.\\n\\n## [PDF page 161]\\n\\nDeterminants of data security…  161\\n\\n1.1.  The essence of an outsourcing venture\\n\\nThe essence of an outsourcing project is that an organization outsources specific processes,\\nfunctions, or activities to external service providers, which allows it to focus on key areas of\\nactivity  and  manage  resources  more  effectively  (Pearson,  Benameur,  2010).  Outsourcing  is\\na  practice  that  has  gained  popularity  in  many  sectors,  including  information  technology,\\nlogistics,  finance,  and  administration  (Zhang,  Liu,  2010)  .  The  decision  to  implement\\noutsourcing usually results from the need to optimize costs, improve the quality of services,\\naccess to specialist knowledge, or flexibility in adapting to changing market conditions (Zhen,\\nXie, Dong, 2021). The fundamental assumption of outsourcing is to use the experience and\\ninfrastructure of an  external provider, which allows the ordering party to avoid the need to\\ninvest  in  resources  that  could  be  expensive  and  time-consuming  to  build  and  maintain.\\nOutsourcing  service  providers  typically  offer  specialized  solutions  based  on  industry  best\\npractices that increase operational efficiency and process quality (Wang, Chow, Wang, Ren,\\nLou, 2011).\\nHowever, an outsourcing undertaking involves not only benefits but also challenges that\\nrequire appropriate management (Cullen, Seddon, Willcocks, 2005). A key element is building\\na  partnership  relationship  between  the  outsourcing  company  and  the  service  provider.\\nThis cooperation should be based on trust, transparency and clearly defined rules (Ateniese et\\nal.,  2007).  In  particular,  outsourcing  agreements  must  contain  precise  provisions  regarding\\nquality  standards,  deadlines,  responsibilities  of  the  parties  and  monitoring  and  reporting\\nmechanisms (Chow et al., 2009). The lack of clear rules can lead to misunderstandings and\\npotential financial losses (Subashini, Kavitha, 2011).\\nAn  important  aspect  of  an  outsourcing  project  is  managing  the  risk  that  results  from\\ntransferring part of the company’s activities to external entities. This applies in particular to data\\nprotection, process integrity and compliance with legal regulations (Quelin, Duhamel, 2003).\\nOutsourcing companies must pay special attention to the selection of suppliers, assessing their\\ncredibility (Nassimbeni,  Sartor, Dus, 2012),  competences  and ability to  ensure security  and\\ncompliance with industry standards. Outsourcing can also affect the organizational culture and\\nemployee  engagement  (Ravichandran,  2016).  Transferring  part  of  the  functions  to  external\\nsuppliers can be perceived by the staff as a threat to their professional position, which requires\\nappropriate change management in the organization. It is important for the company to clearly\\ncommunicate the goals and benefits of outsourcing and to engage employees in the adaptation\\nprocesses (Porter, Heppelmann, 2014).\\nOutsourcing can give organizations greater operational flexibility, especially in the context\\nof  changing  market  conditions  (Bertino,  2009;  Chakrabarty,  2006).  Handing  over  tasks  to\\nexternal  specialists  allows  for  faster  adaptation  to  new  requirements,  introduction  of\\ninnovations and scaling of operations in response to growth or decline in demand. However,\\nfor an outsourcing undertaking to be effective, a strategic approach is necessary, which takes\\n\\n## [PDF page 162]\\n\\n162  D. Kocot, B. Blaszczak\\n\\ninto account both potential benefits and risks. Proper management of outsourcing can bring\\nlong-term  benefits  in  the  form  of  increased  efficiency,  reduced  costs  and  improved\\ncompetitiveness in the market.\\n\\n1.2.  The importance of data security for the company commissioning the outsourcing\\nproject\\n\\nIn the context of an outsourcing undertaking, the security of the outsourcing company’s\\ndata plays an extremely important role (Ren, Wang, Wang, 2012). Modern organizations base\\ntheir  operations  on  data,  which  is  the  basis  for  making  decisions,  building  strategies  and\\nmaintaining a competitive advantage. Transferring part of the processes to an external service\\nprovider means that key company information, such as customer data, financial data or data\\nrelated to operational processes, must be properly protected to prevent their loss, unauthorized\\naccess or breach. Data security in such a context is particularly important due to the complexity\\nof  the  relationship  between  the  company  and  the  service  provider  (Li,  Li,  Chen,  Lee,  Lou,\\n2014). When outsourcing processes, the organization relies to a large extent on the capabilities\\nand  infrastructure  of  the  provider,  which  is  why  it  is  crucial  for  the  outsourcing  partner  to\\ncomply with the highest standards of data protection. The lack of appropriate security measures\\ncan  lead  to  serious  consequences,  such  as  loss  of  customer  trust,  high  financial  penalties\\nresulting  from  non-compliance  with  regulations,  and  even  permanent  damage  to  the\\norganization’s reputation (Turban et al., 2018).\\nOne  of  the  most  important  aspects  of  data  security  in  outsourcing  is  ensuring  its\\nconfidentiality.  Organizations  often  work  with  sensitive  information,  which  may  include\\npersonal  data  of  customers,  trade  secrets  or  details  of  research  and  development  projects\\n(Galvin,  2019).  The  confidentiality  of  this  information  must  be  secured  both  through\\nappropriate technological mechanisms, such as encryption, and clear provisions in outsourcing\\nagreements. It is important that suppliers are obliged to comply with principles consistent with\\ninternational standards, such as GDPR or ISO 27001.\\nData  integrity  is  another  key  aspect  that  is  particularly  important  in  the  context  of\\noutsourcing. This means that data must be stored and processed in a way that guarantees its\\naccuracy  and  completeness.  Any  errors  or  manipulations  can  lead  to  incorrect  business\\ndecisions and, consequently, to financial or operational losses. In practice, this means the need\\nto  use  advanced  monitoring  systems  that  allow  for  the  rapid  detection  and  elimination  of\\npotential breaches (Kamara, Lauter, 2010; Kern, Willcocks, Van Heck, 2013; Murphy, 2024).\\nData availability protection is another pillar of security in outsourcing. Companies must be sure\\nthat their data will be available whenever they  are needed, regardless of the circumstances.\\nThis is especially true in crisis situations, such as system failures, cyberattacks or logistical\\nproblems on the supplier’s side. Therefore, it is important that outsourcing agreements include\\nbusiness  continuity  mechanisms  such  as  backups,  contingency  plans,  and  service  level\\nagreements (SLAs) (Raišienė, Bilan, Smalskys, Gečienė, 2019).\\n\\n## [PDF page 163]\\n\\nDeterminants of data security…  163\\n\\nData security in outsourcing is not limited to technical aspects (Wang, He, Tang, 2015).\\nAn appropriate organizational culture that promotes awareness of threats and responsibility for\\nprotecting information is also crucial. Outsourcing companies must ensure that both their own\\nstaff and the supplier’s staff are properly trained in good security practices (Qureshi, 2016).\\nFinally, the importance of data security in outsourcing also stems from growing regulatory\\nrequirements and market expectations. Customers  and business partners increasingly expect\\norganizations to be able to demonstrate a high level of information protection, which poses\\nadditional challenges for companies in terms of monitoring and reporting security activities.\\nTherefore, proper data security management is becoming not only an operational requirement\\nbut  also  a  strategic  success  factor  in  long-term  outsourcing  cooperation  (Arshad,  Ahmad,\\nMaynard, 2022).\\n\\n1.3.  Factors  that  increase  the  security  of  the  outsourcing  company’s  data  during  the\\noutsourcing process\\n\\nIncreasing the security of the outsourcing company’s data during the outsourcing process\\nrequires a multi-faceted approach that takes into account both technological, organizational and\\neducational aspects. One of the key factors is the development and implementation of a coherent\\ndata security policy. Such a document should clearly define the principles of data management,\\nprocedures  for  handling  incidents  and  requirements  for  outsourcing  service  providers\\n(Annarelli,  Colabianchi,  Nonino,  Palombi,  2021).  The  security  policy  should  be  dynamic,\\nwhich means it should be regularly updated in response to changing threats and technological\\ndevelopments. The use of data encryption is one of the most important technical measures in\\ndata  protection.  Encryption  allows  you  to  protect  information  from  unauthorized  access,\\nboth  during  data  transfer  and  storage.  In  the  context  of  outsourcing,  where  data  is  often\\ntransferred  between  different  locations  and  stored  in  the  cloud,  the  use  of  advanced\\ncryptographic  methods  becomes  particularly  important.  The  implementation  of  encryption\\nshould cover both data in motion and data at rest, which minimizes the risk of their interception\\nor theft.\\nAnother factor that increases data security is the regular conduct of security audits (Wang,\\nWang, Ren, Cao, Lou, 2012). These audits allow for the assessment of the effectiveness of\\nimplemented  data  protection  measures  and  the  identification  of  potential  gaps  and  threats.\\nThey  should  be  conducted  both  internally,  by  the  organization’s  security  department,\\nand externally, by independent auditing entities. The results of audits should be the basis for\\ntaking  corrective  and  improvement  actions,  which  allows  for  continuous  improvement  of\\nsecurity standards (Infinit-O Global, 2022).\\nBuilding awareness among employees is an equally important element of data protection.\\nIn the context of outsourcing, where interaction between the outsourcing company’s staff and\\nthe service provider is inevitable, employee education plays a key role in minimizing the risk\\nof human errors. Training should cover topics such as recognizing social engineering attacks,\\n\\n## [PDF page 164]\\n\\n164  D. Kocot, B. Blaszczak\\n\\nadhering  to  security  policies,  and  responsibility  for  data  protection.  Aware  and  trained\\nemployees  are  the  first  line  of  defense  against  threats  related  to  improper  data  processing\\n(Pandita, Singhal, 2017).\\nIn  addition  to  the  above  activities,  it  is  also  important  to  implement  mechanisms  for\\nmonitoring and reporting data-related activities. Constant supervision over access to data and\\nanalysis of system logs allow for quick detection of unauthorized activities and appropriate\\nresponse. As part of outsourcing, it is important for these mechanisms to also be used by service\\nproviders, which should be included in agreements regulating cooperation (Ghosh, Scott, 2008;\\nGupta, Puranam, Srikanth, 2006). An additional factor that increases data security is the use of\\na  multi-layered  protection  strategy.  This  means  combining  various  technologies  and\\nprocedures,  such  as  encryption,  multi-factor  authentication,  access  control,  or  backup.\\nAn  integrated  approach  provides  greater  resistance  to  various  threats,  both  those  related  to\\ncyberattacks and system failures (Infinit-O Global, 2022).\\nIn  summary,  data  security  in  the  outsourcing  process  can  be  effectively  increased  by\\ncombining  appropriate  technologies,  procedures  and  educational  activities.  Clear  rules  of\\ncooperation with suppliers, appropriately selected technical tools and a conscious approach to\\nsecurity management at every stage of project implementation are of key importance. Only such\\na comprehensive approach allows for minimizing risk and ensuring data protection in a dynamic\\nenvironment of external cooperation.\\n\\n1.4.  Research Methodology\\n\\nThe aim of the conducted research was to determine the key determinants of data security\\nin the context of business process outsourcing and to understand their mutual relations in the\\nperception of people involved in such ventures. The research aimed to deepen knowledge about\\npractices that increase data security, such as developing a security policy, using encryption,\\nconducting audits and building awareness among employees. The research hypothesis assumed\\nthat individual activities related to data security have a different impact on the perception of\\ntheir importance and are to a different extent related to organizational and technical factors.\\nThe  research  asked  questions  about  which  activities  have  the  greatest  impact  on  the\\nperception of data security and what are the relationships between individual determinants in\\nterms of their effectiveness. Particular attention was paid to issues related to technology, audits\\nand  education,  as  well  as  their  mutual  relationships  and  differences  in  the  perceptions  of\\nrespondents.\\nThe research method used was a survey conducted in 2023 on a sample of 723 respondents.\\nThe survey allowed for collecting quantitative data on opinions on the importance of various\\npractices related to data security in outsourcing processes. Multivariate correspondence analysis\\n(MCA) was chosen to analyze the obtained data. The aim of using this method was to identify\\npatterns and relationships between the variables studied, which allowed for presenting their\\ncomplex structure in two dimensions. Thanks to the MCA analysis, it was possible to better\\n\\n## [PDF page 165]\\n\\nDeterminants of data security…  165\\n\\nunderstand the dynamics of the relationships between the determinants of data security, as well\\nas to indicate those activities that play a key role in data protection within outsourcing.\\n\\n1.5. Discussion\\n\\nThe conclusions from the conducted research indicate that the determinants of data security\\nin the context of outsourcing are diverse in terms of importance and perceived effectiveness.\\nThe development of a data security policy, which obtained high values in both dimensions of\\nthe MCA analysis, was identified as one of the most important activities. This results from the\\nfact  that  clearly  defined  rules  and  procedures  are  the  foundation  of  effective  data  security\\nmanagement.  It  also  provides  the  basis  for  other  activities,  such  as  audits  or  employee\\neducation, which can only be effectively implemented within the framework of a well-defined\\nsecurity management system.\\nData  encryption,  which  received  mixed  results  in  two  dimensions  of  the  analysis,  was\\nassessed  as  a  key  element  of  technical  data  protection,  although  its  perception  is  strongly\\ndependent on the specifics of the organization and the level of technological advancement of\\nthe respondents. Respondents who rated encryption highly most often indicated its ability to\\nprotect  data  from  unauthorized  access,  especially  in  the  context  of  external  cooperation.\\nIn turn, lower ratings may result from implementation difficulties, such as costs or the need for\\nspecialist  knowledge.  Security  audit  was  identified  as  a  practice  with  high  control  value.\\nThe results indicate that conducting regular audits increases trust in the security mechanisms\\nused, allowing for early detection of potential gaps and threats. Audits also play a preventive\\nrole, affecting the  responsibility of  external entities for compliance with  security standards.\\nNevertheless, some respondents indicated limitations of this practice, such as time consumption\\nand dependence on the quality of the procedures performed.\\nCreating  awareness  of  security  among  employees  was  assessed  as  an  important,\\nyet  complementary  element  of  the  security  strategy.  The  results  suggest  that  employee\\neducation  increases  the  effectiveness  of  other  activities,  such  as  security  policy  and  data\\nencryption, by reducing the risk of human errors. However, lower values in the first dimension\\nof the analysis may be due to the perception of educational activities as less directly related to\\ntechnological aspects of security, which does not reduce their importance in the overall strategy.\\n\\n## [PDF page 168]\\n\\n168  D.
