Introduction\\n\\nModern  organizations  operate  in  a  dynamically  changing  environment  that  requires\\nflexibility, innovation, and the ability to respond quickly to changing conditions. In this context,\\nagile organizations are becoming one of the key management models that allow for effective\\nfunctioning in a demanding market environment (Routledge, 2020; Sajdak, 2021). At the same\\ntime, the importance of employer branding as a tool for attracting and retaining talents, which\\nare a strategic resource of every organization, is growing. When these two perspectives are\\ncombined, there is a need for a thorough understanding of how an agile approach affects the\\nbuilding of the employer’s image and what determinants of employer branding are key in this\\norganizational model (Akkaya, 2021).\\nThe topic is particularly important in the face of changing employee expectations, for whom\\nthe  traditional  approach  to  work  and  management  is  no  longer  sufficient. Agile organization in theoretical approach – essence and determinants\\n\\nAgile organization in theoretical terms is a management concept that focuses on the ability\\nof an organization to quickly and effectively adapt to changing market, technological and social\\nconditions  (Chen,  Li,  2021;  Fiddler,  2017;  Nath,  Agrawal,  2020).  It  is  an  approach  that\\nemphasizes flexibility, innovation and the ability to quickly respond to challenges and needs of\\nthe environment (Alshehhi, Nobanee, Khare, 2018). In the literature, organizational agility is\\nsometimes defined as the ability to dynamically adjust processes, structures and strategies in\\norder  to  achieve  competitiveness  and  sustainable  development.  The  essence  of  an  agile\\norganization  is  its  ability  to  anticipate  and  use  changes  as  an  opportunity  for  development,\\nnot  a  threat  (Luo,  Ren,  Cao,  Hong,  2020).  Such  an  organization  is  characterized  by  flat\\nmanagement  structures  that  enable  rapid  information  flow  and  decision-making.  Employee\\nengagement  at  all  levels  is  also  crucial,  supporting  a  culture  of  openness,  collaboration,\\nand continuous improvement (Doz, Kosonen, 2008). Organizational agility assumes that a key\\nfactor for success is the ability to learn and adapt in the face of uncertainty and risk (García-\\nGranero, Piedra-Muñoz, Galdeano-Gómez, 2020).\\nThe determinants of an agile organization can be divided into several main areas. The first\\nof  them  are  structural  factors,  which  include  the  flexibility  of  the  organizational  structure,\\nsimplified procedures, and decentralization of the decision-making process. Agile organizations\\nabandon excessively complex hierarchies in favor of management models based on cooperation\\nbetween  teams  and  individuals  (Jones,  Adam,  2023).  Another  important  determinant  is  the\\norganizational culture, which promotes innovation, trust, and openness to change. Values such\\nas  responsibility,  transparency,  and  willingness  to  take  risks  play  a  key  role  in  creating\\nan environment conducive to agility (Gao, Zhang, Gong, Li, 2020).\\nTechnology and digitalization are other key determinants of an agile organization. Agility\\nrequires the skillful use of modern technologies to optimize processes, improve communication,\\nand quickly respond to changing customer needs. Organizations that effectively integrate digital\\ntools into their operations gain an advantage in a dynamic business environment. In the context\\nof  technology,  tools  supporting  team  collaboration,  knowledge  management,  and  process\\nautomation  are  also  important.  An  important  aspect  of  organizational  agility  is  also  human\\nfactors, which include employee competencies and attitudes (Sedej, Justinek, 2021). In agile\\norganizations,  skills  such  as  creativity,  the  ability  to  work  in  teams,  quick  learning,\\nand openness to change are particularly valued. Leaders in agile organizations act as mentors\\nand catalysts for change, inspiring employees to take the initiative and engage in innovation\\nprocesses (Rosário, Raimundo, 2021).\\n\\n## [PDF page 230]\\n\\n230  M. Employer Branding Concept\\n\\nThe concept of employer branding refers to building and managing the employer’s image,\\nwhich is perceived by both current and potential employees. It is a strategic approach that aims\\nto  create  an  organization  as  an  attractive  place  of  work,  where  employees  can  fulfill  their\\nprofessional  ambitions,  develop  skills  and  achieve  professional  satisfaction  (Martin,  2008).\\nThe  contemporary  approach  to  employer  branding  assumes  that  it  is  a  multidimensional\\nprocess,  combining  marketing,  management  and  social  aspects,  which  together  create\\na coherent image of the employer on the market (Szkudlarek, 2022).\\nOne of the key assumptions of employer branding is to adapt the organization’s strategy to\\nthe expectations of employees and market trends. The employer’s image is not based solely on\\npromotional activities, but on the actual value offered to employees, called Employee Value\\nProposition  (EVP)  (Rzewuska,  Majewska,  Berłowski,  Wo{niak,  Marciniak,  2013).\\nEVP  includes  financial  benefits,  professional  development,  organizational  culture,\\nand the possibility of balancing professional and private life. A properly defined EVP allows\\nthe organization to attract talents that are consistent with its mission and values, which affects\\nthe quality of recruitment and the level of employee engagement (Zając-Pałdyna, 2020).\\nThe concept of employer branding includes two main dimensions: external and internal.\\nIn the external dimension, activities focus on building a positive image of the organization on\\nthe labor market through recruitment campaigns, presence in social media and participation in\\nindustry  events.  External  employer  branding  focuses  on  attracting  new  talents  and  building\\nawareness of the employer’s brand among potential candidates (Lane, 2016). In the internal\\ndimension,  this  concept  refers  to  creating  a  work  environment  that  supports  employee\\ndevelopment,  builds  their  commitment  and  loyalty  to  the  organization.  Internal  activities\\ninclude  development  programs,  motivational  systems,  integration  initiatives  and  transparent\\ncommunication (Matuszewska-Kubicz, 2020).\\n\\n## [PDF page 231]\\n\\nEmployer branding determinants…  231\\n\\nThe literature emphasizes the growing importance of employer branding in the context of\\nchanging employee expectations and the labor market (Gillis, 2006). Employees increasingly\\nexpect  not  only  employment  stability,  but  also  development  opportunities,  work  flexibility,\\nand alignment of the organization’s values with their own beliefs (Mayo, 2001; Burke, 2007).\\nThis phenomenon leads to a change in the approach of employers, who must constantly adapt\\ntheir strategies to these expectations in order to attract and retain the most talented employees\\n(Jenner, Taylor, 2008).\\nEmployer branding is also important in building an organization’s competitive advantage.\\nCompanies perceived as attractive employers are more likely to attract the best candidates and\\nretain  key  employees,  which  affects  their  efficiency  and  innovation  (Kozłowski,  2016).\\nResearch shows that a strong employer brand reduces recruitment costs, increases retention and\\nimproves the organization’s financial results.  In this context, employer branding is not only\\nan element of HR strategy, but also an important component of business strategy (|ółkiewicz,\\nOlszewski, Czarnecki, 2021).\\nThe importance of technology in employer branding is constantly growing, especially in the\\ndigital era. Tools such as social media, recruitment platforms and talent management systems\\nallow  organizations  to  reach  a  wide  audience  and  personalize  communication  (Dąbrowska,\\n2014).  Data  analysis  allows  companies  to  better  understand  the  expectations  of  potential\\ncandidates and adapt their activities to their needs. The modern approach to employer branding\\nalso includes the aspect of social responsibility and sustainable development. Employers who\\nactively  engage  in  pro-social  and  ecological  activities  are  perceived  as  more  attractive  by\\nyounger  generations  of  employees  (Grzybowska,  2022).  Transparency  and  authenticity  in\\nemployer branding activities are becoming key in building trust among both current and future\\nemployees (Rosethorn, Mensink, 2008).\\nIn summary, the employer branding concept is a multidimensional approach that combines\\nmanagement, marketing and communication activities to build a strong and attractive employer\\nbrand. It is a dynamic process that requires continuous monitoring of the labor market, analysis\\nof employee needs and adjustment of strategies  to changing conditions. Thanks to properly\\nplanned and implemented employer branding activities, organizations can not only attract and\\nretain talent, but also build their competitive position on the market.\\n\\n2.3.  Employer Branding in an Agile Organization\\n\\nEmployer  branding  in  an  agile  organization  is  a  key  element  in  building  its  image  as\\nan  attractive  employer,  especially  in  a  dynamically  changing  market  environment.\\nIn agile organizations, which are characterized by flexibility, speed of action and the ability to\\nadapt,  employer  branding  must  take  into  account  the  specificity  of  this  type  of  work\\nenvironment. Kaplan  and  Haenlein  as  a  group  of  applications  based  technologically  and\\nideologically on Web 2.0 and allowing the creation and exchange of user-generated content.\\nOther researchers developed the term  and related elements (Larimo  et al., 2021; Oprea,\\n2023; Rhee et al., 2021), and a summary of the definition was provided by T. Even  today,  due  to  the  multitude  of\\nscientific  possibilities,  it  is  still  a  topic  that  is  being  addressed,  mainly  in  connection  with\\nspecific entities such as cultural institutions, museums, local government units and many other\\nforms of activities (Nawrocka, Zaprucka, 2022; Jeż, 2020; Jankowska, 2024).\\nPeople  around  the  world  are  largely  engaged  and  attached  to  web  2.0  technologies  and\\nsocial media platforms. Similarly, related issues of social\\nmedia marketing have also become the focus of scholars and researchers to expand the current\\nknowledge of such phenomena in the field of marketing (Alalwan et al., 2017).\\n\\n## [PDF page 245]\\n\\nInformation management through social networks…  245\\n\\nSocial  media  such  as  blog,  Facebook,  Twitter,  Instagram,  WhatsApp,  etc.,  have  gained\\npopularity worldwide (Razak, Latip, 2016; Vinerean et al., 2013; Maryam 2015).\\nThere is a very high correlation between social media and marketing. Social media also enables\\ncommunication between companies and customers around the world, at any time (Rapp, 2013;\\nBrogi, 2013; Sarangan, Ragel 2014).\\nSocial media marketing can be seen as the business practice of marketing brands, goods,\\nservices, information and opinions through a social media platform. In today’s business world,\\nmarketing  activities  through  social  media  applications  enable  companies  and  customers  to\\ndiscuss and share information with each other. As an interactive platform, social media enables\\ncompanies to engage existing customers and attract new ones, generate more sales, build brand\\nawareness  and  brand  image  (Kietzmann  et  al.,  2011;  Chanthinok,  2015;  Karimi,  Naghibi,\\n2015).\\n\\n2.  Social media in marketing od sport\\n\\nAs already mentioned, social media marketing has been defined as 8the use of social media\\ntechnologies, channels and software to create, communicate, deliver and exchange offers that\\nhave value to an organisation\'s stakeholders9 (Cartwright, 2021; Tuten, Solomon, 2014).\\nThe proliferation of social networks means that their functionality is expanding all the time.\\nSocial media allows you to showcase yourself, your company or the products you offer. Profiles\\ncan  contain  all  sorts  of  information  on  the  subject,  as  well  as  enabling  people  to  network,\\nexchange information and maintain relationships with site members. In this way, they become a tool for creating a company’s image. Each service,\\nalthough providing similar functions, is based on the different nature of the links and contacts\\nthat exist between its users.\\nThe use of social media and its use in business management also depends on generational\\ndifferences (Karasek, Hysa, 2020). Social media engagement can be understood in many ways.\\nEach  social  media  can  also  be  assessed  separately.  Engagement  is  then  examined  as  the\\nintensity of interactions and their implications, vis-à-vis the offers and activities of a brand,\\nproduct  or  company,  regardless  of  whether  the  initiator  is  an  individual  or  a  company.\\nAlongside  traditional  marketing  channels,  social  networks  are  being  integrated  into  the\\n\\n## [PDF page 246]\\n\\n246  S. Kowalski\\n\\nmarketing mix. Social media have changed the dynamics of interaction between companies and\\nconsumers, who favour this relationship.\\nIn the context of media use, a very important aspect is defining who the audience of media\\ncontent is (Jacobson et al., 2020). This article uses the Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA test,\\nwhich  is  a  non-parametric  alternative  to  the  one-way  analysis  of  variance.  Using  this  test,\\nwe compare the distributions of several variables (Cole, 1993; Swallow, 1984; Kruskal, Wish,\\n1978).\\nThe research subjects in this case are respondents who are social media users of sports clubs,\\nand the article is part of a larger research project. Looking more broadly, sports companies are\\nspecific in that they hardly compete with each other. The primary method of communication\\nmanagement  here  is  benchmarking,  a  method  that  involves  comparing  the  processes  and\\n\\n## [PDF page 247]\\n\\nInformation management through social networks…  247\\n\\npractices of one’s own entity with those of companies considered to be the best in the field under\\nanalysis. Another peculiarity of sports organisations is the high level of social media activity.\\nThis is due to the nature of the audience of the content (the fan), for whom sport is associated\\nwith personal emotions. In most other businesses, this need is not present.\\nThe  result  of  these  conditions  is  a  situation  in  which,  theoretically,  marketing\\ncommunications  in  sports  clubs  should  be  almost  identical,  undifferentiated,  homogeneous.\\nSimilarly homogeneous, therefore, should be the assessments of the types of social media or\\nthe factors influencing the attractiveness of these media. Research methods\\n\\nThe research is part of a larger research project dedicated to the issues of sports companies’\\ncommunication on the Internet. The aim of this analysis is to verify the degree of similarity in\\nthe use of online communication tools by speedway sports clubs in Poland. The basis for the\\nconsideration is the evaluations of social media users regarding both the types of media and the\\nfactors influencing the attractiveness of individual profiles. The main survey was conducted on\\n345 people, from which only those with accounts on individual social media sites were selected.\\nThe survey ran from 21 to 31 October 2024, until a number of more than 300 respondents was\\nobtained  to  ensure  the  desired  representativeness  of  the  study.  Based  on  these  figures,\\nit  was  hypothesised  that  the  different  types  and  factors  influencing  the  perception  of  their\\nattractiveness are homogeneous.\\nTo verify this hypothesis, the numerical data were statistically analysed using the Kruskal-\\nWallis ANOVA test.  Initially, the use of  a one-way analysis of variance ANOVA test  was\\nconsidered  to  determine  whether  there  were  statistically  significant  differences  between  the\\npredictor  groups  being  compared  and  the  dependent  variable.  After  a  preliminary  analysis,\\nit was found that the factors did not have a normal distribution. A Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA test,\\nbased on ranks, was therefore applied in this case. Discussion\\n\\nThe conducted research has shown that, thanks to the modified Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA\\nmethod, it can be determined that there are differences in assessments between the types of\\nindividual  social  media  and  the  factors  influencing  the  perception  of  their  attractiveness.\\nThe main aim of the article is to verify the similarity of the use of communication tools on the\\nInternet by speedway sports clubs in Poland. An additional goal is to find differences in the\\nperception of the variety of factors influencing the attractiveness and quality of social media\\nsites.  Therefore,  it  was  verified  whether  the  differentiation  of  the  studied  groups  was\\nstatistically justified. These differences are important because they require a different approach\\nto the management of these media. In practice, this means that companies (sports clubs in this\\n\\n## [PDF page 254]\\n\\n254  S. It highlights the potential risks\\nthese lakes pose to public health, especially in terms of waterborne diseases, due to fluctuations\\nin water quality influenced by seasonal variations, human activities, and environmental factors.\\nBy evaluating the microbiological contamination levels of lakes that are not part of the formal\\nmonitoring system, this research seeks to fill a gap in understanding the risks posed by these\\nbodies of water.\\nDesign/methodology/approach:  The  research  employs  a  combination  of  water  sample\\ncollection and microbiological analysis to determine the contamination levels of Enterococcus\\nspp. and E. coli in various water samples taken from a non-regulated lake (Wyspowo Lake).\\nThe study compares contamination levels in nearshore and lake center areas during different\\nmonths to assess variability in water quality. Future research could involve more frequent sampling and explore\\nthe effects of local human activities on water quality.\\nPractical implications: Improved monitoring systems for non-regulated lakes are essential for\\nprotecting public health. It  adds  value  to  this  field  by  addressing  the\\nmicrobiological  safety  of  lakes  not  covered  by  official  regulatory  systems  and  proposing\\npractical solutions for improving water quality monitoring and risk management. The article is\\nintended  for  local  authorities,  environmental  health  experts,  and  public  health,  water\\nmanagement, and environmental policy researchers\\nKeywords: quality management, risk assessment, microbiological quality, public health, non-\\nregulated lakes.\\nCategory of the paper: research paper.\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nSurface  water  contamination  is  a  significant  global  challenge,  driven  by  both  natural\\nprocesses  and  human  activities  (Vadde  et  al.,  2018).  Key  contributors  to  this  issue  include\\nindustrial development, agricultural practices, industrial waste from food production, surface\\nrunoff, natural events, and insufficient water supply and wastewater treatment infrastructure.\\nThe release of untreated waste into aquatic ecosystems exacerbates water pollution, leading to\\nwidespread contamination of water bodies (Lin et al., 2022; Yesilay et al., 2023). The health\\nconsequences of water pollution are complex and multifaceted. Exposure to contaminated water\\ncan  lead  to  both  short-term  and  long-term  health  issues,  depending  on  the  nature  of  the\\ncontaminants and the level and duration of exposure (Krishan et al., 2023).\\n\\n1.1. Health risks and the need for effective management of recreational waters\\n\\nDuring the swimming season, the primary risk of contracting bacterial, protozoal, and viral\\ngastroenteritis  is  typically  linked  to  contact  with  recreational  water,  rather  than  food\\nconsumption  or  drinking  water.  Illnesses  associated  with  recreational  water  exposure  are\\nfrequent,  with  activities  such  as  swimming,  paddling,  boating,  and  fishing  contributing\\nsignificantly to annual cases of gastrointestinal, respiratory, and skin, ear, and eye infections\\n(Sanborn, Takaro, 2013; Staley et al., 2013; Russo et al., 2020). Swimmers are estimated to\\ningest between 10 and 150 mL of water per hour, with children under the age of 10 being\\nparticularly  vulnerable  due  to  prolonged  exposure  in  shallow,  contaminated  areas,  frequent\\nimmersion of the head, and hand-to-mouth contact (Sanborn, Takaro, 2013). The identification\\nof contamination sources and the development of effective management strategies are essential\\nfor  minimizing  public  health  risks  (Lin  et  al.,  2022).  Bathing  waters  host  numerous\\nmicroorganisms,  including  viruses,  bacteria,  fungi,  algae,  protozoa,  and  their  metabolic\\nproducts. The abundance and species composition of these microorganisms, as well as their\\nactivity, are largely influenced by climatic and trophic conditions (Kacprzak, 2019). Swimming\\nin  contaminated  beach  waters  significantly  increases  the  risk  of  skin  infections  and  other\\nillnesses. Pathogenic microorganisms commonly found in polluted water are often the cause of\\n\\n## [PDF page 261]\\n\\nMicrobiological quality and risk assessment…  261\\n\\nskin conditions in swimmers. Individuals exposed to bacterial levels above safety thresholds\\nface a significantly higher risk of developing skin diseases. Research indicates that swimmers\\nreport  skin  infections  3.5  times  more  frequently  than  non-swimmers  (Yau  et  al.,  2009;  Lin\\net  al.,  2022).  Given  the  intersection  of  public  health,  environmental  management,  and  risk\\nmanagement, addressing water quality issues at recreational sites is critical for protecting user\\nhealth.  Moreover,  improving  quality  management  practices  in  water  safety  is  necessary  to\\nreduce these risks and safeguard public well-being.\\n\\n1.2. International guidelines on water quality and risk management\\n\\nInternational guidelines, including those from the World Health Organization (WHO) and\\nthe European Union, set water quality standards for bathing sites to protect user health through\\nregular monitoring and risk assessment. WHO recommends systematic microbiological testing,\\nwith  fecal  coliforms  used  as  indicators  of  fecal  contamination  and  overall  water  quality\\n(Doe  et  al.,  2016).  The  EU’s  Bathing  Water  Directive  (Directive  2006/7/EC)  emphasizes\\nbathing site profiling and preventive measures to reduce health risks. These guidelines provide\\na regulatory framework that aids in reducing public health risks through proper water quality\\nmanagement.  Together,  these  standards  offer  a  structured  approach  to  water  quality\\nmanagement and risk assessment, improving the overall health protection of recreational water\\nusers.\\n\\n1.3. National water quality management and regulatory framework\\n\\nThe Water Law establishes a water quality management system for bathing areas aimed at\\nenhancing  the  health  safety  of  bathers  and  predicting  potential  hazards.  The  implementing\\nregulations set standards for water quality monitoring, bathing area profiling, registration and\\nsignage of these areas, and outline the authority of the State Sanitary Inspectorate (Kacprzak,\\n2019;  Zwierzyna,  2022).  Waters  in  bathing  areas  are  classified  by  the  State  Sanitary\\nInspectorate  based  on  two  microbiological  parameters:  Escherichia  coli  and  intestinal\\nenterococci, in accordance with the provisions of the Minister of Health’s Regulation (2019).\\n\\n1.4. Factors hydrological and ecological profile of the Wejherowo district\\n\\nWejherowo district, located in northern Kashubia, is a picturesque area positioned along\\na major transportation corridor connecting Gdańsk and Szczecin. Situated just a few kilometers\\nin a straight line from the Baltic Sea, over half of the commune’s area is part of the Tricity\\nLandscape Park. The entire region falls within the catchment area of rivers flowing into the\\nBaltic,  with  a  well-defined  hydrological  network.  Primary  watershed  boundaries  divide\\nWejherowo into four river basins: Reda, Pia\\\\nica, Zagórska Struga, and Gizdepka. Beyond its\\nextensive river network, Wejherowo features several scenic lakes, mainly concentrated on the\\nplateau of the Kashubian Lake District near the terminal moraine. These are mostly kettle lakes,\\n\\n## [PDF page 262]\\n\\n262  A. KukuBowicz, W. Jaroniec\\n\\nlacking surface outflow, with prominent examples including Wyspowo, Bieszkowice, Zawiat,\\nBorowo,  PaBsznik,  and  Wygoda.  Additionally,  the  commune  encompasses  ecologically\\nvaluable areas protected under various conservation designations, such as the ecological sites\\n<Szuwary Jeziora Wyspowskiego= and <Wyspowska Aąka=, underscoring the importance of\\nadhering to protective measures for these natural habitats. (Mieloch-Stojczyk, 2021).\\n\\n1.5. Research problem and aim of the study\\n\\nAt public bathing sites, the health of individuals using water attractions should be protected\\nthrough systematic water sampling and the temporary closure of sites that exceed microbial\\nlevels specified by regulations. The supervision of bathing sites and areas occasionally used for\\nswimming, particularly regarding water quality management, falls under the responsibility of\\nlocal  sanitary  inspectors  (Zwierzyna,  2022).  However,  not  all  bathing  areas  are  subject  to\\nregular  microbiological  inspections.  These  inspections  are  mandatory  only  at  officially\\nregistered sites designated as bathing areas by local authorities, whereas sites used occasionally\\nfor swimming, lacking official status, are not systematically monitored. This lack of oversight\\nraises  a  critical  health  risk  management  issue:  Are  users  of  unmonitored  recreational  lakes\\nexposed  to  higher  risks  of  waterborne  illnesses?  The  aim  of  this  study  was  to  evaluate  the\\nmicrobiological safety of a recreational lake that lacks official sanitary controls, addressing the\\npublic health risks posed to users and highlighting the need for improved risk management\\npractices in water quality supervision.\\n\\n2.  Material and Method\\n\\n2.1. Study area\\n\\nThe Wyspowo Lake, located in northern Poland at the edge of the Kashubian Lake District,\\nis a forest-enclosed lake bordered by a large meadow, southeast of Wejherowo near the village\\nof  Zbychowo  in  the  Wejherowo  commune,  Pomeranian  Voivodeship,  within  the  Tricity\\nLandscape Park (coordinates: 54°332333N 18°182123E). Encompassing an area of 23.0 hectares\\nand bordered by a shoreline measuring 1,910 meters, Wyspowo Lake reaches a maximum depth\\nof nearly 5 meters, with an average depth of 2.6 meters. The Cedron River flows through the\\nlake. Primarily serving as a recreational and tourist site for residents of the nearby Small Tricity\\nregion (Wejherowo, Reda, Rumia), Wyspowo Lake is especially popular among members of\\nthe Rumia Chapter No. 50 of the Polish Angling Association. The area around the lake features\\nseasonal cottages and the village of Wyspowo, part of the Zbychowo district. Nearby, a large\\nforest parking area accommodates numerous camper trailers during the summer season (Jezioro\\nWyspowo, 2013).\\n\\n## [PDF page 263]\\n\\nMicrobiological quality and risk assessment…  263\\n\\n2.2. Research materials and Microbiological analyses\\n\\nThe study material comprised water samples collected from Wyspowo Lake, specifically\\nfrom nearshore water layers (n = 32) and the lake center (n = 32). Samples were collected in\\nsterile containers from a depth of approximately 0.5 m below the water surface. Immediately\\nafter collection, the samples were stored in an insulated cooler at 4±1°C and transported to the\\nlaboratory within 2 hours for analysis. Each analysis was performed in four replicates to ensure\\naccuracy  and  reliability  of  the  results.  The  traditional  plate  count  method  was  used  for\\nmicrobiological assays.  Sampling procedures followed the Water  Law Act of 20 July 2017\\n(Journal of Laws of 2021, item 624, as amended), which defines the bathing season from 1 June\\nto 30 September. In accordance with the Regulation of the Minister of Health of 17 January\\n2019 on water quality supervision in bathing and occasionally used bathing sites (Journal of\\nLaws  of  2019,  item  255),  each  water  sample  was  analyzed  for  Escherichia  coli  and\\nEnterococcus spp. counts.\\nMicrobiological tests were carried out to determine the number of:\\n\uf0b7  Escherichia coli on Coli ID medium from bioMerieux (incubation at 37°C for 48 h),\\n\uf0b7  Enterococcus  spp.  on  D-coccosel  medium  from  bioMerieux  (incubation  at  37°C  for\\n48 h).\\n\\n2.3. Statistical analysis\\n\\nThe normality of the samples was checked using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Differences between\\ngroups in bacterial counts for water samples taken from different locations (lake shore and lake\\ncenter) were tested using the Mann-Whitney U  test. The significance level was set at 0.05.\\nThe data were processed using Statistica software (StatSoft, Inc.).\\n\\n3.  Results and Discussions\\n\\nIn  2023,  the  Wejherowo  district  hosted  two  designated  bathing  areas:  Lake  Wysoka  -\\nWycztok in Kamień and the Lubiatowo Sea Bathing Area located between beach entrances\\n43 and 44. Additionally, there were four occasional bathing sites organized at scout camps and\\none publicly accessible occasional bathing area at Lake Zawiat in Bieszkowice. At the Wysoka\\n3 Wycztok bathing area, a temporary bloom of blue-green algae was observed at the end of the\\nsummer  season,  while  Lake  Zawiat  experienced  a  temporary  bacteriological  contamination\\nbefore the start of the bathing season. In response to these identified issues and to protect public\\nhealth, the State District Sanitary Inspector in Wejherowo implemented a temporary bathing\\nban at these bathing sites until water quality improved (Informacja o stanie..., 2024). Similarly,\\nthe  analysis  of  water  samples  from  Wyspowo  Lake,  which  included  samples  from  both\\n\\n## [PDF page 264]\\n\\n264  A. KukuBowicz, W. Jaroniec\\n\\nnearshore and lake center locations, revealed that while average microbiological contamination\\nof  the  water  met  the  required  standards  for  bathing  water  quality  (f1000  and  f400  CFU/\\n100 mL, respectively), as outlined in the Journal of Laws (2019, item 255), exceedances of the\\npermissible  Enterococcus  spp.  count  were  detected  in  several  samples.  These  exceedances\\nsuggest that the water quality in some areas of the lake may be compromised due to ongoing or\\nepisodic  sources  of  contamination.  Heavy  rainfall  in  July  may  increase  fecal  coliform  and\\nenterococci  levels,  as  stormwater  runoff  introduces  fecal-origin  bacteria  into  water  bodies,\\nworsening contamination (Staley et al., 2013). Specifically, two shore samples collected in June\\nand  five  samples  collected  in  July  exceeded  the  permissible  limits  for  Enterococcus  spp.\\nThe highest concentration of Enterococcus spp. recorded was 1200 CFU/100 mL, which is three\\ntimes the allowable limit, suggesting the potential for long-standing fecal contamination of the\\nwater (Stec et al., 2022). No samples exceeded the permissible E. coli levels, though one sample\\ncollected from the shore in September contained E. coli at 800 CFU/100 mL. These results\\nhighlight the variability in water quality during different times of the year, especially during\\nmonths when fewer bathers were present. Although no statistically significant difference was\\nfound  between  the  sampling  sites  (shore  vs.  lake  center)  and  E.  coli  counts  (z  =  1.44;\\np = 0.1507), a noticeable increase in E. coli levels4approximately 50% higher4was observed\\nin the samples collected from the shore (Table 1). However, a statistically significant difference\\nwas found between shore and lake center samples regarding Enterococcus spp. counts (z = 2.88,\\np = 0.0040).\\n\\nTable 1.\\nAverage microbial content depending on sampling location [cfu/100mL]\\nKind of  Lake shore (LS)  Center of the lake (CL)\\nbacteria  n = 32  n = 32  Z  p\\nM  SD  M  SD\\nE.coli  178.1  171.8  115.6  88.4  1.44  0.1507\\nEnterococcus  246.9  256.6  93.7  66.9  2.88  0.0040\\nM - Mean; SD 3 standard deviation; z (with correction): value of the Mann-Whitney U test statistic with\\ncorrection; p - significance level.\\nSource: own studies.\\nThe literature confirms that nearshore waters are typically the most contaminated (Pandey,\\net al., 2014), as evidenced by the results of this study (Table 1). People bathing in these areas,\\nespecially children, are at increased risk of gastrointestinal illness, as they often spend extended\\nperiods  in  the  water,  playing  both  in  the  water  and  on  the  sand  (Sanborn,  Takaro,  2013).\\nAccording  to  the  World  Health  Organization,  over  50%  of  deaths  caused  by  water-related\\ndiseases  are  due  to  bacterial  intestinal  infections  (Lin  et  al.,  2022;  Stec  et  al.,  2022).\\nIn comparison to July and August, some of the water samples collected in June and September\\nwere free from the examined bacteria, which may be attributed to the lower number of bathers\\nduring these off-peak months. The risk of illness is determined by both the concentration of\\npathogens in the water and the level of human interaction with it. Activities that involve close\\n\\n## [PDF page 265]\\n\\nMicrobiological quality and risk assessment…  265\\n\\ncontact with water, such as swimming or bathing, carry a higher risk compared to those with\\nlimited  exposure.  Water  quality  standards  are  primarily  established  to  protect  public  health\\nduring  such  high-contact  recreational  activities  (Russo  et  al.,  2020;  Guidelines  on\\nrecreational…,  2021).  Integrating  quality  management  and  risk  management  principles  into\\nmonitoring and control systems  can  enhance the  effectiveness of these  guidelines, ensuring\\nconsistent  protection  of  public  health  and  minimizing  exposure  to  harmful  pathogens.\\nWyspowo Lake, while surrounded by forest and adjacent to a meadow, is also in proximity to\\nseasonal summer cottages and a large forest parking lot that accommodates numerous camping\\ntrailers during the summer months. These human activities contribute to the vulnerability of\\nsurface  waters,  which  are  prone  to  rapid  and  significant  microbiological  quality  changes.\\nSuch  fluctuations  often  stem  from  municipal  wastewater  discharge,  agricultural  runoff,  and\\nrainwater  carrying  pollutants  into  water  bodies  like  lakes  and  rivers,  posing  risks  to  their\\necological balance and public health (Staley et al., 2013; Stec et al., 2022). Given the increasing\\nrisk  of  microbiological  contamination  in  lakes  not  covered  by  the  sanitary-epidemiological\\nsupervision system, there is an urgent need for regular water quality monitoring in these water\\nbodies. Monitoring such lakes is crucial, especially when they are used for recreational and\\neconomic  purposes,  as  it  allows  for  early  identification  of  potential  health  risks  and  the\\nimplementation of appropriate preventive measures\\n\\n4.  Summary and Conclusions\\n\\nBased  on  the  findings  of  this  study,  it  is  evident  that  lakes  not  covered  by  the  formal\\nmonitoring system can still pose significant microbiological risks, especially when used for\\nrecreational and economic purposes. Variations in water quality, influenced by seasonal factors,\\nhuman  activities,  and  environmental  conditions,  were  observed.  Despite  compliance  with\\nregulatory limits on average, exceedances of fecal indicator bacteria, such as Enterococcus spp.,\\nwere detected, particularly in shore samples during months with higher rainfall and increased\\nstormwater runoff. This highlights the importance of monitoring non-regulated lakes to ensure\\npublic health safety and mitigate the potential risks of waterborne diseases. Effective integration\\nof quality management and risk management strategies into water quality monitoring systems\\nis essential to protect the health of individuals engaging in recreational activities, particularly\\nin high-contact areas such as nearshore waters. Further research and regular surveillance of\\nthese water bodies are crucial to maintaining water safety standards and  minimizing public\\nhealth risks.\\n\\n## [PDF page 266]\\n\\n266  A. Ligarski\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nNowadays, a city can be treated as a complex system influenced by many elements and the\\nnetwork of relationships between them. A unit composed of many elements, functioning in\\na specific area, in a specific environment, should be treated as a dynamic, functional whole,\\ni.e.  a  territorial  social  system  (Chojnicki,  1988).  Urban  development  planning  requires\\nknowledge of the individual elements of the city system and the relationships between them,\\nand the adaptation of these assumptions to local conditions (Sneddon et al., 2006). It is therefore\\nnot possible to directly replicate solutions taken from other geographical or socio-economic\\nrealities. It is necessary to obtain information from the city level, with a particular focus on\\ninformation from the residents living in the area. This is reflected in the smart city concept and\\ndefinitions  of  the  concept  (Giffinger  et  al.,  2007;  Caragliu  et  al.,  2011;  Nam,  Pardo,  2011;\\nBakici  et  al.,  2013;  Albino  et  al.,  2015;  Kubina et  al.,  2021;  Hajek  et  al.,  2022).  The  most\\nwidespread smart city model assumes that six areas are linked, identifying a number of factors\\nin each area (Giffinger et al., 2007). The smart city concept is still evolving and in its third\\ngeneration, citizens should take the initiative (Alexopoulos et al., 2019; Pira, 2021; Kubina\\net  al.,  2021).  Residents  should  provide  the  information  needed  and  be  involved  in  the\\ndevelopment of the city. There are different forms of resident involvement, both individual and\\ncollective. The municipal government should create the right conditions for expressing needs\\nand expectations. It should develop methods to collect opinions and comments from citizens.\\nMoreover,  these  methods  should  ensure  that  data  is  collected  in  a  cyclical  manner.\\nMany authors point out the need to obtain information from different sources (Huovila et al.,\\n2016; Bosch et al., 2017; Allam, Newman, 2018; Desdemoustier et al., 2019; Camboim et al.,\\n2019; Jonek-Kowalska, Wolniak, 2023). Adequate acquisition of this information and, later,\\nits proper processing should lead to specific decisions and actions. The concept of bottom-up\\ninformation transfer has many proponents (Caragliu et al., 2011; Bakici et al., 2013; Albino\\net al., 2015; Macke et al., 2018; Kubina et al., 2021; Hajek et al., 2022). In contrast, relatively\\nfew  authors  highlight  the  difficulties  and  barriers  associated  with  obtaining  and  processing\\ninformation  from  citizens  (De  Guimarães  et  al.,  2020;  Tan,  Taeihagh,  2020;  Treude,  2021;\\nMouratidis, 2021). One method of obtaining information from citizens is through quality of life\\nsurveys.  To  date,  these  surveys  have  been  used  to  assess  the  satisfaction  of  citizens  and to\\nevaluate the performance of the city government (Insch, 2010; Macke et al., 2018; Rodríguez\\nBolívar, 2021). In contrast, they have not been used to obtain information that can be useful for\\nthe wider development of the city (Papachristou, Rosas-Casals, 2019; Moeinaddini et al., 2020;\\nGoerlich, Reig, 2021; Mouratidis, 2021; Przybyłowski et al., 2021). The author of the study and\\nhis  research  team  conducted  extensive  research  to  investigate  how  cities  understand  and\\nconduct quality of life surveys so that information useful for sustainable urban development\\ncan be extracted. Two stages of research were carried out, the first stage analysed cities that\\n\\n## [PDF page 271]\\n\\nDifficulties in obtaining data…  271\\n\\nconduct structured quality  of life surveys (Ligarski, 2021;  Ligarski, Wolny, 2021a,  2021b).\\nIn the second stage, a comparative study of cities with and without structured quality of life\\nsurveys was conducted (Ligarski, 2022; Ligarski, Owczarek, 2023, 2024). Based on the results\\nobtained, it was clearly confirmed that quality of life surveys can provide information that can\\nbe used for sustainable urban development. For this to happen, however, a proper understanding\\nand preparation of quality of life research is needed. This publication focuses on the issue of\\ndata collection in the quality of life survey process. How should the municipality organise the\\ndata collection stage so that information useful to the city can be obtained. For the purpose of\\nthis paper, some of the results obtained in the second stage of the research procedure were used.\\nThe aim of the paper is to examine how city halls acquire data in the quality of life survey\\nprocess and to highlight the difficulties that arise at this stage.\\n\\n2.  Methods\\n\\nWhen embarking on the research, an attempt was made to cover the largest possible group\\nof  municipal  offices  located  in  Poland.  Ultimately,  all  city  offices  in  cities  with  more  than\\n50,000 inhabitants were selected for the study. Thus, the subject of the research are 84 city\\noffices in cities with more than 50,000 inhabitants. A research methodology was developed and\\nhypotheses  and  research  questions  were  formulated.  A  research  tool  was  selected  -\\na questionnaire survey was chosen. An original survey form was developed for the research.\\nThe form included 30 survey questions and a metric. Closed questions were used, allowing\\nrespondents to choose one or more answers, depending on the question. Some of the questions\\nalso allowed for other answers - where the respondent could formulate the answer themselves.\\nThe anonymity of the research was ensured. At no point did the cities provide information that\\ncould unambiguously indicate the name of the city. The surveys in the offices were carried out\\nby an organisation that professionally deals with this type of activity, between November 2021\\nand January 2022. Out of a population of 84 offices, 80 offices responded, giving a survey\\nreturn rate of 95.2%. Based on the survey results, the offices were divided into two groups.\\nThe first that conducts structured quality of life surveys (29 offices in total) and the second that\\ndoes not conduct structured quality of life surveys (51 offices in total). For the purposes of this\\nstudy, part of the survey results for the 29 city offices that conduct structured quality of life\\nsurveys were used.\\n\\n## [PDF page 272]\\n\\n272  M.J. Discussion\\n\\nThe  research  carried  out  provided  a  great  deal  of  information  on  data  collection  in  the\\nquality of life research  process. The important issues at this stage have  been identified and\\nreference  has  been  made  to  the  perception  of  the  phenomena  taking  place  here  from  the\\nperspective of those responsible for conducting the research. By relating the research results\\nobtained  to  other  publications,  several  regularities  can  be  identified.  Many  publications\\nhighlight the need to obtain information from residents from a variety of sources (Bosch et al.,\\n2017; Allam, Newman, 2018; Desdemoustier et al., 2019). Quality of life surveys can provide\\nvaluable  information  that,  when  properly  processed,  can  be  used  for  sustainable  urban\\ndevelopment (Ligarski, Wolny, 2021b; Ligarski, Owczarek, 2024). A prerequisite for obtaining\\nuseful information is the proper organisation and preparation of the data acquisition process,\\nwhich is also confirmed by other publications (Kaklauskas et al., 2018; Macke et al., 2018).\\nThe results obtained highlight the limitations and problems associated with obtaining data from\\n\\n## [PDF page 278]\\n\\n278  M.J. As a result of the research, it was possible to obtain information\\non the knowledge and awareness of those responsible for conducting research. Based on the\\nanalysis  of  the  research  results  obtained,  an  attempt  can  be  made  to  formulate  potential\\ndifficulties that may arise in any city office:\\n1.  The involvement of the office management in the data collection process.\\n2.  Selection of an appropriate survey frequency.\\n3.  Selection of indicators and determination of their number.\\n4.  Preparation for data collection.\\n5.  Clearly define what data is needed.\\n6.  Training of staff on the purpose and methods of data collection.\\nAwareness of these difficulties should make the office better prepared to conduct quality of\\nlife surveys and prevent problems from arising at this stage. The involvement of the authority’s\\nmanagement seems crucial. It is the management that takes responsibility for the entire data\\ncollection  process.  It  defines  the  aims  and  objectives  of  the  research  to  be  carried  out  and\\nidentifies the people responsible for the process. The second issue is the appropriate selection\\nof the frequency of the surveys. The survey should be conducted at such a frequency as to obtain\\nthe necessary and up-to-date data. In order to gather the necessary information, it is useful to\\ndefine indicators. These indicators should describe the issues to be surveyed in a way that is\\nunderstandable to the residents. It is also important to select an appropriate number of indicators\\nto ensure that all issues are addressed. In order to carry out the data collection process properly,\\ngood preparation is needed. When starting to collect data, it is necessary to clearly define what\\ndata will be needed and for which purposes it will be used. In order for the data collection\\nprocess to be carried out properly, it is necessary to train staff on the purpose and methods of\\ndata  collection.  In  conclusion,  a  recommendation  can  be  offered  to  those  responsible  for\\nconducting quality of life surveys:\\n1.  Inform and cooperate with the municipal management at the survey planning stage.\\n2.  Conduct quality of life surveys annually.\\n3.  When preparing the surveys, identify the indicators and adapt the number of indicators\\nto the needs of the municipality.\\n4.  Prepare for each survey cycle.\\n5.  Clearly define the data needed.\\n6.  Organise training for staff on the objectives and methods of data collection.\\n\\n## [PDF page 279]\\n\\nDifficulties in obtaining data…  279\\n\\n5.  Summary\\n\\nThe survey research carried out on a sample of 29 cities that conduct structured quality of\\nlife surveys provided interesting information on data acquisition. City halls conduct surveys\\nwith varying frequency. The frequency of surveys has a significant impact on the quantity and\\nquality of data obtained. It seems that the solution to ensure access to an adequate database is\\nto conduct quality of life surveys annually. Authorities that conduct surveys less frequently are\\nthemselves condemned to a shortage of the necessary data. In most surveyed cities, quality-of-\\nlife indicators are defined and a number of them are selected. Sometimes indicators are divided\\ninto groups. The definition of indicators is a form of preparation for data collection. If a city\\nhas indicators, in a reasonable number, it will be easier for it to collect the necessary information\\nand compare them in subsequent survey cycles. In the research conducted, attention was paid\\nto the awareness and knowledge of those responsible for conducting quality of life surveys.\\nThe  majority  of  those  surveyed  did  not  explicitly  confirm  that,  when  embarking  on  data\\ncollection, they know for what purposes the information will be used in the future and to which\\norganisational  units  it  should  go.  This  raises  the  issue  of  inadequate  preparation  for  data\\ncollection. If the person entering the survey does not have the necessary knowledge, it will be\\ndifficult for him or her to properly prepare for the survey and identify the issues that should be\\ninvestigated. This, in turn, may lead to a failure to obtain the needed data. The research found\\nthat those responsible for conducting quality of life surveys are aware of the need for change\\nand improvement in the data collection process. They most often indicate the need to better\\nprepare the process and to be clear about what data is needed. They call for training of staff on\\nthe purpose and methods of data collection and involvement of the office management in the\\npreparation for the surveys. They also draw attention to defining for which purposes the data\\nwill be used and to which organisational units and positions the data should reach. On this basis,\\nit can be concluded that there are problems in the offices related to the proper acquisition of\\ndata. These problems are noticed by those appointed to conduct quality of life surveys and these\\npeople are able to propose measures aimed at removing these problems.\\nThe  research  results  obtained  highlight  the  limitations  and  problems  associated  with\\nobtaining data from residents. By analysing the results of the research, it has been possible to\\nidentify a list of six basic difficulties that should be taken into account at the planning and\\npreparation stage of data collection in each town hall. Recognising these difficulties provides\\nan opportunity to better organise the data collection process and prevent problems from arising\\nin the process. Good preparation for data collection should result in an adequate amount of\\nuseful data. The municipality will then have data which, when properly analysed, can be used\\nto make decisions and take action.\\n\\n## [PDF page 280]\\n\\n280  M.J. Introduction\\n\\nThe COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant impact on businesses in European Union\\ncountries, leading to numerous changes in economic activity, the labour market and production\\nstructures  (Lopez-Garcia,  Szörfi,  2021;  Żak,  Garncarz,  2020;  Privara,2022).  As  a  result  of\\nlockdowns,  border  closures  and  restrictions  on  international  trade,  many  businesses,\\nparticularly in sectors such as tourism, catering, transport and retail, experienced a drastic drop\\nin  turnover  (Meyermans,  Rutkauskas,  Simons,  2021;  Bloom,  Brynjolfsson,  Davis,  Mizen,\\n2021). Countries heavily dependent on tourism, such as Spain and Italy, have suffered the most.\\nTurnover per person employed in these sectors fell significantly, which meant a reduction in\\nrevenue per employee.\\nThe COVID-19 pandemic has significantly affected turnover and thus turnover per person\\nemployed  in  companies  in  EU  countries.  Many  industries,  especially  tourism,  retail  and\\nservices,  experienced  declines  in  turnover  per  employee  due  to  lockdowns  and  business\\nrestrictions. Countries such as Spain, Italy and Belgium have seen declines in this indicator as\\na  result  of  business  closures  and  reduced  demand.  Nevertheless,  some  countries,  such  as\\nGermany, remained stable due to better economic conditions.\\nThe pandemic has also caused liquidity problems for many companies, especially in the\\nsmall  and  medium-sized  enterprise  (SME)  sector  (Fana,  Tolan,  Torrejón,  Urzi  Brancati,\\nFernández-Macías,  2020;  Hamann,  Niebuhr,  Roth,  Sieglen,  2023;  Sapir,  2020)  Declining\\ndemand  and  difficulties  in  raising  investment  capital  have  resulted  in  reduced  investment.\\nCompanies have had to delay or abandon planned investment projects, negatively affecting their\\nlong-term growth.\\nIn response to the pandemic, many companies have had to adapt their procedures, increasing\\noperational  costs.  Examples  include  costs  associated  with  complying  with  new  hygiene\\nstandards,  the  introduction  of  remote  working  and  the  reorganization  of  supply  chains.\\nCompanies  have  also  had  to  adapt  to  changing  national  health  and  safety  regulations.\\nThe pandemic has resulted in redundancies and job cuts in many sectors.\\n\\n## [PDF page 285]\\n\\nThe impact of the COVID-19 virus…  285\\n\\nFrims  have  been  reducing  the  number  of  employees  in  response  to  reduced  demand.\\nAt the same time, there has been a surge in flexible working arrangements, such as remote\\nworking,  which  has  affected  the  structure  of  employment  in  the  EU.  Sectors  related  to\\ninformation technology and services have been able to adapt more quickly to this change, while\\nother, more traditional sectors, have found it more difficult.\\nIn response to the pandemic crisis, many companies have accelerated their digitalization\\nprocesses,  investing  in  technologies  related  to  e-commerce,  remote  working  tools  and\\nautomation.\\nCompanies began to look for more local suppliers and to invest in technology that would\\nenable  greater  automation  and  independence  from  global  disruptions  to  international  trade.\\nSectors such as technology, e-commerce and pharmaceuticals have seen increases, while others\\nsuch as tourism, air transport and catering have experienced the biggest declines. In countries\\nsuch as France, Croatia, Spain and Italy, where tourism is an important part of the economy,\\nthe  pandemic  caused  severe  difficulties,  while  in  technologically  strong  countries  such  as\\nLuxembourg, Sweden and Ireland, the impact was milder.\\n\\n2. Conclusion\\n\\nAnalysis  of  indicators  W1-W6  confirms  the  strong  economic  divergence  between\\nEU  countries.  Countries  with  stable  economic  foundations,  such  as  Ireland,  Germany  or\\nLithuania,  have  been  able  to  continue  their  growth  despite  global  challenges.  In  contrast,\\ncountries struggling with structural problems and economic crises, such as Greece, Spain or\\nItaly,  have  experienced  declines  in  a  number  of  key  indicators,  which  may  require  further\\nreforms and a review of these countries’ economic policies and especially investment decisions.\\nThe  discrepancies  in  the  turnover  per  employee  index  between  countries  such  as\\nLuxembourg and Ireland and Croatia and Bulgaria are the result of differences in the structure\\nof  the  economy,  the  level  of  technological  advancement,  investment  in  human  capital  and\\ninvestment  attractiveness.  Countries  with  dominant  high-value-added  sectors  and  a  strong\\npresence  of  multinational  corporations  generate  significantly  higher  turnover  per  worker\\ncompared to countries whose economies are based on labour-intensive and low-value-added\\nsectors.  More  developed  countries,  led  by  the  technology  and  financial  sectors,  are  able  to\\ngenerate significantly higher value added per worker. In contrast, countries with a lower level\\nof  development,  dominated  by  traditional  and  lower  productivity  sectors,  have  a  limited\\ncapacity to achieve high values for this indicator. In order to improve performance, Romania\\nand Bulgaria, Latvia and Greece need to increase investment in innovation and infrastructure\\ndevelopment to gradually improve labour efficiency and increase the value added generated per\\nworker.\\n\\n## [PDF page 295]\\n\\nThe impact of the COVID-19 virus…  295\\n\\nIn countries such as Poland and Slovakia, wages are relatively lower compared to Western\\nEuropean countries, which means that the share of labour costs in total production costs remains\\nrelatively low. In Poland and Slovakia, foreign companies play a significant role in the economy\\nas  thry  relocate  production  to  these  countries  in  order  to  reduce  costs.  Low  labour  costs,\\ncombined with relatively high productivity, mean that the share of labour costs in production\\ncosts  remains  low. The  purpose  of  the  research  was  to  investigate\\nchanges in customer behavior especially in terms of product return, that may have occurred\\nduring the Covid-19 pandemic. The most interesting thing was to find out whether the behavior\\nforced by restrictions turned into a habit after the pandemic. Discussions and conclusion\\n\\nThere is no doubt that the Covid-19 pandemic has had  a significant impact on the way\\npeople behave, think and shop. Many experts believe that the surge in online shopping will\\ncontinue the positive trend. As more people become accustomed to the convenience of shopping\\nat home, it is likely  that e-commerce will  continue to  grow  and evolve into new  and more\\nconvenient forms for consumers in the coming years. The Covid-19 pandemic has had long-\\nterm effects on global trade, and the increase in online shopping is just one of many changes.\\nAs we progress and develop, it is important to understand the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic\\non the exponential growth of online shopping and the likely evolution of e-commerce in a post-\\npandemic world (Szasz et al., 2022).\\nIn our study, we’ve formulated three research questions. Thanks to the precise answers of\\nthe respondents, accurate answers were obtained:\\n\uf0b7  RQ1: How the Covid-19 pandemic changed consumer behavior? The pandemic has\\ncontributed to changes in consumer purchasing behavior. It can be clearly stated that\\nthe  majority  of  respondents  noticed  changes  in  their  behavior.  42%  of  respondents\\nadmitted  to  changing  their  shopping  habits  towards  online  shopping,  35.6%  of\\nrespondents are switching towards cashless payments, which contributed to leaving the\\ntraditional method of settlements. A small percentage of respondents noticed changes\\nin the increase in the frequency of returns (7.5%) or preference for stationary purchases\\nonline (9.5%). However, 40.3% of respondents did not change their shopping behavior,\\nwhich may involve the active use of online shopping in the period before the pandemic\\nand the same degree of stationary purchases in the field of goods available immediately.\\n\\n## [PDF page 311]\\n\\nThe purchasing patterns…  311\\n\\n\uf0b7  RQ2:  Does  age  influence  differences  in  respondents’  purchasing  behavior?\\nYes, age differentiates respondents’ purchasing behavior:\\n\uf0b7  People up to the age of 18 were much less likely to make such returns (19.0%),\\nwhile  people  over  60  years  of  age  (50.0%)  make  returns  more  often  than  in  the\\npre-pandemic period. Pre-pandemic research by Source et al. (2005) suggests that\\nage affects online shopping behavior and product returns, especially if the consumer\\nsearched for the product online (Sorce et al., 2005). The results of this research show\\nthat the percentage of purchases by age category is very similar. Comparing this\\nresult  to  the  study  described  in  the  article  (the  younger  generation  makes  fewer\\nreturns), we can see a difference indicating an increase in the number of returns over\\ntime. Comparing our study to the Basak et al. (2022) survey, according to which the\\nonline shopping return rate among young Indian consumers is close to 50%, there is\\na noticeable difference in consumer awareness about return policy. Such a difference\\nis due to a much more reduced risk in the return policy of online stores in India.\\nThe  return  policy  in  Poland  is  friendly  to  consumers,  but  in  parallel  with  this,\\ncompanies are introducing changes to make the return policy more environmentally\\nfriendly.\\n\uf0b7  The respondents over the age of 60 (50.0%) also paid more attention to whether the\\ncompany is pro-ecological than it was for people under 18 (14.3%). According to\\nour  research,  students/disciples  (13%)  are  more  willing  to  shop  stationary  than\\nbefore the pandemic, but such dependence was not noticed among working people\\n(3.6%). Our research shows that students/students are more likely to shop stationary\\nthan  before  the  pandemic,  but  among  other  studies,  this  data  is  not  confirmed.\\nThe  pandemic  has  accelerated  the  development  of  e-commerce  and  consumers\\nspend more time on online shopping platforms (Ingaldi, Brožová, 2020; Akçagün\\net al., 2021; Ludin et al., 2022). International students, especially those from Asia,\\nhave shown a greater change in buying habits, including increased online shopping\\nand preferences for local products (Szlachciuk et al., 2022). This trend is attributed\\nto factors such as convenience, pandemic restrictions and the adaptation of brick-\\nand-mortar  stores  to  online  platforms  (Ludin  et  al.,  2022).  These  results  suggest\\na  significant  transformation  of  consumer  behaviour,  especially  among  students,\\nas a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.\\n\uf0b7  RQ3: Which gender prefers more online shopping? Among statistically significant\\nbehaviors, it can be indicated that women prefer online shopping more than before the\\npandemic (50.3%), men only (36.0%), and they pay much more with non-cash payments\\nthan  before  the  pandemic  (44.8%),  men  only  (26.7%).  Many  studies  from  different\\ncountries show us that female consumers were more likely to shop online during the\\nCovid-19 pandemic than before the pandemic, paying particular attention to cashless\\npayment (Kráľ et al., 2022; Ohata et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2022). As we can see from\\n\\n## [PDF page 312]\\n\\n312  K. Lysenko-Ryba, M. Reveniuk\\n\\nthe  results  of  that  research,  the  trend  continues.  Post-covid  behavior  related  to  the\\nconvenience of online shopping and the favorable factors for non-cash payments and\\na  consumer-safe  return  policy,  which  began  to  grow  during  the  pandemic  became\\nestablished in the consumer behavior of both sex groups.\\nInternational events, such as the economic, geopolitical or biological crisis, introduce many\\nchanges in consumer behavior. Until recently, we have been dealing with the global crisis of\\nthe Covid-19 pandemic, and today we are facing a political crisis. Such phenomena clearly\\nindicate  not  only  changes  in  the  market,  but  also  changes  in  consumer  expectations  and\\nbehavior. In this article, the authors presented the results of an online survey among Polish\\nconsumers conducted in April-May (N = 305). The authors also compared consumer behavior\\nbefore, during and two years after the outbreak of the pandemic. The results have led to some\\nconclusions: the age and gender of consumers have a direct impact on the way purchases are\\nmade and their returns. Introduction\\n\\nCrisis  migration,  particularly  when  driven  by  conflict,  persecution,  or  environmental\\ncatastrophes, has become one of the most pressing challenges in the field of migration studies\\nand  sustainable  development  (Black,  2018;  Estevens,  2018;  Hugo,  2008;  Raleigh,  2011).\\nAs populations are displaced due to war, natural disasters, or political instability, the impact on\\nboth  host  and  origin  regions  is  profound,  affecting  social,  economic,  and  environmental\\nsustainability.  Given  the  magnitude  and  complexity  of  migration  in  crisis  situations,\\nit is essential to understand the dynamics at play in order to design policies that can both manage\\nmigration  flows  and  contribute  to  long-term  sustainable  development.  This  is  particularly\\nimportant as migration is not just a result of crisis events but also an important factor in shaping\\nregional and global development trajectories (Black, 2018).\\nThis study provides an overview of the literature on crisis migration, refugee movements,\\nand sustainable regional development. Using a systematic review approach, it evaluates recent\\ntrends, key subject areas, and the most commonly used terms in research publications from\\nWeb of Science (WoS) and Scopus databases. The focus of this paper is to address research\\nquestions related to current research trends, subject areas, and keywords in crisis migration and\\nsustainable development, as well as to explore recent issues, challenges, and emerging future\\ntrends in this field. This paper seeks to answer important questions regarding the relationship\\nbetween migration and sustainable development, the factors influencing the displacement of\\npopulations,  and  the  ways  in  which  these  phenomena  are  studied  and  understood  in\\ncontemporary scholarship.\\nThe  primary  aim  of  this  study  is  to  map  out  the  growing  body  of  literature  on  crisis\\nmigration, refugee migration, and sustainable development by examining the period from 1989\\nto 2022, utilizing data from the WoS and Scopus databases. In doing so, this study identifies\\nthe key research topics and geographical regions that have been central to the discussion in\\nrecent decades. The focus on crisis migration and refugee flows has intensified, particularly in\\nthe  aftermath  of  significant  global  events,  such  as  the  Syrian  civil  war,  the  COVID-19\\npandemic,  and  the  ongoing  Russia-Ukraine  conflict.  Furthermore,  this  paper  highlights  the\\nshifting terminology used in the literature, such as the introduction of terms like \\"pandemic\\",\\n\\"Brexit\\",  and  \\"Syrian  refugee\\",  in  response  to  these  events,  while  also  noting  the  lack  of\\nattention to more recent crises, such as the displacement resulting from the 2022 war in Ukraine.\\nThis systematic review aimed to evaluate the key trends in academic literature on these\\ninterconnected  topics  and  to  identify  gaps  in  the  research,  especially  concerning  the\\nunderrepresentation of certain refugee groups in mainstream studies. The study highlights that\\nwhile research interest in crisis migration and sustainable development has surged, the literature\\non  some  of  the  most  current  refugee  crises,  such  as  the  Ukrainian  migration  crisis,  is  still\\nunderdeveloped,  potentially  due  to  delays  in  publication  and  indexing  in  major  academic\\n\\n## [PDF page 319]\\n\\nMigration driven by crises…  319\\n\\ndatabases. The COVID-19 pandemic has reshaped the scope of migration research, introducing\\nnew dimensions such as health crises, border management, and migration governance.\\nSeveral  scholars  have  addressed  the  complex  relationship  between  migration  and\\nsustainable development. Castles (2010) and Martin (2022) discussed migration as both a cause\\nand a consequence of sustainability challenges, noting its influence on economic inequality,\\nenvironmental change, and social stability. More recent works, such as those by Betts (2011)\\nand  Zetter  (2018),  have  examined  the  implications  of  crisis-induced  migration  for  host\\ncountries,  particularly  in  terms  of  policy  responses  and  the  integration  of  migrants.\\nThese studies suggest that crisis migration presents both opportunities and risks for host regions,\\ndepending on the political, economic, and social context in which migrants arrive.\\nHowever, despite this growing body of literature, research gaps remain in addressing the\\nlong-term impacts of crisis migration on sustainable regional development. Pécoud (2014) and\\nHynie  (2018)  have  argued  that  while  migration  can  offer  developmental  benefits,\\nthese  outcomes  are  often  contingent  on  effective  management  and  integration  strategies.\\nMoreover, recent trends highlight that while much attention has been focused on the Middle\\nEast and South Asia, emerging crises in Eastern Europe, such as the displacement caused by\\nthe war in Ukraine, have yet to receive adequate scholarly attention.\\nIn  addition  to  addressing  these  gaps,  this  paper  draws  on  the  work  of  scholars  such  as\\nMcAuliffe and Triandafyllidou (2021), who noted that the COVID-19 pandemic significantly\\naltered  the  migration  landscape,  with  new  keywords  and  areas  of  focus  appearing  in  the\\nliterature,  including  \\"health\\",  \\"hygiene\\",  and  \\"pandemic  migration\\".  The  research  further\\nexplores  how  these  events  have  led  to  an  increased  focus  on  migration  governance,  border\\ncontrol, and the socio-political dimensions of migration, as well as the role of international\\ninstitutions in managing these crises.\\nUsing WoS and Scopus data, this paper addresses research questions related to the current\\ntrends, subject areas, and terms in research publications on crisis migration, refugee migration,\\nand sustainable regional development. In particular, this study highlights recent shifts in the\\nfield, such as the impact of geopolitical events like BREXIT, migration resulting from wars in\\nSyria and Afghanistan, and the European Union’s role in managing refugee crises. These shifts\\npoint  to  the  evolving  nature  of  migration  studies  and  underscore  the  need  for  continued\\nexploration of the intersection between migration, sustainability, and policy in times of crisis.\\nThe findings of this study contribute to the growing body of literature on crisis migration\\nand sustainable development, offering valuable insights into the directions of future research.\\nFurthermore, this paper seeks to provide actionable recommendations for policymakers, NGOs,\\nand international organizations working to address the challenges posed by migration in crisis\\ncontexts. By synthesizing current research and identifying gaps in the literature, this paper aims\\nto guide future studies and provide a foundation for policy interventions that align migration\\nresponses  with  sustainable  development  goals  (OECD,  2020).  This  study  employs  a  novel\\napproach to provide a comprehensive overview of the evolving landscape of crisis migration\\n\\n## [PDF page 320]\\n\\n320  K. Aukaniszyn-Domaszewska, K.
