Discussion\\n\\nThe findings of this study reveal a clear upward trajectory in the volume of research on\\ncrisis  migration,  refugee  movements,  and  sustainable  development  between  1997  and  2022\\n(WoS)  and  1989  to  2022  (Scopus).  This  surge  in  publications  highlights  the  growing\\nrecognition  of  migration  as  a  critical  area  for  research,  particularly  given  its  increasing\\ncomplexity and its close ties to sustainable development objectives. Castles (2010) and Koser\\n(2007) have long argued that migration and development are inextricably linked, with migration\\nboth  influencing  and  being  shaped  by  broader  socio-economic  and  political  dynamics.\\nThe  upward  trend  in  publications  may  also  reflect  the  broader  global  political  and\\nenvironmental crises, which have made migration a focal point for academic inquiry, policy\\ndiscussions, and public debate.\\nThis study shows that the most frequent contributors to research on these topics come from\\nRussia, Germany, and the United Kingdom, with the highest number of citations originating\\nfrom the United States. This geographic trend aligns with previous research, which found that\\nmigration studies often focus on regions heavily impacted by refugee inflows and those that are\\ncentral to international migration policies (Scholten, Penninx, 2016). However, recent shifts in\\nglobal  migration  patterns,  such  as  the  Syrian  and  Afghan  refugee  crises,  have  increasingly\\ndriven research towards specific refugee groups, as documented by Betts and Collier (2017)\\nand Zetter (2021).\\nA  particularly  striking  finding  from  this  study  is  the  relative  lack  of  research  on  the\\nUkrainian refugee crisis, despite its significant scale following the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.\\nThis may be attributed to delays in indexing articles in databases such as WoS and Scopus,\\nwhich can take weeks or months to include new publications (Elsevier, 2021). These delays\\nmay also reflect a lag in the availability of relevant studies, as research on the Ukrainian refugee\\ncrisis is still in its early stages. As highlighted by Pécoud (2014), it is essential for migration\\nscholars to rapidly respond to such emergencies in order to document and analyze emerging\\ntrends in real-time. However, as geopolitical priorities often influence which crises receive the\\nmost  attention  (Pécoud,  2014),  it  is  also  important  to  ensure  that  all  migration  crises  are\\nadequately represented in academic discourse.\\nThis  study  reveals  several  important  trends  in the  literature  on  crisis  migration,  refugee\\nmovements,  and  sustainable  development.  Key  areas  of  focus  include  the  intersection  of\\nmigration  and  public  health,  the  gendered  dimensions  of  crisis  migration,  the  impact  of\\nEuropean  migration  policies,  and  the  relationship  between  migration  and  sustainable\\ndevelopment.  Below,  these  trends  are  discussed  in  greater  detail,  along  with  an  expanded\\nexploration of recent research.\\n\\n## [PDF page 333]\\n\\nMigration driven by crises…  333\\n\\n4.1.  Migration and health in the context of global crises\\n\\nThe  COVID-19  pandemic  has  had  a  profound  impact  on  migration  patterns  and  has\\nsignificantly  reshaped  research  into  migration  and  health.  In  particular,  the  pandemic  has\\nhighlighted the vulnerabilities of migrant populations, whose health and wellbeing are often\\ncompromised  due  to  inadequate  access  to  healthcare,  overcrowded  living  conditions,\\nand limited resources. The increased use of terms such as <pandemic=, <health=, and <hygiene=\\nin  migration  studies  underscores  the  growing  recognition  of  the  need  to  integrate  health\\nconsiderations  into  migration  management  (McAuliffe,  Triandafyllidou,  2021).  Migrants,\\nespecially those in temporary accommodation or refugee camps, face heightened exposure to\\ninfectious diseases due to poor sanitary conditions and lack of healthcare infrastructure (Hynie,\\n2018).\\nAs  McAuliffe  and  Triandafyllidou  (2021)  argue,  the  pandemic  exacerbated  the\\nvulnerabilities  of  migrants  by  restricting  access  to  essential  health  services  and  increasing\\ndiscrimination  and  stigmatization.  These  challenges  have  prompted  a  call  for  more\\ncomprehensive policies that address the health needs of migrant populations, particularly in\\ntimes of crisis. Scholars such as Koser (2007) and Castles (2010) stress the need for migration\\ngovernance frameworks that prioritize health equity and provide essential services to migrants\\nduring  health  crises.  Recent  literature  also  suggests  that  migration  policies  should  integrate\\nhealth  preparedness  strategies  to  mitigate  the  impacts  of  future  pandemics  on  migrant\\ncommunities (Scholten, Penninx, 2016).\\n\\n4.2.  Gendered dimensions of crisis migration\\n\\nResearch on the gendered aspects of crisis migration has seen considerable growth in recent\\nyears,  with  a  particular  focus  on  the  vulnerabilities  of  women  and  children  in  refugee  and\\nconflict settings. As Hynie (2021) notes, women refugees are often exposed to higher risks of\\nsexual  violence,  exploitation,  and  discrimination,  particularly  in  conflict  zones.\\nThese  vulnerabilities  are  further  compounded  by  cultural  and  structural  barriers  that  limit\\nwomen’s  access  to  resources,  legal  protection,  and  integration  opportunities  (Zetter,  2021).\\nRefugee women are often subject to gender-based violence, including sexual assault, forced\\nmarriages, and trafficking, exacerbating their already precarious situations.\\nThis  growing  body  of  research  emphasizes  the  need  for  gender-sensitive  policies  that\\nconsider  the  specific  needs  of  women  and  children  in  refugee  settings  (Al-Husban  Adams,\\n2016). Such policies must address issues such as access to healthcare, legal protection, and safe\\nliving conditions. Zetter (2021) underscores the importance of including gender considerations\\nin refugee assistance programs, particularly in post-conflict settings where women often face\\nheightened  risks.  Moreover,  studies  by  Pécoud  (2022)  have  suggested  that  gender-sensitive\\nmigration  policies  can  improve  both  the  short-term  wellbeing  and  long-term  integration  of\\nrefugee women (Denaro, Giuffré, 2022; Gammage, Stevanovic, 2019).\\n\\n## [PDF page 334]\\n\\n334  K. Aukaniszyn-Domaszewska, K. Mazur-WBodarczyk\\n\\n4.3.  Regional migration and European politics\\n\\nMigration within and towards Europe continues to be a central focus of academic research,\\nespecially in relation to the ongoing crises in Syria, Afghanistan, and other conflict-affected\\nregions.  The  European  Union  (EU)  remains  a  key  destination  for  migrants  and  refugees,\\nwhich has led to the development of complex migration policies. Scholten and Penninx (2021)\\nprovide  a  comprehensive  analysis  of  the  political  challenges  faced  by  European  states  in\\nmanaging  migration  flows.  They  argue  that  the  EU’s  migration  policies,  which  emphasize\\nborder control and the enforcement of asylum procedures, are often at odds with the need for\\neffective integration programs.\\nRecent research indicates that EU policies have been both a source of protection and a cause\\nof friction within host societies. For instance, while the EU’s refugee relocation scheme was\\nintended to share the burden of asylum seekers more equitably, it has faced significant political\\nresistance in many member states, especially in countries like Hungary and Poland. Betts and\\nCollier (2017) suggest that regional migration policies must balance the protection of refugees\\nwith  the  integration  of  migrants  into  local  labor  markets,  education  systems,  and  social\\nstructures. This balance is critical for achieving long-term social cohesion and stability in host\\ncountries.\\nMoreover, the European migration context is further complicated by the rise of far-right\\npopulism, which has influenced migration policies in many European countries. Research by\\nKoser (2020) explores the political dynamics of migration in Europe, arguing that nationalism\\nand anti-immigrant sentiment often shape policy decisions, with detrimental effects on migrant\\nand refugee populations. Given the complexity of migration governance in Europe, there is\\na need for more research into how regional migration policies can be reformed to better meet\\nthe challenges of refugee integration while respecting human rights and international law.\\n\\n4.4.  Sustainability, migration, and development\\n\\nIn  recent  years,  scholars  have  increasingly  explored  the  intersection  between  migration\\ngovernance  and  sustainable  development,  particularly  in  relation  to  the  United  Nations’\\nSustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Betts and Collier (2017) argue that migration can be\\nan engine of economic development, both in host countries and countries of origin, provided\\nthat migration governance frameworks are designed to foster integration and support the long-\\nterm development of migrant populations. However, achieving this vision requires overcoming\\nsignificant  obstacles,  such  as  resource  constraints,  political  opposition,  and  the  need  for\\ninternational cooperation.\\nRecent  studies  by  Pécoud  (2014)  emphasize  the  importance  of  developing  sustainable\\nmigration practices that contribute to both the economic development of host countries and the\\nwellbeing of migrants. These practices include promoting social inclusion, improving access to\\neducation and healthcare, and ensuring that migrant labor is integrated into the local economy.\\n\\n## [PDF page 335]\\n\\nMigration driven by crises…  335\\n\\nSuch policies not only improve the lives of migrants but also benefit host societies by boosting\\nproductivity and fostering social cohesion.\\nMoreover,  sustainable  migration  practices  can  play  a  key  role  in  achieving  the  SDGs,\\nparticularly  Goal  10  (Reduced  Inequalities)  and  Goal  16  (Peace,  Justice,  and  Strong\\nInstitutions). Summary\\n\\nThe purpose of the article was to define current trends, subject areas and terms in research\\npublications on crisis, refugee migration and sustainable development, as well as recent issues,\\nchallenges and future trends in this area. In the case of both databases, there is an upward trend\\nin  the  number  of  documents,  which  allows  for  a  conclusion  about  the  increase  in  research\\ninterest  in  this  topic  in  the  period  1997  to  2022  for  WoS  and  1989  to  2022  for  Scopus.\\nPublications within the database Scopus indicate that most documents of the issues studied\\ncome from Russia, Germany, and the United Kingdom. While the most cited papers come from\\nthe United States.\\nThe  changes  occurring  over  the  last  two  years,  primarily  the  SARS-CoV-2  pandemic\\n(December 2019), have been marked by the appearance in scientific texts of the words: Covid,\\npandemic, hygiene and health and within the area of international integration: union, European\\nUnion, BREXIT and Schengen, as well as migrations resulting from conflicts between given\\nsocial  groups:  war,  Syrian  refugee  and  Afghan.  The  lack  of  a  topic  dedicated  to  Ukrainian\\nrefugees, related to the war started by Russia, which has been ongoing since February 24, 2022,\\nwas  observed.  This  may  be  related  to  the  fact  that  a  publication  appearing  in  print  is  not\\nimmediately indexed in WoS and Scopus, and may be associated with a longer period between\\nits publication and actual appearance in the databases. However, according to the information\\nprovided by the Journal Article Publishing Support Center (Elsevier, 2021), it takes 4-8 weeks\\nfrom the publication of the issue to the indexing of the text. In the case of Scopus, the document\\nis usually indexed within four days (Elsevier, 2023b). However, when analyzing the entries\\n(asked  questions  and  answers)  of  scientists  active  within  Research  Gate,  one  can  get  the\\nimpression that indexing takes a little longer, even up to two months. It can also mean that texts\\ndevoted to this issue appear mainly in journals not indexed or awaiting acceptance by WoS or\\nScopus.\\nRecent trends indicate research interest primarily in topics: Syrian refugees, Afghan and\\nwomen. Limitations of the study\\n\\nThe limitations of this study include the following, using:\\n\uf0b7  only two databases \uf0e0 which eliminated many high-quality documents that are indexed\\nin databases less popular in social sciences, or databases from which it is currently not\\npossible to easily obtain files for analysis as part of the soft tool used,\\n\uf0b7  databases  where  not  all  publications  on  crisis  migration,  refugee  migration  and\\nsustainable regional development are indexed \uf0e0 which eliminates many high-quality\\nworks published in regional journals,\\n\uf0b7  databases in which the dominant language of publication is English \uf0e0 which eliminates\\nmany high-quality texts published in less popular languages,\\n\uf0b7  narrow search criteria (stage 1) \uf0e0 which may exclude some of the documents devoted\\nto the studied area (it is however one of a characteristic feature of SLR).\\nIn general, this study offers a comprehensive review of the current state of research on crisis\\nmigration, refugee movements, and sustainable development. It highlights several key trends,\\nincluding an increasing focus on health and gender in the context of migration, the continuing\\nprominence of European migration patterns, and the integration of migration governance with\\nsustainability. However, important research gaps remain, particularly regarding the Ukrainian\\nrefugee crisis and the longer-term impacts of crisis migration on host regions. Aukasik\\n\\nTherefore,  as  emphasized  by  Helena  Sęk  (2000),  professional  burnout  is  a  sequence  of\\nrelationships  caused  by  factors  found  in  the  employee  as  well  as  in  the  surrounding\\nenvironment. Introduction\\n\\nThe dynamic growth in demand for software and the in-creasing digitization of society are\\nhaving  a  significant  impact  on  organizations  involved  in  IT  projects.  The  rapidly  changing\\nbusiness environment is driving more and more companies to adopt Agile approaches in project\\nmanagement  to  increase  their  flexibility  and  enhance  their  competitiveness  in  the  market.\\nClassical  project  management  methodologies  (also  referred  to  as  waterfall)  assume  fixed\\nproject scope that is the input of long-term planning, which tries to answer how long it would\\ntake  to  implement  the  given  set  of  requirements.  On  the  other  hand,  Agile  methodologies\\npromote adapting project scope to  a fixed timeframe of one Sprint (Kosztyan et  al., 2020).\\nBut this short-term Agile planning cannot guarantee the success of some outsourcing projects\\n(Krancher, 2020). Outsourcing IT projects means hiring an external vendor to handle IT tasks\\nor entire projects, leveraging their expertise and reducing costs (Nicolas et al., 2018).\\nThis  study  focuses  on  projects  with  uncertain  requirements,  realized  by  outsourcing\\ncompanies for which planning improvements are needed. The objective of this paper is twofold.\\nThe  first  objective  is  to  identify  outsourcing  company  project  types  that  need  planning\\nimprovements and the second one is to suggest and discuss potential planning improvements.\\nWhat is more, a sample method based on Kano model is presented that allows to incorporate\\nthe  discussed  improvements.  The  method  development  is  not  the  objective  of  this  paper,\\nbut it has been presented to demonstrate how easy is to apply the improvements.\\nThe Software Extension to the PMBOK® Guide defines software projects as endeavors that\\ninvolve  creating  new  software  products,  modifying  existing  software,  integrating  multiple\\nsoftware  components,  expanding  software  capabilities,  or  modifying  software  infrastructure\\nwithin  an  organization.  Furthermore,  software  projects  can  be  initiated  to  address  service\\nrequests, meet software maintenance needs, or provide operational support. These activities are\\nconsidered projects if they are defined as temporary undertakings aimed at delivering specific\\noutcomes (PMI, 2013).\\nThe  article  is  structured  as  follows:  Section  2  presents  a  literature  review,  Section  3\\ndescribes the research methods used to achieve the objectives of the study, Section 4 presents\\nthe obtained results, including the identification of issues in IT project planning and an analysis\\nof the underlying causes of these problems. Section 5 discusses potential improvements aimed\\nat addressing these issues. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the conclusion of the study.\\n\\n## [PDF page 357]\\n\\nPlanning improvements based on agile requirements…  357\\n\\n2.  Literature review\\n\\nBelow  a  literature  review  in  the  areas  related  to  the  topic  of  this  articles  are  presented.\\nThe  related  areas  are  IT-project  planning,  effort  estimation  techniques,  prioritization\\ntechniques, Kano model and IT project planning.\\n\\n2.1.  IT-Project planning\\n\\nWhen using Agile approach, only minimal planning is promoted (Fernandez-Diego et al.,\\n2020). Simultaneously, in Agile approach only Sprint planning horizon is usually considered,\\nand mid-term planning seems to be neglected in the literature. But mid-term planning can still\\nbe  an  important  topic  in  many  IT  projects  (Kosztyan,  2022;  Kosztyan  et  al.,  2023),\\nalso including the Agile ones or in the projects that use hybrid approach (Kosztyan et al., 2020).\\n\\n2.2.  Effort estimation techniques\\n\\nNo matter in which context (Agile, hybrid or classic) project planning is considered and no\\nmatter  what  planning  horizon  is  the  focus  of  the  research  (short  term  or  mid-term),  effort\\nestimation techniques (Fernandez-Diego, 2020) are required and very important in all project\\nplanning applications and methods. The following estimation techniques can be listed: planning\\npoker, expert judgement, wideband Delphi, machine learning, neural network, functional size\\nmeasurement,  regression,  algorithmic  methods,  fuzzy  logic,  swarm  intelligence,  Bayesian\\nnetwork, Monte Carlo, Statistical combination, Principal Component Analysis, COCO-MO II,\\nuse  case  point,  change  effort  prediction,  ontology  model,  experience  factory,  stories\\nprioritization.  It  should  be  noted  that  uncertainty  is  a  common  characteristic  of  estimation\\n(because  of  many  factors,  including  risks  that  may  materialize  during  project  execution).\\nTo handle un-certainty, it is a common practice (Shirazi et al., 2017) and common Agile practice\\n(Cao et al., 2010), to make scope changes as the project progress-es. In Agile it is the time not\\nthe scope that should be fixed (Kosztyan, 2020). Scope changes may include adjusting the scope\\nof single user stories, but it can also mean changes made on the project level, when some of the\\nnon-important user stories need to be excluded from the scope (Kosztyan, 2020). This is when\\nprioritization techniques come into play.\\n\\n2.3.  Prioritization techniques\\n\\nRequirements techniques are very popular in Agile planning context (Kosztyan et al., 2020;\\nKosztyan, 2022; Kosztyan et al., 2023), including the context of global software development\\n(Ali, Lai, 2021). Some popular examples of prioritization include Must-Should-Could-Would\\nTechnique (MoSCoW), Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Binary-Search Tree (BST), Voting\\nTechniques and Kano model (Saher et al., 2018).\\n\\n## [PDF page 358]\\n\\n358  E. Marchwicka, T. Cybulski\\n\\n2.4.  Kano model and IT project planning\\n\\nKano model is a popular model for assessing the quality of products and services and it\\nappears most frequently in the context of quality (Vavpotic et al., 2019; Golrizgasthi et al.,\\n2019). What is more, Kano model is often cited in reference to product development (Francisco,\\nSantAnna, 2019; Li, Zhang, 2021) and requirements engineering (Campese, Hornos da Costa,\\n2019). What was already mentioned above, there are Kano model applications to requirements\\nprioritization  (Saher  et  al.,  2018).  Some  other  literature  positions  include  applications  to\\nminimal viable product development (Lee, Geum, 2021).\\nNo literature positions were found that incorporate Kano model for IT project planning.\\nTo the best knowledge of authors this paper is the first one that discusses Kano model in the\\ncontext of IT project planning. Of course, there is an indirect reference from Kano to IT project\\nplanning as Kano is listed as one of the prioritization techniques used for Agile planning (which\\nwas  described  above),  but  this  paper  presents  an  original  approach  for  Kano  model\\nrepresentation  and  incorporates  an  original  and  dedicated  questionnaire  for  assessing  Kano\\nmodel quality categories. Additionally, no literature positions were found that consider Kano\\nmodel in the context of long-term Agile planning.\\n\\n3.  Methods\\n\\n3.1. Identifying project types that need planning improvements\\n\\nTo identify project types that need planning improvements, the standard deviation of the\\nestimated project durations is calculated for each type of project undertaken. Analysis of the causes of the problem in project planning area\\n\\nThe  identified  problem  was  further  analyzed  to  determine  its  causes.  For  this  purpose,\\nthe documentation of selected completed projects was reviewed in detail, and semi-structured\\ninterviews  were  conducted  with  project  managers.  Based  on  this,  the  causes  related  to  the\\nproblem were identified.\\nOne of the causes of the problem that was frequently indicated by project managers is the\\nvariability of requirements during project execution. This is an inherent challenge in IT projects\\nbecause early requirement analysis cannot fully determine the software users’ needs.\\nIn  the  case  of  internally  developed  product  development  projects,  the  planning  phase\\ninvolves collecting and analyzing requirements, which are then used for implementing novel\\nfunctionalities by the programming team.  Implemented functionalities are then presented to\\ninternal stake-holders who verify the produced software. At this stage, overlooked requirements\\nand defects can be identified, or requirement coverage by implemented functionality can be\\nvalidated.  Since  such  projects  are  executed  internally  (which  is  in  fact  not  typical  for  the\\noutsourcing companies), the project duration is mainly constrained by internal decisions within\\nthe organizations, creating a tendency to include a large number of new requirements extending\\nthe project scope and causing scope creep. It should be noted that in this case, the software is\\nnot evaluated by external users, suggesting that some internally identified requirements may\\nnot provide business value.\\nIt is also worth noting that each implemented software functionality in the project aims to\\nmeet the needs of users defined during the requirements analysis. In the examined internally\\ndeveloped  product  development  projects,  it  is  often  mentioned  that  user  requirements  are\\ndetermined based on interviews with software users and their own industry experience.\\nThe  problem  of  ad-hoc  determination  of  the  functionalities  priorities  mentioned  above\\nresults  in  lower-priority  requirements  being  implemented  earlier  than  those  associated  with\\nhigher-priority requirements, even though they may have lower business value. As a result,\\nthe project duration is extended because most of the necessary functionalities are implemented\\nin a later order.\\nIn the literature there exist some formal methods that can be used to prioritize requirements\\nin projects, for example MoSCoW method, which is a technique used to determine the priority\\nof requirements based on stakeholders’ positions. Other popular examples incorporate AHP,\\nBST, voting techniques or Kano model (Saher et al., 2018).\\n\\n## [PDF page 364]\\n\\n364  E. Marchwicka, T. Cybulski\\n\\n5.  Discussion\\n\\nBased  on  the  conducted  analysis  that  ended  up  with  identified  causes  for  the  planning\\nproblems  and  supported  by  the  literature  review  (Figure  1),  some  selected  planning\\nimprovements  can  be  proposed.  When  developing  these  improvements,  the  focus  was  on\\ngeneral solutions that can be applied in any organization carrying out IT projects. Additionally,\\nthe  proposed  improvements  were  assumed  to  be  simple  and  easy  to  implement  as  part  of\\nexisting  software  development  processes.  The  improvements  needed  to  address  the  main\\nproblems  described  above,  i.e.  they  need  to  address  requirements  uncertainty  and  need  to\\nincorporate the process of selecting user story priorities that includes business value.\\n\\n5.1.  Improvements regarding reducing requirement uncertainty\\n\\nThe  problem  of  requirement  uncertainty  is  a  well-known  issue  in  IT  projects.\\nIn the literature, requirement volatility in a project is often described as an almost inevitable\\npart  of  IT  projects,  and  it  is  also  reflected  in  one  of  the  principles  mentioned  in  the  Agile\\nManifesto: \\"Welcome changing requirements, even late in development\\" (Beck et al., 2023).\\nThe causes of requirement volatility can be identified already during the requirement gathering\\nstage.  Communication  problems  may  arise  when  gathering  information  about  requirements\\nfrom clients or potential system users by business analysts, as well as during the transfer of\\nrequirements  to  the  implementation  team,  leading  to  misinterpretation  of  the  conveyed\\ninformation  by  one  of  the  parties.  Presenting  requirements  in  the  form  of  extensive\\ndocumentation  also  does  not  solve  the  problem  because  the  recipient  may  lose  important\\nelements related to the requirements amidst the overload of details. Furthermore, each party\\nmay rely on existing knowledge that may not be relevant to the current situation. Additionally,\\nsome  knowledge  within  organizations  may  not  be  formalized,  making  it  difficult  to  codify\\nrequirements derived solely from the context and culture of the organization. Another cause is\\nthe temporary nature of requirements described in requirement documents. They only address\\nthe  requirements  specified  at  the  time  of  document  development.  If  the  document  is  not\\nregularly updated during software implementation, the resulting software will not incorporate\\nrequirement changes that occurred between their collection and the delivery of the software.\\nAnother  factor  contributing  to  requirement  volatility  is  the  prior  experience  of  potential\\nsoftware users. If the existing software is being replaced, it is often due to a lack of expected\\nfeatures. Therefore, users expect the new system to include previous features as well as new\\nfeatures  that  were  not  available  in  the  previously  used  software.  This  leads  to  the  constant\\nexpansion of the requirement list throughout the implementation of the new software (Kelly,\\n2024). To minimize requirement uncertainty, an iterative process is proposed, that allows to\\nupdate the plan, after development team gains more knowledge about the requirements. It leads\\nto the conclusions that the standard Sprint-based approach can be applied, which is not a great\\n\\n## [PDF page 365]\\n\\nPlanning improvements based on agile requirements…  365\\n\\ndiscovery. But it is important is that this iterative approach can be applied not only to the set of\\nrequirements  that  are  planned  to  be  implemented  in  the  current  Sprint,  but  to  all  the\\nrequirements available for the project. On the other hand, when time needed for delivering new\\nfunctionalities is long (which corresponds to the waterfall approach), it is difficult to obtain\\nfeedback from end users regarding the usefulness of the introduced changes. Therefore, internal\\nproduct development projects should be aligned with the Sprint release cycle, allowing for the\\ninclusion  of  previously  developed  functionalities  in  the  next  software  release,  rather  than\\nincorporating all changes only when the project scope has been completed. When requirements\\nare frequently refined and prioritized (which will be described in the following subsection),\\nit is easier to stop product development or re-negotiate the cost with the client, after project\\nexceeds too much the time that was initially agreed with the client. This perfectly fits in the\\noutsourcing company scenario for the fixed-price project that was described in the Introduction\\nsection.  The  above  observations  led  to  the  following  recommendations  that  should  be\\nconsidered for an internal product development project:\\n1.  Developing a minimum viable product (MVP) should be the objective of the project\\nfrom its very beginning. A minimum viable product refers to a product or its part that\\nhas  a  minimal  set  of  functionalities  providing  value  to  the  end  user.  Focusing  on\\ndelivering the MVP helps avoid pro-longed and ultimately unnecessary work.\\n2.  Additional effort of automating manual testing tasks should be considered in project\\nplanning, which pays off in later development phases when releasing subsequent soft-\\nware versions. Other repetitive manual tasks should also be automated. This can include\\nautomated testing and practices such as continuous integration and continuous delivery.\\nThis also seems to be obvious, but it is easy to be forgotten when planning internal\\nproduct development projects with a fixed price model, considering that the client can\\nrefuse  the  plan,  when  the  forecasted  time  horizon  becomes  too  long  or  may  sign\\na contract with a competition in such a case.\\n\\n5.2.  Improvements regarding prioritizing software features\\n\\nThe literature suggests that one of the reasons for failures in traditional project planning are\\nthe  requirements  (and  requirements  risks)  that  are  not  handled  correctly  (Krancher,  2020).\\nIn particular, the prioritization of requirements that is based on the value it brings to users and\\nclients is very important (Saher et al., 2018). The assumption in traditional planning is that all\\nidentified work will be completed (Kosztyan et al., 2020), which means that work is performed\\nin  the  most  favorable  order  from  the  perspective  of  the  implementation  team.  Therefore,\\ntowards the end of the project, if not all features have been implemented, some of them are\\nabandoned. Because the implementation was not carried out in the order of the most valuable\\nbusiness  features,  some  features  with  higher  value  than  those  delivered  are  left  out  (Cohn,\\n2006).\\n\\n## [PDF page 366]\\n\\n366  E. Marchwicka, T. Cybulski\\n\\nTo improve the process of prioritizing features to be implemented, the use of the Kano\\nmodel has been proposed, and a complete novel procedure for prioritizing based on this model\\nhas  been  developed.  Despite  the  extensive  description  of  the  Kano  model  in  the  literature,\\nthere is a lack of a comprehensive procedure that incorporates the Kano model in software\\nrelease  planning,  taking  into  account  all  steps  from  requirement  gathering  to  priority\\ndetermination for software features.\\nTo enhance the process of prioritizing software features to be implemented within the scope\\nof internal IT project planning, the following proprietary procedure utilizing the Kano model\\nhas been developed. The procedure consists of five steps as presented in Figure 7.\\n\\nFigure 7. New procedure for internal product development project planning.\\nTo  illustrate  the  practical  application  of  the  developed  prioritization  procedure,\\nthe implementation of each step of the procedure is described in detail below:\\n1.  Defining  the  project  goal  and  gathering  requirements.  Prior  to  project  planning,\\nthe  organization  establishes  a  high-level  vision  and  product  roadmap.  At  this  stage,\\nthe  product  manager  is  responsible  for  preparing  the  initial  project  goal  and,\\nconsequently,  the  product  developed  within  the  project.  Before  starting  to  gather\\nrequirements  and  analyzing  stakeholders,  the  product  manager  should  determine  the\\nstrategic  reason  for  developing  the  product  according  to  the  product  manager’s\\nassumptions. To achieve this, the product manager should analyze current opportunities\\nand threats, ideally based on both historical and current data. SWOT analysis can be\\na helpful method (Benzaghta et al., 2012). Based on this analysis, the product manager,\\ntogether with the forming project team, can justify why the proposed product vision is\\nthe  right  direction  for  development.  The  next  step  is  gathering  requirements,\\nwhich  enables  the  preparation  of  a  formal  requirements  specification.  To  do  this,\\nit is recommended to use techniques such as brainstorming, documentation analysis,\\ninterface  analysis,  focus  groups,  interviews,  observations,  prototyping,  reverse\\nengineering, or questionnaires (Young, 2002; Maguire, Bevan, 2002).\\n\\n## [PDF page 367]\\n\\nPlanning improvements based on agile requirements…  367\\n\\n2.  Mapping requirements to user stories. The identified requirements should be presented\\nin the form of user stories. Expressing needs in this format facilitates understanding of\\nthe  planned  software  features  that  will  address  the  discovered  user  requirements.\\nIt is important to ensure that the user stories are at an appropriate level of generality,\\ndetailed  enough  to  understand  the  expected  functionality  but  without  unnecessary\\ndetails that overshadow the overall vision of the software features. To accomplish this,\\na hierarchical approach can be used. For example, identified general requirements are\\nlisted in the top of the hierarchy. Then, for each requirement, the user activity related to\\nthe software is described. In the final step, for each user activity, low-level details should\\nbe specified in the form of a user story. The user story template \\"As a <user>, I want\\n<need>, so that <goal to achieve>\\" can be used for this purpose. Similar hierarchical\\napproach, together with similar user story template is presented in (Wautelet et al., 2014)\\nbut requirements are called functionalities there. An example table illustrating mapping\\nof requirements to user stories is presented in Figure 8.\\n\\nFigure 8. Illustrative example of mapping requirements to user stories.\\n3.  Preparation  of  the  Kano  evaluation  form  and  conducting  attractiveness  assessment.\\nFor each defined user story (NOTE: the subsequent text refers to user stories, although\\nthey are not in a standard form of a user story template) a Kano evaluation form can be\\ndeveloped to assess the attractiveness of the planned user stories among its potential\\nusers.  The  evaluation  form  suggested  in  this  paper  consists  of  a  list  of  functional\\n(i.e.,  <How  would  you  assess  the  software  if  the  user  story  is  implemented=)  and\\ndysfunctional questions (i.e., <How would you assess the software if the user story is\\nNOT implemented=) for each examined user story. Cybulski\\n\\nTable 2.\\nUser stories evaluation form template\\nHow would you rate the  Like it  Like it  Neutral  Don’t like it  Don’t like it\\nproduct if:  very much  very much\\nSatisfaction  2  1  0  -1  -2\\n1a. you could …\\n1b. you couldn’t …\\n2a. you could …\\n2b. you couldn’t …\\n…  …  …  …  …  …\\n\\nThe Kano model suggests five possible quality categories for the products and services,\\nthat are based on the customer satisfaction level and the degree to which the product or service\\ncan be delivered (Aslamiyah, 2023). These categories are: Must-be (here referred to as MB),\\nOne-dimensional  (here:  1D),  Attractive  (here:  AT),  Reverse  (here:  RV)  and  Indifferent\\n(here: IN). These categories are usually depicted in two listed dimensions of satisfaction level\\nand  a  degree  of  implementation.  MB  category  means  that  when  this  product  or  service  is\\nimplemented,  customers  are  neutral  but  are  not  satisfied  when  it  is  not  implemented.\\n1D category means that customers are satisfied when the product or service is implemented and\\ndissatisfied when not. AT means satisfaction when product/service is achieved fully, but it does\\nnot cause dissatisfaction when it is not implemented. RV means high level of dissatisfaction\\nwhen implemented and IN is reserved for product/services that neither cause satisfaction nor\\ndissatisfaction  and  are  indifferent  for  the  customer. Introduction\\n\\nDevelopment  is  perceived  as  an  interdisciplinary  and  very  broad  meaning  (Mitra  et  al.,\\n2023; Hajian, Kashani, 2021; Payán-Sánchez et al., 2021; Sen, Kumar, 2023). It is also difficult\\nto  clearly  define  development  in  the  area  of  transport  (Guirao,  2021;  Wiktorowska-Jasiak,\\n2016). This may result from the specificity of transport and its types (Oviedo, Nieto-Combariza,\\n2021; Wiśniewska et al., 2017). The role of transport and (more broadly) logistics infrastructure\\nin economic growth is one of the most frequently discussed topics in recent times. Compared\\nto development expenditures such as education and health, which produce results in a very long\\ntime horizon, the progress of investments in infrastructure is physically visible and can bring\\nresults in a shorter time. In the field of economics (especially political), it is widely believed\\nthat the development of the logistics sector can change the economy in a few years (Guirao,\\n2021;  Chia-Lin2021;  Arshed  et  al.,  2022).  Road  infrastructure  is  part  of  the  transport\\ninfrastructure. It includes elements of the transport network used by means of transport during\\nmovement and standstill (Harańczyk, 2015). The road transport infrastructure is divided into\\nlinear  infrastructure  (road  network)  and  point  infrastructure  (passenger,  cargo,  means  of\\ntransport  and  people  services)  (Wojciechowski  et  al.,  2009).  However,  the  development  of\\ninfrastructure to a large  extent, if we consider its pace, depends on the  number and size of\\nproblems, deficiencies, incompatibilities, etc. The linear infrastructure of road transport can be\\nclassified  according  to  the  criterion  of  the  function  performed  and  the  following  roads  are\\ndistinguished: national,  voivodship, poviat, commune, company, local and municipal roads.\\nSuch a correlation may occur, for example, between regional development and the condition of\\nroad infrastructure or public transport (Guirao, 2021; Oviedo, Nieto-Combariza, 2021; Vulevic,\\n2018). Therefore, an important element of development is improvement. Transport logistics\\ninfrastructure  is  defined  as  a  complex  of  interconnected  elements  ensuring  material  flows.\\nIts  key  functions  include,  among  others,  improving  the  regional  level  of  socio-economic\\ndevelopment  (thanks  to  the  efficient  functioning  of  various  types  of  transport  and  building\\na sustainable transport network), meeting the needs of economic entities for transport facilities\\n(including logistics), or improving the functioning of the storage system.\\nIn recent years, the problems of transport logistics require a comprehensive study, namely,\\na thorough consideration of the processes and objects of transport logistics infrastructure in the\\ncontext  of  their  interaction  as  a  complex  system  (Bychkov  et  al.,  2016).  The  term\\n\\"infrastructure\\"  comes  from  the  Latin  language,  namely  the  word  \\"infra\\"  is  understood  as\\nfoundations  or  foundations,  while  \\"structure\\"  means  the  arrangement  of  elements  of  some\\nundefined  configuration.  As  defined  in  the  Cambridge  Advance  Learner’s  Dictionary\\n& Thesaurus (2016), \\"infrastructure\\" is basic systems and services such as transport and power,\\nthat a country or organization uses to operate effectively. Infrastructure is an element of the\\nterritorial structure of the national economy, which consists of transport, communication, trade,\\n\\n## [PDF page 377]\\n\\nSelected problems of infrastructure development…  377\\n\\nenergy and water management, as well as housing (Skorobogatova, Kuzmina-Merlino, 2017).\\nIn the case of the development of transport infrastructure, three of the many effects that are of\\nparticular importance are mentioned. Among other things, these are direct benefits for users,\\nachieved  through  the  impact  of  investment  projects  in  road  infrastructure  on  traffic  safety.\\nThe effects include a smaller number of road accidents, which are not only personal tragedies,\\nbut above all financial. For over several decades, in efficient and developed economies, the loss\\nof health or life has been converted into measurable economic and financial losses (lower tax\\nrevenues, lower consumption, loss of part of the national income, payment of compensation,\\ncosts of treatment and rehabilitation, etc.) (Górczyńska, Krawczyk, 2014). Improvement is one\\nof  the  significant  determinants  of  pro-development  activities,  in  particular  in  terms  of\\norganizational, material and social conditions, including in the area of transport (Wojewódzka-\\nKról,  ZaBoga,  2016).  This  may  result  from  the  necessity  and  essence  of  the  implemented\\nchanges, in particular to increase the existing transport potential (of the  country, individual\\nterritorial  units)  as  well  as  the  satisfaction  of  market  stakeholders  (Kaczyńska,  Korycińska,\\n2014).  Because it is them: entrepreneurs, residents, offices, tourists, etc. who build loyalty,\\nimage and also affect the profitability of investments (e.g. road, public transport infrastructure)\\nand transport entities. By increasing the safety of road users, both individual and public, we can\\ninfluence the individual location decisions of the stakeholders of a given market. Therefore,\\nit should be remembered that by improving the  quality of life of the society, as part of the\\ndevelopment of infrastructure, we increase the socio-economic and economic opportunities of\\nboth local government units in a given region and entities operating there (Olkiewicz, 2020).\\nThe analysis of the literature shows that all transport development activities are carried out\\naccording to identified needs (area of aware market needs), action planning and action (method\\nof achieving technical parameters in accordance with the assumptions), compliance control and\\nimprovement of previous stages (verification and standardization of the effect achieved) form\\na comprehensive whole (Gibbons et al., 2019; Meijer et al., 2018). Therefore, they cover the\\nareas of strategic management (e.g. creating long-term development of  road infrastructure),\\noperational  management  (e.g.  efficiency  and  optimization  of  executive  processes),\\norganizational (e.g. making activities related to issuing permits, tender procedures, etc.) more\\nflexible, resources (e.g. financial ), safety (e.g. in environmental protection aspects), quality\\n(e.g.  performance  of  individual  elements  of  infrastructure  (technology  and  raw  material\\napplications),  projects  (e.g.  implementation  of  innovation  or  creating  cooperation  between\\nvarious research and development centers, etc.), and others (Persia et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2020;\\nReshetnikova et al., 2021). It also indicates the complexity of identifying factors determining\\nthe  development  of  transport.  Each  of  the  above-mentioned  areas  of  management,  or  its\\ncomponents, may have a greater or lesser impact on the implementation of changes in transport.\\nGlobal threats to the development of the transport system (passenger and freight) resulting,\\namong  others,  from  transport  congestion,  climate  change,  negative  impact  on  the  natural\\nenvironment and living conditions of society, make it necessary to apply a sustainable transport\\n\\n## [PDF page 378]\\n\\n378  M. Olkiewicz, J.A. Dyczkowska\\n\\npolicy. According to the OECD, the transport policy should be based on the principles of: access\\nto transport services while maintaining the requirements of health and environmental safety;\\nreducing  the  negative  impact  on  the  environment;  economic  efficiency  or  intergenerational\\njustice (OECD, 2004; Farhadi, 2015; Churchill et al., 2021). Meeting such expectations requires\\na broader perspective on the region’s logistics, mobility, access to the infrastructure of \\"green\\nzones\\", etc. through the prism of time and investment financing opportunities. It is also in line\\nwith  the  state’s  transport  policy,  as  it  is  aimed,  among  others,  at:  reducing  the  nuisance  of\\ntransport for residents; protection of the natural environment and its non-renewable resources;\\nreduce  the  risk  of  accidents;  ensuring  equality  in  access  to  means  of  transport,  or  creating\\nappropriate conditions for the functioning of public, freight and individual transport (Kalisiak-\\nMędelska,  2017;  Wolniak  et  al.,  2019).  Poland’s  road  infrastructure  still  requires  large\\nexpenditures on development and ensuring appropriate standards of the existing network in\\norder to be able to meet the needs of the market resulting from the increase in the exchange of\\ngoods and the constantly growing passenger traffic. A well-developed and modern network of\\nmotorways,  expressways  and  expressways  is  a  prerequisite  for  the  proper  functioning  of\\neconomically developed countries (regions).\\n\\n2.  Materials and methods\\n\\nThe aim of the study was to show the impact of selected infrastructure elements on the sense\\nof development of the region  among the inhabitants. As part of the research, the  following\\nhypotheses were put formulated:\\n\uf0b7  H1 – an increase in expenditure on the modernization and development of infrastructure\\nincreases the attractiveness and satisfaction of the inhabitants of a given region.\\n\uf0b7  H2 – an increase in the number of individual infrastructural linear elements increases\\nthe efficiency of communication and improves the quality of life of residents.\\nThe research conducted in December 2022 in the Middle Pomeranian region focused on\\ntwo  main  cities  (of  this  region),  i.e.  Koszalin  and  Slupsk,  making  a  comparative  analysis.\\nRespondents in the amount of 100 people (50 people from each city) took part in the survey in\\nJune 2022. In Koszalin, 37 women and 14 men, aged 18-30 (47%), 30-45 (17%) and 56 and\\nover (36%) participated in the study. Due to the specificity of the scope of the study, it was\\nfound  that  as  many  as  92%  of  the  respondents  are  professionally  active  in  the  surveyed\\npopulation. In Slupsk, 32 women and 18 men, aged 18-30 (58%), 30-45 (14%) and 56 and over\\n(28%), participated in the study. Due to the specificity of the scope of the study, it was found\\nthat as many as 91% of the respondents are professionally active in the surveyed population.\\n\\n## [PDF page 379]\\n\\nSelected problems of infrastructure development…  379\\n\\n3. Conclusions\\n\\nThe plan of road investments in the area of Middle Pomeranian Region for the coming years\\nassumes  high  investments.  It  plans  to  expand  national  roads,  bypasses,  motorways  and\\nexpressways on a large scale. The most important goal of the Program adopted by the Council\\nof  Ministers  is  to  shorten  the  travel  time  between  major  Polish  cities  by  at  least  15%.\\nIt is important that the government allocates funds for this, as well as for the maintenance of\\nexisting  roads,  which  is  proved  by  the  analysis  presented  in  the  article.  One  of  the  major\\nproblems related to the road infrastructure is the poor condition of the road surface, which is\\nemphasized  by  the  inhabitants  of  Koszalin  and  Slupsk,  and  the  related  renovation  needs.\\nOnly half of the national roads managed by the GDDKiA (General Directorate for National\\nRoads and Highways) meet the conditions for classifying them as being in good condition.\\nRenovation of linear infrastructure elements (such as viaducts in Koszalin) may affect not only\\nthe quality of movement of the city’s inhabitants, but also the entire area of Middle Pomeranian\\nregion.\\nThe transport and logistics integration of Middle Pomeranian region is based on the concept\\nof  the  Northern  Transport  Corridor  and  a  number  of  key  projects  in  the  development  of\\ntransport.  The  transport  network  that  has  not  been  completed  should  be  supplemented  as\\ncurrently  S11. One  of  such  modern  innovative  solutions  is  the  use  of  drones  for  military\\napplications  (Li  et  al.,  2022;  Rozmirez-Montoya  et  al.,  2022).  The  issue  of  innovation  is\\nimportant for the development of the contemporary military industry because as a result of the\\nuse of innovations, including open innovations, the effectiveness of technical solutions used in\\nthe  military  can  be  significantly  improved  (Sloane,  2011;  Gajdzik,  Wolniak,  2021,  2022;\\nLee et al., 2018, Bober et al., 2017). Such solutions are in line with the contemporary trends in\\nthe  implementation  of  the  so-called  Industry  4.0  concept,  which  is  based,  inter  alia,\\non digitization, robotization and application of artificial intelligence (Olkiewicz et al., 2019;\\nDrozd,  Wolniak,  2021).  The  innovative  use  of  drones  presented  in  this  publication  is\\nan example of this. In the literature, there are currently three parallel terms related to the subject\\nof drones: (UE, 2019) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) (Tice, 2009), unmanned aerial system\\n(UAS) and the most popular 3 drone. All of these terms refer to an aircraft that does not require\\na  flight  crew  on  board  and  is  not  able  to  board  passengers  (Fowler,  2014).  The  aircraft  is\\nremotely piloted (guided by a pilot that does not have to see the drone) or performs the flight\\nautonomously (by itself, using the autopilot or other system on-board). In addition, the term\\nunmanned aerial system refers to a system comprising several components. The components\\ninclude a drone, a control system, a telecommunication link to pilot the drone and the drone’s\\nequipment (Aroosa, 2021; Fairehead, 2021).\\nSoon, wars could be fought without the participation of humans. Intelligent drones will start\\nto appear on the battlefields, and other autonomous machines will join them (Johnson, 2019;\\nHallaq et al., 2017). Such innovations in the military constitute a revolution on the modern\\nbattlefield, changing many aspects of the warfare, especially in the case of asymmetric conflicts,\\nwhere one of the sides is weaker in terms of conventional military (Bousquet, 2017; Boyle,\\n2015; Mack, 1975; Jacob, 2017; Yun, Liu, 2019). The issue of asymmetric wars is important\\nbecause contemporary armed conflicts are usually of this nature (Cianciara, 2021).\\nThe ongoing war in Ukraine and the previous conflicts of recent years have proven that\\ndrones are becoming increasingly used equipment on the battlefield (Byman, 2013). They have\\nbeen  an  effective  weapon  against  military  units  armed  with  Russian  equipment  in  the  past.\\nThey got a lot of publicity during the clashes over the Nagorno-Karabakh region between the\\narmed  forces  of  Azerbaijan  and  Armenia  in  the  fall  of  2020  (Rauch,  2021).  It  needs  to  be\\nemphasized that the former one was largely modernized by Turkey in an ongoing process since\\nthe 1990s. This cooperation has intensified over the next years. Drones, in particular, achieve\\ngood  results  in  asymmetric  warfare,  where  one  side  has  a  major  military  advantage\\n(Wolfendale, 2021; Jeangène, 2023).\\nDrones have also been used by guerrilla groups in recent years. It was probably the Syrian\\nguerrilla  who  was  behind  the  spectacular  attack  on  Russian  military  bases  in  that  country\\n(Baggiarini,  Rupka,  2020;  Malaviya,  2020).  The  operation  was  carried  out  by  a  swarm  of\\ndrones, which were programmed with specific targets along with the GPS data, thus they were\\nautonomous. Some of the drones attacked a Russian support vessel. The attack was mostly\\n\\n## [PDF page 389]\\n\\nDrone swarms 3 as an innovative tool…  389\\n\\nprevented. The Saudis, however, failed to prevent the attack of 10-25 drones carried out by the\\nYemen rebels aimed at one of Saudi’s largest oil refineries (Johnson, 2020; Behnke, 2020).\\nThe anti-aircraft defence system was ineffective due to the low flight path and numerous angles\\nof  attack.  The  operation  resulted  in  a  massive  fire  at  this  oil  installation  (Ruschi,  2020;\\nGusterson, 2019).\\nDrones are capable of destroying ground targets no worse than bombers. At the same time,\\nbeing  much  more  precise.  Contemporary  combat  drones  are  becoming  an  increasingly\\nimportant component of weaponry (Bauer et al, 2022).\\nIn order not to waste the potential of the purchased combat drones and the taxpayers’ money,\\nthe  army  has  to  combine  innovative  technology  and  new  tactics.  The  drone  swarms  tactic,\\nin particular, has great potential in terms of innovation (Bergen, Sims, 2021).\\nThe analysis of the respected literature (Fowler, 2014; Aroosa, 2021; Fairehead, 2021; Borg,\\n2021; Antebi, 2016; Dekel et al., 2017; Benjamin, 2013; Kostenko et al., 2022; Schilling, 2022;\\nRagab  et  al.,  2022;  Soria  et  al.,  2022;  Iacovelli,  Grieco,  2021)  indicates  a  research  gap\\nconcerning  the  use  of  drones  on  the  contemporary  battlefield,  in  particular  regarding  the\\nso-called  drone  swarms.  There  are  publications  on  drone  swarms  and  drone  swarms\\nmanagement,  but  there  are  no  detailed  publications  on  the  military  use  of  this  innovation.\\nSwarms of drones can be used in search operations, transport networks or monitoring. The point\\nis  for  the  swarm  to  not  only  control  its  surroundings  but  also  itself  and  should  not  need\\nan  operator  (Kostenko  et  al.,  2022;  Schilling,  2022;  Ragab  et  al.,  2022;  Soria  et  al.,  2022;\\nIacovelli, Grieco, 2021). It is also possible to use them for military purposes. From the military\\nstandpoint, a swarm is an autonomous, interconnected group of small unmanned aerial systems\\nthat are working together to achieve a shared objective with the operator on or in the loop.\\nCoordination  and  responsiveness  are  what  distinguish  between  a  real  swarm  and  the\\nemployment of the drones en masse. The latter occurs when a large number of drones are used\\nagainst a single target, mainly to incapacitate it by overpowering its defences (Gagaridis, 2022).\\nIn  particular,  no  studies  focusing  on  the  analysis  of  the  possibility  of  using  simulation\\nmethods to manage innovative drone swarms for military purposes were found. This publication\\ntries to fill in this gap by examining the options of employing such innovative solutions in the\\narmed forces.\\nThe objective of this publication is to analyse the possibilities of using drone swarms as\\nan innovative battlefield tool.\\nThe research includes simulation methods by using computer simulation methods based on\\nthe so-called random walk 3 Brownian motion and Brownian bridge. Journal  of  Physics:  Conference\\nSeries, 2213(1), 012007.\\n\\n## [PDF page 409]\\n\\nS I L E S I A N  U N I V E R S I T Y  O F  T E C H N O L O G Y  P U B L I S H I N G  H O U S E\\n\\nSCIENTIFIC PAPERS OF SILESIAN UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY  2025\\nORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT SERIES NO. 215\\n\\nAPPLICABILITY OF SERIOUS GAMES TO PROJECT’S MANAGER\\nCOMPETENCIES ASSESSMENT – LITERATURE REVIEW\\n\\nMarcin OPAS1*, Marcin WARDASZKO2\\n\\n1 Kozminski University, Warsaw; mopas@kozminski.edu.pl, ORCID: 0000-0003-3941-1846\\n2 Kozminski University, Warsaw; wardaszko@kozminski.edu.pl, ORCID: 0000-0001-5411-7894\\n* Correspondence author\\n\\nPurpose: Assessing project manager competencies is a complex but essential factor in ensuring\\nproject  success.  Traditional  assessment  methods  may  not  adequately  address  project\\nmanagement’s  dynamic  and  multifaceted  nature.  Serious  games  have  shown  promise  in\\neducation and training, providing a realistic, interactive, and risk-free environment to develop\\nand assess skills. However, their application to project manager competency assessment needs\\nto be explored. The research aimed to investigate the current state of serious games used in\\nproject management, particularly their role in assessing project manager competencies.\\nDesign/methodology/approach: The authors use systematic and classical literature reviews\\nand analyze the current research areas of simulation games adoption for project management,\\nlearning goals and skills, and assessment models. The literature review findings are compared\\nto the competence model of the IPMA and analyzed for similarities and differences.\\nFindings: The findings of this research confirm that serious games could be used not only to\\ntrain but also to assess (certify) the competencies of project managers formally, understood as\\nan assessment of a project manager9s ability to apply knowledge, skills, and abilities in practical\\nsituations.\\nResearch limitations/implications: The study relies on articles published between 2000 and\\n2023 and available in English, which may exclude relevant works in other languages or older\\nfoundational  studies.  The  selection  was  limited  by  the  accessibility  of  articles  in  specific\\ndatabases, potentially omitting key contributions from less accessible or alternative sources.\\nThe analysis was conducted on only two serious games, which may not represent the full range\\nof serious games available for project management competency assessment.\\nPractical implications: The research suggests that serious game developers should expand the\\nscope  of  competencies  assessed,  including  behavioral  and  contextual  dimensions,  to  offer\\na more holistic evaluation.\\nSocial  implications:  By  aligning  serious  games  with  international  competency  models  like\\nIPMA,  the  research  supports  the  development  of  globally  recognized  standards  for  project\\nmanagement skill assessment.\\nOriginality/value:  The  study  innovatively  uses  the  IPMA  Level  C  certification  process  as\\na  benchmark  to  evaluate  the  potential  of  serious  games  in  formal  competency  assessment.\\nThis  approach  bridges  the  gap  between  gamification  in  learning  and  formal  professional\\ncertification standards.\\nKeywords: serious games, project manager, competencies assessment, complexity.\\nCategory of the paper: Literature review.\\n\\nhttp://dx.doi.org/10.29119/1641-3466.2025.215.25  http://managementpapers.polsl.pl/\\n\\n## [PDF page 410]\\n\\n410  M. Opas, M. Wardaszko\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nProject management is an increasingly important specialty nowadays. Currently, more than\\n20% of global economic activity takes place as projects (de Rezende, 2019; Gemunden, 2013),\\nand  in  some  emerging  economies,  it  exceeds  30%  (Bredillet  C.  N.,  2010).  Moreover,  the\\n8projectification9 of organizational work is today observed in almost every industry (Kuura,\\n2020; Bakker, 2010; Sydow, 2004), and organizations increasingly use projects to achieve their\\nstrategic objectives (Morris, 2004).\\nEffective project management helps organizations improve  efficiency and reduce waste,\\nwhich  results  in  cost  savings  and  improved  profitability  (Kaufmann,  2022).  Organizations\\nskilled in project management can develop a competitive advantage by delivering projects more\\nefficiently and effectively than their competitors (Milosevic, 2003).\\nWith the increasing complexity of projects in various industries (de Rezende, 2019), project\\nmanagement has become a critical skill set for organizations (Maylor, 2017) to successfully\\ncomplete  projects  on  time,  within  budget,  and  with  the  desired  level  of  quality.  There  are\\nnumerous reasons why project management has become an important profession. In industries\\nsuch as construction, engineering, IT, and healthcare, there is a need for professionals who can\\nmanage these projects effectively. Kriz  et  al.  (Kriz,  2022,  p.  4)  define  a  serious  game  as  <a  reconstruct  of\\nimportant aspects of the reference system; therefore it is an abstract model of reality with less\\ncomplexity and fewer details=. The major challenge of project management is its complexity\\nand  decision-making  in  a  rapidly  changing  environment.  Therefore,  the  simulation  of\\na  simplified  reality  model  lays  solid  grounds  for  various  applications  of  serious  gaming  in\\nproject management.\\nSerious  games  are  typically  created  to  teach  or  develop  specific  skills,  knowledge,\\nor behaviors and can be used in various contexts, including education, training, and personal\\ndevelopment. The  very  important  debriefing  is  represented  in  the  ELC\\n(Reflective  Observation  and  Abstract  Conceptualization)  (Schwagele,  2014). Medical simulators are used to train and certify healthcare professionals in various skills\\nand  procedures,  such  as  surgical  techniques,  diagnostic  imaging,  and  emergency  medicine.\\n\\n## [PDF page 420]\\n\\n420  M. Opas, M. Wardaszko\\n\\nThese simulators can provide a realistic and immersive learning experience, allowing learners\\nto practice their skills in a safe and controlled environment. For example, Lap Sim (LapSim,\\n2023)  is  used  for  laparoscopic  surgery  training  and  assessment,  da  Vinci  Surgical  System\\n(Da Vinci, 2023) for robotic-assisted surgery training and assessment or VirtaMed ArthroS™\\n(Medical training simulators, 2023) for arthroscopic surgery training and assessment.\\n\\n4.4.  Project management, serious games, and competencies assessment\\n\\nThe main purpose of the research was to review the literature, investigate the application of\\nserious  games  in  project  management,  and  analyze  their  utilization  for  the  project  manager\\ncompetency assessment. The research question was: are there any serious games that formally\\nassess  project  manager  competencies?  The  identification  and  selection  of  games  were  the\\nsubject  of  several  stages.  From  January  2023  to  May  2023,  intensive  research  was\\nsystematically  performed  using  multiple  sources,  i.e.,  research  papers,  international  gaming\\nawards,  and  contacts  with  experts,  to  identify  the  project  management  games  available.\\nThis investigation led to the identification of over thirty serious games that were relevant to the\\nscope  of  research,  i.e.,  Construction  Project  Management  Game  (Hassan,  2021),  GRAPM\\n(Miler, 2016), SiMSE (Navarro, 2004), DELIVER! (von Wangenheim, 2012), PMQUIZ (Petri,\\n2016) and others. However, a selection was required to select the games that were suitable for\\nthe scope of the research. The following criteria were followed to undertake this selection:\\n\uf0b7  the game should be available and used for project management training,\\n\uf0b7  adequate  and  publicly  accessible  documentation  should  be  available  to  evaluate  the\\ngame9s applicability to the competency assessment process,\\n\uf0b7  the serious game scoring system should assess the player in as many CEs as possible\\nusing IPMA9s project manager competency assessment model.\\nAs a result, two games were selected. The first is SimulTrain (SimulTrain, 2023), developed\\nby  STS  Sauter  Training  &  Simulation  SA  (STS).  SimulTrain  is  a  project  management\\nsimulation that allows participants to manage a virtual project from start to finish. Its general\\nobjective is to train in three fundamental areas, divided into various learning points. The first\\none is project leadership, where participants learn to lead a project in its entirety, which includes\\ndealing  with  the  project\'s  stakeholders,  the  project9s  functions  complexity,  and  priorities\\nmanagement.  The  second  one  is  project  management,  where  participants  learn  to  manage\\na project on a day-to-day basis by making decisions which being a project manager requires\\nupdating,  planning,  checking  progress,  managing  quality,  and  organizing  project  reviews.\\nThey also learn how to make decisions as a team. They have to make decisions requiring them\\nto negotiate cost, deadline, quality, and motivation goals, as well as manage conflict within the\\nteam and consider each participant’s views. The last one is resource management, designed to\\nteach  how  to  plan  the  involvement  of  resources  for  maximum  efficiency.  There  are  eleven\\nsimulated project manager functions, such as project planning, budgeting, risk management,\\ndecision-making, or project controlling.\\n\\n## [PDF page 421]\\n\\nApplicability of serious games…  421\\n\\nFigure 2. SimulTrain users dashboard.\\nSource: SimulTrain, 2023.\\nSimulTrain  is  primarily  used  in  combination  with  classroom  activities  but  can  also  be\\nplayed completely online. Training is conducted with teams of four participants where learners\\nplay the  role of the project manager. The teams  must plan and execute  a typical mid-sized\\nproject  in  two  or  three  sessions  of  3-4  hours  each.  The  teams  are  confronted  with  many\\nsituations requiring quick decisions while considering all project parameters (cost, deadlines,\\nquality,  and  human  factors).  The  teams  are  scored  against  five  parameters:  cost,  schedule,\\nquality, motivation, and risk. The trainer can adjust the weight of each parameter to accomplish\\nvarious learning objectives, i.e., focus of players on project cost management. The SimulTrain\\nis used in trainings for project managers, project participants, top management, managers and\\ntheir reports, and students of business schools and technical universities. The game is available\\nin more than 22 languages, and there are up to 10 scenarios, reflecting project simulations in\\ndifferent  areas. According to STS, the simulator  is used in more than 51 countries and has\\ncontributed to the training of more than 200.000 project managers (About STS, 2023).\\nThe  second  one  is  <Project  Management=  (PM),  developed  by  REVAS  (Games,  2023).\\nSimilarly to SimulTrain, it is a simulation that allows participants to manage a virtual project\\nfrom start to finish the game and its main objective is to train in three fundamental areas of\\nproject  leadership,  operational  management,  and  resource  management.  Players  can  play\\nindividually or in small (three to four people) teams. The game scenario starts with the endeavor\\norientation session, where project objectives and stakeholders are identified, and the company9s\\norganizational structure, budgets, and resources are reviewed. In the second part, players are\\nexpected  to  develop  the  project  plan,  including  the  project9s  schedule,  budget,  resource\\nallocation, and risk management plan. The third phase focuses on project execution with several\\nrounds,  each  representing  one  calendar  month.  To  simulate  real-life  project  challenges,\\nunexpected events are introduced, such as late materials delivery, conflict with stakeholders,\\nor  project  team  members  getting  sick.  During  the  game,  players  score  against  eight  key\\ncompetence areas presented in Figure 3.\\n\\n## [PDF page 422]\\n\\n422  M. Opas, M. The article sample was limited to both period\\nand online availability, search engines, and language (English). The authors are aware that there\\nare significantly more articles and papers published in the area of concern and that the selection\\nis limited due to the methods applied and other constraints. The authors9 future efforts will aim\\nto broaden and study the underlying design methodologies, narratives for serious game design,\\nand project management competency assessment methods in more detail. The planned future\\nwork aims to extend the classifications of project management serious game usage and look for\\nopportunities to create a model of the project manager competency assessment serious game to\\nimprove the project manager education and assessment process.\\nThis research confirms that serious games could be used not only to train but also to assess\\n(certify) formally project managers’ competencies, understood as an assessment of a project\\nmanager9s  ability  to  apply  knowledge,  skills,  and  abilities  in  practical  situations.  Firstly,\\nthey are designed to simulate real-life scenarios. Therefore, assessing competencies is more\\nrealistic and comprehensive as project managers apply their knowledge and skills in a simulated\\nenvironment resembling real-life situations. Secondly, serious games may simplify the major\\nchallenge of real-world project management 3 their complexity, as serious games are an abstract\\nmodel of reality with less complexity and fewer details. Thirdly, serious games can provide\\nimmediate feedback from senior project management experts to project managers, allowing\\nthem  to  understand  their  mistakes  and  correct  them  in  real  time.  At  the  same  time,  senior\\nmanagement experts9 observations and performance evaluations can also be used to perform\\nthe project manager assessment center role. However, the analysis of the two selected project\\nmanagement  serious  games  depicts  the  current  deficiencies  of  game-based  project  manager\\ncompetencies assessment compared to the IPMA Level C assessment process. The first one is\\nthat only a few of twenty-eight project manager competencies are assessed, which results in\\n\\n## [PDF page 424]\\n\\n424  M. Opas, M. Wardaszko\\n\\na very selective assessment of a minority of them. Additionally, as game scenarios focus on\\nproject life cycle management, their scoring systems reflect the project operational management\\nmastery level, not the overall project manager competencies assessment. Finally, although the\\nbriefing  sessions  are  foreseen  in  games9  scenarios,  their  ultimate  objective  is  reflection  or\\ndiscussion  of  activities  performed,  not  a  formal  assessment  of  project  management\\ncompetencies  in  an  interview  or  assessment  center.  Such  a  situation  creates  a  research\\nopportunity through the identified research gap in finding the balance between game design,\\nthe IPMA competence model, and simulation games as an assessment tool. It also creates the\\nchallenge of marring the diverging angles of these competing research areas.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1.  Global Alliance for Project Performance Standards.
