Introduction\\n\\nThe advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) represents a pivotal moment in the\\nevolution of technology, exerting a significant influence across a range of sectors, including\\ninformation  technology  (IT)  project  management.  GenAI  comprises  sophisticated  machine\\nlearning models that are capable of creating content, generating solutions and solving complex\\nproblems autonomously based on specific inputs and constraints. Such capabilities facilitate the\\nautomation  of  intricate  tasks  and  enhance  decision-making  processes,  rendering  GenAI\\na  particularly  pertinent  technology  in  the  context  of  the  dynamic  landscape  of  IT  project\\nmanagement.  The  IT  sector  is  distinguished  by  a  high  degree  of  complexity  and  rapid\\ndevelopment cycles, which in turn requires the implementation of innovative approaches to the\\neffective  management  of  resources,  schedules  and  risks.  Conventional  project  management\\nmethodologies are often insufficient for addressing the growing volume and intricacy of data,\\nevolving  expectations  of  diverse  stakeholders,  and  the  necessity  for  continuous  innovation.\\nThe complexity and demands of IT projects have increased, necessitating the implementation\\nof effective management strategies to ensure their success. In this context, project management\\nassumes a pivotal role in orchestrating the tasks, resources, and stakeholders in a manner that\\nensures the efficient achievement of project objectives within defined constraints. Nevertheless,\\nthe  efficacy  of  project  management  methodologies  is  subject  to  question  in  light  of  the\\ninherently dynamic and complex nature of IT projects.\\nThe ability of GenAI to generate predictive insights, optimise workflows, and support real-\\ntime decision-making makes it a uniquely positioned technology to address these challenges.\\nBy enhancing operational efficiency and strategic foresight, GenAI offers a transformative tool\\nfor IT project managers to navigate the intricacies of modern projects.\\nDespite the considerable promise that GenAI holds for the field of IT project management,\\nit  remains  a  relatively  unexplored  area  within  both  academic  and  practical  discourse.\\nWhile  existing  studies  have  provided  extensive  examination  of  the  integration  of  artificial\\nintelligence in broader organisational functions, limited attention has been paid to the specific\\nuse  cases  and  impact  of  GenAI  in  managing  IT  projects.  The  extant  literature  frequently\\nconcentrates on general AI applications, thereby neglecting the distinctive characteristics and\\ndemands  of  IT  project  environments.  These  include  adaptive  planning,  cross-functional\\ncollaboration, and rapid technological shifts.\\nFurthermore, the potential of GenAI to enhance decision-making, resource optimisation,\\nand project lifecycle management has  yet to be systematically studied. There is a dearth of\\nempirical  evidence  on  how  GenAI  tools  can  be  tailored  to  align  with  established  project\\nmanagement  methodologies,  such  as  Agile,  Scrum,  or  Waterfall.  Addressing  these  gaps  is\\ncrucial  for  understanding  how  GenAI  can  be  effectively  leveraged  to  improve  IT  project\\noutcomes.\\n\\n## [PDF page 433]\\n\\nUsing GenAI in IT Project Management…  433\\n\\nAnticipating challenges, dealing with disruptions and minimising risks have constituted the\\ncore responsibilities of project management professionals for decades (Tominc et al., 2023).\\nFurthermore,  they  are  an  integral  component  of  contemporary  discourses  pertaining  to  the\\nprospective applications of GenAI in project management. Despite their daily familiarity with\\nthese concepts, many project professionals may find themselves ill-prepared for the manner in\\nwhich their organisations will utilise GenAI, as well as the precise impact that it will have on\\ntheir work. While it is not possible to predict the full extent of the impact that GenAI will have\\non business operations and processes, it is clear that this emerging technology will enhance the\\nrole of many workers, including project professionals. GenAI is having a significant impact on\\nthe  structure  of  project  work  (Curcirito  et  al.,  2023).  In  light  of  the  accelerated  pace  of\\ndevelopment and adoption of GenAI, there is an increasing imperative for project professionals\\nto  cultivate  expertise  in  artificial  intelligence.  This  will  result  in  increased  productivity,\\nefficiency and project success (Taboada et al., 2023).\\nFor those in project management roles, GenAI  has the potential to automate a range of\\ncomplex  tasks  across  multiple  project  activities.  These  include  the  generation  of  reports,\\nupdates to schedules, data analysis, cost estimation, and more. Those project professionals who\\nare able to harness the power of artificial intelligence will ultimately be able to free up their\\ntime and focus on higher value tasks that contribute to project success. Consequently, project\\nprofessionals are able to dedicate more time and attention to the generation of new business\\nvalue,  the  development  of  leadership  skills  and  the  advancement  of  innovation  within  the\\norganisation, in alignment with the organisation’s business objectives (Kerzner, 2017).\\nThis  paper  presents  the  findings  of  a  study  conducted  on  the  data  extracted  from  ten\\nIT  companies  currently  utilising  GenAI.  The  objective  is  to  demonstrate  how  GenAI  can\\nfacilitate project management activities within IT companies. To this end, the paper will present\\na  series  of  practical  examples  from  IT  companies,  illustrating  the  potential  benefits  of\\nintegrating GenAI into project management.\\n\\n2.  Literature review\\n\\nPrior  research  has  examined  the  incorporation  of  technology  into  project  management\\nmethodologies,  underscoring  its  capacity  to  enhance  project  performance  and  outcomes.\\nAlthough  it  is  unlikely  that  artificial  intelligence  will  entirely  supplant  the  role  of  the\\nprogrammer in the near future, if ever, it is already capable of markedly enhancing the quality\\nand productivity of IT departments (Taboada et al., 2023). As posited by Wolf and Company,\\nAI has the potential to enhance the efficiency of programmers by up to 10 times by the year\\n2030 (Curcirito et al., 2023). As reported by McKinsey, over half of companies are utilising AI\\nin at least one business area (McKinsey&Co, 2024). An analysis conducted by Goldman Sachs\\n\\n## [PDF page 434]\\n\\n434  S. Ostrowski\\n\\nsuggests that AI could potentially displace 300 million full-time positions while simultaneously\\nenhancing global productivity by 7% (McKinsey&Co, 2024). The statistics pertaining to the\\nintegration of AI and project management are noteworthy. As indicated in a Gartner report,\\nthe  use  of  AI  in  project  management  is  expected  to  reach  80%  by  2030,  representing\\na significant increase from the current 2% (Gartner, 2024). A further survey conducted by PMI\\nrevealed that 81% of project managers consider AI to be a significant factor in the future of\\nproject management (Grandview Research, 2024; Maphosa et al., 2022). The results of recent\\nresearch appear to reinforce the view that the use of AI in the field of project management is\\nbeneficial.  As  might  have  been  anticipated,  at  the  conclusion  of  January  2024,  Microsoft\\ndeclared  a  commitment  of  $10  billion  to  the  advancement  of  artificial  intelligence.\\nA few months ago, it would have been challenging to envisage the potential implications of this\\nfor us. It is possible that, in the near future, many people’s imaginations may be transformed\\ninto  tangible  outcomes  (Grandview  Research,  2024).  The  field  of  artificial  intelligence  is\\nprogressing at a rapid pace. Notable corporations such as Google are engineering devices with\\nartificial  neural  networks,  which  imitate  the  functionality  of  the  human  brain.\\nSuch a proposition would have been deemed implausible a few years ago. It will be of interest\\nto observe the future development of AI (Gartner, 2024).\\nIn order to address these challenges, there is a growing interest in integrating a range of\\nemerging AI technologies, such as GenAI and machine learning (ML), into project management\\npractices within the IT domain. GenAI comprises a variety of AI techniques that are capable of\\nautonomously  generating  solutions,  models  or  designs  based  on  specified  criteria  and\\nconstraints. The potential benefits of this technology in IT projects include improvements in\\ndecision-making  processes,  optimisation  of  resource  allocation  and  acceleration  of\\ndevelopment cycles. Despite the potential benefits, the integration of GenAI with IT project\\nmanagement methodologies remains relatively unexplored in the existing literature. Therefore,\\nthis  study  seeks  to  address  this  gap  by  investigating  the  feasibility  and  effectiveness  of\\nintegrating  GenAI  with  established  project  management  practices  in  the  context  of  IT.\\nThis article aims to provide valuable insights into the synergies between GenAI and project\\nmanagement in IT, thereby contributing to the advancement of both theoretical knowledge and\\npractical applications in this area.\\n\\n2.1.  GenAI in Industry\\n\\nGenAI represents a transformative innovation with applications across a range of industries,\\nincluding  healthcare,  manufacturing,  finance  and  logistics.  By  employing  sophisticated\\nmachine  learning  methodologies,  GenAI  is  capable  of  autonomously  generating  content,\\ndevising solutions, and conducting predictive analysis, thereby addressing intricate challenges\\nin  real-time  (Hashfi,  Raharjo,  2023).  Such  capabilities  render  GenAI  a  vital  instrument  for\\naugmenting  efficiency,  curbing  operational  expenses,  and  facilitating  innovative  solutions\\n(Bahai et al., 2024).\\n\\n## [PDF page 435]\\n\\nUsing GenAI in IT Project Management…  435\\n\\nGenAI is particularly impactful in domains that require high degrees of adaptability and\\ncreativity. For example, it is widely employed in the fields of automated content generation,\\nreal-time data analysis, and scenario modelling, assisting businesses in navigating uncertainty\\nand making data-driven decisions (Bodea et al., 2020; Hess, Kunz, 2024). The integration of\\nGenAI with existing workflows frequently results in notable increases in productivity. This is\\nevident in sectors such  as healthcare, where it is employed in diagnostic imaging and drug\\ndiscovery,  and  in  finance,  where  it  is  utilized  to  enhance  fraud  detection  and  portfolio\\noptimization.\\nDespite  the  considerable  potential  of  GenAI,  the  adoption  of  this  technology  is  often\\nimpeded  by  a  number  of  factors,  including  technological  challenges,  ethical  concerns  and\\norganisational resistance. It is emphasised in studies that these barriers must be addressed in\\norder to fully capitalise on the benefits of GenAI in different domains (Bodea et al., 2020; Hess,\\nKunz, 2024).\\n\\n2.2.  IT Project Management\\n\\nIT  project  management  is  inherently  complex,  necessitating  the  coordination  of  diverse\\nteams,  technologies,  and  resources  to  achieve  project  objectives  within  specified  time  and\\nbudget constraints. The traditional methodologies of the Waterfall and Agile models have long\\nbeen regarded as the cornerstones of IT project management. While the Waterfall methodology\\nplaces  an  emphasis  on  the  completion  of  tasks  in  a  sequential  manner,  the  Agile  approach\\nemphasises  iterative  development,  flexibility  and  the  fostering  of  close  collaboration  with\\nstakeholders (Hashfi, Raharjo, 2023).\\nHowever, these methodologies are constrained in their ability to effectively manage the\\nincreasing  complexity  and  dynamism  of  modern  IT  projects.  The  management  of  cross-\\nfunctional collaboration, the addressing of rapidly evolving requirements and the mitigation of\\nrisks in an effective manner represent significant challenges (Bodea et al., 2020; Hess, Kunz,\\n2024). The advent of new technologies has led to the emergence of tools that facilitate enhanced\\nvisibility and control over projects, including collaborative platforms and project management\\nsoftware.  However,  these  tools  frequently  lack  the  sophisticated  analytical  capabilities\\nnecessary to optimise decision-making and resource allocation in real time.\\nThe integration of AI into project management has provided a solution to some of these\\nissues,  facilitating  predictive  analysis,  automated  scheduling  and  enhanced  risk  assessment.\\nNevertheless,  the  integration  of  more  advanced  AI  tools,  such  as  GenAI,  remains\\nunderexplored, particularly in terms of aligning these tools with established methodologies like\\nAgile and Scrum (Hashfi, Raharjo, 2023).\\n\\n## [PDF page 436]\\n\\n436  S. Ostrowski\\n\\n2.3.  Conjunction of GenAI and IT Project Management\\n\\nThe conjunction of GenAI and IT project management signifies a substantial leap forward\\nin the resolution of the challenges inherent to contemporary projects. The capacity of GenAI to\\nautomate  intricate  processes,  generate  actionable  insights  and  facilitate  decision-making\\nrenders it particularly well-suited to the dynamic nature of IT projects (Bodea et al., 2020; Hess,\\nKunz, 2024).\\nThe applications of GenAI in IT project management include:\\n\uf0b7  Automation  of  tasks:  GenAI  automates  routine  tasks,  including  the  generation  of\\nreports, updates to schedules, and estimation of costs. This allows project managers to\\ndirect their attention to activities of a more strategic nature (Hashfi, Raharjo, 2023).\\n\uf0b7  Enhanced  collaboration:  is  facilitated  by  NLP  capabilities  facilitate  enhanced\\ncommunication and alignment among project stakeholders by summarising meetings,\\ngenerating  real-time  translations,  and  analysing  stakeholder  sentiment  (Bodea  et  al.,\\n2020).\\n\uf0b7  Predictive analytics: The application of predictive analytics enables the forecasting of\\nfuture  outcomes  based  on  historical  data.  GenAI  models  facilitate  enhanced  risk\\nassessment  and  decision-making  by  identifying  patterns  and  predicting  project\\noutcomes based on historical data (Hashfi, Raharjo, 2023).\\nNevertheless, the incorporation of GenAI into project management remains in its nascent\\nstages. A review of the literature reveals significant gaps in knowledge, including a lack of\\nempirical  evidence  on  the  long-term  impacts  of  GenAI  and  the  absence  of  structured\\nframeworks  for  its  implementation  within  traditional  project  management  methodologies\\n(Bodea et al., 2020; Bahai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ethical concerns pertaining to data privacy\\nand algorithmic transparency remain pivotal challenges.\\nThe reviewed literature evinces the considerable potential of GenAI to transform IT project\\nmanagement  by  augmenting  efficiency,  collaboration,  and  decision-making.  Nevertheless,\\nsubstantial gaps and challenges must be addressed to fully harness its capabilities. This study\\naims to bridge these gaps by investigating the practical applications of GenAI in IT project\\nmanagement, thereby providing actionable insights for researchers and practitioners.\\n\\n3. The selection criteria were designed to encompass a diverse range\\nof  sectors  within  the  IT  industry,  thereby  ensuring  a  comprehensive  perspective  on  the\\napplication  of  GenAI. Discussion\\n\\nThis  study  demonstrates  the  considerable  impact  that  GenAI  can  have  on  IT  project\\nmanagement.  It  illustrates  the  capacity  of  GenAI  to  optimise  processes,  enhance  decision-\\nmaking and improve collaboration among stakeholders. The findings demonstrate how GenAI\\ntools, such as predictive scheduling and resource allocation algorithms, facilitate more efficient\\nproject  management  in  organisations,  whilst  addressing  long-standing  challenges  such  as\\nresource conflicts, scheduling delays and risk management.\\nThe capacity of GenAI to analyse extensive datasets and generate actionable insights is\\nespecially  beneficial  in  the  context  of  managing  the  complexities  inherent  to  IT  projects.\\nTo illustrate, the predictive capabilities of GenAI permit project teams to anticipate potential\\nrisks  and  address  them  in  a  proactive  manner,  thereby  enhancing  project  resilience  and\\nstakeholder satisfaction. Similarly, the deployment of GenAI for the automation of repetitive\\ntasks, such as reporting and quality assurance, has the effect of reducing the manual workloads\\nof project managers, thereby enabling them to focus on strategic priorities.\\nNevertheless, the study also uncovers significant obstacles to the successful implementation\\nof GenAI. The quality and availability of data remain significant concerns, as the efficacy of\\nAI-driven tools is contingent upon the integrity and comprehensiveness of the datasets upon\\nwhich they rely. The necessity for robust frameworks to ensure fairness and accountability is\\nunderscored by ethical challenges, including those pertaining to algorithmic bias and the lack\\nof transparency in decision-making processes. Furthermore, organisational resistance, driven\\nby  scepticism  or  concerns  about  job  displacement,  serves  to  further  complicate  integration\\nefforts.  Furthermore,  the  interpretability  of  GenAI  models  remains  a  significant  challenge.\\nIn  order  to  build  trust  and  confidence,  stakeholders  require  clear  explanations  of  AI-driven\\ndecisions.\\nIn order to address these challenges, organisations should develop and implement ethical\\nAI  frameworks  with  the  aim  of  mitigating  the  risks  associated  with  bias  and  transparency.\\nIt is similarly crucial to invest in training and capacity-building programmes, with the objective\\n\\n## [PDF page 445]\\n\\nUsing GenAI in IT Project Management…  445\\n\\nof  equipping  project  teams  with  the  requisite  skills  to  utilise  GenAI  tools  effectively.\\nThe  implementation  of  incremental  adoption,  commencing  with  pilot  projects,  enables\\norganisations to refine their strategies, cultivate expertise and identify potential impediments\\nprior to the comprehensive deployment of GenAI.\\nThis  study  makes  a  contribution  to  the  theoretical  discourse  on  GenAI  in  IT  project\\nmanagement  by  providing  empirical  evidence  on  its  applications  and  effectiveness.\\nFurthermore, the study identifies shortcomings in existing research, including the necessity for\\ninvestigations  into  the  long-term  consequences  of  GenAI,  sector-specific  applications,\\nand hybrid methodologies that integrate traditional project management frameworks with AI-\\ndriven tools.\\nIt is recommended that future research explore these areas while addressing the ethical and\\nsocial implications of  GenAI  adoption. Summary\\n\\nThis  study  illuminates  the  potential  for  transformative  change  in  the  field  of  IT  project\\nmanagement through the application of GenAI, drawing insights from case studies conducted\\nin ten IT companies. Introduction\\n\\nNational parks are organisations entrusted with a special task – the protection of biodiversity\\nand  landscape  in  the  most  beautiful  and  valuable  natural  areas.  In  recent  years,  significant\\nchanges  have  taken  place  in  their  organisation,  legal  form  and  financing  rules.  In  place  of\\nnational parks – budget units, state legal entities were established, which are obliged to protect\\nboth animate and inanimate nature, and at the same time are obliged to take care of its financing\\nby conducting specific economic activities limited by the obligation to protect this nature (Pater,\\n\\nhttp://dx.doi.org/10.29119/1641-3466.2025.215.27  http://managementpapers.polsl.pl/\\n\\n## [PDF page 450]\\n\\n450  B. The greatest consequence of the change in the legal form, from the point of view\\nof accounting for national parks, is the transition from the budget accounting system, which is\\nbased  on  the  cash  basis,  to  accounting  in  the  income  and  cost  (accrual)  system.  There  is\\nan exception to that rule, such as the settlement of budget subsidies in the cash system and\\nplanning both on a cash basis and on an accrual basis. The documents that since 2012 have been\\nprovided  by  the  national  park  to  the  minister  responsible  for  the  environment,  who  is  to\\nsupervise its activities and control it, include primarily: financial statements, reports on the\\nimplementation of the financial plan, reports on the implementation of subsidies, as well as\\nother ad hoc reports or reports about the national park.\\nThe  role  of  national  parks  in  preserving  biodiversity,  their  importance  for  society  and\\ndescendants, as well as the affiliation of national parks to public finance sector entities make\\nmanaging these organisations a challenge for their directors. Managing a national park, like any\\neconomic entity, requires planning, organising, leading and controlling. Among the numerous\\ntools  that  organisations  have  at  their  disposal  to  best  fulfill  these  functions,  there  is  also\\naccounting.\\nThe aim of the work is to present the nature of managing national parks in Poland and to\\nindicate the impact of accounting on managing a national park. Legal and organisational conditions for managing a national park\\n\\nThe protection of natural resources is global in nature, which is why it is dealt with by\\ninternational  organisations,  and  is  subject  to  international  agreements  and  conventions.\\nThis results from the need to protect biodiversity. Legal protection fulfills this task best. Nature\\nall over the world, including Poland, is protected due to systemic solutions, through the creation\\nof  protected  areas  (national  parks,  nature  reserves,  landscape  parks,  \\"Natura  2000\\"  areas,\\nprotected  landscape  areas),  species  protection  and  individual  protection,  including  natural\\nmonuments, documentation sites, ecological sites, nature and landscape complexes (Article 6\\nof the Act of 16 April 2004 on Nature Conservation. Journal of Laws 2004, No. 92, item 880).\\nTerritories covered by various forms of protection occupy a total of 32.3% of Poland’s area,\\nmost of which are protected landscape areas with a relatively low protection regime. National\\nparks  cover  a  total  area  of  315.2  thousand  ha,  constituting  only  1%  of  the  country’s  area.\\nThe structure of the parks’ area is dominated by forest land (63% of the area), agricultural land\\nconstitutes 15% of their area, and water 6% (GUS, 2023).\\n\\n## [PDF page 451]\\n\\nThe impact of accounting on the management…  451\\n\\nCurrently,  there  are  23  national  parks  in  Poland.  The  Act  of  16  April  2004  on  Nature\\nConservation (Journal of Laws 2004, No. 92, item 880, art. 8, section 2) defines a national park\\nas an area distinguished by special natural, scientific, social, cultural and educational values,\\nwith an area of no less than 1000 ha, in which all nature and landscape values are protected.\\nNational  parks,  as  an  organisation  protecting  nature,  ensure  the  implementation  of  tasks\\nimposed on them by the legislator. A national park is therefore established in order to preserve\\nbiological diversity, resources, formations and components of inanimate nature and landscape\\nvalues,  as  well  as  to  restore  the  proper  state  of  resources  and  components  of  nature  and  to\\nrecreate distorted natural habitats, habitats of plants, animals or fungi.\\nIn  a  national  park,  the  most  important  thing  are  the  natural  resources  and  therefore  the\\nproper protection of the ecosystems. This does not mean that their use should be abandoned.\\nThey have been entrusted to national parks to protect them and to use these resources wisely,\\nin  accordance  with  the  concept  of  sustainable  development  as  defined  by  Brundtland,\\ni.e. meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to\\nmeet their own needs (Brundtland, 1989; Nasza wspólna przyszło\\\\\\b, 1991).\\nNature conservation activities should be planned, which is why the Nature Conservation\\nAct requires national parks to prepare a conservation plan, which is prepared individually for\\neach park. However, until the plans are prepared, the way conservation activities are carried out\\nis described  in  conservation  tasks. These  are  documents  that identify  existing  and  potential\\nthreats  to  the  park’s  ecosystems  and  describe  methods  to  reduce  or  eliminate  them.\\nThe  document  also  identifies  areas  of  the  park  under  strict,  active  or  landscape  protection.\\nIt  specifies  the  method  of  active  protection  of  ecosystems,  together  with  the  size,  type  and\\nlocation for the tasks described. The process of drawing up protection plans is time-consuming\\nand complex. Under the current law, national parks had until 15 November 2018 to do so.\\nAccording  to  the  post-audit  information,  in  more  than  half  of  the  national  parks,\\nthe conservation tasks have been defined in regulations issued by the Minister of the Climate\\nand Environment, not in protection plans, even though the deadline for their preparation has\\npassed. To date, 11 national parks have approved conservation plans. This means that not all\\nnational parks have documents setting out specific conservation objectives for the park and its\\nnatural assets. Draft protection plans that have already been submitted to the Ministry of the\\nClimate and Environment have been under evaluation for almost 10 years, despite the fact that\\nArticle 19(5) of the Nature Conservation Act sets a deadline of 6 months (NIK, 2024).\\nThe area of a national park includes land with different ownership structures - both state\\nand private. It is extremely important for the nature of a national park and for the management\\nof such an organiation that its territory is accessible. A national park can be accessible for the\\nfollowing purposes: scientific, educational, tourist, recreational, sporting, which is in line with\\nthe objectives of the Nature Conservation Act.\\n\\n## [PDF page 452]\\n\\n452  B. Pater\\n\\nTourist traffic in parks, in addition to its many benefits for each visitor, brings a great threat\\nto the nature of national parks (\\u0007wiek, Pater, 2020). In 2022, 16 million people visited national\\nparks in Poland, while in 2023 it was 15.5 million tourists (GUS, 2023, 2024). The Nature\\nConservation Act contains a list of restrictions that must be respected by visitors, and the park\\ndirector sets the access policy for national park by means of a regulation. Among other things,\\nthese regulations determine the number of people who can visit a site at the same time and the\\namount of the entrance fee to the national park. It is the director’s duty to ensure the safety of\\nvisitors,  which  includes the  provision  and  maintenance  of  appropriate  tourist  infrastructure.\\nEducational activities also require appropriate infrastructure, such as museums, nature trails or\\nclassrooms. In this way, the need to educate the public about nature and how to enjoy its richnes\\nin accordance with the principles of sustainable development is met.\\nParks  perform  a  number  of  socially  useful  functions:  firstly,  they  are  created  to  protect\\nnatural resources, but within this overarching function they also perform scientific, didactic,\\nhistorical  and  cultural,  tourist  and  recreational  functions,  as  well  as  an  economic  function.\\nThe latter can be understood in two ways: as a business entity and as part of the economic\\nsystem at regional and state level.\\nA park is not only a form of area-based nature conservation, but also an organisational unit,\\nwhich has its own structure and functions according to rules set out in the Act. Pursuant to\\nArticle 8(1) of the Public Finance Act of 27 August 2009 (Journal of Laws 2009, No. 157, item\\n1240), national parks are created in forms specified by law. In 2012, national parks gained legal\\npersonality by changing their legal form from unincorporated state budgetary units to a state\\nlegal person. Pursuant to Article 9(14) of the Public Finance Act of 27 August 2009, the public\\nfinance  sector  is  co-created  by  state  legal  persons  established  under  other  acts  in  order  to\\nperform  public  tasks,  excluding  enterprises,  research  institutes,  banks  and  commercial  law\\ncompanies.\\nTherefore, in accordance with the regulation of article 8a, paragraph 1 of the Act of 16 April\\n2004 on Nature Conservation, a national park is a legal entity within the meaning of article 9,\\nitem. 14 of the Act of 27 August 2009 on public finance, in relation to which it can be the\\nsubject of civil law relations.\\nThe  basic  legal  act  regulating  the  operation  of  national  parks  in  Poland  is  the  Nature\\nConservation Act. According to article 10(2) of the Public Finance Act, the regulations of the\\nPublic Finance Act apply to state legal entities operating on the basis of separate legal acts,\\nwhich constitute the basis for their establishment, so that in the case of a conflict of regulations,\\nthe principle of lex specialis derogat legi generali can be applied - a law with a higher degree\\nof specificity should be  applied before a more  general law,  which in this case allows us to\\nconclude  that  the  Nature  Conservation  Act  takes  precedence  over  the  Public  Finance  Act.\\nIt  should  be  noted  that,  due  to  the  complexity  of  the  legal  issues  related  to  national  parks,\\nthe Nature Protection Act also refers to other laws.\\n\\n## [PDF page 453]\\n\\nThe impact of accounting on the management…  453\\n\\nParks operate on the basis of their statutes, which are granted by way of an ordinance by\\nthe minister responsible for the environment. The statutes define the internal structure of the\\npark, the functioning of its authority and the way in which powers are delegated to ensure the\\nproper functioning of the national park and the fulfilment of its tasks. The internal organisation\\nof a national park is defined in detail in the organisational regulations, which are issued by\\ndecree of the park director, and the statutes provide a framework for the internal organisation\\nof the park.\\nNational  parks  are  equipped  with  the  necessary  material  resources  (natural  resources,\\nbuildings,  structures,  infrastructure,  means  of  transport,  machinery  and  other  necessary\\nequipment),  organisational  resources  (employees,  organisational  structure)  and  financial\\nresources, i.e. revenues generated by the park in connection with providing access to tourist\\nattractions and the area of the national park, as well as educational activities, sale of timber\\nfrom reforestation, timber after natural disasters and from cultivation treatments (in national\\nparks there is no forest management as understood in commercial forests) and other revenues\\nlisted in the Nature Conservation Act (Art. 8 h), including a subsidy from the state budget.\\nThe property of the national park is wholly owned by the state. The method of management is\\nbased  on  self-financing,  i.e.  the  costs  of  carrying  out  the  activities  of  the  National  Park,\\nincluding the fulfilment of its tasks, are covered by its revenues. The catalogue of costs and\\nrevenues is precisely defined in the article 8h of the Nature Conservation Act.\\nThe  specificity  of  national  park  management  is  influenced  by  many  factors,  but  what\\ndistinguishes the management of a national park from the management of other entities is the\\nlegislation that regulates in detail the various areas of management of such an organisation.\\nThis is because parks subordinate all actions and decisions to the need and priority of nature\\nconservation.\\nIt is also very important to note that national parks in Poland are very diverse entities in\\nterms of attractiveness for tourists, natural resources, location, accessibility, the amount of the\\nbudget they have at their disposal, including the amount of subsidies from the state budget,\\nthe amount of revenue generated from their business activities and, of course, the size of the\\norganisation itself - as parks in Poland employ from a few to more than 100 people (Pater,\\n2020).\\n\\n3. Accounting in the management of national parks\\n\\nA national park, not only as an economic entity with legal personality, but also as a public\\ninstitution, has an obligation to properly document its activities, and the information it collects\\nshould become the basis for reasoned decision-making.\\n\\n## [PDF page 454]\\n\\n454  B. Pater\\n\\nIn this respect, the accounting system, i.e. the information system of an economic entity,\\nperforms  the  functions  of  identification,  measurement,  collection  and  processing  of  data.\\nOn this basis, it is possible to analyse and evaluate phenomena and management processes in\\nthe organisation. It has an important, even key role to fulfil in an entity. It also communicates\\nfinancial  information  to  interested  users  (Nowak,  2011).  In  other  words,  it  supports\\nmanagement functions. In performing these functions, accounting identifies, measures, collects\\nand processes data, analyses and evaluates economic phenomena and processes. The accounting\\nsystem in national parks is used to record economic operations, provide data for analysis and\\nevaluation of the organisation’s activities and for the day-to-day management needs of the entity\\n(Czubakowska  et  al.,  2006).  In  practice,  accounting  is  a  set  of  techniques  and  methods  for\\nmeasuring and communicating economic information in such a way that various stakeholders\\nand managers can make valid, rational judgements in the decision-making process  (Dobija,\\n1999).\\nThe amount of information generated in the accounting system of the national parks has\\nbeen greatly affected by the changes that took place in 2012, when the national parks were\\ntransformed from budgetary units to state legal entities. The changes experienced by the parks\\nat  that  time  also  affected  their  accounting,  as  they  were  obliged  to  fully  comply  with  the\\nregulations of the Accounting Act of 29 September 1994. Journal of Laws of 1994, No. 121,\\nitem 591. As budget units, the parks kept accounts mainly for the purpose of settling accounts\\nwith the state budget. This change therefore brought new obligations, but also opened up the\\npossibility of collecting data to produce information for management purposes. Such solutions\\nsupport the proper fulfilment of the tasks of any organisation, so national parks can also benefit\\nfrom them, especially as they are entities with very specific functional characteristics.\\n\\nTable 1.\\nThe Structure of the Income of the selected national parks in the Malopolska for the Years 2019-\\n2022\\nNational park  Year  State budget subsidies  Own revenue  Other\\nW %\\nPieninski  2019  35.4  48.4  16.2\\n2020  37.5  42.1  20.4\\n2021  29.2  52.7  18.1\\n2022  39.4  50.3  10.3\\nOjcowski  2019  44.9  40.6  14.5\\n2020  53.6  24.1  22.3\\n2021  37.9  48.5  13.6\\n2022  47.0  37.5  15.5\\nGorczanski  2019  59.7  9.0  31.3\\n2020  62.3  5.9  31.8\\n2021  62.6  9.8  27.6\\n2022  62.6  8.6  28.8\\nTatrzanski  2019  16.0  62.3  21.6\\n2020  13.4  67.8  18.8\\n2021  7.9  71.7  20.4\\n2022  9.4  74.5  16.2\\nSource: own work based on the financial reports of the national parks.\\n\\n## [PDF page 455]\\n\\nThe impact of accounting on the management…  455\\n\\nThe change in the legal form and the fact that the national parks are engaged in economic\\nactivities  allows  them  to  retain  the  income  generated  and  use  it  for  nature  conservation\\npurposes. In the most parks,\\nthe  subsidy  from  the  state  budget  does  not  even  cover  these  costs,  which  means  that  the\\nimplementation of the basic tasks of the park is financed with funds generated by the business\\nactivity  or  obtained  from  external  sources.  Such  a  situation  can  lead  to  delays  in  the\\nimplementation of conservation plans and tasks.  In this regard, the situation in the selected\\nnational parks does not differ from the situation in parks all over Poland. Among the selected\\nparks, only the budget subsidy for the Gorce Park covered remuneration with overhead costs.\\n\\n## [PDF page 456]\\n\\n456  B. Pater\\n\\nIn the Tatra National Park, on the other hand, the budget subsidy covered about 40% of the cost\\nof remuneration with overheads (Figure 1).\\nThe basis of the Park‘s activities is an annual financial plan, which is prepared in a task-\\nbased manner for the budget year and the following two years. Such a draft of the financial plan\\nof a state legal entity is submitted to the Minister of Finance in accordance with the procedure\\nand  within  the  term  established  by  the  regulations  on  work  on  the  draft  of  the  budget.\\nThe financial plan, as well as the financial plan in the task-based system, is prepared both on\\na cash basis (recording only realised revenues and expenses) and on an accrual basis, recording\\nall  earned  revenues  accruing  to  the  entity  and  costs  charged  to  it  in  connection  with  such\\nrevenues for a given financial year (Kiziukiewicz, 2014).\\nNational parks, when accounting for the subsidy received from the state budget, are obliged\\nto provide information taking into account the cash basis, and as state legal entities they should\\nconduct financial management on an accrual basis (Winiarska, 2012). Despite the change in\\nlegal form, no obligation to standardise accounting policy has been introduced, nor has a model\\nchart  of  accounts  been  developed.  Each  of  the  23  national  parks  has  shaped  its  accounting\\nsystem autonomously.\\nThe information on the finances of the national parks and their detail is derived from the\\nway  in  which  the  national  parks  keep  their  accounts.  The  chart  of  accounts,  which  is\\na systematic list of accounts with their names and symbols used to organise the recording of\\neconomic events, is important in this aspect. The layout of the chart of accounts is not the same\\nfor each of the parks, although it is clear that in each of the national parks the accounts are kept\\nin accordance with the regulations of the Accounting Act. In addition, the Regulations on the\\ndetailed manner of conducting the financial management of the national park (Rozporządzenie\\nRady Ministrow, 2012) do not provide any guidelines for the accounting policy. As a result,\\nit is difficult to compare the financial data of the national parks, primarily costs. As mentioned\\nabove, the accounting of national parks is based on the accrual method and the profit and loss\\naccount is prepared on a comparative basis. The accounting of the national parks as budgetary\\nunits  was  based  on  the  cash  method.  At  that  time,  particularly  in  terms  of  reporting,  little\\nattention was paid to costs in the parks’ charts of accounts, which generally confined themselves\\nto recording costs by nature.\\nIn the current legal form, costs are also reported by nature, which means that the financial\\nstatements only provide information on the nature of costs incurred. In the accounting of the\\nnational parks, the accounts related to the tasks performed by the parks have been separated,\\nbut only for the purpose of preparing reports on the implementation of the financial plan in\\na task-based arrangement and preparing reports on the implementation of the annual financial\\nplan in the arrangement compliant with the Public Finance Act for state legal entities, in which\\nthe operating costs and the costs of task performance are shown. However, the management of\\nnational parks should take place both at the level of an individual park and at the level of the\\nwhole group of national parks. It would therefore be useful to have a reliable assessment of the\\n\\n## [PDF page 457]\\n\\nThe impact of accounting on the management…  457\\n\\nindividual  tasks  in  each  national  park.  Financial  plans  make  possible  to  compare  between\\nindividual  parks  in  terms  of  their  general  costs,  whereas  task-based  planning  does  not.\\nThis is because national parks plan and report their activities as a single task (Revenues and\\ncosts of national parks are realised in the following task system: State function 12 Environment,\\ntask 12.1 W Shaping biodiversity, subtask 12.1.1 W Nature and landscape protection, activity\\n12.1.1.2 W National parks).\\nAs a consequence of the lack of legal norms regarding the necessity of reporting on the\\ncosts of individual tasks of the national parks, the way in which they are recorded varies greatly.\\nFrom the information gathered in the course of the research, it is clear that the layout of the\\naccounts  in  Unit  5  is  very  different.  As  a  result,  it  is  not  possible  to  extract  comparable\\ninformation about where costs are incurred. The weak point here is the lack of a consistent\\naccounting policy. As a result, it is virtually impossible to obtain information on the costs of\\nindividual tasks of the national parks, e.g. the costs of providing access, the costs of carrying\\nout research, the costs of education, the costs of nature conservation tasks, etc. The method of\\naccounting used by the national parks is not uniform. The present way of accounting in the\\nnational parks does not allow cost comparisons to be made, even with regard to the three main\\ntasks  of  the  national  parks,  i.e.  nature  conservation,  access  and  education.  These  cannot  be\\nderived from the financial reports. Although in the majority of parks records are kept that make\\nit possible to separate the costs of nature conservation, provision, education, research and nature\\nmonitoring, salaries and administrative costs, there are also parks where the costs of the tasks\\nare divided differently, i.e. into costs related to education, nature conservation and providing\\naccess. In a report by Babczuk & Kachniarz (2015), carried out and financed at the request of\\nthe  Association  of  Employers  of  Polish  National  Parks,  the  authors  admittedly  carried  out\\nan analysis of the survey data received on the level of costs of tasks performed, but they also\\nconfirm  that  their  comparability  between  parks  is  not  entirely  possible.  For  example,\\nthe maintenance of forester’s lodges is treated as an administrative cost in some parks and as\\na conservation cost in others. There are more such discrepancies as a result of the different\\naccounting policies adopted by the national parks.\\n\\n4. Conclusions\\n\\nAccounting as an information system within an organisation can provide information not\\nonly for reporting but also for management purposes. A uniform accounting policy is essential\\nfor  analysing  the  economic  situation  of  parks  and  for  making  comparisons  between  them.\\nOf particular importance is cost accounting, which in its current form does not provide a means\\nof understanding the costs of the functions performed and making reliable comparisons between\\nparks. The lack of consistency in the accounting policy makes the picture of the functioning of\\n\\n## [PDF page 458]\\n\\n458  B. Pater\\n\\nthe parks, including their financial management, not very transparent, which is contrary to the\\nneed for transparency in public finances.\\nTherefore, the establishment of a uniform chart of accounts for national parks, together with\\nthe establishment of a model and uniform accounting policy, becomes indispensable. Of course,\\nin such a model chart of accounts, parks could expand the scope of independent analysis by\\nintroducing more detailed horizontal and vertical divisions of accounts, while maintaining the\\nuniformity and comparability of information coming from the accounting system. In addition,\\nthe  information  from  the  financial  and  accounting  system  should  be  useful  not  only  from\\na  financial  accounting  perspective,  but  also  from  a  management  accounting  perspective.\\nBased on the observation of the way accounting works in these companies, the conclusion is\\nthat managers underestimate the role of financial information and the accounting system and\\ndo not realise how much useful information for management they could obtain by implementing\\nsolutions  developed  within  the  framework  of  management  accounting  as  well  as  financial\\naccounting.  This  may  be  due  to  a  conservative  approach  aimed  solely  at  fulfilling  legal\\nobligations.  Of  course,  these  are  public  institutions,  so  costly  solutions  should  not  be\\nintroduced. However, consideration could be given to introducing a uniform way of recording\\ncosts,  as  cost  accounting  tailored  to  the  activities  carried  out  provides  the  knowledge  to\\neffectively manage not only a single park, but its entire system.\\n\\nAcknowledgements\\n\\nThe  publication  was  financed  by  a  subsidy  from  the  Ministry  of  Science  and  Higher\\nEducation for the University of Agriculture in Krakow, for 2024.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Piwowar-Sulej, A. Austen\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nOver  the  last  few  years,  the  topic  of  sustainability  has  gained  enormous  popularity\\nworldwide. Increased public awareness of the impact of human activity on the environment,\\nclimate  change,  and  the  need  for  sustainable  resource  management  has  made  sustainability\\na key area of interest for society, companies and institutions at various levels (Piwowar-Sulej,\\n2022a).  Social  needs  have  also  gained  in  importance,  which,  alongside  economic  and\\nenvironmental needs, is one of the three pillars of sustainable development (Elkington, 2004).\\nAccording  to  Jonker  et  al.  (2011),  companies  have  a  high  capacity  to  react  quickly  to\\nexisting problems and implement corresponding changes. Therefore, their role in achieving the\\nSustainable  Development  Goals  at  national  or  international  level  cannot  be  overestimated.\\nThis has given rise to the concept of organizational sustainability, which promotes management\\nthat simultaneously and equivalently takes into account economic, social and environmental\\nissues related to the functioning of a company (Dyllick, Hockerts, 2002). Moreover, the concept\\nof  sustainable  human  resource  management  (HRM)  has  also  emerged,  which  incorporates\\nbusiness, social and environmental aspects in the management of people. Its main objective is\\nto  create  a  harmonized  approach  that  contributes  to  a  balance  between  organizational\\neffectiveness, employee satisfaction, as well as social and environmental values (cf. Ehnert,\\n2009). One of the main activities of sustainable HRM is the development of human resources,\\nwhich  is  part  of  the  company’s  long-term  growth  orientation  (Piwowar-Sulej,  2022b).\\nIndeed,  no  concept  can  be  implemented  effectively  without  a  properly  prepared  workforce.\\nIn this connection, the need to provide organizations with so-called sustainable competencies\\n(competencies  in  sustainability,  competencies  for  sustainability/sustainable  development,\\nsustainability competencies) is exposed (Piwowar-Sulej, 2023).\\nSustainable competencies are becoming increasingly important in today’s dynamic business\\nenvironment.  Furthermore,  society  is  becoming  increasingly  aware  of  sustainability  issues.\\nIt is therefore important to provide an understanding of  what competencies are  and will be\\nimportant in the long term, not only for the development of individual careers, but also for\\nsociety as a whole. It is also worthwhile to analyze the existing body of knowledge devoted to\\nthese competencies in an objective and reproducible way. Therefore, the aim of the article was\\nset to answer the following questions:\\n1) What are sustainable competencies? What are the components of these competencies?\\n2) What does the science map for sustainable competencies look like?\\nThe first part of the article 3 to answer the first question 3 uses a narrative literature review.\\nIn turn, the second part of the article uses science mapping which is a bibliometric data analysis\\ntechnique  that  helps  to  understand  the  structure  and  dynamics  of  scientific  knowledge,\\nto identify research trends, and to assess the impact of specific studies or scientific areas (Chen\\net al., 2015). This was carried out using the Scopus database of scientific publications.\\n\\n## [PDF page 463]\\n\\nSustainable competencies: terminology…  463\\n\\n2.  Sustainable competencies: their scope and justification of the need\\nfor shaping them across groups of employees\\n\\nCompetencies for sustainable development have been broadly defined as a combined set of\\nknowledge,  skills,  attitudes  and  values  that  enable  effective  global  action  on  real-world\\nsustainability issues, challenges and opportunities, according to the context (Brundiers et al.,\\n2021).  On  the  one  hand,  these  competencies  will  form  the  basis  for  certain  professions  -\\ncommonly referred to as \\"green jobs\\" (Sulich et al., 2020). These professions of the future will\\nmake  a  significant  contribution  to  the  successful  transformation  of  organizations  towards\\nsustainability,  focusing  primarily  on  the  businesses’  environmental  goals.  However,\\non  the  other  hand,  according  to  the  definition  presented  in  the  introduction  of  the  article,\\nsustainability  is  not  only  about  protecting  the  environment.  The  literature  advocates,\\nfor example, the implementation of so-called frugal innovation, which refers to the development\\nand  implementation  of  new  products,  services  or  processes  that  are  both  economical  and\\nenvironmentally friendly. These innovations are usually focused on creating low-cost solutions\\nthat  meet  specific  needs,  especially  in  areas  with  limited  financial  resources. Conclusions\\n\\nSustainable competencies are essential to address a wide range of environmental, social and\\neconomic challenges. They enable individuals and organizations to make responsible, ethical\\nand sustainable choices that lead to positive outcomes for individuals, the planet, society and\\nthe economy. Employers should therefore value employees who possess not only traditional\\nprofessional  skills,  but  also  sustainable  competencies  such  as  flexibility,  collaboration,\\nthe ability to solve socially-oriented problems and concern for the environment, among others.\\nDisseminating knowledge about sustainable competencies is essential for raising awareness\\nand  bringing  about  change.  This  article  educates  readers  about  the  role  of  sustainable\\ncompetencies in today’s working world. It can help them to better understand what skills are\\ncrucial for their career success. Giving concrete examples of sustainable competencies and their\\nrole in different professional fields can provide practical guidance for people who are looking\\nfor  career  development  tips.  Furthermore,  the  article  shows  how  3  i.e.,  through  the  use  of\\nsustainable competencies 3 employees can contribute to social and environmental progress.\\nWith  a  view  to  the  contribution  of  this  article  to  management  theory,  the  authors  have\\nidentified  different  approaches  to  the  analyzed  competencies.  In  addition,  they  proposed\\na  division  of  sustainable  competencies,  taking  into  account  different  professional  groups.\\nUsing bibliometric analyses, they showed that the greatest research attention has so far been\\nfocused on education for sustainable development taking place in institutions set up for this\\npurpose  (e.g.,  universities).  As  this  article  demonstrates,  there  is  a  paucity  of  research  on\\npractices  undertaken  by  employers  as  part  of  staff  development.  Furthermore,  most  of  the\\nresearch to date has been carried out in Spain, the US and Germany and has focused on selected\\ncompetencies,  including  those  related  to  environmental  protection.  As  sustainable\\ncompetencies  require  knowledge  from  multiple  disciplines  such  as  environmental  sciences,\\nsocial  sciences,  economics  and  management,  researchers  3  in  future  international  research\\nprojects  also  bringing  together  authors  from  e.g.  Central  Europe  3  should  also  work  in\\ninterdisciplinary teams to develop and test comprehensive theories and models. It would be\\nimportant to recognize which competencies are particularly needed in different industries and\\nhow this phenomenon changes over time.\\n\\n## [PDF page 470]\\n\\n470  K. Introduction\\n\\nLocal governments have become important policy actors for sustainable development and\\nplay  a  key  role  in  initiating  and  supporting  the  transition  to  sustainability.  In  particular,\\nthe significance of cities in this process is emphasized, as they are places where environmental,\\nclimate, demographic, and social problems converge, as well as opportunities and resources for\\naccelerating  change  towards  sustainable  and  smart  development  (Dawes,  2019;  Hölscher,\\nFrantzeskaki, 2021; Wolfram et al., 2016; Wolfram, Frantzeskaki, 2016). Cities can also play\\nan important role in achieving deep greenhouse gas emission reductions and climate-resilient\\ndevelopment (IPCC, 2023). The role of local governments (including those operating in smaller\\ntowns and villages) in the transition to sustainable development is highlighted by Goal 11 of\\nthe 2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (Transforming Our World: The 2030\\nAgenda  for  Sustainable  Development,  2015),  which  was  directly  dedicated  to  developing\\nSustainable Cities and Communities. Most of the other goals implicitly address the local level.\\nAchieving  at  least  105  of  the  169  SDG  targets  requires  appropriate  engagement  and\\ncoordination with local and regional governments (OECD, 2020).\\nSustainable  and  smart  development  of  municipalities  requires  radical  transformation  of\\nlocal  systems  to  solve  complex,  long-term  problems  (Hölscher,  Frantzeskaki,  2021).\\nThis  transformation  involves  making  fundamental  irreversible  changes  in  infrastructure,\\necosystems, lifestyles, service delivery systems, urban innovation, institutions and governance\\n(Elmqvist  et  al.,  2019).  Sustainability-oriented  local  leadership  has  been  identified  as\\na  facilitator  of  the  transition  to  sustainability,  and  as  key  to  the  implementation  of  the\\nSustainable Development Goals (Krellenberg et al., 2019; Valencia et al., 2019). According to\\nWittmayer et al. (2016) a clear focus of local authorities on radical change is a prerequisite for\\nmanaging sustainability in a way that addresses the root causes of local challenges. In addition\\nto  prioritizing  the  goals  of  sustainable,  smart  development  in  local  policies,  effective\\ntransformation requires appropriate governance. Managing the transformation of local systems\\nin  line  with  the  Sustainable  Development  Goals  is  a  major  challenge  for  local  authorities\\n(Wolfram et al. 2016), as they need to facilitate alignment, foresight and reflexive learning in\\norder to recognise, anticipate and shape transformation dynamics and leverage points (Hölscher\\net al., 2019a; Hölscher, Frantzeskaki, 2021).\\n\\n## [PDF page 475]\\n\\nCollaborative and inclusive governance…  475\\n\\nIn practice, sustainability management in local government faces a number of structural,\\ncultural  and  attitudinal  barriers  (Raffer  et  al.,  2022).  The  article  addresses  the  issue  of\\nsustainability  transition  governance  at  the  local  level  in  Poland  and  attempts  to  answer  the\\nquestion of whether Polish municipalities are ready for transition governance. On the formal-\\nlegal  side,  the  localization  of  sustainability  goals  in  Poland  has  been  ensured  by  legal\\nregulations  such  as,  for  example,  the  Act  on  the  Principles  of  Development  Policy  (2006),\\nthe Environmental Protection Act (2001), the Act on Planning and Spatial Development (2003).\\nThey  have  guaranteed  legitimacy  and  opportunities  for  the  implementation  of  sustainable\\ndevelopment activities and investments in Polish municipalities. Ways to implement SDG goals\\nat the local level have also been identified in national sectoral strategies such as the National\\nUrban Policy 2030, regional strategies and regional sectoral programs, and local development\\nstrategies. However, data from the Sustainable Development Report 2022 indicates that the\\nimplementation of SDG11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, which assumes making cities\\nand  human  settlements  inclusive,  safe,  resilient  and  sustainable,  still  faces  significant\\nchallenges in Poland (Sachs et al., 2022). In particular, the air pollution index remains poor in\\ncomparison with other European countries, despite the slight improvement recorded. Previous\\nresearch results also highlight the low involvement of Polish local governments (about 20%) in\\nsustainable development activities and the rather high percentage of local governments still\\nunaware  of  sustainable  development  challenges  (about  38%)  (Boguszewski  et  al.,  2023).\\nThey  also  diagnosed  insufficient  leadership  and  low  prioritization  of  current  sustainability\\nchallenges by Polish mayors (Przywojska et al., 2019).\\nAccordingly,  the  purpose  of  our  article  is  to  gain  deeper  insight  into  the  process  of\\ntransformative  governance  in  Polish  municipalities.  We  analyze  two  of  its  dimensions:\\nthe municipality’s ability to develop collaborative, inclusive governance and the mayor’s local\\nleadership  oriented  toward  sustainable,  smart  development.  We  try  to  get  an  answer  to  the\\nfollowing  research  question:  (1)  What  is  the  capacity  of  Polish  municipalities  to  develop\\ncollaborative,  inclusive  governance?  (2)  How  do  mayors  prioritize  the  challenges  of\\nsustainable,  smart  development?  (3)  Does  the  capacity  of  Polish  municipalities  to  develop\\ncollaborative,  inclusive  governance  affect  the  mayor’s  prioritization  of  sustainable,  smart\\ndevelopment challenges?\\nThe article contributes to theory on collaborative, inclusive governance and its impact on\\nthe priorities assigned by local leaders for interventions toward sustainable smart development.\\nWhat is new is the clarification of the importance of the interplay between the individual and\\norganizational  aspects  of  collaborative  governance  for  the  declared  priorities  of  local\\ndevelopment by mayors.\\n\\n## [PDF page 476]\\n\\n476  A. Literature review\\n\\nTransformational  governance  refers  to  the  management  of  radical  changes  in  social-\\nenvironmental systems to achieve  a more sustainable state of these systems (Chaffin et  al.,\\n2016). It involves defining and mainstreaming sustainability issues and setting a transformation\\nagenda,  i.e.  introducing  a  vision  of  sustainability  and  possible  transformation  pathways,\\nfollowed  by  implementing  innovations  and  experiments  and  monitoring  the  progress  of\\ntransformation (Rotmans & Loorbach, 2009). Each of these stages of governance requires close\\ncollaboration  between  interdependent  actors  who  work  together  to  make  decisions  (Chang\\net al., 2017; Loorbach, 2010). Networked, interactive governance is considered a fundamental\\ncharacteristic of the transition to sustainability (Chang et al., 2017).\\nTransformational management is also applied at the regional and local levels. Sustainable\\nlocal transformation is a process of structural, multi-dimensional and radical change that can\\neffectively guide the development of cities and municipalities towards sustainable development\\ngoals (McCormick et al., 2013). According to Westman and Castán Broto (2022) managing the\\ntransition  to  sustainability  should  be  inclusive,  collaborative,  integrated,  experimental  and\\nreflective. The sustainable governance approach necessitates that local governments collaborate\\nwith  a  multiplicity  of  stakeholders  in  order  to  achieve  harmonisation  of  priorities,\\nthe development of shared visions, experimentation and the combination of disparate ideas and\\nsolutions (Hodson et al., 2017). Furthermore, the literature on urban climate change policy,\\nwhich  is  regarded  as  a  component  of  the  transition  to  sustainability,  indicates  that  similar\\nfeatures  of  transformative  climate  governance  can  be  observed,  including  learning,\\nparticipation,  knowledge  co-production,  long-term  thinking,  experimentation  and  flexibility\\n(Hölscher et al., 2019b). Additionally, researchers in the field of smart community development\\ngovernance  propose  a  governance  approach  predicated  on  participation  and  inclusion.\\nThe  objective  of  such  governance  is  to  empower  local  communities  in  digital  development\\nplanning  and to  ensure that all interests, perceptions, expectations and needs are taken into\\naccount in the process (Angelidou, 2015; Podgórniak-Krzykacz et al., 2020). Consequently,\\nall three forms of governance (sustainable, climate and smart) are characterized by distributed\\npower (polycentric governance), participation, high levels of information sharing, innovation\\nsupported by experimentation and learning in governance networks.\\nGovernance of local transformation requires specific capacities of local actors to mobilize\\nand  direct  the  driving  forces  and  dynamics  of  transformation  (Hölscher  et  al.,  2019a).\\nResearchers  agree  that  actors’  capacities  to  create  conditions  for  cooperation  with citizens,\\npublic  actors,  private  actors,  NGOs  and  participatory  learning,  as  well  as  Orchestrating\\ncapacity, meaning the ability to coordinate multi-stakeholder governance processes and share\\nknowledge,  play  an  important  role  (Hölscher  et  al.,  2019a,  2019b).  Indeed,  at  the  stage  of\\nsustainable  development  policy  formulation  and  implementation,  open  discussion,\\n\\n## [PDF page 477]\\n\\nCollaborative and inclusive governance…  477\\n\\nconsideration of the interests of different actors, involvement of different forms of knowledge,\\nand consensus based on common goals and trust are essential (Christie, 2001). For this reason,\\nthe ability of local authorities to build flexible institutions, networks and cooperation is seen as\\nplaying  an  important  role  in  effectively  managing  transitions  to  sustainable  development\\n(Evans et al., 2006; George, 2018; Grin et al., 2010; Loorbach, 2010; Meadowcroft et al., 2005;\\nWittmayer et al., 2014).\\nSimilar conclusions were reached by Evans et al. (2006). They argue that local government\\ncoping with long-term sustainability challenges requires high institutional capacity manifested\\nthrough  strong  local  leadership  with  a  vision  for  sustainability  and  a  commitment  to\\ncollaboration with stakeholders that shapes institutional learning capabilities. Bridging social\\ncapital, or the ability to build collaborative ties between organizations and groups in society,\\nis also crucial. Public authorities can help to create and mobilize bridging social capital and\\nincrease civil society activity through appropriate policies (such as supporting the voluntary\\nsector, promoting citizen participation, and the ability to listen to and channel citizen demands).\\nIn turn, the institutional capacity of local governments to mobilize and lead cooperation and to\\nengage civil society is important for generating local innovation and experimentation. Indeed,\\nniche, innovative solutions play an important role in transforming entrenched, unsustainable\\nsystems (McCormick et al., 2013; Raffer et al., 2022). Evans et al. (2006) call for a \\"dynamic\\napproach\\" to sustainable development management, based on the high social and institutional\\ncapacity of local governments, allowing them to better respond to the need for good governance\\nand reflective management, and to more effectively achieve sustainable development goals.\\nCooperation  between  local  governments  and  local  actors  as  the  foundation  of  local\\ntransformation  management  is  based  on  mutual  interactions  and  enables  joint  institutional\\nlearning.  This  process  involves  the  integration  of  local  and  expert  knowledge.  Institutional\\nlearning  is  in  turn  translated  into  urban  practice  or  policy  (MacDonald  et  al.,  2022).\\nHealey (2006) explains this mechanism as follows: the collective learning that occurs during\\ncollaborative  initiatives  feeds  mainstream  urban  governance  and  ultimately  transforms\\nembedded  cultural  values  and  formal  and  informal  mechanisms  for  policing  governance.\\nIn  this  context,  it  is  particularly  important  to  include  marginalized  perspectives  so  that\\ntransformative governance is inclusive and equitable.\\n\\n## [PDF page 478]\\n\\n478  A. Research assumptions\\n\\nThis section illustrates the data, methods and models used in this study to assess the impact\\nof municipalities’ ability to develop collaborative governance on the prioritization of sustainable\\nand  smart  development  challenges.  We  assume  that  Polish  local  governments  are  moving\\ntowards a more sustainable system by collaborating with stakeholders, learning and using the\\nbest available information. Chaffin et al. (2016) describe this approach as proactive.\\nWe consider the capacity of local authorities to develop collaborative governance through\\nthe  prism  of  two  aspects:  (1)  mayors’  attitudes  toward  collaboration  and  (2)  municipality’s\\ninvolvement in cooperation. We analyze the municipality’s orientation toward shaping a more\\nsustainable  system  through  the  prism  of  the  mayor’s  prioritization  of  the  challenges of\\nsustainable, smart growth in municipal governance. In our study, we analyze mayors’ attitudes\\ndue to their strong position in the municipal power system.
