Discussion\\n\\nThe  findings  of  our  research  have  led  to  several  significant  preliminary  conclusions.\\nFirst, the capacity of Polish local authorities to develop collaborative, inclusive governance is\\nconsiderable,  which  should  facilitate  the  creation  of  more  equitable  and  inclusive\\nmunicipalities.  According  to  Hambleton  (2015)  cities  that  implement  policies  that  are\\nconducive  to  the  environment  and  also  beneficial  to  residents,  while  embracing  diversity,\\nare  able to  guarantee  equity, inclusiveness, and  sustainability. A local leader in such  a city\\nshould  serve  as  a  facilitator,  orchestrating  the  efforts  of  numerous  local  actors  to  construct\\na just city and collaborating with stakeholders. The high capacity for collaborative, inclusive\\ngovernance in the surveyed sample of municipalities is determined by the attitudes of mayors\\ntoward cooperation. The mayors in this sample are generally open and ready to include various\\nstakeholder groups in local policy-making. They also recognize the need to build and strengthen\\nlocal  partnerships,  although  this  recognition  is  somewhat  less  pronounced.  The  lowest\\npercentage of mayors indicated that they perceived the need to include ethnic and minority\\ngroups in decision-making on municipal issues. This is likely due to the low participation or\\nabsence of such groups in the populations of the surveyed municipalities at the time of the\\nsurvey.  It  is  important  to  note  that  this  situation  underwent  a  significant  transformation\\nfollowing the outbreak of the war in Ukraine.\\n\\n## [PDF page 492]\\n\\n492  A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, J. Przywojska\\n\\nThe ability of local authorities to develop collaborative, inclusive governance also stems\\nfrom municipalities’ involvement in cooperation with various stakeholders. Other researchers\\nhave indicated that collaborative ventures confirm the municipality’s ability to seek external\\npartners (Tuurnas et al., 2019), the ability to establish and manage relationships with partners\\n(Blomqvist,  Levy,  2006),  as  well  as  learning  from  shared  experiences  and  transferring  that\\nknowledge  to  subsequent  collaborative  ventures  (Ulbrich  et  al.,  2009).  The  findings  of  our\\nresearch  demonstrate  that  Polish  municipalities  engage  in  substantial  collaboration  with\\nexternal  stakeholders,  particularly  with  local  non-governmental  organizations  (NGOs),\\nlocal action groups, residents’ groups, and local entrepreneurs. It is noteworthy that the majority\\nof the municipalities’ cooperation is with local stakeholders, rather than with entities of a supra-\\nlocal nature or inter-organizational networks. These include, for example, universities, experts,\\nnational  NGOs,  business  networking  institutions,  and  business  environment  institutions.\\nTo some extent, this is determined by laws that require municipalities to cooperate with local\\nactors,  e.g.  in  the  formula  of  consultation  with  residents  and  with  NGOs.  Additionally,\\nregulations exist that encourage Polish municipalities to foster collaborative relationships with\\nresidents, groups of residents, and NGOs by granting municipalities the right to adopt a civic\\nbudget  or  village  funds  (rural  municipalities).  Cooperation  with  expert  entities  and  inter-\\norganizational networks is not explicitly supported by local government law. The diverse nature\\nof  cooperation  among  Polish  municipalities  can  also  be  linked  to  organizational  culture.\\nThe organizational culture in Polish local government is dominated by clan and hierarchical\\ncharacteristics,  and  only  marginally  manifests  adhocracy  characteristics  (Podgorniak-\\nKrzykacz, 2021). This configuration indicates that conditions are favorable for initiating and\\nconducting cooperative ventures with local stakeholders. However, conditions are unfavorable\\nfor  experimentation  and  generating  innovations,  which  require  cooperation  with  support\\nnetworks and expert organizations. In contrast, research (Springer et al., 2020) conducted in\\nrural  municipalities  of  the  Wielkopolska  region  indicates  the  dominance  among  leaders  of\\ntransactional leadership, which, according to the authors, is associated with the use of only basic\\nforms of participation of residents in local governance, resulting from legislation.\\nIn  our  analysis,  the  independent  variable  we  looked  for  as  a  determinant  was  mayors’\\nprioritization of the challenges of sustainable, smart growth. The literature indicates that the\\ntransition to sustainable development requires local leaders who are aware of contemporary\\nchallenges, which is the starting point for implementing sustainable development policies and\\ninitiatives  (Alshumrani  et  al.,  2018;  Boguszewski  et  al.,  2023;  Przywojska  et  al.,  2019;\\nWittmayer et al., 2016; Wolfram et al., 2016). Also, the motivation of local actors and their\\ngoal  orientation  matters  for  the  results  of  digital  projects  (Akterujjaman  et  al.,  2022).\\nIn the sample analyzed, prioritization of sustainable smart growth is at a moderately high level.\\nHigher  priority  was  assigned  by  mayors  to  economic  and  social  challenges  than  to\\nenvironmental challenges. The lowest priority was given to the challenges of digitization and\\ndeveloping smart cities, as well as improving the integration of minorities and emphasizing\\n\\n## [PDF page 493]\\n\\nCollaborative and inclusive governance…  493\\n\\ndiversity and tolerance in the local community. In a recent survey on this topic conducted by\\nBoguszewski et al. (2023), similar results were obtained among local governments of different\\ntypes  (provinces,  counties,  municipalities)  (local  governments  attach  the  most  significant\\nimportance to the socio-economic aspects, environmental issues, but to a small extent to low-\\nemission  transport  or  green  building  and  equality  aspects).  Thus,  the  configuration  of  local\\ndevelopment  priorities  in  Polish  municipalities  still  indicates  a  preference  for  traditional,\\nestablished  paths  of  sustainable  transformation  over  more  progressive  ones  and  mayors’\\nunderstanding of sustainable development is not always comprehensive and all-encompassing.\\nThe  correlation  and  regression  analyses  conducted  in  this  article  confirm  the  impact  of\\nmunicipalities’  capacity  for  collaborative,  inclusive  governance  (both  municipal  attitudes\\ntoward  cooperation  and  its  two  components,  as  well  as  municipality’s  involvement  in\\ncooperation) on mayors’ prioritization of sustainable, smart growth challenges. Consequently,\\nit can be concluded that the attitudes of mayors who are open to cooperation, as well as the\\nmunicipality’s involvement in cooperation itself, allow mayors to perceive diverse perspectives\\nand  to  learn  from  partners,  which  in  turn  directs  local  policies  towards  sustainable,  smart\\ngrowth. These findings support the conclusions of other researchers about the importance of\\nmunicipality’s involvement in cooperation for implementing sustainable development practices\\n(Swann,  2017),  the  role  of  municipalities’  collaboration  with  residents  and  local  support\\nnetworks for improving sustainability initiatives (Hawkins, Wang, 2012), the importance of\\na  mayor’s  conciliatory  leadership  style  for  policy  agendas  that  promote  an  inclusive and\\nequitable city (Umberto et al., 2016), as well as the design and implementation of smart cities\\nand villages (Broccardo et al., 2019).\\nOur  analysis  further  showed  that  Mayors’  Attitude  Toward  Cooperation  moderates  the\\nrelationship between Municipality’s Involvement in Cooperation and Mayors’ Prioritization of\\nSustainable, Smart Growth Challenges. Considering both components of the Mayor’s Attitude\\nToward  Cooperation  (F1  -  the  mayor’s  attitude  toward  including  stakeholders  in  the  local\\ndevelopment management process, F2 - the mayor’s attitude toward initiating, mobilizing and\\nstrengthening partnerships), we confirmed a stronger moderating effect for the mayor’s attitude\\ntoward  including  stakeholders  in  the  local  development  management  process.  Identifying\\nan increase in the degree of explanation of the variability of the prioritization of sustainable,\\nsmart development challenges as a result of the inclusion of the moderator helped clarify the\\ninterplay of the individual and organizational dimensions of collaborative, inclusive governance\\non mayors’ prioritization of sustainable, smart development challenges.\\nThe moderating effect identified is surprising. The higher the mayor’s cooperative attitude\\nis, the lower the effect of the municipality’s involvement in cooperation on the prioritization of\\nsustainable,  smart  development  challenges,  and  conversely,  when  the  mayor’s  cooperative\\nattitude decreases, the prioritization of sustainable development challenges is accompanied by\\na higher level of cooperation between the municipality and stakeholders. Thus, on this basis,\\nit can be concluded that the importance of cooperation projects (organizational experiences) for\\n\\n## [PDF page 494]\\n\\n494  A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, J. Przywojska\\n\\nthe mayor’s adopted development priorities decreases as the mayor’s willingness to cooperate\\n(personal  beliefs  of  the  leader)  increases.  The  importance  of  organizational  experiences  of\\ncooperation  for  the  prioritization  of  sustainable  growth  challenges  increases  as  the  mayor’s\\nattitude towards cooperation (the leader’s personal beliefs) decreases.\\nThus, our research shows that past cooperative ventures enable municipalities to learn and\\ninfluence the determination of preferred transit paths to sustainable development, at the same\\ntime, the role of past experiences for learning is less than the attitudes and beliefs of the leader,\\nwhen  these  are  largely  oriented  towards  cooperation.  This  result  can  be  explained  by  the\\npredominance  of  cooperation  of  the  surveyed  municipalities  with  local  actors  (residents,\\nentrepreneurs,  NGOs)  over  cooperation  with  organizations  with  a  broader  scope  and  more\\nexpert  nature  of  activity  (experts,  universities,  business  environment  institutions,  economic\\nself-government,  NGOs  with  national  scope  of  activity).  Although  the  latter  are  not\\na homogeneous category, they share some characteristics. They certainly integrate knowledge,\\nhave broader visions of  transformation  and experience in building partnerships, which may\\ntranslate  into  a  greater  importance  of  working  with  them  for  learning  communities  and  the\\ndevelopment  of  sustainable,  smart  transit  paths.  In  particular,  the  support  of  such  actors  is\\nessential to integrate and mediate between different local policy interrelations or to define and\\ndesign the digital and green development (ecosystems, biodiversity) of municipalities (Ferraris\\net al., 2018; Jayasena et al., 2019; Ugolini et al., 2018). A study conducted by Soberón et al.\\n(2023)  on  the  support  of  the  municipality  of  Madrid  in  the  operationalization  of  transition\\ninitiatives  by  the  Center  for  Innovation  and  Technology  for  Development  of  the  Technical\\nUniversity  of  Madrid  (itdUPM),  confirms  the  important  role  of  this  type  of  specialized\\norganization in supporting municipalities in developing the capacity to collaborate and manage\\na sustainable transition On the other hand, an explanation for these correlations can be found\\non  the  side  of mayors’  attitudes  towards  cooperation,  and  in  particular  the  somewhat  lower\\ndeclared support of mayors for the involvement  of ethnic and minority  groups and socially\\nexcluded  groups  in  the  creation  of  local  policies  or  in  the  building  of  local  partnerships.\\nThis  may  suggest  that  the  smaller  and  less  inclusive  (and  therefore  including  fewer\\nperspectives) the mayor’s attitude towards cooperation, the less important it is for the mayor to\\nadopt sustainable inclusive development priorities.\\n\\n6.  Conclusions\\n\\nThe  results  of  the  survey  presented  in  this  article  provide  a  deeper  insight  into  the\\nrelationship  between  collaborative,  inclusive  governance,  as  manifested  in  the  degree  of\\nmunicipal  involvement  in  stakeholder  cooperation  and  local  leaders’  attitudes  toward\\ncooperation, and the mayor’s prioritization of sustainable, smart growth challenges. Based on\\n\\n## [PDF page 495]\\n\\nCollaborative and inclusive governance…  495\\n\\nthe results of surveys conducted in 1,236 municipalities in Poland, we confirmed the existence\\nof  a  relationship  between  municipal  involvement  in  collaboration  and  the  prioritization  of\\nsustainable,  smart  growth  challenges,  as  well  as  between  municipal  attitudes  toward\\ncooperation and the prioritization of sustainable, smart growth challenges. Greater capacity for\\ncollaborative,  inclusive  governance  fosters  mayors’  more  comprehensive  perceptions  of\\nsustainability challenges. We further demonstrate that attitudes toward collaboration moderate\\nthe  relationship  between  municipal  engagement  in  collaboration  and  the  prioritization  of\\nsustainable, smart growth. Our survey results shed new light on this relationship. They captured\\nthat the importance of personal factors, mayors’ attitudes, and their willingness to cooperate for\\nadopted  local  policy  priorities  is  particularly  high  under  conditions  of  low  municipal\\ninvolvement  in  cooperation  networks.  Thus,  we  confirm  the  significant  impact  of  the  local\\nleader’s  beliefs  on  the  municipality’s  entry  into  the  path  of  transition  to  sustainable,  smart\\ndevelopment. When the mayor’s collaborative mindset is low, the role of the municipality’s\\nengagement  with  stakeholders,  and  thus  the  role  of  the  mayor’s  administrative  background\\nexperience in prioritizing sustainable development challenges, increases. The importance of\\ninstitutional factors in determining the preferred path of the municipality’s transformation thus\\nincreases  The  predominance  of  personal  over  organizational  factors  in  the  mayor’s\\ndetermination  of  development  priorities  in  a  situation  of  high  declarative  openness  to\\ncooperation is explained by the nature of past cooperation. We found a significantly larger scale\\nof cooperation between municipalities and local actors than with supra-local and expert actors.\\nIn addition, the smaller the scale of cooperation, the more it is limited to traditional local actors\\n(residents,  NGOs),  which  may  have  an  impact  on  its  lower  importance  for  prioritizing\\nsustainable smart growth than in the case of expanding cooperation with expert partners.\\nBased on these results, a recommendation can be made to expand municipal cooperation\\ninto partnerships with supra-local expert actors with broader resources, skills, knowledge, and\\nvisions, in order to improve the effectiveness of municipal collaborative learning and to transfer\\nthis experience to cooperation with traditional actors (e.g. residents), and consequently to adopt\\nsustainable and smart transformation pathways. Collaborative ventures with such actors can be\\neducational, training, experimental, and address transformations towards sustainability.\\nThe  results  presented  also  highlight  the  importance  of  the  mayoral  candidate  selection\\nprocess in local elections and the role of residents who are aware of current local challenges.\\nThrough the electoral process, residents appoint their representative to the position of mayor,\\nand the selection of a candidate with a consensual attitude, open to dialogue and cooperation,\\naccording  to  our  survey  results,  should  contribute  to  the  formulation  of  local  policies  with\\na greater focus on sustainable and smart development. These survey results point to the need to\\neducate residents about the challenges of sustainable and smart development and to influence\\nthe topics of debate during the municipal election campaign period.\\n\\n## [PDF page 496]\\n\\n496  A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, J. Przywojska\\n\\nOur analysis has several limitations. First, we do not take into account other factors that\\nmay  determine  local  policy  priorities,  such  as  the  ability  to  obtain  funding  for  sustainable\\ndevelopment and smart community development projects. Future analyses should therefore also\\nconsider  the  importance  of  financial  factors  in  the  priorities  adopted  by  mayors.  Second,\\nour research is limited to an analysis of priorities and does not take into account completed\\nsustainable smart community projects. This approach does not allow us to draw conclusions\\nabout  the  importance  of  mayors’  attitudes  towards  and  involvement  in  cooperation  for  real\\nprogress in the transition to sustainable smart development.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Przywojska, A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, M. Kalisiak-M delska\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nThe challenge of demographic transition is currently affecting many countries in the EU,\\nincluding  Poland.  Demographic  transition  is  a  result  of  persistently  low  fertility  rates  and\\nincreasing life expectancy, which results in an aging population (Li et al., 2019; Podgórniak-\\nKrzykacz,  Przywojska,  Warwas,  2020;  Podgórniak-Krzykacz,  Przywojska,  Wiktorowicz,\\n2020a; Zhang et al., 2021). The share of people aged over 65 in the total EU population will\\ngrow by 2050 from 17% to 30% (Podgórniak-Krzykacz, Przywojska, Wiktorowicz, 2020b).\\nThe  population  of  Poland  will  also  become  increasingly  older;  by  2060,  the  number  of\\nindividuals  over  60  in  Poland  is  expected  to  rise  by  21.0%  compared  to  2022,  reaching\\n11.9  million  seniors,  which  will  account  for  38.3%  of  the  total  population  (GBówny  Urząd\\nStatystyczny, 2023). This trend necessitates an urgent reorganization of living conditions, the\\nlocal environment, social services, and the adaptation of product and service offerings to make\\nthem more friendly for the elderly (Fulmer et al., 2020; Hoof, Marston, 2021; Kowalczyk-AnioB\\net al., 2021).\\nAt the same time, scientists and international organizations emphasize the importance of\\ntaking  action  for  social  inclusion  and  environmental  protection  in  line  with  the  concept  of\\nsustainable development. The pursuit of sustainable development has also become a goal of the\\nage-friendly cities movement. The WHO, as the originator of the age-friendly cities concept,\\nemphasizes  the  importance  of  sustainable  development  within  the  local  environment.\\nAn environment better adapted to the needs of older adults should also provide broader benefits\\nfor the entire community, including the advantages of sustainable development (Hoof, 2023;\\nvan Hoof et al., 2024; WHO, 2018).\\nAt the same time, individual consumer attitudes and behaviors are crucial in the pursuit of\\nsustainable  development  (Oosterveer,  Spaargaren,  2013).  Sustainable  consumption  is\\nsignificant  for  ensuring  both  social  and  environmental  sustainability  (Vargas-Merino  et  al.,\\n2023).  Among  sustainable  consumer  behaviors  aimed  at  minimizing  their  negative\\nenvironmental impact, three main groups can be distinguished: choosing sustainable options\\n(organic  and  eco-friendly  products,  as  well  as  local  goods  and  environmentally  friendly\\npackaging),  avoiding  the  purchase  of  new  products  (circular  practices  and  recommerce,\\npurchasing  second-hand  items,  or  participating  in  the  second-hand  market),  and  supporting\\ncollective  actions  (group  purchasing,  social  initiatives  within  the  sharing  economy,\\nand borrowing) (Bi et al., 2024).\\nThe first group of behaviors, which involves choosing sustainable products and packaging,\\nis  widely  discussed  in  the  literature.  However,  significantly  less  attention  has  been  paid  to\\nconsumer attitudes and behaviors aimed at avoiding the purchase of new products and reducing\\nwaste generation through circular practices. Researchers emphasize that the circular behaviors\\nof individuals contribute to increasing resource efficiency and reducing waste. These behaviors\\n\\n## [PDF page 503]\\n\\n<Rethink and use product smarter=…  503\\n\\nalign with the circular economy, which promotes sustainable development and has a strong\\npotential to transform society towards a more sustainable future by extending the life cycle of\\nproducts and encouraging responsible consumption (Ma et al., 2021). Responsible consumption\\ninvolves  conscious  and  rational  resource  consumption  that  seeks  to  mitigate  the  negative\\nenvironmental impact by preventing environmental degradation (Jain et al., 2023; Jiang et al.,\\n2024). Responsible consumption has many dimensions. It can be considered as sustainable,\\nethical, rational, local consumption, as well as a lifestyle defined as minimalism.\\nCircular behaviors help reduce the use of new products by extending the usefulness of those\\nalready  in  use.  Ali  and  Choe(2022)  categorized  the  following  circular  behaviors:  Care  3\\nmaintaining and repairing products, Upgrade 3 improving the functionality and aesthetics of\\nproducts to extend their lifespan and reduce the need for purchasing new ones; Repurpose 3\\nreusing  unused  products  (through  selling,  giving  away,  or  applying  them  in  new  ways);\\nAppreciate 3 using the product one already owns and resisting the urge to discard it due to\\npsychological obsolescence.\\nCurrently,  we  also  have  several  Frameworks  R  that  comprehensively  classify  circular\\nbehaviors.  These  are  sets  of  strategies  that  indicate  how  to  achieve  a  circular  economy.\\nThese frameworks are useful for both researchers and businesses to understand the pathways to\\na  circular  economy.  One  of  the  more  developed  frameworks,  the  Framework  9R,  lists  ten\\ncircular  economy  strategies,  starting  from  the  \\"Refuse\\"  (R0)  strategy  to  \\"Recover\\"  (R9),\\nshowing different levels of priority in waste management and the associated circular behaviors\\n(Kirchherr et al., 2017; Potting et al., 2017). At the top of the hierarchy, and thus the most\\nprioritized, are Refuse (R0), Reduce (R2), and Rethink (R3), which focus on smarter and more\\nsustainable practices in the production and use of products. The strategies Reuse (R4), Repair\\n(R5), Refurbish (R6), Remanufacture (R7), and Repurpose (R8) aim to extend the lifespan of\\nproducts and their parts. For the useful application of materials, the strategies Recycle (R8) and\\nRecover (R9) are highlighted.\\nIn our article, we focus on the circular behaviors of seniors related to smarter product use\\nthrough the Rethink strategy. This strategy is one of the priority strategies in the Framework\\n9R and pertains to consumers. It encourages them to share products with each other to maximize\\ntheir  usage  and  suggests  reconsidering  how  products  are  used  and  disposed  of.  Consumer\\nbehaviors associated with the \\"Rethink\\" strategy include, among others, borrowing, renting,\\nand sharing products.\\nThe main aim of this article is to assess the attitudes of individuals aged 55+ in Poland\\ntowards  responsible  consumption  and  to  identify  circular,  sustainable  behaviors  among  this\\ndemographic,  focusing  on  smarter  product  use  through  the  Rethink  strategy,  undertaken  in\\nresponse  to  environmental  issues  and  excessive  waste  production.  We  focused  on  older\\nconsumers for several reasons. Firstly, the dynamic aging of the Polish population means that\\nseniors  represent  a  significant  consumer  segment.  Secondly,  studies  on  consumer  behavior\\nthroughout the lifespan are becoming increasingly popular as the number of consumers aged\\n\\n## [PDF page 504]\\n\\n504  J. Przywojska, A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, M. Kalisiak-M delska\\n\\n55+ steadily increases (Carpenter, Yoon, 2015; Venn et al., 2017). Thus, we contribute to the\\nongoing  discussion  on  consumer  behaviors  among  older  adults.  Thirdly,  we  fill  the  gap  in\\nknowledge regarding Rethink-type circular behaviors. Existing research has not addressed this\\nissue. Few studies to date have focused on responsible and sustainable consumption among\\nmature  adults  (Grasso  et  al.,  2019;  Zbuchea  et  al.,  2021)  or  responsible  consumption  in\\na broader - generational 3 context (Bulut et al., 2017; Diprose et al., 2019; Gordon-Wilson,\\nModi, 2015; Morrison, Beer, 2017; Pinto et al., 2011). On the other hand, studies concerning\\nolder  adults  in  Poland  have  focused  on  assessing  the  environmental  awareness  of  seniors\\n(Ministerstwo  Klimatu  i  [rodowiska,  2020;  WBodarczyk,  2019)  and  identifying  sustainable\\nshopping  behaviors  (Zalega,  2018,  2024).  Fourthly,  understanding  consumer  behaviors  in\\nrelation to R-strategies is, according to researchers (Zimmermann et al., 2024), essential for\\nbusinesses to adjust their marketing strategies to meet the needs and preferences of consumers,\\nand ultimately to ensure the successful adoption of a circular economy.\\nIn the article, we present the results of representative research among Polish consumers\\naged 55 and older. The study allowed us to answer the following research questions:\\n1.  What environmental problems are considered the most burdensome by individuals aged\\n55+?\\n2.  What is the attitude of individuals aged 55+ towards responsible consumption?\\n3.  To what extent do individuals aged 55+ use products in a smarter way, applying the\\nRethink strategy?\\n\\n2. Discussion and conclusion\\n\\nThe Rethink behaviors  analyzed in our study  among Poles aged 55+ are  undertaken by\\nrespondents  with  moderate  frequency.  Particularly  rarely  practiced  is  the  sale  of  their  own\\nclothes and equipment on online platforms such as olx.pl, vinted.pl, and allegro.pl. This may\\nbe hindered by lower digital competencies of older adults in Poland, as pointed out by other\\nresearchers(Garwol,  2019;  SusBo  et  al.,  2019).  On  the  other  hand,  respondents  in  our  study\\nrecognize the burden of environmental problems. The most pressing issues they highlight are\\nair  pollution,  water  pollution,  and  overcrowded  landfills.  These  problems  significantly\\ndetermine the quality of life for older adults, who are one of the groups particularly vulnerable\\nto the negative consequences of such threats (e.g., the increased mortality of older adults due to\\ndiseases resulting from poor air quality) (Michalak et al., 2022).\\n\\n## [PDF page 511]\\n\\n<Rethink and use product smarter=…  511\\n\\nExisting studies indicate that women tend to have stronger pro-environmental attitudes than\\nmen. They are significantly more likely to engage in various environmental activities (Tindall\\net al., 2003; Zelezny et al., 2000). Our research findings also confirm that women aged 55+ are\\nmore sensitive to the issue of climate change. They are more concerned than men about the\\nongoing  degradation  of  the  natural  environment  (air  pollution,  water  pollution).\\nWomen  are  slightly  more  likely  than  men  to  adhere  to  the  principles  of  responsible\\nconsumption. They are more inclined to produce goods (such as food or clothing) themselves\\nrather  than  purchasing  them.  These  attitudes  are  not  solely  a  result  of  disposable  income,\\nbut also influenced by trends, the desire to stand out, or social sensitivity (e.g., donating clothing\\nto those in need). For women, emotional and sentimental values attached to goods are also\\nimportant. However, women engage in Rethink circular behaviors with the same, equally low\\nfrequency as men.\\nMen,  as  respondents  in  our  study,  similarly  to  women,  recognize  the  importance  of\\nenvironmental  issues,  although  they  attach  more  significance  to  the  problem  of  waste.\\nLike women, they also follow the principles of responsible consumption. They see the rationale\\nin producing goods themselves or sharing products. However, it is difficult to clearly observe\\na connection between circular behaviors and gender, as indicated by other researchers (Bassi,\\n2023; Patel et al., 2017).\\nAn important variable influencing pro-environmental behaviors is income, as it is a key\\nfactor determining purchasing power. For most older adults, the primary source of income is\\npensions,  which  are  typically  allocated  to  meet  basic  needs.  As  highlighted  in  the  Green\\nGeneration  report  (Mobile  Institute,  2020),  there  is  a  common  belief  among  individuals\\naged 55+ that living according to ecological principles involves additional costs.\\nInterestingly, the results of our study indicate that respondents with relatively high incomes\\n(above 4,000 PLN) are less likely to follow the principles of responsible consumption in their\\nconsumer choices. They apply the principle of minimalism to the least extent. On the other\\nhand, individuals with lower incomes are more inclined to produce goods themselves or share\\nitems (such as tools, devices, books, etc.) with others. For Polish seniors, such behaviors may\\nstem from habits acquired in the past, personal experiences, or values passed down from their\\nfamilies. Thus, some circular behaviors seem to be \\"inherited\\" from generation to generation\\nrather than the result of ecological awareness development. On the other hand, these behaviors\\ncould also have an economic  basis. As indicated by the report on the economic security of\\nhouseholds in Poland (Derkacz et al., 2024), seniors, compared to other age groups, assess their\\nability to engage in current consumption less favorably. Their incomes often do not allow them\\nto achieve financial stability. The lack of sufficient financial  resources to meet basic needs\\nlimits the tendency to waste resources and forces a more rational approach to their use. Younger\\ngenerations entering retirement carry with them consumption behaviors and habits shaped in\\nmarket economy conditions. These behaviors are often revised due to a decrease in disposable\\nincome.\\n\\n## [PDF page 512]\\n\\n512  J. Przywojska, A. Podgórniak-Krzykacz, M. Kalisiak-M delska\\n\\nConsidering  the  criterion  of  place  of  residence,  our  study  shows  that  the  ranking  of\\nenvironmental issues is the same for  respondents living in rural and urban areas.  However,\\nthose living in rural areas were more likely to point out water pollution as a major problem.\\nOn the other hand, city dwellers are more sensitive to climate change. In cities, especially large\\nones, a range of phenomena related to air pollution accumulates, such as the urban heat island\\neffect and the lack of biologically active surfaces. These issues have a significant impact on the\\nhealth of older adults.\\nOur study focused on the attitudes and pro-environmental behaviors of individuals aged 55+\\nin Poland, with particular emphasis on the implementation of the \\"Rethink\\" strategy within\\nresponsible  consumption.  The  research  reveals  a  positive  attitude  among  seniors  towards\\nresponsible consumption, though it also highlights limitations related to the adoption of more\\nsustainable  and  digital  solutions,  such  as  online  sales  or  shared  purchasing.  The  findings\\nprovide valuable insight into the consumer behavior of older adults and indicate the need for\\neducational  and  systemic  support  to  increase  their  involvement  in  circular  consumption.\\nCampaigns should emphasize the importance of environmental issues, such as climate change,\\nwhich, according to our research, are less recognized by individuals aged 55+. Education should\\nalso promote \\"Rethink\\" behaviors as simple and accessible ways to protect the environment.\\nAn  important  direction  for  action  should  also  involve  promoting  local  circular  economy\\ninitiatives,  particularly  by  facilitating  access  to  product  exchange  and  rental  platforms.\\nFor individuals aged 55+, education regarding sharing, selling, or exchanging goods online is\\ncrucial. Future research is also recommended to explore in greater depth the underlying factors\\ninfluencing the consumer behaviors of older adults.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1.  Ali, M.I.M., Choe, P. (2022). Introduction\\n\\nPersonal development and improvement of women’s social and professional situation are\\nimportant factors behind their involvement in organizations. The Rural Homemakers’ Club is\\na voluntary, independent, social and professional organization of women that operates in rural\\nareas.  Important  factors  behind  the  establishment  of  women’s  organizations  are  political\\nfactors, actually the influence of politically active persons on women. The Rural Homemakers’\\nClub  in  SBobódka  BoBszowiecka,  which  was  the  first  such  club  in  the  Polish  territory,\\nwas established in 1877 in JanisBawice by a socialist activist, Filipina PBaskowicka. Therefore,\\nthe factors related to the transfer of innovations are crucial. In that case Filipina PBaskowicka\\nacted as such factor, although she was not the one who came up with the model of the Club as\\nan  organization  because  a  similar  organization  called  the  Association  of  Homemakers\\n(Towarzystwo Gospodyń) operated since 1866 in Piaseczno in the Gdańsk Pomerania.\\nWomen’s  associations  that  were  established  were  ancillary  to  agricultural  clubs.\\nSuch agricultural clubs were voluntary, social and economic organizations associating farmers\\nand their purpose was to boost and improve agricultural production. Thanks to access to state-\\nof-the-art  knowledge  in  the  area  of  hygiene,  health  and  nutrition,  members  of  female\\norganizations were to support the development of rural communities. In other words, the first\\nwomen’s organizations in rural areas were established partly due to the necessity of convincing\\nwives to let their husbands out of the house to take part in training sessions. Wives discouraged\\ntheir husbands from participating in agricultural associations as they believed that they spent\\ntime  there  chatting  and  drinking  alcohol.  In  1866  Julian  Kraziewicz  established  the\\n\\n## [PDF page 519]\\n\\nDeterminants of rural women’s…  519\\n\\n<Association  of  Homemakers=  (Towarzystwo  Gospodyń)  to  persuade  women  that  their\\nsuspicions towards their husbands were wrong, to present the purpose of the associations and\\nteach women useful homemaking skills.\\nAt present the Rural Homemakers’ Clubs mostly cherish local traditions, draw connections\\nto roots, inspire to take action and contribute to building bridges between generations in local\\ncommunities. They successfully complete local projects, take civic initiatives and perform tasks\\nprovided for in the SoBectwo Fund. The Rural Homemakers’ Clubs get involved in cultural\\nevents  organized  in  gminas  (communes),  poviats  and  capitals  of  voivodeships,  including,\\namong other things, harvest festivals or  exhibitions of handicrafts. The  RHCs cherish local\\ncustoms, cultivate culture and promote culinary traditions. The Clubs cultivate the traditions of\\nfamily  and  neighborly  life  and  keep  forgotten  local  traditions  alive.  They  create  amazing\\nhandicrafts keeping cultural heritage for future generations. Together with village heads they\\norganize various ceremonies such as harvest festivals, games for children, youth and adults that\\nbring together entire generations. The activities of the RHCs are not just limited to cooking and\\nsinging but also include staging theatre performances, doing needlework, making decorations,\\ncultivating local traditions, celebrating religious and other holidays and recovering customs.\\nThe Rural Homemakers’ Clubs make life in the country more attractive. Despite many socio-\\ncultural changes and ongoing march towards modernity the Rural Homemakers’ Clubs have\\nsurvived, remain faithful to traditions and bravely implement their goals.\\nMotivation  is  very  important  to  the  organization  and  refers  to  forces  that  determine\\ndirections, intensity and duration of human activities. Motivating people to act is not easy, let\\nalone become engaged in social work, hence the idea to research the motivation of women who\\nget  involved  the  activities  of  the  Rural  Homemakers’  Clubs’.  There  are  numerous  theories\\nrelated to motivation. Maslov’s Hierarchy of needs theory (Maslov, 1954; McClelland, 1987)\\npoints to the hierarchy of needs from physiological ones to self-fulfillment being the motivating\\nfactors. The equity theory or social comparison theory (Adams, 1965) points to a psychological\\nphenomenon  of  drawing  conclusions  regarding  oneself  in  terms  of  comparisons  to  others\\n(abilities, values, attitudes). According to the expectancy theory (Vroom, 1964), motivation\\ndepends on two factors: on how strongly we desire something and on the expected likelihood\\nof fulfilling that desire. A goal-setting theory, a theory of motivation (Locke, Latham, 1990)\\nposits that clear, well-defined and measurable goals improve performance much better than\\nthose  which  are  unclear.  The  Job  design  model  (the  job  characteristics  theory)  is  a  model\\ndeveloped  by  Richard  Hackman  and  Grieg  Oldham  (Hackman,  Oldham,  1976,  1980)  that\\ndescribes the job whose five basic characteristics include: diversity of skills, task idiopathy,\\ntask meaning, independence and feedback. The self-determination theory (Deci, Ryan, 1985;\\nRyan, Deci, 2000) is based on the assumption that the desire to reach a specific goal is a basic\\nsource of motivation. The goal is what we intend to achieve within a specific period of time.\\n\\n## [PDF page 520]\\n\\n520  J. PuchaBa\\n\\nThe research into the participation of women in non-governmental organizations discovers\\nseveral  motivating  factors,  including  willingness  to  make  a  contribution  to  the  society,\\nacquiring knowledge and skills, networking, increasing career perspectives and building self-\\nesteem. Women are also interested in  working for non-governmental organizations because\\nthey  care  about  social  issues,  search  for  educational  experiences,  express  idealism  and\\nappreciate flexibility and independence. The involvement in NGOs may strengthen women’s\\nposition in economic and social terms, particularly in developing countries where traditional\\ncustoms  frequently  make  the  involvement  of  women  difficult  (Panday,  2016). Despite  those\\ndifficulties a growing number of women’s NGOs is an indication of growing recognition of\\nwomen’s important role in social growth and their potential to influence politics and the process\\nof solving women’s problems.\\n\\n2. Introduction\\n\\nMaintenance  management  involves  organizing  resources  to  deal  with  the  problems  of\\nmaintaining production equipment and obtaining maximum benefits from the decisions made.\\nMaintenance decision-making includes but is not limited to selecting maintenance strategies,\\nsetting  maintenance  priorities,  scheduling  work  orders,  etc.  Computerized  maintenance\\nmanagement  systems  (CMMS)  are  commonly  used  to  support  maintenance  management\\nprocesses. These systems enable integrating related data on equipment, work performed and\\ncosts,  spare  parts  suppliers,  and  inventory  to  manage  maintenance  workflows,  including\\nproactive  maintenance  planning,  reactive  maintenance  ordering,  order  fulfillment  tracking,\\nand maintenance performance benchmarking.\\nHowever,  few  CMMS  systems  on  the  market  provide  decision-making  capabilities,\\nso maintenance personnel must make decisions based on their experience, the information in\\nthe  operator’s  system  event  report  and/or  maintenance  manual,  or  a  combination  thereof.\\nThis  empirical  approach  to  decision-making  usually  does  not  produce  the  expected  results.\\nPoor decisions can result in unnecessary or inappropriate maintenance, inefficient use of human\\nresources and time, and unnecessary spare parts purchases.\\nThe operational data collected in CMMS systems is significant and large enough to be used\\nto make decisions regarding the scope  and frequency of preventive maintenance. However,\\nif  a  decision  is  made  about  reactive  actions  (i.e.,  actions  taken  after  a  failure),  appropriate\\nanalysis of historical data in connection with the information contained in the failure report in\\nthe CMMS system will enable better resource allocation and shorten the service implementation\\ntime.  Historical  data  contains  information  about  emergency  events  that  occurred  on  the\\nproduction  line,  their  causes,  and  actions  taken.  With  this  data,  it  is  possible  to  automate\\ndecision-making processes based on a data-driven approach.\\nData-driven  approaches,  particularly  machine  learning  (ML),  are  attracting  attention\\n(Bousdekis et al., 2021; Justus et al., 2024). The concept of ML is not new, but it still enjoys\\ngreat  interest.  Thanks  to  advances  in  algorithms,  computing  power,  inexpensive  memory,\\nand large amounts of data, recent years have seen a significant increase in the applicability of\\nML in various areas of engineering practice, such as maintenance processes (Çınar et al., 2020;\\nCline et al., 2017; Arena et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2022; Antosz et al., 2023; Vanderschueren\\net al., 2023). According to Quatrini et al. (2020), <by using ML tools it is possible to discover\\nthe  relationship  between  different  factors  and  analyze  the  degree  of  influence  of  related\\n\\n## [PDF page 545]\\n\\nIdentification of the causes…  545\\n\\nvariables=. ML-based approaches can be applied to high-dimensional and unstructured data and\\nextract hidden relationships within data in the manufacturing environment.\\nDecision tree (DT) and random forest (RF) models are important ML tools for decision\\nanalysis due to their visualization and interpretability features (Kaparthi, Bumblauskas, 2020;\\nAmruthnath Gupta, 2019; Misaii et al., 2022). The article aims to present the possibility of using\\nDT and RF to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of maintenance activities by identifying\\nthe probable cause of a failure based on historical data stored in the enterprise’s CMMS system.\\nThe paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides literature reviews. Section 3 explains\\nthe methods and materials used in the study. Section 4 presents the study’s results. Finally,\\nSection 5 presents the conclusions of this research.\\n\\n2.  Background\\n\\nMaintenance is defined as <a set of all technical, organizational, and managerial activities\\nduring the life cycle of an object, the purpose of which is to maintain or renew the state in which\\nit  can  be  used  to  fulfill  the  required  function=  (EN  13306:  2017).  Maintenance  plays\\nan important role in every manufacturing company, and its costs, depending on the industry,\\nmay constitute a significant percentage of the company’s production costs (Rebaiaia, Ait-Kadi,\\n2023).\\nEffective  and  efficient  implementation  of  maintenance  processes  allows  you  to  achieve\\nnumerous benefits, including reduced operating costs, stable level of product quality, reduced\\nenvironmental  impact  (e.g.,  energy  consumption,  consumables),  and  more  efficient  use  of\\nresources (Hallioui et al., 2023). Maintenance management professionals implement various\\nmaintenance strategies to avoid unexpected production downtime and increase the efficiency\\nof production assets (Mahmud et al., 2024; Gatta et al., 2024). Broadly speaking, maintenance\\nstrategies  can  be  divided  into  three  main  categories:  corrective,  preventive,  and  predictive\\nmaintenance. In reactive strategy, maintenance actions are taken when anomalies or failures\\noccur. This approach leads to high costs of unexpected production downtime. Additionally,\\nemergency repairs often require expedited parts shipping, overtime costs, and higher service\\nfees  from  third-party  vendors,  further  increasing  overall  expenses.  Preventive  maintenance\\n(PM) is <carried out intended to assess and/or to mitigate degradation and reduce the probability\\nof failure of an item= (EN 13306:2017). PM can be considered the most common maintenance\\npolicy in which a system is maintained preventively at set intervals regardless of the system’s\\nfailure history. Despite the various benefits that PM can bring, there are many shortcomings,\\nwhich  result  mainly  from  the  fact  that  maintenance  activities  are  generally  carried  out\\nprematurely, resulting in reduced availability and increased costs (Polenghi et al., 2023).\\n\\n## [PDF page 546]\\n\\n546  I. Rojek, M. Jasiulewicz-Kaczmarek, M. Piechowski, D. MikoBajewski\\n\\nAs  modern  production  systems  become  increasingly  complex  and  involve  highly\\ninterconnected  machines,  traditional  maintenance  strategies  (reactive  and  preventive)  are\\ninsufficient. The answer to these challenges is a predictive maintenance strategy supported by\\nthe development of digital technologies (Pinciroli et al., 2023; Sanchez-Londono et al., 2023;\\nWanget  al.,  2023).  Maintenance  is  an  area  that  can  benefit  the  most  from  digitalization\\n(Shaheen, Németh, 2022; Saihi et al., 2023) because acquiring and processing data from both\\nmachines and the environment in which the production process is carried out can significantly\\nimprove  maintenance  decision-making  processes.  Regardless  of  the  maintenance  strategies\\nadopted  in  the  company,  historical  data  on  emergency  events,  maintenance  activities\\nundertaken  and  their  effectiveness  are  very  important.  In  the  case  of  reactive  maintenance,\\nthe response time is important, i.e. the time from reporting the incident by the operator to taking\\ncorrective actions. The length of this time depends on the quality of the information contained\\nin the notification, as it allows for the identification of the job, the estimation of the required\\nlabor force, the identification of spare parts, and the determination of whether and what tools\\nare needed. Analysis of the data contained in the CMMS system allows you to make the right\\ndecision and shorten both the response time and the service implementation time.\\nConcerning  the  preventive  strategy,  it  is  important  to  define  the  plan  and  schedule  of\\nmaintenance interventions (e.g., time intervals and scopes of individual services) so that they\\nare  not  performed  in  excessive  amounts  and  scope.  Availability  of  resources  must  also  be\\nensured.  According  to  Campbell  et  al.  (2015),  planning  determines  what  needs  to  be  done,\\nin what order, and with what skills. The degree to which companies can derive value from data\\nprocessing and draw actionable conclusions can be an important factor in improving production\\nprocesses, reducing costs and resource consumption, and thus meeting customer demands.\\nAccording to (Carvalho et al., 2019; Emmanouilidis, 2023), one of the promising tools in\\nthe proactive maintenance approaches is machine learning (ML) methods. Machine learning is\\ndefined as <a set of methodologies and algorithms capable of extracting knowledge from data,\\nand  continuously  improving  their  capabilities,  by  learning  from  experience  (i.e.,  from  data\\naccumulating over time)= (Bertolini et al., 2021). According to Ruiz-Sarmiento et al. (2020),\\nML techniques <are data-driven approaches that find complex and non-linear patterns in data\\nand  build  models  from  them  that  can  be  used  for  prediction,  detection,  classification  or\\nregression=.  The  literature  analysis  indicates  that  the  use  of  ML  models  in  maintenance  is\\nbecoming more and more popular (Dalzochio et al., 2020; Campos et al., 2019; Abidi et al.,\\n2022; Surucu et al., 2023; Arena et al., 2022; Alsina et al., 2018; Alvarez Quiñones et al., 2023;\\nChakroun et al., 2024). Problem statement\\n\\nThe present study covered a medical device company. To formulate the research problem,\\nit was assumed that the response time (i.e. the time that elapses from the notification of a failure\\nto the start of the repair process of a localized damaged technical object) is a key indicator of\\nthe effectiveness of maintenance activities and translates into the economic efficiency of the\\nenterprise (downtime is a loss). For the aforementioned reasons, particular emphasis should be\\nplaced on effectively reducing the aforementioned response time. This is important not only for\\nreducing machine downtime itself but consequently also for optimizing the production process\\nas a whole. To minimize the response time, several preventive measures are taken, starting with\\nmaintaining  an  adequate  number  and  level  of  training  of  maintenance  services,  ensuring\\nmonitoring and rapid alarming of equipment anomalies and failures that have occurred, to the\\nrapid and accurate identification and classification of the causes of failures, determining the\\nhuman resources, tools, materials, and spare parts required for their removal. Mistakes or delays\\nin the latter activities (e.g., the location and identification of failure causes) can significantly\\naffect the efficiency of maintenance operations. The consequences can be costly, leading not\\nonly  to  increased  machine  downtime  but  also  to  increased  repair  and  downtime  costs.\\nFor  the  aforementioned  reasons,  solutions  that  explore,  support,  and  automate  this  area  are\\nscientifically  and  economically  important.  Effective  methods  and  tools,  including  AI-based\\nones, are constantly being sought to support human service decision-makers with easier, faster,\\nmore  efficient  maintenance  activities  using  prediction  and/or  classification.\\nFor the aforementioned reasons, ML is increasingly used to speed up failure identification and\\ndiagnosis processes.\\n\\n3.2.  Data set\\n\\nThe company under study uses a CMMS system and operators enter emergency reports into\\nit. The emergency event thus entered is described in a uniform procedure using line segment,\\nunit, component, and type of failure. In this way, it is possible to identify where the failure\\noccurred. As part of the same procedure, information on the cause of the failure, the extent of\\nthe maintenance work carried out (this may be only adjustment, for example), and the resources\\ninvolved are entered into the CMMS after the failure has been rectified. These are entered post-\\nhoc by the maintenance technicians.\\n\\n## [PDF page 548]\\n\\n548  I. Rojek, M. Jasiulewicz-Kaczmarek, M. Piechowski, D. MikoBajewski\\n\\nIn the study, the computational analyses were based on actual data over 18 months from the\\ncompany studied. The data comprised 5000 occurring failure reports and the maintenance staff’s\\nassociated responses (service actions). The following input parameters were assumed:\\n\uf0b7  line segment,\\n\uf0b7  unit,\\n\uf0b7  component,\\n\uf0b7  type of failure.\\nIt was also assumed that the following output parameters would be used in the system:\\n\uf0b7  task type,\\n\uf0b7  type of repair.\\nThis treatment of the data set enabled the design and testing of the computational tools\\npresented next.\\n\\n3.3.  Statistical and Computational Methods\\n\\nIn this study, Statistica 13 software (StatSoft Power Solutions Inc., Tulsa, USA) was used\\nto perform statistical analyses of the data and develop computational models. This software is\\nrelatively often used in scientific research, including the analysis and modelling of industrial\\nissues (Ciężak, KutyBowska, 2023; MusiaB et al., 2023).\\nVarious statistical and computational methods and tools have been used to achieve such\\na goal (Rojek et. al., 2023; Scaife, 2024). This study used classifiers based on General Chi-\\nsquare  Automatic  Interaction  Detector  (CHAID)  and  random  forests.  Using  this  group  of\\nclassifiers brings with it faster u performance, the possibility to process symbolic data directly,\\nand the possibility to add a tree as part of interactive tree building. A separate tree was built for\\neach input parameter to aggregate the results from both trees by considering them together.\\nThe choice of this solution is based on the need to compromise between the large amount of\\ndata to be processed, accuracy, and speed. For the aforementioned reasons, preprocessing or\\nedge processing, i.e., the reduction of the entire input data set to a vector of the most relevant\\nfeatures, is increasingly used, saving computational complexity at the expense of classification\\naccuracy. In our solution, we also applied feature (input data) importance analysis (example for\\ntask type: Figure 1).\\n\\n## [PDF page 549]\\n\\nIdentification of the causes…  549\\n\\nFigure 1. Feature importance for <type of task=.\\nThe  tree-building  algorithm  analysis  presented  below  aims  to  find  a  set  of  logical\\nIF partitioning conditions that ensure an unambiguous classification of objects. In this study,\\nwe  compared  the  results  of  two  computational  methods:  CHAID  and  the  random  forest\\nalgorithm obtained on the studied data set.\\nCHAID enables the construction of an optimal tree using cross-validation (optional) for\\nclassification problems with quantitative and qualitative predictors. The program can determine\\nvarious statistics of results (predicted classes). For classification, the basis for splitting the node\\nis  the  chi-square  test  (p-value  with  Bonferroni  correction).  The  advantages  of  this  solution\\ninclude the automatic selection of n-way splits in the node, but the disadvantage is that this\\napproach requires quite large data sets.\\nThe random forest algorithm involves creating and combining many different classification\\ntrees. Each tree is created on a random sample of n observations taken with replacement from\\nthe training set (bootstrap sample). For classification, random forest is an ensemble ML method\\nthat  involves  constructing  many  decision  trees  during  training  and  generating  a  class  -\\nthe dominant of the classes of individual trees. In this way, random decision forests improve\\noverfitting to the training set. Random forests provide smoother results with large data sets than\\ntraditional  decision  trees.  However,  the  disadvantage  is  a  certain  opacity  of  decisions:\\nthe final decision of the random forest is the average of many independent partial decisions,\\nand it is difficult to simply explain the reasons for making it.\\n\\n## [PDF page 550]\\n\\n550  I. Based on the research, we have shown that using ML techniques can improve the\\naccuracy of decisions regarding the type of maintenance work that should be carried out to\\nefficiently and effectively remove failures and reduce losses caused by machine downtime.\\nRelatively simple AI-based solutions such as CHAID and random forests have yielded fairly\\nhigh  accuracy  with  very  short  execution  times,  which,  within  edge  processing,  fulfills  the\\ncomplex  trade-off  between  accuracy  and  speed  in  predictive  maintenance  applications.\\nThe presented families of simple algorithms should be developed as a transparent source of\\nopinion for industrial decision-making processes.\\nDue to enterprises’ need to effectively use their resources and reduce losses, automating the\\ndecision-making process regarding identifying the causes of emergency events and determining\\nmaintenance works may be of key importance for improving the efficiency of processes in the\\nenterprise. Although the issue of \\"failure prediction\\" dominates the literature, we cannot forget\\nabout enterprises in which the use of the predictive maintenance approach is limited due to,\\namong others, machine age and implementation costs. However, it should be noted that failures\\noccur  in  every  enterprise,  regardless  of  the  chosen  maintenance  strategy,  and  the  approach\\npresented in the article can reduce losses.\\nCurrent  research  focuses  on  eliminating  the  most  important  limitations  of  the  described\\nsolutions, occurring to varying extents and intensity in both described solutions (CHAID and\\nrandom forests):\\n\uf0b7  The impact of data set quality and size, particularly by limiting employees’ ability to\\nselect classifications to drop-down menu items or numerical values.\\n\uf0b7  Unbalanced data set in classes, especially in the case of training, when one group of\\nfailures occurs more often than others or some components are new and simply do not\\nfail for a long time.\\n\uf0b7  Risk of overfitting, which can be reduced by using hybrid solutions, including random\\nforests.\\n\uf0b7  Some  approaches  require  real-time  response  due  to  data  entry  and  classification\\nduration.\\nFurther research will focus on:\\n\uf0b7  Comparison of the effectiveness of various ML methods and techniques that can be used\\nto develop the above-mentioned solutions.\\n\uf0b7  Standardization of data acquisition, collection, and analysis, both from employees and\\nusing IIoT.\\n\uf0b7  Flexibility,  adaptation,  and  combination  of  solutions  according  to  needs,  including\\ndepending on the area of application or the form of data (numerical, descriptive) or their\\ncharacteristics (e.g., predominance of one type of damage).\\n\uf0b7  Imaging the results of analyses as part of human-machine interaction.\\n\\n## [PDF page 554]\\n\\n554  I. Introduction\\n\\nAgriculture plays a crucial role in the European Union (EU) economy, not only as a source\\nof food, but also as an important element in sustainable development, environmental protection\\nand the maintenance of biodiversity. The agricultural sector in the EU is diverse, ranging from\\nintensive farms in countries such as France and Germany to smaller, family-run farms in regions\\nsuch  as  Central  and  Eastern  Europe.  Agriculture  is  also  a  key  factor  in  sustaining  rural\\ncommunities, providing employment and supporting local economies. However, as the world\\ngrapples with the challenges of sustainability and resource efficiency, it is necessary to study\\nagriculture in this aspect to ensure its long-term viability (Corato, Cancellara, 2019; Santos,\\nAhmad, 2020).\\nThe European Union9s agriculture is undergoing constant transformation, the dynamics of\\nwhich intensified especially after the EU enlargement in 2004. It was the accession of ten new\\nMember States, including Poland, that fundamentally changed the structure of the European\\nagricultural  sector,  introducing  significant  production  resources  into  the  community,\\nbut also new challenges related to modernisation and farming efficiency. Literature review\\n\\nThe  technical  efficiency  of  agriculture  in  the  European  Union  (EU)  is  a  critical  area  of\\nresearch,  particularly  in  the  context  of  the  Common  Agricultural  Policy  (CAP)  and  its\\nimplications for Member States, including Poland. The CAP has undergone significant reforms\\nsince  its  inception,  aiming  to  increase  agricultural  productivity,  ensure  food  security  and\\npromote sustainable rural development.\\nThis  literature  review  synthesises  key  findings  from  various  studies  to  clarify  the\\nrelationship between CAP subsidies and technical efficiency in EU agriculture and also takes\\ninto account the research-applied divisions of European agriculture into different groups due to\\ndifferences in CAP effects.\\nPrevious  research  suggests  that  CAP  subsidies  play  an  important  role  in  shaping  farm\\ntechnical efficiency across the EU. For example, Latruffe et al. highlight that while subsidies\\ncan increase technical efficiency, their effects are diverse and vary depending on the type of\\nsubsidy and the specific agricultural context (Latruffe et al., 2016). This is further supported by\\nthe meta-analysis by Minviel and Latruffe, showing that public subsidies can have both positive\\nand negative effects on  farm  efficiency, depending on their structuring  and implementation\\n(Minviel, Latruffe, 2016). This is also reflected in the findings of Galluzzo, who notes that the\\nfirst pillar of the CAP, which includes direct payments, has played a key role in supporting farm\\nefficiency in the EU Member States. The findings revealed the positive  impact of financial\\nsubsidies granted to disadvantaged rural areas on increasing technical efficiency and the low\\nimpact of decoupled payments paid under the first pillar of the CAP on the Romanian farms\\nstudied. He also showed that, although CAP subsidies have generally improved productivity,\\nthe benefits are not evenly distributed, with some regions experiencing greater improvements\\nthan others (Galluzzo, 2020).\\nRadlinska  (2023)  found  that  EU  agriculture  showed  high  technical  efficiency  (90.24%)\\nbetween  2004  and  2020,  with  very  small  and  very  large  farms  being  the  most  efficient.\\nHowever,  the  relationship  between  farm  size  and  efficiency  is  not  straightforward.\\nIn  turn,  regional  differences  in  agricultural  efficiency  in  the  context  of  cohesion  policy  are\\npointed out by (Cie\\\\lik, Rokicki, 2013; Nazarczuk, 2015). Several studies have also analysed\\nthe impact of the CAP on agricultural efficiency  in Poland. For  example, Wilczyński et al.\\nconducted an empirical study on dairy farms in Poland revealing that technical efficiency is\\nsignificantly affected by the level of CAP support received (Wilczyński et al., 2020). Similarly,\\n\\n## [PDF page 561]\\n\\nDevelopment trajectories and technical efficiency…  561\\n\\nSmędzik-Ambroży et al. analysed the sustainability of Polish farms after the EU accession,\\nfinding that CAP instruments positively influenced the sustainability and efficiency of farms\\n(Smędzik-Ambroży et al., 2018). This is confirmed by later research by BCażejczyk-Majka who\\nemphasises  the  importance  of  the  CAP  in  increasing  agricultural  efficiency  and  reducing\\nregional differences in the level of this efficiency  (BCażejczyk-Majka, 2022).  It  can  also be\\nnoted  that  previous  studies  have  indicated  that  higher  specialisation  correlates  with  better\\ntechnical efficiency. This was found in a study of the technical efficiency of specialised dairy\\nfarms in Poland by apička and Smutka, who used regional data to assess efficiency levels.\\nThis is in line with broader findings across the EU, where specialised farms tend to show higher\\nefficiency compared to mixed farms, especially in older EU regions (apička, Smutka, 2014).\\nKocur-Bera, on the other hand, discusses how the EU membership and participation in the CAP\\nhas changed land management practices and agricultural property prices in Poland, which has\\nalso further affected efficiency scores (Kocur-Bera, 2016).\\nThe  dual  structure  of  the  CAP  3  comprising  direct  payments  and  rural  development\\nmeasures  3  has  played  a  key  role  in  shaping  agricultural  practices  and  productivity.\\nDirect payments under the first pillar aim to stabilise farmers9 incomes, while the second pillar\\nfocuses on rural development, which includes investments in technology and innovation that\\ncan increase productivity (Constantin et al., 2021). The integration of precision farming tools,\\ndiscussed  by  Vecchio  et  al.  is  one  such  innovation  that  can  significantly  improve  the\\nproductivity and sustainability of agriculture in the EU (Vecchio et al., 2020).\\nIn  summary,  the  literature  shows  a  complex  interaction  between  CAP  subsidies  and\\ntechnical  efficiency  in  EU  agriculture,  especially  in  Poland.  While  the  CAP  has  generally\\ncontributed  to  farm  efficiency,  the  effects  depend  on  various  factors,  including  the  type  of\\nsubsidies, farm specialisation and regional characteristics. Recommendations\\n\\nIn order to improve the efficiency of agriculture in the different groups of countries in the\\nEuropean Union, different agricultural policies can be proposed to address the specific needs\\nand  challenges  of  each  group.  The  recommendations  for  each  of  the  identified  groups  are\\npresented below:\\nGroup 1: Efficient innovators\\nNetherlands, Denmark, Belgium, Germany\\nRecommended policies:\\n\uf0b7  Support  for  research  and  innovation:  Increase  funding  for  agricultural  research  to\\ndevelop new technologies and practices that can increase productivity.\\n\uf0b7  Sustainability: Promote agricultural practices that are environmentally friendly, such as\\nprecision  agriculture  that  minimises  resource  use.  Support  for  projects  related  to\\na circular economy.\\n\uf0b7  Educational  programmes:  Training  for  farmers  on  new  technologies  and  innovative\\nfarming practices.\\nGroup 2: Rapid modernisers\\nCountries: Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary\\nRecommended policies:\\n\uf0b7  Access to finance: Facilitate access to credit and grants for farmers to invest in modern\\ntechnology and infrastructure.\\n\uf0b7  Support  programmes  for  young  farmers:  Initiatives  to  attract  young  people  to  the\\nagricultural sector, which can contribute to innovation and modernisation.\\n\uf0b7  Cooperation with the environment: Encourage consolidation and partnerships between\\nfarmers and technology companies to implement modern solutions.\\nGroup 3: Stable performers\\nFrance, Italy, Spain, Austria, Sweden, Ireland, Finland\\nRecommended policies:\\n\uf0b7  Preserving  traditional  practices:  Promote  local  agricultural  traditions  that  can  be\\nsustainable and efficient.\\n\uf0b7  Quality certification schemes: Support for the introduction of certification schemes that\\npromote the quality of agricultural products, which can increase their market value.\\n\uf0b7  Sustainability: Support agricultural practices that are sustainable to maintain production\\nstability. Rusielik\\n\\nGroup 4: Challenged adaptors\\nGreece, Croatia, Portugal, Slovenia, Slovakia\\nRecommended policies:\\n\uf0b7  Support for climate change adaptation: Programmes that help farmers adapt to changing\\nclimate conditions, such as training in sustainable water management.\\n\uf0b7  Investment  in  infrastructure:  Improve  infrastructure,  such  as  irrigation  systems,\\nto increase production efficiency.\\n\uf0b7  Promoting crop diversity: Encourage the cultivation of a variety of crops, which can\\nincrease resilience to climate and market changes.\\nGroup 5: special cases\\nEstonia, Latvia, Lithuania\\nRecommended policies:\\n\uf0b7  Support for the development of local markets: Initiatives to develop local markets for\\nagricultural products, which can increase farmers9 incomes.\\n\uf0b7  Education and training programmes: Training for farmers in modern farming practices\\nand farm management.\\n\uf0b7  Increasing access to technology: Facilitate access to modern technologies and tools that\\ncan help increase production efficiency.\\nEach  group  of  countries  in  the  EU  has  its  own  unique  challenges  and  opportunities.\\nThe implementation of appropriate agricultural policies that take into account the specificities\\nof  each  group  can  contribute  to  improving  the  efficiency  of  agriculture  across  the  EU.\\nIt is also crucial to monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of these policies to adapt them to the\\nchanging conditions and needs.\\n\\n6.  General conclusions\\n\\nBased  on  the  analysis  of  the  technical  efficiency  of  agriculture  in  the  European  Union\\ncountries from 2007 to 2023, taking into account the impact of the Common Agricultural Policy\\n(CAP), general conclusions can be drawn:\\n\uf0b7  The analysis showed an overall increase in the technical efficiency of agriculture in the\\nEU  over  the  period  studied.  Most  member  countries  achieved  high  efficiency  rates,\\nsuggesting a positive impact of CAP reforms and investments in modern technologies.\\nIn  particular,  country  groups  such  as  the  8Productive  Innovators9  and  8Rapid\\nModernisers9  showed  significant  progress  in  efficiency,  which  may  be  the  result  of\\nsuccessful implementation of innovation and adaptation to changing market conditions.\\n\\n## [PDF page 573]\\n\\nDevelopment trajectories and technical efficiency…  573\\n\\n\uf0b7  There is a clear variation in technical efficiency levels between different country groups.\\nCountries in the 8Efficient Innovators9 group (e.g. Netherlands, Denmark, Germany)\\nhave  achieved  the  highest  efficiency  rates,  while  the  8Challenged  Adaptors9\\n(e.g. Greece, Croatia) face a variety of structural and economic challenges, which affect\\ntheir ability to improve efficiency.\\n\uf0b7  The CAP has played a key role in shaping the technical efficiency of agriculture in the\\nEU. Policy reforms, such as the introduction of direct payments and rural development\\nprogrammes,  have  contributed  to  increased  investment  in  modern  technologies  and\\nimproved living conditions in rural areas. However, these effects have varied depending\\non the specific characteristics of the countries and their initial circumstances.\\n\uf0b7  Against the backdrop of increasing challenges related to food security, climate change\\nand  sustainability  pressures,  agriculture  in  the  EU  needs  to  adapt  to  new  realities.\\nThe  implementation  of  green  transformation  and  the  digitalisation  of  agriculture  is\\nbecoming crucial for the further development of the sector. Countries that successfully\\nimplement innovative agricultural practices will be more likely to achieve long-term\\nefficiency.\\n\uf0b7  The conclusions of the analysis point to the need for further research on the technical\\nefficiency of agriculture in the context of changing market and policy conditions. It is\\nimportant  for  the  EU  agricultural  policy  to  be  flexible  and  adapt  to local  needs  and\\ncountry  specificities.  In  the  future,  it  will  also  be  necessary  to  diversify  support\\ninstruments  to  better  respond  to  the  challenges  and  needs  of  different  groups  of\\ncountries.\\n\uf0b7  Investment in R&D and knowledge transfer is crucial to increasing technical efficiency\\nin agriculture. Countries that make effective use of technological innovation and support\\nthe development of human capital are more likely to achieve high production efficiency.\\nCooperation between member countries in sharing experiences and best practices can\\nfurther increase efficiency across the EU.\\n\uf0b7  The future of agriculture in the EU will largely depend on the ability of countries to\\nadapt to the changing market, technological and environmental conditions. The balance\\nbetween  production  and  environmental  protection  will  be  vital,  which  requires\\ninnovative  solutions  and  the  involvement  of  all  stakeholders  in  decision-making\\nprocesses. The Common Agricultural Policy should continue its reforms to effectively\\nsupport farmers in adapting to these challenges.\\nIn conclusion, the analysis of the technical efficiency of agriculture in the EU between 2007\\nand  2023  shows  positive  trends,  but  also  variation  in  performance  between  countries.\\nThe  Common  Agricultural  Policy  is  crucial  for  the  further  development  of  the  sector,  but\\nrequires continuous adaptation and innovation to meet today9s challenges. These findings and\\nrecommendations  can  form  the  basis  for  shaping  the  future  EU  agricultural  policy  and\\nagricultural development strategies in individual Member States.\\n\\n## [PDF page 574]\\n\\n574  R. Summary\\n\\nThe study analyses the technical efficiency of agriculture in the European Union countries\\nfor the 2007-2023 period, taking into account the development paths in each country and the\\nimpact of the Common Agricultural Policy. A set of variables was adopted that reflects the\\nspecifics of the business model of agricultural production and is also relevant to the analysis of\\ntechnical efficiency. In the first stage of the research, on the basis of observations and analysis\\nof the trajectory of the adopted variables, five groups of countries with similar development\\npaths and efficiency were identified. An attempt was made to estimate the impact of different\\nCAP instruments on the formation of these paths. In the second stage, the Data Envelopment\\nAnalysis (DEA) method was used, which, in the context of the adopted variables, allowed for\\nan accurate assessment of the technical efficiency of agriculture, taking into account differences\\nin the structure of production and the level of technological development. The results indicate\\na  general  upward  trend  in  technical  efficiency  in  the  EU  agriculture,  but  with  marked\\ndifferences between the separate groups of countries. The study also showed that the impact of\\nthe CAP on technical efficiency varies and depends on the initial conditions and development\\nstrategies  adopted  in  each  country.  The  results  of  the  study  made  it  possible  to  formulate\\nrecommendations aimed at raising and levelling the efficiency levels.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n1. Introduction\\n\\nEmployers  increasingly  value  industry-recognized  certifications  to  assess  candidate\\ncompetencies  and  readiness  for  professional  roles  in  today’s  competitive  job  market.\\nFor students and early-career professionals, certifications can serve as vital tools for bridging\\nthe gap between academic learning and industry standards, validating theoretical knowledge\\nand practical skills. In project management, where effective planning, execution, and evaluation\\nare  essential,  certifications  such  as  IPMA-Student  offer  individuals  a  structured  path  to\\ndemonstrate their capabilities.\\nThe International Project Management Association (IPMA) Poland developed the IPMA-\\nStudent certification to introduce students and young professionals to core project management\\ncompetencies. This transition significantly increased workers’ demands, particularly regarding\\ntheir  competencies. This  may\\nsuggest a greater readiness or need among women to enhance their qualifications in project\\nmanagement.  Women  are  also  more  likely  to  pursue  equal  job  opportunities  and  break  the\\nso-called \\"glass ceiling\\" by obtaining additional qualifications. Responses to salary questions\\nindicate  that  these  are  mainly  women  with  work  experience  who  view  certification  as\\nan  investment  leading  to  further  financial  benefits.  However,  some  individuals  who  also\\nupgraded did not disclose their earnings, which may suggest other motivations independent of\\nmonetary gain. When asked about their motivations for certification, respondents indicated the\\npotential  of  using  IPMA  to  gain  a  professional  advantage  and  improve  career  prospects.\\nIt can also be suggested that IPMA’s prestige and marketing activities serve as a desirable asset\\nfor those starting their careers.\\n\\n## [PDF page 591]\\n\\nThe Importance of Competencies…  591\\n\\nCertification Timeline\\n\\nAll individuals who upgraded their IPMA level completed only the basic (D) level in 2017\\nor later. None of the earlier graduates among respondents continued their studies, which may\\nsuggest that IPMA certification was less popular 7-8 years ago than it is now. This may be\\nattributed to lower globalization at that time, which drove fewer competency requirements in\\nthe workplace. However, only some individuals upgraded their certification from IPMA D to\\nhigher levels. They felt less need for accreditation or were satisfied with their current career\\nstatus and earnings. It is also possible that their initial motivation for IPMA D came solely from\\nencouragement by a program coordinator rather than intrinsic motivation.\\n\\n6.  Study Limitations and Future Research\\n\\nThis  study  provides  insights  into  the  motivations  and  career  impacts  of  IPMA-student\\ncertification  among  students  and  early-career  professionals.  However,  several  limitations\\nshould be acknowledged. First, the sample size is relatively limited, and the study’s participants\\nare drawn from a specific certification program, which may only partially represent the diversity\\nof students and professionals pursuing project management certifications globally. This limits\\nthe generalizability of the findings to other regions and certification programs.\\nSecond,  the  study  relies  on  self-reported  survey  data,  which  may  introduce  bias,\\nas  respondents  may  provide  socially  desirable  answers  or  be  influenced  by  retrospective\\nevaluation of their career motivations and outcomes. Additionally, while the study explores\\nmotivations for certification, it does not capture detailed longitudinal data on participants’ career\\ntrajectories  over  time,  which  would  provide  a  more  comprehensive  understanding  of  how\\ncertification impacts long-term career development.\\nThe study’s findings highlight several potential directions for future research. Expanding\\nthe  sample  size  and  diversity,  including  participants  from  multiple  regions  and  various\\ncertification programs, would improve the generalizability of results and help identify trends\\nacross different demographic and industry contexts. A longitudinal study tracking certification\\nholders over time would also provide valuable insights into the sustained impact of certification\\non career advancement, role transitions, and income growth.\\nFurthermore, future studies could explore the role of certification in helping professionals\\novercome specific career barriers, such as gender-related challenges or \\"glass ceiling\\" effects.\\nResearch  focused  on  how  certification  influences  career  paths  in  particular  industries,\\nsuch as IT, healthcare, and engineering, where project management skills are highly sought\\nafter, would also be beneficial. Finally, examining the cost-benefit analysis from participants’\\nperspectives, particularly how perceived financial and time investments influence certification\\npursuit  and  progression,  could  inform  strategies  for  certification  bodies  and  educational\\ninstitutions to support and encourage certification uptake.\\n\\n## [PDF page 592]\\n\\n592  J.
