SoBtysiak, D. Zaj\\u0006c\\n\\n1.  Introduction\\n\\nResearch issues related to socioeconomic development on a regional and local scale have\\narouse  wide  interest  among  economists.  The  main  reasons  for  this  are  the  danger  of\\ndisappearing the specific features of regions and local environments, their cultural identity and\\nhistorical  heritage,  as  well  as  the  growing  threats  to  the  values  of  the  natural  environment.\\nIn turn, from an economic point of view, the key issue is the optimisation and efficiency of the\\nuse of resources in the management and development process. Another significant problem is\\nthe  growing  interregional  and  intraregional  disproportions  in  the  level  of  socioeconomic\\ndevelopment and quality of life of residents, which generally leads to migration of people from\\nless developed regions  and local communities, and consequently  weakens the possibility of\\ntheir further functioning (BBachut, CierpiaB-Wolan, Czudec, Kata, 2018).\\nSocioeconomic development, understood as the  scale,  pace, and direction of changes in\\nregional and local communities leading to better conditions and quality of life, as well as the\\nresulting spatial structure and forms of space development, are spatially diverse and are the\\nresult of many conditions. They can be divided into the following groups regarding conditions:\\nhistorical, related to the location in geographical space and economic structures, the natural\\nenvironment and the quality of the human environment, the level of infrastructure development\\n(social, technical, economic, institutional), the activity and effectiveness of local government\\nactivities,  and  also  the  entrepreneurship  and  innovation  of  residents.  From  a  different\\nperspective, we can also mention site conditions, environmental conditions, conditions resulting\\nfrom  space  development,  and  conditions  related  to  the  quality  of  the  regional  or  local\\ncommunity.  The  literature  on  the  subject  emphasises  the  key  importance  of  sustainable\\ndevelopment of local government units (including counties and communes), because it leads\\ndirectly to improvement of the functioning of the economy and society, as well as the condition\\nand quality of the natural environment (Heffner, 2007; 2011a, 2011b; Dziekański, 2018; MiBek,\\n2018;  Grzebyk,  Miś,  Stec,  Zaj\\u0006c,  2019;  Józefowicz,  Smolińska,  2019;  Utzig,  Raczkowska,\\nMikuBa, 2023).\\nLocal development is a multidimensional concept, but it is usually perceived as a process\\nof positive quantitative and qualitative changes taking place in the social and economic sphere\\nof  a  given  local  government  unit  (i.e.,  poviat  or  commune),  taking  into  account  the  needs,\\npreferences,  and  hierarchy  of  values  specific  to  its  inhabitants  (Sztando,  2012;  Król,  2015;\\nJóźwiakowski, 2016).\\nLocal development can be considered on many levels, which is why it stands out (Balcerek-\\nKosiarz, 2018):\\n\uf0fc  local development that concerns a given area, i.e. changes in the territorial system;\\n\uf0fc  local development, which focusses on the needs of the local government community\\nliving in a given area;\\n\\n## [PDF page 595]\\n\\nDifferences in local development conditions…  595\\n\\n\uf0fc  local development, which is a process, i.e., ongoing and therefore not a one-time action;\\n\uf0fc  local  development,  which  is  an  expression  of  the  activity  of  entities,  institutions,\\nand organisations.\\nThe main goal of local development should be to guarantee the inhabitants of a given local\\ngovernment  unit  (i.e.,  poviat  or  commune)  the  possibly  lasting  improvement  in  their  living\\nconditions  and  quality.  This  can  occur  primarily  by  providing  them  with:  work  (income),\\nconditions of material existence (food, housing, living in an environment that is not harmful to\\nhealth), a positive environment for spiritual development (opportunity for education, recreation,\\nparticipation in culture and entertainment, access to information, the possibility of travelling\\nand contact with the wider environment), as well as the basic need for security and prospects\\nfor the future (sense of stability) and development opportunities for future generations (Król,\\n2015).\\nA  characteristic  feature  of  local  development  is  the  relatively  low  mobility  of  the  main\\ndevelopment factors, which include: the condition of infrastructure, qualifications of the labor\\nforce, social structure and branch structure of the economy, as well as general and technical\\nknowledge of the local community. Therefore, the goal of local development policy should be\\nthe best possible use of these resources and factors (Król, 2015; Jóźwiakowski, 2016).\\nEffective implementation of local development policy depends on many factors, including\\nprimarily: understanding the essence and meaning of local development, willingness to act in\\nthis  area,  knowledge  and  ingenuity  of  the  entities  of  this  policy  and  the  local  economy,\\nresources enabling development, unmet social needs that this development stimulate and direct,\\nas well as on collecting appropriate financial resources, gathering people around the idea of\\nlocal development and creating the right social climate, as well as on the effectiveness of the\\nexisting organisational structures of this development. However, the basic structure initiating\\nand organising the local development process will always be the local government (district,\\ncommune), in relation to which the following conditions for the effectiveness of development\\npolicy are distinguished: pro-development activity, entrepreneurship, openness to innovation,\\nnew  ideas  and  cooperation,  inducing  a  collective  process  learning,  readiness  to  build\\npartnerships  and  create  social  capital  (Guzal-Dec,  2015;  Parysek,  2015;  Zwolińska-Ligaj,\\n2019).\\nLocal development factors can be divided into four basic groups,  i.e., economic, social,\\ntechnical  and  technological,  and  ecological.  In  the  group  of  economic  factors,  the  most\\nimportant variables are: the size and the related functioning of the local market for goods and\\nservices, the situation on the local labour market, the amount and variability of income of the\\npopulation, enterprises, and local government bodies. The rank and quality of local marketing\\nand the level of management by local authorities should also be taken into account. The local\\neconomic  situation  is  also  influenced  by  external  factors,  including  the  country’s\\nmacroeconomic  situation.  Some  of  the  most  important  social  factors  include  demographic\\nchanges and the pace and nature of urbanisation processes. The development and improvement\\n\\n## [PDF page 596]\\n\\n596  M. SoBtysiak, D. Zaj\\u0006c\\n\\nof social infrastructure, changes in the level and lifestyle of residents, the level of education,\\nand  the  activity  and  participation  of  the  authorities  and  the  local  community  also  play\\nan important role. Technical and technological factors include: the quantity and quality of fixed\\ncapital  and  changes  in  its  structure,  development  of  research  and  development  activities,\\nthe level of cooperation between the science and industry sectors, production diversification,\\nand  the  development  and  improvement  of  technical  infrastructure.  However,  the  ecological\\nfactors of local development include access to natural resources, rationalisation of management\\nof  natural  environment  resources,  implementation  of  the  so-called  \\"clean\\"  technologies,\\nstimulating the production of healthy food, improving the ecological awareness and culture of\\nsociety and implementing modern environmental protection instruments. It should be added\\nthat the above factors usually influence development processes in a cumulative manner, making\\nup a bundle of determinants of local development. There is often a coupling between individual\\nfactors.  The  issue  of  local  development  should  therefore  be  considered  comprehensively,\\nbearing in mind that many processes have a cause-and-effect nature. Causes and effects are\\ninterconnected  and  connect  to  all  mentioned  aspects  of  development.  They  can  constitute\\nfactors  of  local  development,  but,  on  the  other  hand,  they  can  also  effectively  inhibit  this\\ndevelopment  (Kiczek,  Pompa-Roborzyński,  2013;  ZióBkowski,  2015;  Jóźwiakowski,  2016;\\nBalcerek-Kosiarz, 2018).\\nMoreover,  in  the  case  of  local  development,  attention  should  be  paid  to  its  internal\\n(endogenous), external (exogenous) factors, and various types of centrifugal forces. In the case\\nof  endogenous  factors,  the  basis  for  local  development  is  the  existing  resources  of  basic\\nproduction factors (i.e., human, property, raw materials, etc.), but their development, quality,\\navailability, and efficiency of use as well as adequacy to the generally accepted and accepted\\ndevelopment  strategy  are  very  important.  Exogenous  factors,  in  turn,  include  the  state’s\\neconomic policy and its entire environment, as well as spatial policy. Also of great importance\\nin this respect are: state-wide social policy, state-wide basis for shaping the level and quality of\\nsocial life, the country’s situation in the international system, and the nature of trade with other\\ncountries (import and export policy). In the modern economy, despite the increasing importance\\nof  exogenous  factors  of  local  development,  mainly  related  to  national  and  European  Union\\npolicies and the dynamic development of the international flow of human and financial capital,\\nspecial attention is paid to endogenous factors. They constitute very important conditions for\\nlocal development and the functioning of local government, because they have a significant\\nimpact  on  the  scale,  directions,  and  dynamics  of  socioeconomic  development  and  also\\nconstitute the primary (somehow natural) conditions in which local government functions and\\nconducts its own development policy (Zakrzewska-PóBtorak, 2011; Król, 2015; Jóźwiakowski,\\n2016; Józefowicz, Smolińska, 2019; Grzebyk, SoBtysiak, Stec, Zaj\\u0006c, 2020).\\n\\n## [PDF page 597]\\n\\nDifferences in local development conditions…  597\\n\\n2.  Research aim, empirical material, and research methods\\n\\nThe aim of the article is to identify and evaluate selected endogenous conditions of local\\ndevelopment  in  land  counties  in  Poland,  depending  on  changes  in  the  number  of  their\\ninhabitants.\\nThe  article  presents  a  research  hypothesis  that  assumes  that  the  conditions  of  local\\ndevelopment vary between land counties in Poland, depending on changes in the number of\\ntheir inhabitants, with the best conditions in the group of counties characterised by an increase\\nin this number.\\nThe empirical material of the article concerns all land districts in Poland. The numerical\\ndata come from the Local Data Bank of the Central Statistical Office in Warsaw and concern\\n2023. The collected and organised empirical material was developed in descriptive, tabular,\\nand graphic form, using the method of comparative analysis.\\nTo identify and assess the conditions of local development in rural districts in Poland, the\\nfollowing  diagnostic  features  illustrating  them  in  2023  were  analysed:  population  density\\n(population per 1 km2), percentage of the working-age population, nonworking-age population\\nper 100 working-age people, natural increase per 1,000 population, net migration for permanent\\nresidence per 1000 population, percentage of population using water, sewage and gas networks,\\naverage  monthly  gross  salary  (PLN),  total  income  of  poviat  budgets  per  capita  (PLN),\\nown income of poviat budgets per capita (PLN), the share of own income in the total income\\nof  poviat  budgets  (%),  total  expenditure  of  poviat  budgets  per  capita  (PLN),  investment\\nexpenditure of poviat budgets per capita (PLN) and share of investment expenditure in total\\nexpenditure of poviat budgets (%).\\nWhen analysing the diversity of local development conditions in land countries in Poland,\\nit was assumed that the leading feature in this respect is changes in the number of inhabitants,\\ni.e.  a  clear  increase,  stagnation  or  a  clear  decrease  in  this  number.  For  the  purposes  of  the\\nresearch, the article divided all land counties in Poland into three groups, i.e.:\\n\uf0d8  I – land counties (poviats) with an increase in the number of inhabitants in the years\\n1995-2023 (these are units in which the population dynamics in the years 1995-2023,\\nwith 1995 = 100, is above 110.0);\\n\uf0d8  II – land countries (poviats) with stagnation in the number of inhabitants in the years\\n1995-2023 (these are units in which the population dynamics in the years 1995-2023,\\nwith 1995 = 100, ranges from 90.0 to 110.0);\\n\uf0d8  III – land countries (poviats) with a decrease in the number of inhabitants in the years\\n1995-2023 (these are units in which the population dynamics in the years 1995-2023,\\nwith 1995 = 100, is below 90.0).\\n\\n## [PDF page 598]\\n\\n598  M. Summary and conclusions\\n\\nThe conditions of local development in poviat local government units in Poland are a very\\nimportant,  interdisciplinary,  extensive,  and  broad  issue,  constituting,  among  others,\\nan important research issue for both economic theory and economic practice.\\nThe analysis of the collected statistical data carried out in the article shows that:\\n\uf0fc  The  demographic  and  infrastructure  conditions  of  local  development  vary  between\\ndistricts in Poland, depending on changes in the number of their inhabitants in the years\\n1995-2023. They are clearly the best in the group of land counties with an increase in\\nthe  number  of  inhabitants,  while  the  worst  are  in  the  group  of  land  counties  with\\na decrease in this number.\\n\uf0fc  The economic and financial conditions of local development are similar in all separate\\ngroups  of  land  counties  in  Poland,  depending  on  changes  in  the  number  of  their\\ninhabitants  in  the  years  1995-2023,  and  similar  to  the  average  for  all  land  counties\\nthroughout the country.\\n\uf0fc  In  turn,  a  point  assessment  of  all  analysed  conditions  of  local  development\\n(i.e.  demographic,  infrastructural  and  economic  and  financial  together),  in  separate\\ngroups  of  land  counties  in  Poland,  depending  on  changes  in  the  number  of  their\\ninhabitants in the years 1995-2023, against the background of all land counties in the\\ncountry, showed that the studied groups of local government units are diversified in this\\nrespect - in favor of the group of counties with an increase in the number of mixed\\ninhabitants. This allows us to confirm the research hypothesis, which assumes that the\\nconditions of local development vary between land counties in Poland, depending on\\nchanges  in  the  number  of  their  inhabitants,  with  the  best  conditions in  the  group  of\\ncounties characterised by an increase in this number.\\nThe results of the analysis of the collected statistical data presented in the article provide\\nimportant  and  up-to-date  knowledge  that  may  be  useful  for  local  government  officials\\nresponsible  for  the  conditions,  possibilities,  and  directions  of  local  socio-economic\\ndevelopment of poviat local government units in Poland, as well as for other decision-makers\\ninvolved in the implementation of local development policy.\\n\\n## [PDF page 604]\\n\\n604  M. Introduction\\n\\nProject  management  is  a  crucial  aspect  of  modern,  growing  organizations,  providing\\nstructured approaches to planning, implementing, and controlling activities aimed at achieving\\nproject  success.  Traditional  project  management  methods  follow  a  sequential  process,\\nbeginning  with  the  identification  of  requirements,  followed  by  detailed  planning,\\nand  continuous  progress  monitoring  (Project  Management  Institute,  2008).  While  these\\nmethods are effective in stable environments, they struggle to address the challenges of today’s\\nrapidly  changing  business  landscape,  where  customer  needs  and  technological  innovations\\nevolve at unprecedented speeds.\\nTo respond to these challenges, the Agile Manifesto was introduced at the beginning of the\\n21st century, forming the foundation for various Agile project management methodologies.\\nFrameworks  such  as  Scrum,  Kanban,  and  Extreme  Programming  are  grounded  in  Agile\\nprinciples, emphasizing iterative and incremental approaches to project execution (Hohl et al.,\\n2018).  These  methodologies  aim  to  enhance  project  outcomes  by  fostering  adaptability,\\nincreasing  responsiveness  to  change,  and  improving  alignment  with  customer  and  market\\nneeds.  Practices  derived  from  these  approaches  can  be  collectively  referred  to  as  <project\\nsuccess factors=, as they are specific elements, conditions, and variables that, when effectively\\nimplemented, improve the likelihood of project success (Ika, 2009).\\nThe challenge in the current business landscape lies in understanding project success from\\nmultiple perspectives and these diverse factors that influence it. In 2008, the last time there was\\nextensive research on the relationship between Agile success factors and IT project success\\n(Chow, Cao, 2008). In this work, the authors adopted the success factors that were important at\\nthat time, and the criteria were general statements based on the management triangle. Over the\\nlast  20  years,  this  importance  of  factors  has  changed,  because  the  approach  itself  has  been\\ngradually adapting to market requirements. The same goes for the success criteria. Success is\\nnow multi-dimensional. Studies such as this done by Kerzner (Kerzner, 2017) emphasize that\\nproject  success  is  defined  across  various  perspectives,  including  budget,  schedule,  quality,\\nand stakeholder satisfaction, many at the same time. The research initiated by Chow and Cao\\nwas  continued.  However,  they  did  not  evaluate  the  current  state  of  the  criteria  or  factors\\nthemselves but rather selected parts of them and tried to deepen them (Stankovic et al., 2018).\\nHowever, there is no actual research in the available literature on the relationship between Agile\\nsuccess  factors  and  the  set  of  currently  used  success  criteria.  Specifically,  there  is\\nno comprehensive model that maps a wide range of Agile practices to an extended set of project\\nsuccess  criteria,  divided  into  clear  categories.  This  lack  of  a  detailed  framework  limits  the\\nability of managers to align practices with specific outcomes effectively.\\n\\n## [PDF page 609]\\n\\nSuccess Criteria and Factors…  609\\n\\nThis paper aims to address this gap by linking selected Agile success factors with project\\nsuccess  criteria  specific  to  the  IT  industry.  The  article  seeks  to  bridge  this  gap  through\\na  structured,  three-phase  research  process.  The  first  phase  involved  an  extensive  literature\\nreview to identify key Agile practices and success criteria. This review resulted in a focus on\\n18 Agile success factors and 10 project success criteria - those most frequently mentioned in\\nprior  studies  over  the  years.  The  term  \\"Agile  success  factors\\"  is  used  interchangeably  with\\n\\"Agile practices\\" throughout this work and includes practices, activities, and artifacts derived\\nfrom Agile methodologies. By concentrating on widely recognized factors, the research ensures\\na balance between depth and breadth, avoiding the narrower focus of some previous studies that\\nlimit practical insights. The second of part of the research consisted of qualitative interviews\\nwith Agile practitioners, who evaluated the relationships between the identified success factors\\nand criteria. These insights were synthesized into a detailed mapping that illustrates how Agile\\npractices  influence  different  success  metrics  (Fig.  1).  Finally,  the  third  phase  involved\\nvalidation through expert interviews. Experienced professionals assessed the proposed model,\\nconfirming  its  relevance  to  real-world  project  management  and  suggesting  refinements  to\\nimprove its practical applicability.\\nThe findings reveal that Agile practices are more effective in supporting certain success\\ncriteria, such as team satisfaction and functional quality than others, like meeting budget and\\nschedule compliance. This nuanced understanding addresses the identified research gap and\\nprovides  a  practical  model  for  Agile  teams  and  project  managers.  By  offering  a  detailed\\nframework that links Agile practices to specific project success criteria, this study contributes\\nboth to academic knowledge and to practical advancements in IT project management.\\n\\nFigure 1. Model concept.\\nSource: Own elaboration.\\n\\n## [PDF page 610]\\n\\n610  B. Stec\\n\\n2.  Method\\n\\nThis paper’s research was conducted in three stages. The first stage involved identifying\\nAgile practices, and project success criteria by literature review. Then, part two, examines the\\nlinks between these groups with Agile practitioners 3 resulting in creating a model. The third\\nstage  centered  on  an  initial  validation  of  the  model  by  IT  industry  experts.  This  research\\nstructure and methodology were chosen to provide a well-rounded view of how Agile practices\\ninfluence the success of IT projects (Fig. 2).\\n\\nFigure 2. Research general plan.\\nSource: Own elaboration.\\n\\n2.1.  Systematic literature review – stage I\\n\\nIn this case, the literature review concentrates on providing a general overview of success\\nfactors within Agile work methodology and success criteria specific to Information Technology\\n(IT) projects. The goal is to gather sources that discuss these two areas, critically evaluating\\ntheir  relevance  to  addressing  the  research  question,  which  is  formulated  as  follows:\\n<How, do specific activities, artifacts, and practices from the Agile work methodology (success\\nfactors) impact IT projects’ specific success criteria?=\\nThe sources for this review were drawn from two major global databases, Web of Science\\nand Scopus. The author organized the review in two rounds, each dedicated to one of these\\naspects. Methodology\\nInitially, quantitative approaches - particularly surveys - were considered for their efficiency\\nand scalability in data collection (Babbie, 1990; Fowler, 2009). However, given the task of\\nevaluating  180  (18  potential  success  factors  and  10  success  criteria)  specific  relationships\\nbetween  Agile  success  factors  and  criteria,  there  was  a  high  risk  of  respondent  fatigue.\\nSuch  fatigue  could  lead  to  superficial  responses  or  survey  abandonment  (Bryman,  2016),\\nthereby compromising the reliability of the data - a risk that would undermine the objective of\\nproducing meaningful insights. In contrast, qualitative research offers a way to gather context-\\nrich, nuanced insights directly from participants’ experiences, aligning well with the objectives\\nof this study. Agile project outcomes are often highly contextual, and shaped by factors such as\\nteam dynamics, organizational culture, and individual expertise. Qualitative methods are ideal\\nfor exploring these dimensions, as they allow participants to articulate how and why specific\\npractices  impact  project  success,  beyond  merely  indicating  agreement  or  frequency  on\\npredefined scales (Creswell, 2007; Marshall, 2006). Ultimately, qualitative interviews emerged\\nas the optimal approach, enabling the collection of complex, context-specific insights necessary\\nto understand Agile project success. This approach’s flexibility, coupled with its capacity to\\ncapture in-depth participant experiences, makes it particularly suited to this study’s goals.\\nThe interview format was also carefully chosen. Semi-structured individual interviews were\\nselected over group formats. Given that perceptions of practice impact can vary widely within\\nAgile teams, group settings could lead to response conformity or dominant voices influencing\\nthe  discussion,  potentially  skewing  results  (Butt  et  al.,  2023).  Semi-structured  interviews,\\ncombining open-ended and focused questions, offer a balance of flexibility and consistency.\\nThis format allowed for an in-depth examination of specific factor-criteria relationships and\\ncaptured  individual  perspectives,  while  also  providing  structure  on  critical  areas,  such  as\\nassigning weights to practices and exploring role-specific project contexts (Rubin, 2011).\\n\\n## [PDF page 614]\\n\\n614  B. General findings\\n\\nThis  section  explores  research  findings,  as  shown  in  Figure  5,  through  participant\\ncomments, focusing on the success criteria and selected success factors perspective.\\n\\nPerspective from the criteria position – C1, C2\\n\\nThe study reveals that the first two criteria (C1 3 budget, and C2 - schedule) have lower\\naverage ratings than subsequent criteria, with a notable difference of approximately 0.2 points.\\nAdditionally,  these  criteria  exhibit  more  cells  with  negative  weights,  indicating  that  Agile\\npractices may hinder rather than help meet them. A primary factor affecting these criteria is F3,\\nthe culture of improvement, which respondents found beneficial for learning from mistakes and\\ndeveloping  autonomy.  While  this  approach  benefits  long-term  employee  satisfaction  and\\nquality,  it  introduces  short-term  challenges:  correcting  mistakes  incurs  costs,  time  for  error\\ndetection, and the engagement of senior staff. This factor could become a liability for projects\\nwith tighter deadlines (e.g., six months), although it is expected to yield benefits in longer-term\\nprojects.\\nSelf-organization (F4) also impacts C1 and C2. While respondents acknowledge its positive\\neffect  on  team  satisfaction  and  budget  management,  the  lack  of  a  structured  approach\\noccasionally  leads  to  chaotic  task  management,  which  may  jeopardize  project  timelines.\\nThe feedback culture (F6) was another noteworthy factor; while feedback facilitates quality\\nimprovement, it may extend project costs and timelines. Respondents recognized that Agile\\nfeedback  mechanisms  enhance  project  quality  but  may  compromise  time  and  budget\\nconstraints.  Similarly,  daily  meetings  (F12)  provide  a  limited  positive  impact  on  cost  and\\nschedule,  as  these  meetings  may  devolve  into  unproductive  status  updates,  driven  by\\nparticipants’ need to report rather than engage in genuine problem-solving.\\nA final consideration related to C1 and C2 was the non-life-critical nature of projects (F17).\\nThis factor has a mixed effect, providing a relaxed environment conducive to quality work but\\npotentially reducing productivity for employees who perform better under structured guidance\\n(McGregor, 1960). Overall, respondents noted that Agile principles generally align with team\\nsatisfaction and quality but may fall short on cost and schedule criteria.\\n\\nPerspective from the criteria position – C3-C7\\n\\nThe criteria from C3 to C7 align more closely with Agile methodologies, which focus on\\ndelivering functional outcomes. Five of the top six column averages from Figure 5 fall within\\nthis  group,  highlighting  Agile’s  effectiveness  in  achieving  operational  stability,  reliability,\\nand functional delivery. For example, meeting functional requirements (C6) was rated slightly\\n\\n## [PDF page 625]\\n\\nSuccess Criteria and Factors…  625\\n\\nlower,  partly  because  of  the  dynamic  nature  of  requirements  under  Agile.  Respondents\\nappreciated the flexibility to adapt requirements to the customer’s evolving needs but noted that\\nsuch changes require additional resources. Importantly, these criteria (C33C7) are interrelated:\\na stable system minimizes risks, reduces unplanned outages, and enhances access to tools and\\ndata  -  ensuring  both  team  efficiency  and  service  continuity.  Respondents  emphasized  that\\neffective initial analysis of requirements (Davis, 1989) is essential to meet these goals, though\\nchallenging to achieve. Extensive analysis requires experience, making it resource-intensive.\\n\\nPerspective from the criteria position – C8-C10\\n\\nThis segment covers team, customer, and end-user satisfaction (C8, C9, C10), with team\\nsatisfaction  scoring  the  highest,  followed  by  the  customer  and  then  end-user  satisfaction.\\nAgile practices focusing inward, such as the roles of the Scrum Master (F9), the non-critical\\natmosphere (F17), and self-organizing teams (F4, F18), notably contribute to team satisfaction.\\nFor customer satisfaction, respondents perceived Agile’s impact as moderate. The client’s\\nability to follow progress (F13) contributes to a sense of control, but the extensive interaction\\nrequired with the Agile process can strain customer satisfaction. Agile’s impact on end-user\\nsatisfaction (C8) received surprisingly low ratings. Respondents attributed this to limited direct\\ninteraction with end-users, as Agile processes often assume the client represents the end-user’s\\nperspective. The client is often a business representative rather than an actual user, creating\\na  gap  between  user  needs  and  Agile  team  actions.  Although  Agile  emphasizes  end-user\\norientation, respondents suggested that the lack of direct-user communication limits Agile’s\\nimpact on true end-user satisfaction.\\n\\nPerspective from the position of the factors – F7-F9\\n\\nExamining factors with the highest impact averages across criteria, three factors - F7 (user\\nstories),  F8  (sprint  planning  and  backlog  usage),  and  F9  (Scrum  Master  role)  -  stand  out.\\nUser  stories  (F7)  help  Agile  teams  by  organizing  requirements  and  testing  scenarios,\\nsimplifying  quality  assurance.  However,  implementing  user  stories  effectively  demands\\nrigorous  standardization.  Sprint  planning  (F8)  is  another  fundamental  Agile  practice  that\\nstructures team efforts, though it alone does not ensure project success. The role of the Scrum\\nMaster (F9) emerged as crucial in bridging the team with the Product Owner, who connects the\\nteam with the client. This <double bridge= enhances communication, increasing project success\\nlikelihood and satisfaction for both the team and client.\\n\\nPerspective from the position of the factors – F14, F15\\n\\nRespondents  underscored  the  impact  of  F14  (appropriate  documentation)  and  F15\\n(continuous product delivery). Extensive documentation, though contractually required, often\\nconsumes time and resources that could be used for project tasks. Assigning documentation\\n\\n## [PDF page 626]\\n\\n626  B. Stec\\n\\ntasks to less experienced team members also risks generating low-quality output. Respondents\\nrecommended focusing on essential documentation only, advocating for concise templates to\\nstreamline internal documentation. Continuous product delivery (F15), meanwhile, fosters a\\nhabit of regular development, aligning with Agile principles of iterative progress. However,\\nrespondents cautioned that continuous delivery without periodic reflection may compromise\\nstrategic direction.\\n\\nPerspective from the position of the factor – F18\\n\\nThe team size factor (F18) influenced the efficacy of Agile practices in meeting criteria.\\nRespondents suggested that increasing team size beyond a certain point (e.g., 15-20 members)\\ncould dilute Agile’s impact, potentially excluding developers from vital sprint review meetings\\nand leading to miscommunication. A smaller team, according to respondents, enables a direct\\nconnection between Agile practices and project success.\\n\\nPerspective from the position of the factors – F7, F8, F11\\n\\nFinally, respondents highlighted the time dedicated to Agile practices, particularly F7 (user\\nstories), F8 (sprint planning), and F11 (test cases). These factors, requiring the Product Owner’s\\ninvolvement, were seen as essential for effective Agile implementation. Product Owners play\\na crucial role in translating client priorities into team tasks, underscoring their importance in\\nAgile  project  success.  The  respondents  recommended  including  the  Product  Owner’s\\neffectiveness as a future research success factor, emphasizing their role as a central link between\\nthe Agile team and the client.\\n\\n4.2.  Conclusions\\n\\nThe research findings offer a wide view of how Agile practices relate to project success\\ncriteria,  showing  both  the  advantages  and  challenges  of  using  Agile  methods  in  IT  project\\nmanagement.\\nFrom the perspective of success criteria, Agile works well in areas like team satisfaction\\n(C8) and delivering functional results (C3-C7). However, it is less effective at meeting strict\\nbudget (C1) and schedule (C2) goals. This happens because Agile focuses on flexibility and\\ngradual progress, which improves quality and long-term outcomes but can lead to higher costs\\nand longer timelines in the short term. Practices like self-organization (F4), space for making\\nmistakes  and  changing  them  (F3),  feedback  culture  (F6),  and  daily  meetings  (F12)  reflect\\nAgile’s collaborative nature, but they sometimes lack the structure needed to help staying within\\nbudget and on schedule.\\n\\n## [PDF page 627]\\n\\nSuccess Criteria and Factors…  627\\n\\nThe study also highlights that Agile does not always fully address end-user satisfaction.\\nWhile it emphasizes working closely with the customer, in some cases it is not working with\\na particular end-user. This can result in a gap between what users need and what teams deliver.\\nTeams may benefit from more direct contact with end-users to improve outcomes.\\nLooking at success  factors, certain practices like  sprint planning (F8), user stories (F7),\\nand the Scrum Master role (F9) play a key role in connecting team efforts to project success.\\nThese  practices  help  teams  organize  their  work,  set  priorities,  and  maintain  good\\ncommunication  with  the  client.  Respondents  also  suggested  using  simpler  documentation\\nprocesses and making time for reflection during continuous delivery to avoid losing focus on\\nthe main objectives.\\nAlthough Agile aims to orient teams toward product outcomes, this study found that Agile\\npractices primarily foster internal collaboration. Agile practices are strong tools for building\\nteamwork, flexibility, and quality, but they need to be adapted to fit different project goals,\\nespecially  for  managing  costs,  meeting  deadlines,  and  ensuring  end-user  satisfaction.\\nThese results also highlight areas where Agile methods can be improved, such as better daily\\nmeetings or adjusting for larger teams.\\n\\n5.  Limitations and recommendations\\n\\nThis  chapter  identifies  limitations  in  the  research  methodology  and  provides\\nrecommendations for enhancing the application of research findings and for future studies on\\nAgile project success. These suggestions are intended to improve the study design, address\\nidentified barriers, and propose directions for future investigations.\\n\\n5.1.  Limitations\\n\\n5.1.1.  Extensive response analytics\\nThe research model primarily used averages to calculate the impact of factors, a simplified\\nmeasure  that  limits  the  insights  derived.  A  more  comprehensive  analysis,  using  advanced\\ntechniques  such  as  cluster  analysis  or  regression  analysis,  could  reveal  patterns,  trends,\\nor  deviations  otherwise  unseen.  Such  methods  would  allow  for  a  deeper  understanding  of\\nrelationships between variables and enable the identification of nuanced insights, potentially\\noffering more robust and actionable findings.\\n5.1.2.  Complexity\\nWhile  the  model  aims  to  reflect  real-world  Agile  project  dynamics  by  linking  success\\nfactors directly to success criteria. This simplification overlooks the complexity of Agile project\\nenvironments.  The  nonlinear  and  adaptive  nature  of  Agile  projects,  with  their  dynamic\\nrequirements and dependencies, complicates the possibility of guaranteed outcomes from any\\n\\n## [PDF page 628]\\n\\n628  B. Stec\\n\\nsingle practice. Attempting to model the intricacies of Agile project management in a linear\\nway only partially captures the fluid nature of these projects, which require constant adjustment\\nand are influenced by external, often unpredictable factors.\\n5.1.3.  Answer declaration\\nResponses in the study are influenced by participants’ theoretical or general knowledge of\\nAgile practices, rather than specific, practical experiences. This can lead to a disconnection\\nbetween  declared  practices  and  their  actual  application  and  effectiveness  in  projects.\\nIn Agile IT projects, for instance, development team members may implement practices without\\nfully understanding how these align with broader success criteria (Forlicz, Rólczyński, 2016;\\nMoyer , Syrett, 2019). It makes it challenging to assess the true impact of Agile methods on\\nproject outcomes, as responses may reflect assumptions rather than real practices.\\n\\n5.2.  Recommendations\\n\\n5.2.1.  Connection between Success Criteria and Project Success\\nAlthough  the  study  links  success  factors  and  success  criteria,  it  could  benefit  from\\nincorporating  an  overarching  project  success  metric.  Building  on  principia,  like  Kerzner’s\\napproach (Kerzner, 2013), assigning weighted values to individual success criteria based on\\nempirical data could yield a more nuanced understanding of project success. By leveraging data\\nfrom  managers  with  insights  across  various  projects  or  portfolios,  the  model  would  better\\nrepresent how individual practices contribute to a project’s final success, providing practical\\nand adaptable insights for Agile teams.\\n5.2.2.  Defining project context\\nThe research focuses on IT teams, yet this category includes a wide range of project types,\\nfrom website development to real-time emotion detection models, each with distinct user types\\nand success criteria. This broad scope may dilute the study’s precision. A more context-specific\\napproach - such as focusing on commercial IT projects in a single industry, like education -\\ncould  yield  more  accurate,  actionable  results.  To  balance  applicability  with  depth,  future\\nresearch might investigate a few closely related project types, offering insights that apply to\\nsimilar projects without overgeneralizing findings.\\n5.2.3.  Factors and criteria connections\\nThe model’s focus on linking success factors with success criteria overlooks dependencies\\namong factors  and criteria. For example, the implementation of a factor like sprint reviews\\n(F11)  relies  on  using  a  backlog  (F8),  creating  a  dependency  that  affects  the  model’s\\napplicability. A more advanced mapping approach could incorporate such interdependencies,\\nenabling a more realistic application of the model. By allowing dependencies to be activated\\nonly when prerequisite practices are implemented, the model would more accurately reflect\\nreal-world project dynamics.\\n\\n## [PDF page 629]\\n\\nSuccess Criteria and Factors…  629\\n\\n5.2.4.  Research group, quantitative research\\nThe  research  primarily  used  qualitative  interviews,  which  offered  detailed  insights  but\\nlimited the scope to a smaller sample size. To enable more generalizable conclusions, future\\nstudies should consider a quantitative approach,  allowing for a larger and more statistically\\nrepresentative sample. Although more resource-intensive, quantitative methods could provide\\nbroader insights and a stronger foundation for making widely applicable recommendations.\\n5.2.5.  Partial use of Agile practices\\nIn the current model, Agile practices are assessed on a binary basis4either used (<1=) or\\nnot used (<0=). This simplification fails to capture varying degrees of practice implementation,\\nwhich could provide a more realistic picture. Using a scale from 0 to 1 to represent partial\\nadoption  of  practices  might  offer  more  nuanced  insights,  although  it  presents  challenges  in\\ndetermining non-linear relationships between partial use and project outcomes. Future research\\ncould explore these partial relationships by modeling them for selected success factors, enabling\\na more flexible and detailed analysis.\\n\\n6.  Summary\\n\\nThe primary objective of this paper is to investigate the impact of Agile practices on the\\nsuccess  of  IT  projects,  evaluated  based  on  defined,  industry-specific  success  criteria.\\nThe research-specific aim is to develop a model that delineates the connections between the\\nAgile practices employed by project teams - viewed as success factors - and the success criteria\\nused to evaluate project outcomes.\\nThe  first  stage  of  this  research  involved  an  extensive  literature  review  to  establish\\na  foundation  for  understanding  Agile  practices,  artifacts,  and  tools  that  are  potentially\\nsignificant for IT project success. This review also identified key project success criteria from\\nexisting  research,  though  they  are  not  unique  to  Agile.  Through  this  process,  the  author\\nidentified 18 Agile success factors (Tab. 1)  and  selected 10  general project success criteria\\n(Tab. 2). The literature review concluded that the final model should outline the relationships\\nbetween each Agile factor and each success criterion, providing insights into which factors hold\\nthe most significance for project teams and which success criteria are directly supported by\\nspecific Agile practices.\\nTo  develop  this  model,  the  author  conducted  qualitative  research  involving  in-depth\\ninterviews  with  Agile  practitioners  currently  working  on  projects  managed  with  Agile\\nmethodologies.  Participants  in  this  study  were  asked  to  assign  weights  to  the  relationships\\nbetween individual Agile factors and success criteria, indicating the relative importance of each\\nfactor-criterion connection. A total of 15 practitioners participated, and their responses formed\\nthe basis for constructing the final model (Section 3.2). During these interviews, key success\\n\\n## [PDF page 630]\\n\\n630  B. Stec\\n\\nfactors within Agile practices were highlighted, particularly practices like thorough planning,\\nmaintaining  a  product  backlog,  and  delivering  software  incrementally.  In  contrast,  certain\\npractices,  such  as  daily  meetings,  were  rated  as  having  a  lower  impact  on  project  success\\ncriteria. The research also identified specific criteria that Agile practices in this study supported\\nless  effectively,  such  as  meeting  budget  and  timeline  constraints  and  achieving  high  user\\nsatisfaction.\\nThe  model’s  initial  validation  involved  follow-up  interviews  with  three  domain  experts,\\nwho assessed the model’s accuracy in depicting Agile’s real-world application and evaluated\\nits  consistency  with  practical  experience.  The  experts  affirmed  that  the  model  accurately\\nreflects the connections between Agile practices and project success criteria, as observed in\\nprofessional settings.\\nThe study’s findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how Agile practices affect\\nIT project success, offering a model that both Agile teams and project managers can use as\\na  practical  resource  to  inform  resource  planning  and  project  implementation.  This  model\\nillustrates how different Agile practices carry varying levels of impact on the overall success of\\nIT  projects,  thus  providing  targeted  insights  for  better  project  management  and  resource\\nallocation.\\nDespite certain limitations, this research presents valuable findings that hold potential for\\nboth academic study and practical application in Agile IT project management. Taking into\\naccount the research steps described in the paper, it is fully replicable, and the results should\\ndiffer when selecting respondents from a specific type of IT project or one professional profile\\n(e.g. developers). Additionally, the paper highlights the role of\\nthe teacher in guiding and supporting students in using VR technology for educational purposes.\\nDesign/methodology/approach: The paper utilizes a case study approach to examine the use\\nof a specific virtual reality application in the field of Management and Production Engineering.\\nThe study involves the implementation of VR-based laboratory classes, where students engage\\nin various training modules of the given selected VR application, including both theoretical and\\npractical tasks in a simulated production environment. The methodology includes a presentation\\nof  the  VR  application’s  modules,  the  tasks  for  students,  the  organization  of  VR-supported\\nlaboratories, and the role of the instructor in facilitating the learning process.\\nFindings:  The  study  showed  that  it  is  possible  to  use  virtual  reality  in  higher  education,\\nespecially in the context of classes in the field of management and production engineering.\\nThe possibility of creating and implementing VR applications that realistically reproduce the\\nproduction environment and enable conducting training and classes for students of technical\\nstudies  has  been  confirmed.  The  research  results  confirmed  that  VR  is  a  practical  tool  for\\nteaching production lines, technological processes, machine parameters, equipment operation,\\nquality control, and safety rules in the production hall. All these elements can be effectively\\nimplemented  under  controlled  conditions  in  the  university,  without  the  need  for  physical\\npresence in the industrial plant.\\nOriginality/value: This paper offers a perspective on integrating virtual reality into laboratory\\nclasses  within  the  field  of  Management  and  Production  Engineering,  highlighting  its\\ntransformative potential for traditional teaching methods. The use of VR application in laboratories from Production Engineering\\n\\nIn the application \\"Production Plant\\", selected production processes are generally presented,\\nwhich means that their specificity is not discussed or presented in great detail. The steps include:\\n\uf0b7  Preparing the room\\nTo  conduct  classes  using  virtual  reality,  an  appropriate  laboratory  room  is  necessary.\\nA larger room equipped with several stations with virtual reality  goggles and  controllers is\\npreferred, so that several students from a smaller laboratory group can use virtual reality at the\\nsame time. Small laboratory groups (several people) are also preferred; otherwise conducting\\nclasses  and  monitoring  students’  work,  as  well  as  ensuring  safety,  will  be  very  difficult.\\nThe room must be spacious, and in such a room, any objects such as desks and chairs that may\\npose a threat to those using virtual reality should be avoided.\\n\\n## [PDF page 649]\\n\\nAdvancing education through virtual reality…  649\\n\\n\uf0b7  Equipment purchase and setup\\nThe laboratory must be equipped with several VR stations, each consisting of VR goggles,\\ncontrollers, and a designated space for students to move around safely. The goggles must be\\ncalibrated first. Each station should be preloaded with the VR application \\"Production Plant\\",\\nready for use.\\n\uf0b7  Familiarization of students with regulations\\nBefore students put on the VR goggles, they are introduced to the safety regulations for\\nusing VR  goggles, health and safety instructions and best practices for using virtual reality\\ntechnology. Also, it is important to know contraindications to using virtual reality equipment\\nand possible complications.\\nThe  instructor  must  ensure  that  all  students  are  aware  of  potential  contraindications,\\nsuch as motion sickness or epilepsy, and verify that no student has any medical condition that\\ncould be exacerbated by the use of VR. Students are required to read and understand the safety\\nguidelines (sign a consent form if necessary) and be briefed on emergency procedures in case\\nof discomfort or technical issues.\\n\uf0b7  Initial familiarization\\nEach student starts with the general instructional module of the VR application (described\\npreviously in this paper). This module is crucial to ensuring that all students, regardless of their\\nprevious experience with VR, can use the technology effectively.\\n\uf0b7  Engagement with theoretical and practical modules\\nStudents  use  subsequent  virtual  reality  modules  in  subsequent  laboratories.  During  this,\\nthey learn, familiarize themselves with the theoretical and practical content developed in the\\napplication, develop, expand their imagination, and gain experience and knowledge. They also\\nlearn  independent  thinking,  and  develop  problem-solving  skills,  logical  thinking,\\nand reasoning. It is worth mentioning that during such labs, students engage more senses than\\nduring traditional lectures.\\nAfter  completing  each  task,  students  receive  immediate  feedback  from  the  application.\\nThis  allows  students  to  identify  and  correct  their  mistakes.  Moreover,  if  a  student  makes\\na mistake, they have the opportunity to retry the task without any time pressure. This iterative\\nprocess helps reinforce learning and ensures that students fully understand the correct setup and\\noperation of the technological line.\\n\uf0b7  Broder context and discussion\\nIt is important that the content shown in virtual reality is also discussed during the lecture.\\nIt is suggested that individual technological lines and individual machines are discussed in more\\ndetail during the lecture.\\nAfter the VR lab session, the students meet for a debriefing session. Here, they discuss their\\nexperiences, the challenges they faced, and the lessons they learned. The role of the teacher (trainer) during a VR session\\n\\nThe role of the teacher during a virtual reality session is key, transforming from a traditional\\nteacher  to  an  instructor,  guide  and  mentor.  In  VR  learning  environment,  the  teacher’s\\nresponsibilities extend far beyond conveying information.\\nBefore beginning any VR session, the teacher must conduct a identify if any students have\\ncontraindications to using VR technology. This includes understanding if any students have\\nconditions  such  as  motion  sickness,  epilepsy,  severe  vertigo,  or  other  forms  of  locomotion\\nweaknesses  that  could  be  intensified  by  VR  use.  Students  with  these  conditions  might\\n\\n## [PDF page 652]\\n\\n652  K. StecuBa\\n\\nexperience  discomfort,  disorientation,  or  other  health  risks  when  exposed  to  the  immersive\\nVR environment. What is more, due to some sickness and conditions, some of the students are\\nnot allowed to use VR.\\nTo ensure safety, the teacher should ask students if they have any known issues with VR or\\nsimilar technologies and provide them with a clear explanation of what the VR experience will\\nentail. This allows students to make informed decisions about their participation. In some cases,\\nalternative assignments or accommodations might be necessary to ensure that all students can\\nengage with the course content in a way that is safe and effective for them.\\nDuring the session, the teacher should remain  alert, closely monitoring students for any\\nsigns  of  discomfort  or  adverse  reactions,  such  as  dizziness,  nausea,  or  disorientation.\\nThey should be prepared to pause the VR activity immediately if a student exhibits any of these\\nsymptoms  and  have  a  plan  in  place  to  assist  them,  whether  that  involves  taking  a  break,\\nadjusting the settings, or switching to a different learning activity.\\nAdditionally, the teacher should ensure that students are aware of the importance of taking\\nbreaks  during  VR  sessions  to  prevent  eye  strain  and  reduce  the  risk  of  motion  sickness.\\nRegular breaks are an essential part of maintaining student well-being during extended VR use.\\nThen, the teacher must ensure that students are well-prepared to use the VR equipment,\\nsuch  as  goggles,  controllers,  and  any  associated  software.  This  includes  providing  detailed\\ninstructions on how to operate the technology and addressing any initial technical challenges\\nthat students may face.\\nAs students begin to immerse themselves in the VR experience, the trainer’s role becomes\\none of continuous support and guidance. Introduction\\n\\nIn the face of rapid technological advancements and constantly evolving market demands,\\norganizations are under growing pressure to deliver successful projects that meet both strategic\\ngoals  and  stakeholder  expectations.  Traditional  project  management  approaches,  such  as\\npredictive or plan-driven models, are often inadequate for projects that require adaptability and\\nresponsiveness to change. Consequently, adaptive and hybrid approaches, including Agile and\\nmixed-method models, have gained prominence for their ability to navigate complexity and\\nprioritize flexibility.\\nDespite the popularity of various project management approaches, there remains a critical\\ngap  in  understanding  the  optimal  conditions  and  criteria  for  their  effective  application.\\nThe  objective  of  this  study  is  to  bridge  this  gap  by  providing  a  comparative  analysis  of\\npredictive, adaptive, and hybrid project management strategies, aiming to identify the factors\\ninfluencing  the  choice  of  approach  in  diverse  project  environments.  This  research  not  only\\naddresses the challenges of aligning project characteristics with suitable methodologies but also\\noffers  empirical  insights  based  on  survey  data  to  guide  organizations  in  selecting  the  most\\neffective  project  management  approach.  By  addressing  this  research  gap,  the  findings\\ncontribute to enhancing project efficiency, improving outcome predictability, and ultimately\\nachieving higher levels of project satisfaction among stakeholders.\\n\\n2.  Literature review\\n\\nProject design and implementation have become critical aspects of organizational strategy,\\nas reflected by the increasing volume of publications dedicated to project management and the\\ndevelopment  of  diverse  project  management  approaches  and  methodologies  aimed  at\\nsupporting organizations in achieving their strategic objectives. The origins of modern project\\nmanagement date back to the 1950s, marked by the introduction of network planning techniques\\nsuch as the Critical Path Method (CPM) and the Program Evaluation and Review Technique\\n(PERT)  (Reed  et  al.,  2024;  Stretton,  2007).  Since  then,  project  management  has  evolved\\nsignificantly, from practices primarily used in engineering and construction to comprehensive\\nmethodologies applicable across a wide range of industries.\\n\\n2.1.  Traditional (predictive) project management approaches\\n\\nPredictive,  or  traditional,  project  management  approaches  rely  on  thorough,  upfront\\nplanning  and  assume  that  project  requirements  can  be  clearly  defined  from  the  outset.\\nThe Waterfall methodology and PRINCE2 are well-established examples, structured around\\n\\n## [PDF page 659]\\n\\nOptimizing the selection of project…  659\\n\\nsequential project phases and emphasizing control through detailed documentation and rigid\\nschedules (Bentley, 2020). These methodologies, however, tend to struggle in environments\\nmarked  by  high  levels  of  uncertainty,  where  requirements  may  change  during  the  project\\nlifecycle. Research suggests that projects with fixed or highly regulated scopes, as well as those\\nin industries with lower variability, such as construction or manufacturing, benefit most from\\npredictive approaches (Wright, 2022; Ciric et al., 2021).\\nThe primary advantage of predictive methodologies lies in their ability to provide stability\\nthrough clear scope definitions and fixed budgets, making them suitable for large-scale projects\\nwith multiple dependencies (Sheffield, Lemétayer, 2010; Shiv, Doraiswamy, 2012). However,\\nrigid  adherence  to  initial  plans  can  result  in  costly  overruns  and  delays  if  changes  become\\nnecessary,  a frequent  risk  in  today’s  rapidly  changing  business  environment  (Pace,  2019).\\nStudies  by  Reed  et  al.  (2024)  and  Rotaru  (2021)  also  underscore  that  while  predictive\\napproaches provide  effective structure  and accountability, they  can limit flexibility, making\\nthem less adaptable to the evolving needs and expectations of stakeholders.\\n\\n2.2.  Adaptive project management approaches\\n\\nIn response to the limitations of traditional project management, adaptive methodologies\\nhave gained popularity, especially in industries characterized by high innovation and changing\\nrequirements,  such  as  software  development.  The  Agile  approach  and  its  associated\\nmethodologies,  like  Scrum  and  Kanban,  prioritize  flexibility  and  continuous  feedback  over\\nrigid planning, which enables iterative development cycles that adapt to evolving stakeholder\\nneeds (Cooke, 2014; Reed et al., 2024). The Agile Manifesto, published in 2001, formalized\\nthese  principles,  advocating  for  customer  collaboration,  rapid  response  to  change,\\nand incremental project delivery (Schwaber, Sutherland, 2020).\\nAdaptive methodologies focus on delivering value through frequent iterations, or sprints,\\nwhich help to address stakeholder feedback continuously. Research by Bentley (2020) shows\\nthat Agile approaches are particularly advantageous for projects with uncertain requirements,\\nas  they  allow  project  teams  to  modify  the  project  scope  and  priorities  based  on  real-time\\nfeedback, rather than pre-defined milestones. Wright (2022) emphasizes that adaptive project\\nmanagement has a strong focus on customer satisfaction, with scope defined by the evolving\\nneeds of the customer rather than a fixed project plan.\\nWhile Agile has shown success across various industries, its reliance on less formalized\\ndocumentation and processes requires a cultural shift within organizations, fostering a no-blame\\nenvironment, collaborative teams, and high levels of self-organization (Pace, 2019). Despite its\\nadvantages, the Agile approach may introduce risks in highly regulated environments where\\ndocumentation and fixed scope are mandatory (Azenha et al., 2021). Research by Reed et al.\\n(2024) highlights that, while Agile is widely praised for its adaptability, its lack of a clearly\\ndefined hierarchy and increased dependence on cross-functional teams can create challenges\\nfor organizations accustomed to traditional management structures.\\n\\n## [PDF page 660]\\n\\n660  A. Stronczek, P. ŚcigaBa\\n\\n2.3.  Hybrid project management approaches\\n\\nAs  project  requirements  have  become  increasingly  diverse,  hybrid  methodologies  have\\nemerged, blending elements of both predictive and adaptive approaches to achieve a balance\\nbetween structure and flexibility. This middle ground is particularly valuable for projects where\\ncomponents like regulatory compliance benefit from a structured approach, while customer-\\ndriven  features  demand  adaptability  (Gemino  et  al.,  2021;  Brendzel,  2024).  Hybrid  project\\nmanagement approaches, often combining the upfront planning of Waterfall with the iterative\\nexecution of Agile, enable organizations to harness the stability of traditional models while\\nmaintaining the responsiveness of adaptive methodologies (Wright, 2022).\\nStudies  reveal  that  hybrid  approaches  are  commonly  applied  in  complex  projects  that\\nrequire multiple stakeholder groups and have a broad scope (Reed et al., 2024; Piwowar-Sulej,\\n2021, Wolniak, 2022a, 2020b). By maintaining a predictive framework for regulatory or highly\\nsensitive components and incorporating iterative Agile cycles for development tasks, hybrid\\nmethodologies address a broader range of project needs. Research also indicates that hybrid\\napproaches facilitate improved stakeholder satisfaction by aligning project deliverables with\\nboth regulatory and market-driven requirements (Bentley, 2020; Cooke, 2014).\\n\\n2.4.  Selection criteria for project management approaches\\n\\nThe choice of project management approach depends on several factors, including project\\ncomplexity,  regulatory  requirements,  team  size,  and  customer  involvement.  Wright  (2022)\\nnotes that highly regulated projects with extensive compliance requirements may necessitate\\na predictive  approach,  while  projects  with  evolving  or  uncertain  requirements  benefit  more\\nfrom  adaptive  methodologies.  Additionally,  organizational  culture  plays  a  significant  role\\nin approach  selection;  bureaucratic  organizations  may  struggle  to  adopt  Agile,  while\\ncollaborative  environments  are  often  better  suited  to  adaptive  approaches  (Piwowar-Sulej,\\n2021).\\nResearch by Reed et al. (2024) suggests that the experience and expertise of project teams\\nalso impact approach selection, as teams familiar with Agile can more effectively implement\\nadaptive methodologies. Moreover, factors such as project team structure and communication\\nfrequency  affect  the  feasibility  of  hybrid  approaches,  as  they  require  both  structured\\ndocumentation and iterative, cross-functional collaboration.\\nIn summary, the literature on project management approaches highlights the advantages and\\nlimitations  of  predictive,  adaptive,  and  hybrid  methodologies.  Predictive  approaches  offer\\nstability for projects with defined requirements and minimal need for flexibility, while adaptive\\nmethodologies excel in environments characterized by uncertainty and rapid change. Hybrid\\napproaches combine elements of both, providing a tailored approach to projects with mixed\\nneeds.  However,  selecting  the  optimal  project  management  methodology  requires  careful\\nconsideration of organizational, project-specific, and external factors. As the field of project\\n\\n## [PDF page 661]\\n\\nOptimizing the selection of project…  661\\n\\nmanagement continues to evolve, understanding the optimal conditions for each approach is\\nessential to maximizing project success and stakeholder satisfaction in an increasingly complex\\nbusiness landscape.\\n\\n3.  Research method\\n\\nThis study employs a quantitative research approach to identify optimal application areas\\nfor different project management approaches – predictive, adaptive, and hybrid – and the key\\nfactors  influencing  their  selection.  Given  the  increasing  interest  in  project  management\\nmethodologies  and  the  limited  empirical  research  on  their  practical  effectiveness,\\na hypothetico-deductive method was chosen to provide objective measurements and identify\\nquantitative  relationships  between  project  characteristics  and  methodology  selection\\n(Apanowicz, 2005; SuBkowski et al., 2021)\\n\\n3.1.  Literature review and formulation of research questions\\n\\nThe research process began with a comprehensive review of the literature to understand the\\nevolution, application, and efficacy  of various project management  approaches. The review\\nhighlighted the need for a practical analysis of project management approaches, particularly\\nin assessing their effectiveness across diverse organizational environments. Based on insights\\nfrom the literature, two research questions were formulated:\\n1.  What  are  the  optimal  application  areas  for  predictive,  adaptive,  and  hybrid  project\\nmanagement approaches?\\n2.  What factors influence the selection of a project management approach for a specific\\nproject?\\nThese questions guide the study’s empirical focus on identifying factors that inform the\\nchoice of methodology and examining how different project management approaches align with\\nproject and organizational characteristics.\\n\\n3.2.  Data collection instrument: survey questionnaire\\n\\nTo gather data, a survey questionnaire was developed, a common tool for data collection in\\nproject  management  research  (Reed  et  al.,  2024).  The  questionnaire  is  structured  into  five\\nsections:\\n1.  Demographics  –  questions  capturing  respondents’  background,  including  work\\nexperience,  certifications,  and  familiarity  with  different  project  management\\nmethodologies.\\n2.  Project  characteristics  –  questions  addressing  the  scope,  requirements  stability,\\nand project end-date flexibility.\\n\\n## [PDF page 662]\\n\\n662  A. Stronczek, P. ŚcigaBa\\n\\n3.  Delivery organization characteristics – this section focuses on factors such as senior\\nmanagement  commitment,  customization  of  project  management  methodologies,\\nand organizational type.\\n4. Data analysis approach\\n\\nThe data collected from the survey was analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics.\\nDescriptive  analysis  was  employed  to  understand  the  distribution  of  project  management\\napproaches  and  methodology  customization  across  different  project  and  organizational\\ncharacteristics. Adaptive  approaches,  in  contrast,  are  better  suited  for  projects  with\\nchanging  requirements  and  high  uncertainty,  where  flexibility  and  customer  feedback  are\\ncrucial. Hybrid approaches, which combine aspects of both, prove to be  the most versatile,\\naccommodating projects with diverse needs and varying levels of predictability.\\nThese findings emphasize the importance of a tailored approach to project management.\\nOrganizations benefit from customizing methodologies to suit specific project requirements and\\nadapting to external and internal factors. Introduction\\n\\nThe  modern  world  is  witnessing  a  continuous  technological  transformation,  with  the\\ntechnology available on the market evolving at an unprecedented pace. Advances in areas such\\nas big data, the Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence are not just the domain of the\\nworld’s largest industrial centers, but are transforming the market on a global scale (Rymarczyk,\\n2020).  Businesses  are  facing  challenges  that  were  unimaginable  a  dozen  years  ago.\\nThese include globalization, increasing customer requirements and the need to make decisions\\nquickly in a dynamic environment (Lina, 2022).\\nIn response to these challenges, artificial intelligence could become a key tool (Patalas-\\nMaliszewska et al., 2020), enabling manufacturing companies not only to manage resources\\nefficiently, but also to respond more quickly to changing trends and deliver more personalized\\nservices (Huang, Rust, 2018). With its ability to analyze vast amounts of data, AI is speeding\\nup  decision-making  processes  while  opening  the  door  to  new  business  models  (Patalas-\\nMaliszewska, 2020).\\nAI  encompasses  a  broad  spectrum  of  technologies,  including  machine  learning,  neural\\nnetworks,  and  expert  systems,  which  collectively  enable  machines  to  perform  tasks  that\\ntraditionally required human intelligence. These technologies are instrumental in addressing\\ncontemporary  manufacturing  challenges,  such  as  optimizing  resource  utilization,  reducing\\ndowntime through predictive maintenance, and enhancing product quality through automated\\ndefect  detection.  The  application  of  AI  extends  beyond  operational  efficiency,  offering\\ntransformative  potential  in  areas  such  as  product  personalization  and  sustainable  energy\\nmanagement.\\nDespite  the  growing  interest  in  the  application  of  artificial  intelligence  (AI)  in  the\\nmanufacturing  sector,  there  is  a  significant  gap  in  the  literature  regarding  a  comprehensive\\nunderstanding of where research on the use of AI in manufacturing sector stands. Additionally,\\nmany studies are based on case studies or a specific technology, which limits their generality\\nand universality. Therefore, there is a need for a broad literature review that not only identifies\\nand  summarizes  existing  research,  but  also  highlights  untapped  opportunities  and  future\\nresearch directions. This study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the current state of\\nresearch  on  AI  applications  in  manufacturing,  identifying  key  trends,  thematic  clusters,\\nand  emerging  opportunities.  By  leveraging  bibliometric  analysis  and  a  systematic  literature\\nreview, the study not only highlights the progress achieved in this domain but also identifies\\ngaps and areas for future exploration. The findings serve as a valuable resource for researchers,\\npractitioners, and policymakers, offering insights into the strategic deployment of AI to drive\\nindustrial innovation and sustainability.\\n\\n## [PDF page 679]\\n\\nArtificial intelligence in manufacturing…  679\\n\\n2.  Literature review\\n\\nOne of the most straightforward definitions of artificial intelligence (AI) is that it is a field\\nof study concerned with the development of systems that are capable of performing tasks that\\nwould typically require human intelligence (Boden, 2016). Some researchers, on the other hand,\\npoint to the fact that AI does not just match the capabilities of the human mind, but sometimes\\nsurpasses them (Angelov et al., 2021), this may be due to the fact that this field of science is so\\nbroad (Arinez et al., 2020).\\nThe sub-areas of artificial intelligence include, but are not limited to, expert systems, neural\\nnetworks and machine learning. It should also be noted that these fields are not inseparable.\\nVery often they overlap to form complex structures (Arias, 2022).\\nThe development of expert systems can be traced back to the second half of the twentieth\\ncentury. Subsequently, a system was developed for use in the field of chemistry. The success\\nof  this  system  led  to  the  initiation  of  scientific  research,  which  in  turn  resulted  in  the\\ndevelopment of numerous other systems that were subsequently applied in the field of medicine\\n(Grabarek,  Stasiak-Cieślak,  2019).  Expert  systems  are  limited  to  a  specific  discipline.\\nIn this way, they are regarded as a form of traditional artificial intelligence, although they do\\nnot learn by constructing comprehensive models; instead, they draw on a database that has been\\nencoded  by  humans  (Arias,  2022).  Expert  systems  represent  one  of  the  earliest  tools  to  be\\nemployed in practice. By design, this system is intended to replace the expert in solving more\\ncomplex tasks and problems. By recording the knowledge of experts in a specific field, the\\nsystem can access and apply it repeatedly (Wyskwarski, 2015).\\nAn artificial neural network (ANN) can be defined as a biologically inspired computational\\nmodel  comprising  processing  elements  (referred  to  as  neurons)  and  connections  with\\ncoefficients.  These  connections  constitute  the  neuronal  structure  to  which  the  learning  and\\nrecall algorithms are attached. In simple terms, artificial neural networks are a collection of\\nmathematical  techniques  used  for  signal  processing,  prediction  and  clustering\\n(Shanmuganathan, 2016). Their structure is modelled on the human brain, and their approach\\nto  problem  solving  and  structure  itself  resembles  the  operation  of  the  nervous  system\\n(Wyskwarski,  2015).  However,  the  human  brain  is  much  more  complex  and  many  of  its\\ncognitive functions remain to be discovered (Shanmuganathan, 2016).\\nAnother  part  of  artificial  intelligence,  considered  a  subset  of  it,  is  machine  learning.\\nIt consists of teaching machines the given rules according to which they should act, and then\\nusing them to solve a problem. The model that is prepared is intended to enable a decision to\\nbe made or a phenomenon to be predicted based on the analysis of data that was previously\\nprovided in the learning phase. This data is called training data and is fundamental to the final\\ncreation  of  the  model.  It  is  also  crucial  to  select  an  appropriate  algorithm  responsible  for\\ncarrying out the learning process (Młodzianowski, Rostowski, 2021). There are three variants\\n\\n## [PDF page 680]\\n\\n680  W. Tarasiuk, K. Halicka\\n\\nof  machine  learning  based  on  the  method  of  learning  -  supervised,  unsupervised  and\\nreinforcement learning (Morales, Escalante, 2022).\\nA review of the literature indicates that artificial intelligence is being implemented in the\\nmanufacturing  sector  at  multiple  levels,  including  optimization  of  the  production  process,\\ncollaboration between humans and robots, and resolution of maintenance issues (Arinez et al.,\\n2020).\\nOne  example  of  the  application  of  artificial  intelligence  is  the  machine  learning  model\\npresented  by  researchers  Hrnjica  and  Softic,  which  is  used  in  the  field  of  predictive\\nmaintenance.  Machine  learning  was  used  to  develop  a  model  for  predicting  the  failure  of\\nproduction machine components/parts. The model created in the study achieved high prediction\\naccuracy (99% in test data), suggesting that AI can make a significant contribution to reducing\\nthe costs associated with unplanned downtime, failures and precent the occurrence of machine\\nerrors (Hrnjica, Softic, 2022).\\nAnother  area  of  industrial  application  for  artificial  intelligence  is  quality  assurance.\\nToday, there are a number of solutions for achieving high product quality through the use of\\nhighly automated production machines (Arora, Gupta, 2022). In the context of quality assurance\\nin manufacturing, process automation is becoming a crucial component of industrial strategies.\\nThe  utilization  of  artificial  intelligence,  particularly  machine  learning  algorithms,  not  only\\nfacilitates the expeditious and precise identification of defects, but also the implementation of\\nreal-time monitoring systems. The utilization of models such as convolutional neural networks\\n(CNNs)  enables  the  automatic  identification  of  undesirable  phenomena,  thereby  markedly\\nenhancing the  quality  of  the final  product.  The  implementation of  such  solutions  facilitates\\nan immediate response to detected irregularities, which can result in time and resource savings,\\nas well as increased production efficiency (Patel et al., 2019; Schreiber et al., 2019).\\nIn  the  field  of  manufacturing,  collaborative  robots  (cobots)  are  also  being  deployed.\\nOver  the  past  decade,  research  into  human-machine  relationships  has  concentrated  on  the\\nintricacies of collaboration, in which cobots must not only avoid collisions but also respond\\nadaptively to circumstances and communicate in a manner that is analogous to that of humans\\n(Faccio, Cohen, 2024). Cobots are being applied in a diverse range of industries, reflecting their\\nversatility and high level of accuracy. Their ability to perform tasks requiring precision and to\\nhandle hazardous substances without risk to human operators makes them an attractive option\\nin many workplaces. The potential benefits of cobots, particularly in terms of enhanced safety,\\nflexibility and improved efficiency, are frequently highlighted (Javaid et al., 2022).\\nFurthermore, artificial intelligence can be employed not only in the operational activities of\\nmanufacturing  businesses  but  also  in  planning  and  strategic  decision-making.  In  particular,\\nit can be utilized in forecasting consumer demand (Aktepe et al., 2021). In general, a multitude\\nof  demand  forecasting  techniques  are  based  on  artificial  intelligence  (Mediavilla,  Dietrich,\\nPalm, 2022), in certain cases, these techniques are combined with additional approaches that\\nextend the conventional boundaries of artificial intelligence. For instance, examples include\\n\\n## [PDF page 681]\\n\\nArtificial intelligence in manufacturing…  681\\n\\nhybrids of AI and metaheuristic algorithms (Goli et al., 2018). The use of artificial intelligence\\nalgorithms makes it possible to analyze huge amounts of data, leading to more accurate demand\\nforecasts. These models can identify hidden patterns and changes in consumer behavior that\\ntraditional statistical methods may miss. This can lead to increased operational efficiency and\\nreduced  costs  associated  with  running  the  business  (Kondapaka,  2021).  In  addition  to  the\\npreviously  mentioned  applications,  artificial  intelligence  can  also  be  utilized  to  develop\\ninnovations  that  may  prove  to  be  of  considerable  importance  in  the  field  of  manufacturing\\n(Szymańska, Berbel Pineda, 2024).\\nThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into manufacturing represents a comprehensive\\nstrategy  for  advancing  product  efficiency,  operational  effectiveness,  and  safety  standards.\\nThrough  the  optimization  of  production  processes,  the  efficient  allocation  of  resources,\\nand  the  implementation  of  sophisticated  quality  assurance  methodologies,  AI  enables\\nsubstantial  improvements  in  overall  operational  performance.  Within  the  domain  of  skills\\nanalysis  related  to  manufacturing  processes,  the  adoption  of  AI  assumes  a  critical  role.\\nThis technology facilitates a proactive framework for workforce development by systematically\\nanalyzing historical data, identifying recurring patterns, and forecasting future skill demands.\\nConsequently, it ensures the identification and cultivation of essential competencies necessary\\nfor sustaining industry advancements (Doanh et al., 2023).\\n\\n3.
